units.la: Exhibemus tibi, Lector benevole, philosophemata viri celeberrimi D Guilielmi Amesii, qui quàm subtilo ac solido fuerit judicio, praeter scripta, quae extant, Theologica, hac quoque, quae damus, Philosophica abundè demonstrabunt. Sistimus primum tibi, argumento simplicem, forma duplicem, Technometriam, quâ utrâque omnium disciplinarum ac facultatum limites ac fines accuratè praescribuntur; in priori quidem, omnia dicuntur prefsius, ac lumen ibi est contractius, quod in posteriori per quaestiones fusius & latius explicatur: Technometriae subjungitur gemina Disputatio, adversus Metaphysicam una, adversus Ethicam altera: quâ utramque ex philosophiae ambitu ac pomeriis proscribit Autor, rationibus non exigui ponderis, & ad locum in Technologia alisque disciplinis relegat. Sequitur ejus Demonstratio Logicae verae, quae praecepta divinae artis, veritatémque eorum, simul & explicat & demonstrat, istâc industriâ & sedulitate, ut omnium aliorum, qui hîc desudárunt, labores longè superaverit, ac quod mirerus, tantâ orationis brevitate: ac potest insuper hæc Logica demonstrata commentarii vicem supplere in Theses Logicas, pro disputationis materia sub finem annexas: nam quæ hîc nudè ponuntur, istic accuratissimè demonstrantur. Vale Lector ac fruere, & nostrum rem Philosophicam juvandi conatum bæni consule, ac sicubi veritatis novæ scintillula affulserit, Deo Patri luminum gratias age.
units.tr: We present to you, kind Reader, the philosophical writings of the most celebrated Guilielmus Amesius, which, apart from the theological writings that are extant, these Philosophical writings that we are giving will amply demonstrate how subtle and sound his judgement was. First we set before you the Technometria, simple in its subject matter but twofold in its form, by which the limits and boundaries of all disciplines and faculties are carefully prescribed. In the first form, everything is stated more concisely, and the light there is more compressed; in the second, it is explained more fully and broadly through questions. Attached to the Technometria is a twofold Disputation: one against Metaphysics, the other against Ethics, by which the Author excludes both from the scope and boundaries of philosophy, with arguments of no small weight, and relegates them to their place in Technologia and other disciplines. There follows his Demonstration of True Logic, which both explains and demonstrates the precepts of the divine art and their truth, with such diligence and care that he has far surpassed the labours of all others who have toiled over this subject, and, which is remarkable, in such brevity of expression. Moreover, this demonstrated Logic can also serve as a commentary to the Logical Theses appended at the end as material for disputation; for what is here set down bare is there demonstrated with the greatest precision. Farewell, Reader, and enjoy; take in good part our effort to advance the philosophical enterprise, and if a spark of new truth shines upon you anywhere, give thanks to God the Father of lights.

units.la: HUc usque turpi nubilo pressum caput, Interque cunas artium pectus rude Vinćti tenemur. Ipsa perpero viam Nisu, sciendi cluserat scientia: Et tota dispar, membra ducebat suis Adversa membris, invicemque limites Injurioso quæque stringebant pede. Nunc illa verum monstra ridemus, chaos Cæcumque pondus, sole perfusi novo. Litem diremit artifex viri manus, Et fida solers jura singulis deditLabos Amesi, Proteumque dexteraLigans potente, ferreaque compede, Stupere cunctis, scire vindicat sibi.
units.tr: Until now our head has been pressed down by a shameful cloud, and our untrained breast has been held bound among the cradle-clothes of the arts. Knowledge itself, by a wrong effort, had closed the path to knowing. Everything was disjointed and unlike itself, leading limbs hostile to their own limbs, and each thing, with an injurious foot, kept the boundaries of the others. Now we laugh at those true monsters, the chaos and blind weight, bathed in a new sun. The artist's hand has settled the strife of men and, skilful and faithful, has given each its own laws. The labour of Ames, binding Proteus with a mighty hand and an iron fetter, has made all stand amazed, and claims knowledge for itself.

units.la: ARs est Idea ὁ τεχνικὸς (?) regulis catholicis methodicè delineata.
units.tr: Art is an idea, methodically laid out by universal rules.

units.la: 2. Etsi vocabulum artis τέχνη μέτρον (?) sit, variaq; variis significet, in quam tamen partem, & in qua significatione à nobis accipiatur, manifestum est.
units.tr: 2. Although the word art (technē) may be a measure and signifies various things, it is clear in which sense, and in which meaning, we take it.

units.la: 3. Est idea, non Platonica, in certo quodam terræ angulo exist ens, sed exemplar, ut Plantæ vertit, aut exemplaris delineatio, seu formula in artificis mente ante actionem ad actionem efformata, ut eam repræsentE, & repræsentando regat.
units.tr: 3. It is an idea, not a Platonic one existing in some corner of the earth, but a pattern (as Plautus renders it), or the sketch of a model, or a form conceived in the craftsman's mind before action and shaped for action, so that it may represent the action and, by representing it, guide it.

units.la: 4. Omnis scilicet non ex casu agens, primò propter formam agit, quod fieri nequit nisi eam habeat per similitudinem in se præexistentem: nimirum, vel secundum esse naturale, si sit agens naturaliter; vel secundum esse intelligibile, si sit agens ex consilio, qualiter ex arte agitur. Atqs illa formæ similitudo vocatur idea; ut similitudo domûs in mente Architecti præexistens, vocatur idea domûs.
units.tr: 4. For every agent that does not act by chance acts first for the sake of a form, which cannot happen unless it has that form through a likeness pre-existing in itself: namely, either according to natural being, if it acts naturally, or according to intelligible being, if it acts by design, as art acts. This likeness of form is called the idea, just as the likeness of a house pre-existing in the architect's mind is called the idea of the house.

units.la: 5. Et idea potiùs quàm habitus, doctrina, disciplina, facultas, liber, systema, virtus, quia idea generalem artis essentiam propriissimè & proximè exprimit, omnia, quæ de ea verius dicuntur, comprehendens, & omni omnino arti conveniens.
units.tr: 5. And it is called idea rather than habit, doctrine, discipline, faculty, book, system or virtue, because idea most properly and most closely expresses the general essence of art, comprehending all the things that are more truly said of it, and fitting every art without exception.

units.la: 6. Habitus equidem ars quoque dici potest, vel quia habetur, vel quia habentem fe habilem & potentem ad operandum facit, quò Germanicum kunst à konnen (posse) descendens, collimat. Verùm cùm neutrum horum artis essentiam constituat, sed utrumque eam constitutansequatur, id, ut adjunctum; hoc, ut effectum habitus genus artis minùs convenienter. statuitur.
units.tr: 6. Art may indeed also be called habit, either because it is possessed or because it makes the possessor able and capable of acting; this is what the German kunst, derived from können (to be able), aims at. But since neither of these constitutes the essence of art, and one follows art as an accessory while the other follows as an effect of its constitution, habit is posited as the genus of art less fittingly.

units.la: 7. Dici potest doctrina, quâ docetur; disciplina, quâ discitur; facultas, quâ faciles ad agendum reddit; liber aut systema, quâ literis pluribus inter se compositis, olim libro seu cortici inscriptis, calamo aut typis exprimitur. At nequehæc primò de artis essentia sunt, sed eam in & pro hominibus, sive constituendam anteceduntsive constitutam consequuntur.
units.tr: 7. It may be called doctrine, by which it is taught; discipline, by which it is learned; faculty, by which it makes one apt for acting; or book or system, which is expressed by pen or print through many letters composed together, once inscribed on a book or bark with a stylus. But these are not primarily of the essence of art; they belong to men and are for men, following art either before it is constituted or after it has been constituted.

units.la: 8. Virtus autem dici nequit, nisi quâ vel doctrina virtutis est pars cujusdam artis, vel rei cujuslibet scientia Graecis virtus dicitur, quia hæc ad actionem virtuosam rectiùs exercendam norparùm conducit; unde etiam intellectuales virtutes vulgò appellatæ. Sed quamvis hæc etymologia sufficiens ratio sit illis, qui sive ἀρετῆς, sive ab אריה fortis fuit, a quo ipsa vox ἀρετὴ deducunt artis vocem, nobis tamen generis aut essentiæ generalis ratio esse haud potest.
units.tr: 8. Virtue, however, cannot be said of art, unless either the teaching of virtue is part of some art, or the knowledge of any thing whatever is called virtue by the Greeks (aretē) because it helps more rightly to exercise virtuous action; whence also they are commonly called intellectual virtues. But although this etymology is a sufficient reason for those who derive the word art from aretē, or from the Hebrew אריה (ari), "was strong," from which they derive the word aretē, nevertheless for us it cannot be the reason for the genus or general essence.

units.la: 9. Et est idea εὐσχηματία habens εὐσχηματίαν tum pro objecto, circa quod repræsentandum versetur, tum pro fine, ad quem repræsentando dirigendam tendat.
units.tr: 9. And it is an idea having its euschēmatia [εὐσχηματία], both as to the object about which it is concerned in representing, and as to the end to which it tends in directing the representation.

units.la: 10. Quòd ab aliis mens & voluntas objectum artis, & utriusque rectio aut directio finis ejusdem statuitur, id minùs accuratè fieri, ipsorum addita verba produnt, quibus mentem in cognitione, voluntatem in actione dirigi aiunt. Hinc enim palàm est, cognitionem & actionem principaliter dirigi & objectivè, mentem verò & voluntatem ntatem non nisi subjectivè, quatenus cognitio action in iis radicantur.
units.tr: 10. That others set the mind and will as the object of art, and the governance or direction of each as its end, is done less accurately, as the words they add reveal, by which they say the mind is directed in knowing and the will in acting. For from this it is plain that knowing and acting are directed principally and objectively, but the mind and will only subjectively, insofar as knowing and acting are rooted in them.

units.la: 11. Quod postremum nec nos inficias imus, mentem & voluntatem eatenus ab arte diriac ejusdem subjectum esse, quatenus operationes artis in iis fundantur, ultrò concedimus.
units.tr: 11. What is last, we do not deny either: we freely concede that the mind and will are the subject of art, governed by it, insofar as the operations of art are founded in them.

units.la: 12. At rectio & directio non tam finis artis est, quàm pars essentiæ ejus generalis, ideæ scilicet in repræsentando & regendo absolutè constitutæ.
units.tr: 12. But rule and direction are not so much the end of art as part of its general essence, namely of the idea, absolutely constituted in representing and governing.

units.la: 13. Est autem συμμετρία regularis agentis in agendo motus.
units.tr: 13. Now symmetria [συμμετρία] is the regular motion of an agent in acting.

units.la: 14. Hujus συμμετρίας aptitudinem ars omnis illis, quibus inest, secum affert. Cujus aptitudinis usus, etsi in hominibus non usque adeo perfectus est, tum ob ipsam artium in his imperfectionem, tum ob imbecillitatem virium humanarum ad agendum requisitarum; εὐ συμμετρία tamen propterea finis artis esse non definit.
units.tr: 14. Every art brings with it to those who possess it the aptitude for this symmetria. The use of this aptitude, though in humans it is not so perfect, both on account of the imperfection of the arts in them and the weakness of the human powers required for acting, nevertheless does not cease for that reason to be the end of art, namely good symmetria.

units.la: 15. Porrò hæc συμμετρία, ut & idea ejus ac ipsa, quamvis in Deo aut exercitio Dei exstiens sit actus unicè unus & simplicissimus, quia tamen in opere exercito, rebus nempe creatis, voxque omnes concretæ & divisibiles sunt, quasi ex refractione radiorum multiplex & varia evadit, multiplicata ac divisa à rationis oculo percipiantur, & ab homine exercetur.
units.tr: 15. Moreover, this symmetria, like its idea and itself, though in God, or in God's exercise, it exists as a single and most simple act, nevertheless, because in the exercised work, namely created things, and voices are all concrete and divisible, it becomes manifold and varied, as if by the refraction of rays. It is perceived by the eye of reason multiplied and divided, and it is exercised by man.

units.la: 16. Divisa, inquam, 1. in Genesin & Analysin tanquam partes earum generaliter integrantes, & reciprocationem motus ejus ad vivum exprimentes.
units.tr: 16. Divided, I say, (1.) into Genesis and Analysis, as their general integral parts, vividly expressing the reciprocation of its motion.

units.la: 17. Genesis enim, est progressus regularis à simplicibus ad compositia, hæc ex illis constituendo.
units.tr: 17. For Genesis is the regular progress from simples to composites, constituting the latter from the former.

units.la: 18. Analysis est regressus regularis à compositis ad simplicia, illa in hæc resolvendo.
units.tr: 18. Analysis is the regular regress from composites to simples, resolving the former into the latter.

units.la: 19. Utrumque hic motus, tam progressus seu Genesis, quàm regressus seu Analysis, est in συμμετρία. {Greek}, adeo strictè reciprocus, ut regulariter 1. ubicunque alterutrum eorum definit aut incipit, ibi alter incipiat aut desinat; 2. eadem vestigia utrumque premat.
units.tr: 19. Both this motion, both progress or Genesis and regress or Analysis, belongs to symmetria, and is so strictly reciprocal that regularly (1.) wherever one of them ends or begins, there the other begins or ends; (2.) each treads the same tracks.

units.la: 20. At Genesis illa, quae ad Analysin sequitur, dicitur peculiari nomine Imitatio, quae proprie hujus, non alterius est loci, quoad generalem suam naturam.
units.tr: 20. But that Genesis which follows Analysis is called by the special name Imitation, which properly belongs to this place, not to another, as far as its general nature is concerned.

units.la: 21. Quemadmodum ipsa Genesis & Analysis in genere alibi, quàm hic de arte in genere doceri nequit: si quidem Analyseos & Geneseos speciālis doctrinam quaelibet ars ut persequitur, itā cum exordio suo orditur.
units.tr: 21. Just as Genesis and Analysis in general cannot be taught elsewhere than here, where art in general is treated: for any art pursues the special doctrine of Analysis and Genesis, and so it begins with its beginning.

units.la: 22. Dividitur 2. {Greek} in generalem & specialem. Non dicimus in genus & speciem, quasi altera esset alterius genus aut species: tam illa enim, quàm haec, est species {Greek}, ut communis generis. Sed generalis est alia quoad usum suum, quem habet in omnibus aliis {Greek}, & in seipsa, unde concrescentem eam dicimus cum omnibus aliis, & cum seipsa; specialis alia, cujus usus specialior est, & sic late se non extendit.
units.tr: 22. It is divided (2.) into general and special [aporaxia]. We do not say "into genus and species," as if one were the genus or species of the other: for both this and that are species of the same common genus. But one is general as to its use, which it has in all the others and in itself; whence we call it growing together with all the others and with itself. The other is special, whose use is more particular, and so does not extend widely.

units.la: 23. {Greek} generalis est {Greek} bene differere Ciceroni, hoc est rationes rerum bene inventas bene disponere.
units.tr: 23. General [aporaxia] is "to differ well," in Cicero's phrase, that is, to arrange well the reasons of things well discovered.

units.la: 24. Haec cum omnibus aliis {Greek} ac eum seipsa in usu concrescit, & quidem ex necessitate absoluta, ita ut reliquae {Greek} fine ea nullatenus sciri, esse, aut exerceri possint. Hinc rectè vocatur {Greek}.
units.tr: 24. This grows together in use with all the other [arts] and with itself, and indeed from absolute necessity, so that the remaining arts can in no way be known, be, or be exercised without it. Hence it is rightly called general.

units.la: 25. Nam licet praeter hanc sint alia dua {Greek} generales, loqui nimirum & dicere, quas hujus imago recepta ab homine in homine ad hominem parit. Quia tamen hae non nisi ex hypothetica necessitate cum reliquis {Greek} concrescunt, quatenus scilicet illae ab aliquo cognitæ aliis communicandæ, cum priore illa usû s generalitate certare nequeunt.
units.tr: 25. For although besides this there are two other general [arts], namely speaking and saying, which the received image of this produces from man, in man, to man, yet since these grow together with the rest only from a hypothetical necessity, namely insofar as what someone has known is to be communicated to others, they cannot compete with that former one in generality of use.

units.la: 26. Atque inde talis quidem subdivisio instituì potest, quâ ἂωεραξία generalis dicatur vel magis vel minus talis; magis, ut differere, minus, ut loqui & dicere. Sed ut nihilominus differentia illa utrinque observetur, quæ inter dominam & ancillas ejus esse & observari debet ac solet. Hæ enim illi, ad melius esse ipsius, in hominibus saltem, subservient & ancillantur.
units.tr: 26. And from this a subdivision can indeed be made, by which general aporaxia is called more or less such: more, as to differ; less, as to speak and say. But this difference must be observed on both sides, as ought to be and customarily is observed between the mistress and her maidservants. For these serve and wait upon the mistress, for her better being, at least in humans.

units.la: 27. Specialis ἂωεραξία concrescit in usu, vel ex parte tantum cum quadam alia, vel plane non, unde in minus & magis talem dividi potest.
units.tr: 27. Special aporaxia grows together in use either only partly with some other, or not at all, whence it can be divided into less and more such.

units.la: 28. Specialis ἂωεραξία minus talis est bene mensurare; magis talis est vel bene naturare, vel bene vivere.
units.tr: 28. Special aporaxia less such is to measure well; more such is either to deal well with nature or to live well.

units.la: 29. Speciales dicuntur hæ ἂωεραξία, quia non cum omnibus aliis in usu concrescunt, ad differentiam earum, quæ sic concrescunt, atque ideo generales vocantur.
units.tr: 29. These aporaxiai are called special because they do not grow together in use with all the others, in contrast to those which so grow together and are therefore called general.

units.la: 30. Una vero earum dicitur minus talis, hoc est minus specialis, nimirum bene mensurare, quia cum aliqua, ἂωεραξία nempe bene naturandi, ex parte, quoad dimensiones scilicet corporum, concrescit. Reliquæ magis tales, quia cum nulla ἂωεραξία ulla ex parte in usu concrescunt.
units.tr: 30. One of these is called less such, that is, less special: namely, measuring well, since it combines with some ἂωεραξία (the skill of properly ordering things) on one side, namely as regards the dimensions of bodies. The rest are called more such, because they combine with no ἂωεραξία on any side in their use.

units.la: 31. At naturare forsan non esse ἂωεραξίαν artis, quidam existimabunt ante dictorum immemores, quia humanas vires excedat. Quibus id, inde repetitum, ingerendum, quòd naturandi actum homini omnino detrahere, reclamantibus & agricolarum, & hortulanorum, & opificum, & aliorum quam plurimorum operibus, per imitationem naturatis, non sustinebunt. Quòd verò hic naturandi actus in homine tanta cum impersectione hactenus conjunctus fuerit, quanta vix ip in alia ulla ἀ(nisi forte in bene vivendo) observata est, inde est, quia & ars ejus omnium hucusque fuit imperfectissima in hominibus, & vires ad istum actum exercendum requisitæ in iisdem maximè desiderentur.
units.tr: 31. Perhaps some, forgetting what was said above, will think that to order things is not an ἂωεραξία of art, because it exceeds human powers. To them this must be pressed, drawn from the same source: they will not allow that the act of ordering things is wholly denied to man, since the works of farmers, gardeners, craftsmen and very many others, by imitation of nature, cry out against it. That this act of ordering has hitherto been joined in man with such imperfection as scarcely any other is observed to have (except perhaps in living well) is because the art of it has been the most imperfect of all among men up to now, and because the powers required to exercise that act are chiefly lacking in them.

units.la: 32. Porro cùm omnem motum necessariò & immediatè sequatur aliquid ipso factum seu aliqua res, ut Logici vocant, illo motu facta; motum artis seu ἀ qualemcunque non potest non res motu illo facta, seu ἀ fe-qui.
units.tr: 32. Furthermore, since every motion is necessarily and immediately followed by something made by the motion itself, or some thing, as the Logicians call it, made by that motion; the motion of art, or ἀ of whatever kind, cannot but be followed by a thing made by that motion, or ἀ.

units.la: 33. Unde etiam ex Aristotelis mente omnis disciplina erit ars, quia omnis disciplina est μετὰ λόγου ποιητικὴ opus post se relinquens. Habent enim, ut monitum, singularum disciplinarum ἀ sua ἀ, quemadmodum id quoque inductione facilè potest reddi manifestum. Differere & disciplina differendi relinquit post se argumenta inventa & dispositia; Loqui, orationem congruam; Dicere, orationem ornatam; Mensurare, mensuras; Naturare, naturas; Vivere, vitam.
units.tr: 33. Hence also, in Aristotle's mind, every discipline will be an art, because every discipline is a productive capacity with reason, leaving behind a work. For, as has been noted, each of the disciplines has its own ἀ, as can easily be made plain by induction. Arguing, and the discipline of arguing, leave behind arguments found and arranged; speaking, apt speech; speaking ornately, ornate speech; measuring, measures; ordering nature, natures; living, a life.

units.la: 34. Qui vero opus externum, & in sensus incurrens ab arte relictum volunt, illi primò ἀ id solum significare verè demonstrent, ac sic Principem suum Aristotelem secum concilient, antequam nobis id persuadebunt. Quod non fiet adducendo quædam loca Aristotelis ubi opus artis in sensus incurrens dicitur; cujusdam enim, immo plerarumque artium etiam nostrarum opus in sensus incurrere non diffitemur. At hinc quòd omne omnis artis opus in sensus incurrere debeat, aut quod ποίησις opus in sensus incurrens solummodo significet, nulla omnino est consequentia.
units.tr: 34. But those who want art to leave behind an external work that falls under the senses must first truly demonstrate that ἀ means only this, and so reconcile their own Prince Aristotle to themselves, before they persuade us of it. This will not be done by citing certain passages of Aristotle where the work of an art is said to fall under the senses; for we do not deny that the work of some, indeed of most, of our arts also falls under the senses. But from this it does not follow at all that every work of every art must fall under the senses, or that ποίησις means only a work falling under the senses.

units.la: 35. Quamvis autem <bl>ἀ</bl> inter sese & à sese sint distincta, quemadmodum ipsæ <bl>ἀ</bl>-ma, <bl>ἀ</bl>
units.tr: 35. Although, however, the ἀ are distinct from one another and from themselves, just as the ἀ-themselves are, ἀ

units.la: in De {Greek}αι earúmque præcepta, usus tamen eorum communis est & confusus, ut qui ea conglutinat, ac in quo ars posterior, & præceptum posterius semper utitur prioris operæ. Sic in hoc exemplo; idem mensura, qua vos mensuratis, vobis remetiuntur; communis & confusus distinctorum {Greek}, Logici, Grammatici, Rhetorici, Mathematici, Theologici usus est; sic in hoc, unum novum in utres recentes injiciendum, ubi præterea Physici {Greek} usus quoque est.
units.tr: in De {Greek} and their precepts, yet their use is common and confused, since whatever binds them together, and in which the later art and the later precept always uses the work of the earlier. So in this example: the same measure by which you measure will be measured back to you; the common and confused use of the distinct {Greek} belongs to logicians, grammarians, rhetoricians, mathematicians and theologians; so in this: new wine must be put into fresh wineskins, where moreover the use of physics {Greek} also occurs.

units.la: 36. Sicut autem usu confunduntur {Greek}, ita speculatione abstrahuntur & separantur : dum mediante hac quodlibet eorum ad suum disciplinam defertur. Quemadmodum in arte delineatione fieri consequens jam est, ut oculos promamus.
units.tr: 36. But just as the {Greek} are confused in use, so they are abstracted and separated in contemplation, while through this each of them is referred to its own discipline. As, in the art of drawing, it now follows that we bring out the eyes.

units.la: 37. Idea hæc {Greek} delineata est, non uno, pluribus delineamentis; non uno quippe, sed pluribus actibus singulæ {Greek} absolutæ à Deo concipiuntur, ut supiá, & ab homine absolvuntur.
units.tr: 37. This idea is drawn {Greek}, not with one line but with several lines; for indeed the individual {Greek} are conceived by God as complete, not with one but with several acts, as it were, and are completed by man.

units.la: 38. Delineamenta hæc, quia fideliter repræsentant {Greek} suam & absque ullo fuco, dicuntur {Greek} fide digna; quia {Greek} sequentem regunt, regulæ; quia regunt præcipiendo instar edictorum prætoriorum, præcepta; quia secundum ea, & actuum & actorum judicium ac examen instituitur, {Greek} five Canones; quia {Greek} projecta in iisdem videntur, & apparent, problemata, theoremata, {Greek}.
units.tr: 38. These outlines, because they faithfully represent {Greek} their own, and without any gloss, are called {Greek} worthy of belief; because they govern what follows, they are rules; because they govern by prescribing, like the edicts of the praetor, they are precepts; because according to them the judgement and examination both of acts and of agents is instituted, they are {Greek} or canons; because {Greek} seem to be thrown forward in them and appear there, they are problems, theorems, {Greek}.

units.la: 39. Nos regulas vocare maluimus, quia de ideæ prima essentia est, & vim artis maximè exprimit.
units.tr: 39. We have preferred to call them rules, because this belongs to the first essence of the idea, and most clearly expresses the force of the art.

units.la: 40. At hæ regulæ, cùm primitùs fuerint ac sint in Deo verissimo, justissimo, sapientissimo, non possunt non esse verissimæ, justissimæ, sapientissimæ, hoc est, uno verbo, catholicæ.
units.tr: 40. But these rules, since they were and are in God, who is most true, most just and most wise, cannot but be most true, most just and most wise; that is, in one word, catholic.

units.la: 41. Quinimo cùm certò & infallibiliter debeant (quò rectè respiciunt illi, qui ab arce ar-tem dictam volunt, quoniam instar munitissimæ arcis omnes errores ab ἀδ ασφαλίας arceat) non ex parte saltem veræ, hoc est dubiæ, multò minus injustæ, aut insipientes ulla ratione esse possunt. Hinc delineatam hanc ideam regulæ Catholicæ diximus.
units.tr: 41. Indeed, since they must be certain and infallible (which is rightly seen by those who want art to be named from the citadel, since like a most fortified citadel it keeps off all errors from ἀδ ασφαλίας), they cannot be, for any reason, only partly true, that is doubtful, much less unjust or foolish. Hence we have called this outlined idea catholic rule.

units.la: 42. Veritissimæ autem erunt regulæ, si earum principia Legi veritatis χ̄ πάντος sint consona, id est, talia, ut, cum inter se axiomaticè componuntur, consequens de omni antecedente verum sit. Quæ enim non de omni antecedente consequens enunciant, pro diversitate assumti antecedentis, tam falsa quàm vera sunt, ac sic per se, ac in se, nequevera, neque falsa.
units.tr: 42. The rules will be most true if their principles agree with the Law of truth, that is, are such that, when they are combined with one another axiomatically, the consequent is true of every antecedent. For those that do not state a consequent true of every antecedent are, according to the variety of the assumed antecedent, as false as they are true, and so in themselves and of themselves neither true nor false.

units.la: 43. Horum principiorum, quæ nihil aliud sunt quàm singularia illa singulorum, est Intelligentia. Qui enim, quod in singulis est singulare percipit, hunc intelligentem dicere consuevimus.
units.tr: 43. Of these principles, which are nothing other than those singular things of singulars, there is understanding. For we are accustomed to call understanding the one who perceives what is singular in each singular thing.

units.la: 44. Hæc intelligentia in Deo est Archetypa, in homine Ectypa.
units.tr: 44. This understanding is archetypal in God, and ectypal in man.

units.la: 45. Quippe, cùm Deo ab æterno immediatè infit nullatenus advéniens aut impressa, se verò exprimens per quandam quasi refractionem in rebus creatis & gubernatis, quæ sunt intelligentiæ nostræ typus, ex quo ea colligitur, verè, ut est in ipso, est ἀρχὴ τῆς τύπου ἡ πάντος ἡ σοφία.
units.tr: 45. Indeed, since in God, from eternity, it inheres immediately, not coming to him or being impressed on him from outside, but expressing itself, by a certain kind of refraction, in created and governed things, which are the type of our understanding, from which it is gathered truly as it is in itself, it is the beginning of the type, the wisdom of all.

units.la: 46. Atque hinc est, quod Theologia dicitur, ars autem universim sumta dicenda est; quatenus in Deo existit, Archetypa, quia videlicet nihil est aliud, quam æterna ejus sapientia rerum creatrix & gubernatrix.
units.tr: 46. And hence it is that it is called Theology, while art, taken universally, is to be called so insofar as it exists in God as archetypal, since clearly it is nothing other than his eternal wisdom, the creator and governor of things.

units.la: 47. Etsi autem ars hominis etiam quarundam rerum, & sic alicujus typi causa & principium est per imitationem, cum tamen principium neque que primi neque omnis typi fit, ut intelligentia aut ars Dei; led ipsa, qualiscunque fuerit, typum aliquem pro principio habuerit, Ectypa potius, quàm Archetypa dicitur.
units.tr: 47. Although, however, the art of man, even of certain things, is also the cause and principle of some type through imitation, yet since it is not the principle of the first type nor of every type, as the understanding or art of God is, but whatever it may be, has taken some type as its principle, it is called ectypal rather than archetypal.

units.la: 48. Typus (scilicet, in quo omnis ars refplendet, & ex quo ab homine principia ejus,quæ intelligentiam humanam faciunt, colliguntur,sunt yes primario quidem à Deo creatæ & gubernatæ, secundario vero ab homine simili modo factæ aut fictæ.
units.tr: 48. The type (namely, that in which all art shines, and from which man gathers the principles of art, which make up human understanding) is indeed primarily created by God and governed, but secondarily made or feigned by man in a similar way.

units.la: 49. Hinc Græci artem τέχνην vocant à τεύχεσθαι fabrico, quia nempe fabricatæ rei imprimitur, & ex ea tanquam typo suo elucet.
units.tr: 49. Hence the Greeks call art technē, from teuchesthai, to fabricate, because it is impressed on the thing made and shines out from it as from its type.

units.la: 50. Hæ res, quatenus sunt, dicuntur Ens, hoc est, si resolvas, quod est; quatenus finguntur esse, seu possibiliter, Ens fictum possibile; seu impossibiliter, Ens fictum impossibile. Quamvis id quod fingitur esse, etiam Non-Ens dicatur, quatenus non est verè; & Ens rationis pura, aut ratiocinantis, quatenus in sola ratione aut intellectu alicujus est & existit. Quemadmodum aliàs, quicquid non est, Non-Ens dicitur, & si ita non fit, ut id esse plane repugnet, Non Ens negativum; si ita, ut aliquando esse possit, Non Ens potentiale aut Ens potentiale; si ita, ut esse aliquando debuerit, Non-Ens privativum.
units.tr: 50. These things, insofar as they are, are called Being, that is, if you resolve it, that which is; insofar as they are feigned to be, or possibly, feigned possible being; or impossibly, feigned impossible being. Although what is feigned to be is also called non-being, insofar as it is not truly; and pure being of reason, or of the reasoner, insofar as it is and exists only in the reason or intellect of someone. Likewise, elsewhere, whatever is not is called non-being; and if it is such that its being is plainly contradictory, negative non-being; if such that it can sometimes be, potential non-being or potential being; if such that it ought at some time to have been, privative non-being.

units.la: 51. Nomine harum appellationum, ut & aliarum quarumcunque, quæ rebus, quatenus sunt, impositæ videntur, Metaphysicæ nihil certè laudis debemus, licet aliquid vituperii, quod falcem in alienam messem intromiserit; & quod Lexicis etymologicis proprium est, sibi injustè vindicaverit. Nisi forte pro Lexico Logico, aut Philosophico in genere, sed imperfectissimo, haberi velit.
units.tr: 51. By the name of these appellations, as of all others which seem to have been imposed on things insofar as they are, we certainly owe no praise to Metaphysics, though some blame, because it has thrust its sickle into another's harvest, and has unjustly claimed for itself what belongs to etymological lexicons. Unless perhaps it wishes to be held as a logical or philosophical lexicon in general, though a most imperfect one.

units.la: 52. At si appellationes has aliasve similes, non qua tales, sed quoad rationes suas, sibi deberi contendat, in Scyliam profecto incidet. Tum enim ei Logica merito dicam scribet, ex qua sola rationes harum & quarumcunq; generalium Entis appellationum desumuntur.
units.tr: 52. But if someone claims these terms, or others like them, for himself not as terms but in respect of their grounds, he will certainly fall into Scylla. For then I will rightly say that he is writing a Logic, since the grounds of these and all other general terms of Being are drawn from it alone.

units.la: 53. Quod enim rem aut ens aliquod cognosco aut dico esse unum, verum, bonum, perfectum, prius, posterius, simul, universale, singulare, causam, effectum, possibile, necessarium, contingens, facile, difficile, duratione & loco vestitum, mensuram aut mensuratum, idem cum alio ullo modo, diversum, relatum, apparens, complexum, oppositum, id solum per Logica inventionis & dispositionis praecepta fit, quae has & similes affectiones rerum cognoscere docent, licet plerasque saltem, non omnes hae voces in ea conspiciantur.
units.tr: 53. For whether I know or say that a thing or being is one, true, good, perfect, prior, posterior, simultaneous, universal, singular, a cause, an effect, possible, necessary, contingent, easy, difficult, clothed with duration and place, a measure or a thing measured, the same as or different from anything else, related, apparent, complex, or opposed, this is achieved solely by the precepts of Logic for invention and arrangement, which teach us to know these and similar affections of things, although these terms are found in it at least for the most part, if not all of them.

units.la: 54. An vero, Ens aliquod habeat naturam, sive per se subsistentem, sive alii inhaerentem, hoc est, Substantia aut accidens sit, id ea disciplina monstrat, cujus est totam rerum naturam tradere, Physica nimirum, sicut id cum eo quod praemisimus, ex resolutione Entis (quatenus est Typus artis) quam continuo subjiciemus, cuivis facile erit videre.
units.tr: 54. But whether a being has a nature that subsists through itself or inheres in another, that is, whether it is a substance or an accident, is shown by that discipline whose task is to deliver the whole nature of things, namely Physics. This will easily be seen by anyone who compares it with what we have set out above and with the resolution of Being (as far as it is the type of an art) which we shall presently add.

units.la: 55. Typus hic, quem Res ipsa aut Ens ipsum esse diximus, ex omnium artium principiis concretus est, quae tum circa eum, tum in eo, apparent & refulgent.
units.tr: 55. This type, which we have said is the thing itself or Being itself, is compounded from the principles of all the arts, which appear and shine both around it and in it.

units.la: 56. Cyrca typum undique & ex omni ejus parte fulget ratio, relatio aut affectio rerum mutua, ut mediante ea res ipsae ad intellectum nostrum deferantur, qui quicquid percipit, non aliter quam sub ratione & affectione quadam percipit. Hinc differendi principia.
units.tr: 56. Around the type, on every side and from every part of it, shines reason, relation, or the mutual affection of things, so that through it the things themselves are brought to our understanding. Whatever our understanding perceives, it perceives only under some reason and affection. Hence the principles of reasoning.

units.la: 57. Cum hac & in hac radicaliter quoque conspiciuntur appellationes rerum seu verba, utpote quae a ratione aut affectione aliqua rei denominantur, qui p... muntur, quo mediantibus iis rēs ab homine ad ominem deferantur. Hinc principia loquendi & dicendi.
units.tr: 57. With this, and within it, the names or words of things are also seen at their root, since they are named from some reason or affection of a thing, and through them things are conveyed from one person to another. Hence the principles of speaking and saying.

units.la: 58. In typo 1. videtur quantitas, quia res mnes primò materiatæ, ut sic primò statim à eo differant, & propterea quantæ. Hinc principia mensurandi.
units.tr: 58. In the type, first, appears quantity, because all things, first of all as material, differ from it at once, and are therefore quantified. Hence the principles of measuring.

units.la: 59. 2. Natura, quia res secundò à se invicem istinctæ, ac potissimum quidem per formam, uæ præcipua rerum Natura est. Hinc principia naturandi.
units.tr: 59. Second, nature, because things are distinguished from one another, above all through their form, which is the chief nature of things. Hence the principles of natures.

units.la: 60. 3. Finis, qui est bonitas illa universalis, loria scilicet Dei, quæ in omnibus rebus speatur, & ad quam eædem omnes speɑant, ad andem instar sagittæ alicujus directæ. Quod Plato intellexit, qui nihil unquam sive morale, sive Dialeticum, aut Mathematicum, aut Physicum tractat, quin mox ad contemplationem cumque Dei summa cum pietate reducat. M. Ficinus in procemio theologiæ Platonicæ. Hinc principia vivendi.
units.tr: 60. Third, end, which is that universal goodness, namely the glory of God, which is seen in all things, and toward which all of them tend, like an arrow aimed at a mark. Plato understood this, "who never treats anything, whether moral, dialectical, mathematical, or physical, without at once leading it back, with the greatest piety, to the contemplation of God." Marsilio Ficino, in the preface to the Platonic Theology. Hence the principles of living.

units.la: 61. Omnia hæc typus rerum creatarum perfectissimè initio referebat, homini adhuc in Integritatis statu constituto, facile obvia. At postquam homo lapsus est, bonitas tum reliquarum creaturarum, quæ propter hominem maledicti- ni & vanitati subjectæ sunt, tum ipsius hominis, cujus conscientia præcipuè elucebat (erat enim cordi ejus inscripta) ità obscurata & obtenebrata est, ut non nisi paucissima, & quidem corruptissima ejus principia supersint nobis ibidem conspicienda.
units.tr: 61. The type of created things set all of these before man in the most perfect way at the beginning, while he was still in the state of integrity, and they were easily within his reach. But after man fell, the goodness both of the other creatures, which are subject to vanity and the curse on account of man, and of man himself, in whom his conscience especially shone forth (for it was written on his heart), was so darkened and obscured that only very few, and indeed very corrupt, principles remain there for us to see.

units.la: 62. Benignè tamen Deus ac sapienter hic quoque nobis consuluit, dum deficienti ea in arte rerum typo Scripturas substituit, in quibus bonitatis, hoc est, honestatis, pietatis, justi & qui principia perfectissimè revelavit.
units.tr: 62. Yet God has kindly and wisely provided for us here too, in that, when the type of things failed in this art, he put the Scriptures in its place, and in them he revealed the principles of goodness, that is, of honesty, piety, and justice, most perfectly.

units.la: {63.} Hinc incogitantes aut ingrati & mod non impii jure audiunt illi, qui in sinu Ecclesi educati horum principiorum & obscuratione in typo rerum, quam aliis quisque, proh dolo per se in se sat sentit, & revelationem novam Scripturis perdidicerunt, ab his tamen ad illu principia practica quam vocant Philosophia Judis, petitum confugiunt, aliósque secum r piunt.
units.tr: 63. Hence those who are thoughtless or ungrateful, and who are not, I suppose, altogether impious, rightly hear this: those who were brought up in the bosom of the Church and have lost the new revelation in the Scriptures, because of the obscuring of these principles in the type of things, which each of us, alas, feels within himself, nonetheless turn away from these and take refuge in those practical principles which they call "the philosophy of the Jews," and they draw others along with them.

units.la: {64.} Quod tacitè innunt ipsi Ethnici, quo S. Scripturæ in parte præferunt, exemplo suo quibus nimirum pudor non fuit, principia bonitatis, quæ veriora deesse suis naturis sentiebant ex Hebræorum, sive inter se, sive alibi degentium, Scripturis, tum directè tum indirectè, pe tere, ut historiis proditum est.
units.tr: 64. The heathen themselves tacitly admit this when, by their example, they prefer the Scriptures of the Hebrews to their own. Those who had no shame, namely, felt that the truer principles of goodness were lacking in their own natures, and so sought them, both directly and indirectly, from the Scriptures of the Hebrews, whether among themselves or living elsewhere, as history records.

units.la: {65.} Atque hinc tot laudabilia honestatis vestigia in scriptis eorum apparent; quæ propterea non excusa manibus omnium planè optamus modo S. Scripturis subordinentur, & ad eas examinentur, non regula & Canon vitæ seu morum ac Juris, neglectâ Sacrâ Scripturâ, amplius ha beantur.
units.tr: 65. Hence so many praiseworthy traces of honesty appear in their writings. We therefore wish that these writings, which we indeed do not wholly reject, be subordinated to the Holy Scriptures and examined by them, and that they no longer be held as the rule and canon of life, morals, and law, while Holy Scripture is neglected.

units.la: {66.} Reliqua principia præter bonitatem typi rerum adhuc perfectè satis refert, sed nonni indefesâ Analysi interiora ejus penetrantibus intimè videnda & colligenda.
units.tr: 66. As for the other principles, apart from the goodness of the type of things, a sufficient account has not yet been given, but they must be seen and gathered inwardly by an untiring analysis that penetrates their interior parts.

units.la: {67.} Quin nec bonitatis principia in Sacri Scripturis revelata quis intimè cognoverit & perspecta habebit, nisi factâ Sacrarum Scriptu rarum etiam ipsarum Analysi dextrâ, apertis fi mul à Spiritu Sancto oculis mentis ejus. Quo postremum hîc quidem summè & absolutè necessarium, ibi verò, ad principia nimirum reliqua indaganda non parum utile.
units.tr: 67. Nor will anyone know and thoroughly understand the principles of goodness revealed in the Holy Scriptures unless he has also performed an analysis of the Holy Scriptures themselves with a skilful hand, while the eyes of his mind are opened by the Holy Spirit. This last is absolutely and supremely necessary here, and for seeking out the remaining principles it is not a little useful.

units.la: {68.} Analysis Sacræ Scripturæ perficitur Logi cæ præceptis ritè applicatis.
units.tr: 68. The analysis of Holy Scripture is completed by applying the precepts of Logic properly.

units.la: §9. Analysis rerum inchoatur αἰ ἆντ sensu, omnia sive in se, sive ratione effectorum φαγόμεν & αἰ ἀντ, hoc est, apparentia & sensibilia ne alterius interventu apprehendente. Provehitur ἱστορίᾳ, observatione, sensu percepta, eo ūmq; choatam cognitionem sedulò notante & retinente. Perficitur ἐπαγωγῇ inductione, sensu saepe percepta, & observatione retenta inter se serio comparante, & certi quid indè concludente. Confirmatur ἐμπειρίᾳ, Experientiâ, ac quâvis occasione data accuratè & solidè examinante.
units.tr: 69. The analysis of things begins [ἀπὸ αἰσθήσεως] from sense: all things, whether in themselves or in respect of their effects, are [φαινόμενα] and [αἰσθητά], that is, apparent and sensible, apprehended without the intervention of another. It advances by [ἱστορία], observation, perceived by the senses, carefully noting and retaining the knowledge begun in this way. It is completed by [ἐπαγωγή], induction, in which what has often been perceived by the senses and retained by observation is seriously compared among itself, and something certain is concluded from it. It is confirmed by [ἐμπειρία], experience, examining it accurately and soundly on any occasion given.

units.la: §10. Hue pertinent historiae singularum artium, tam Notativae aut Observativae quam Inductivae (quae experimenta aut experimentalia vocantur) quarum contexendarum modum D. Velamius in Novo Organo praepingit, & exemplar ipse, tum Plinius, & Aristoteles in historia animalium reliquerunt. Summi profecto usus ad disciplinas, tum verius constituendas tum faciliter intelligendas & corrigendas, nisi Dictatoria Aristotelis Potestas & nimia illa Credulitas usque hadeo praevaleret.
units.tr: 70. To this belong the histories of the individual arts, both notative or observational and inductive (which are called experiments or experimental works). The method of compiling them is outlined by Lord Verulam in the Novum Organum, and Pliny and Aristotle in his History of Animals have left us examples of it. These are of the highest use for establishing the disciplines more truly and for understanding and correcting them more easily, were it not that the dictatorial power of Aristotle and that excessive credulity prevail so greatly.

units.la: §11. Ex hilce jam 1. quis in singulis discipliniis primus & praecipuus errorum, defectuum ac controversiarum (studiis literarum in eo statu perannentibus nunquam finiendarum) fons fit, proclive est judicare, nimirum, ante dictorum, & colligenda verissima principia necessariorum, antus neglectus.
units.tr: 71. From these things it is easy to judge that the first and chief source of errors, defects, and controversies in each discipline (which, in the present state of letters, never come to an end) is the neglect, mentioned above, of collecting the most true principles of necessary things.

units.la: §12. Qui neglectus, quo major in Physicis, eo luribus quoque ipsa mendis scatet, ut vix ulla jus materia ab iis libera sit. Quia scilicet plerique ejus Mystae non saltem ulla ipsi experimenta rerum naturalium faciunt, ex quibus aut eriora ejus principia colligerent, aut collecta examinarent & emendarent, sed etiam scriptis eterum quorundam vix accuratis ita superstitiosè sè innituntur, ut sacrilegium ab iis recedend fe commissuros, credant, licèt manifesta per a os hâc ratione exquisita & explorata veritas summe suadeat, quærentes quippe priùs quàm quid dixerit.
units.tr: 72. This neglect, the more it occurs in Physics, the more the subject itself is full of errors, so that scarcely any subject is free of them. For most of its initiates not only make no experiments on natural things from which they might gather its truer principles, or test and correct what has been gathered, but they also lean so superstitiously on the writings of certain men, scarcely accurate, that they believe they would commit sacrilege by departing from them, although truth, sought and tested in this way, plainly urges the contrary, since they ask first what he said rather than what is so.

units.la: 73. Ex hisce 2. veterum hoc in genere fcr ptis licet suus debeatur respectus & honos,qua tus tamen debeatur, palàm fit: Nimirum ut r centiorum, caeteris paribus, iis præ-non poftp nantur, cùm oculi plus videant quàm oculu diem dies doceat, cogitationes fecundæ prim sint meliores.
units.tr: 73. From these things, second, it is plain how much respect and honour is due to the writings of the ancients in this field, and how much is not due. Namely, other things being equal, the more recent are not to be ranked below the older ones, since eyes see more than a single eye, as the day itself teaches, and second thoughts are better than first.

units.la: 74. Ex hisce 3. Ethnicorum scriptis lic suus debeatur honos, quantus tamen debeatu palàm fit. Nimirum ut Christianorum, caeter paribus, iis præ non-post-ponantur, ut quorum oculos divinâ gratiâ magis apertos esse, magi consentaneum est.
units.tr: 74. Of these, the writings of the Gentiles (3) deserve their own respect and honour, but only as much as is due. Namely, other things being equal, they should not be put before Christian writers, since it is more fitting that the eyes of Christians have been opened more widely by divine grace.

units.la: 75. Ex hisce 4. inter ipsos Christianos Scr ptores discrimen, quod habendum fit, appare Nempe opera per cacoëthes scribendi & philautiam enixa non tanti sint facienda, quan ex sincero veritatis amore ab amicis Dei probitate vitæ fe demonstrantibus profeEta.
units.tr: 75. From these points (4), the difference that must be recognised among Christian writers themselves appears. Namely, works produced by an itch for writing and by self-love are not to be valued as highly as those which come forth from a sincere love of truth, from friends of God who show their uprightness in their lives.

units.la: 76. Ex hisce 5. in Theologia & Jurisprudentia fi ullorum sententiis adhærere liceat in r valde obscura, Christianorum potiùs quàm Ethnicorum, piorum quàm impiorum (etiam plurimorum) adhærendum est.
units.tr: 76. From these points (5): in theology and jurisprudence, if it is permitted to adhere to anyone's opinions in matters that are very obscure, one should adhere to those of Christians rather than Gentiles, of the pious rather than the impious (even of the many).

units.la: 77. Sic tamen, ullius mancipia ne fiamus, fe sub liberæ veritatis vexillo militantes, eam ducentem, & ab hallucinationibus superiorum no ftrorum, ut qui homines ad imaginem Adam etiam geniti sunt, avocantem, liberè & animos sequamur; omnia probantes, quod bonum est reti nentes: amicus Plato, amicus Aristoteles; at magi amica Veritas.
units.tr: 77. Yet, so that we do not become the slaves of anyone, let us follow the mind freely, as soldiers under the banner of free truth, which leads us and calls us away from the delusions of our ancestors, since men were born in the image of Adam: testing all things, holding fast what is good. Plato is a friend, Aristotle is a friend, but truth is a greater friend.

units.la: 78. Principia porrò verissima, si juxta Legem statia ςῦ̈ τὸ αὐτὸ homogenè (seu ejfentialiter componantur, fiunt regulæ justissimæ. Ubi enim cuique suum tribuitur, ibi justissimè agitur.
units.tr: 78. Moreover, the most true principles, if they are composed according to the Law of Stability [ςῦ̈ τὸ αὐτὸ] homogeneously (or essentially), become the most just rules. For where each thing is given its due, there justice is done.

units.la: 79. Horum principiorum ità compositorum Scientia. Causas quippe & effectias rerum esse; quod tum ante compositionem in component requiritur, & ex compositione, in verè cognoscente, exurgit, prima veriflimáque scientia est.
units.tr: 79. Science of these principles so composed. For that causes and effects of things exist, which is required before composition in what is to be composed, and arises from composition in the one who truly knows, is the first and most true science.

units.la: 80 Sic autem composita principia talia, si juxta Legem Sapientiæ ςῶ ἀδςquate reciprocè diducantur, fiunt tandem regulæ sapientissimæ. Quæ enim justo nec latius, nec angustiùs extenduntur, ea sapientissimè extensa erito dicuntur. Hinc eorum etiam Sapientia.
units.tr: 80. Principles so composed, if they are according to the Law of Wisdom [ἀδεκάτως?] and reciprocally drawn out to an exact equality, finally become the most wise rules. For those things which are extended neither more widely nor more narrowly than the measure requires are said to be extended wisely. Hence also their Wisdom.

units.la: 81. Atque hic est usus harum Legum in omnibus & singulis disciplinis, quoad omnia & singula præcepta essentialia, quæ, nisi eis congruant, vitiosa jure habentur.
units.tr: 81. And this is the use of these Laws in all and each discipline, with respect to all and each essential precept, which, unless they agree with them, are rightly held to be faulty.

units.la: 82. Commorationes verò quod attinet, eæ idem ex parte ab ipsis eximuntur, ast non nisi iustis de causis, & paucissimæ sunt admittendæ.
units.tr: 82. As for digressions, these too are in part removed from them, but only for just reasons, and very few are to be admitted.

units.la: 83. Canones & regulas alii eximunt, & denitiones ac divisiones solas ad eas exigendas se contendunt. At, ne repetam dicta, appellationem & finem Canonis, aut regulæ tantùm considerent, ac quin manus dent non poterunt. Quomodo nomen regulæ rectæ ac quidem κατ' κανὸν merebitur, quod quodammodo curvum aut quomodo juxta, id quod tale, abfolutam alicujus rei rectitudinem examinem?
units.tr: 83. Some remove canons and rules, and claim that definitions and divisions alone are to be demanded from them. But, not to repeat what has been said, they will not be able to consider the nature and end of a canon or rule, nor to hold back. How will a rule deserve the name of a straight rule [κατὰ κανόνα], if what is curved in some way, or what is near to it, may examine the absolute straightness of anything?

units.la: 84. Si denique idea hæc, regulis catholicis constans, methodicè juxta Legem Prudentiæ seu Methodi, delineetur, Prudentia indè exurgit. Quæ intelligentia, Scientia, Sapientia adjuncta absolutam reddit Artem.
units.tr: 84. Finally, if this idea, consisting of catholic rules, is outlined methodically according to the Law of Prudence, or of Method, Prudence arises from it. When this is joined with understanding, science, and wisdom, it makes an Art complete.

units.la: 85. Atqj
units.tr: And

units.la: 85. Atque hæc est genuina horum vulgò & eorum habituum natura ac scaturigo, ut videt, ceu ex diétis apparuit, in omni arte itá necessariò colligentur, quò, eorum qualicunque deficiente ipsâ ideâ defitiat, & ad artis complementum justam non deveniat.
units.tr: 85. And this is the genuine nature and source of these habits, as commonly understood, as appears from what has been said. In every art they must thus be gathered together, so that if any one of them is lacking, the idea itself is lacking, and the art does not reach its completion.

units.la: 86. Quod diversum sentientes licèt inscii præter propositum, plerumque tamen justè cum supposito de omnibus illis ideis & difciplinis produnt, quas artes esse pernegant.
units.tr: 86. Those who think otherwise, though unaware and against their intention, for the most part reveal, rightly and by implication, all those ideas and disciplines which they deny to be arts.

units.la: 87. Qui autem alicui Disciplinæ, five Scientiam, five Sapientiam, five Prudentiam, detrahunt, illi eatenus eam laude suâ spoliant, five heterogenea, five inadæquata, five amethodica ejus præcepta, tacitè & per interpretationem dicant.
units.tr: 87. Those who deny any discipline to be science, or wisdom, or prudence, to that extent strip it of its praise, by tacitly saying, through interpretation, that its precepts are either foreign, or inadequate, or without method.

units.la: 88 Sic fuit natura & effentia artis, divisa ejus sequitur. Quæ in Theoreticam & Practicam vulgò quidem recepta, ac multis modis vitiosa ideóque repudianda est.
units.tr: 88. Thus the nature and essence of art is followed by its division, which is commonly accepted into theoretical and practical, but is faulty in many ways and therefore to be rejected.

units.la: 89. Est fine ulla vera differentia, itá ut unum ejus membrum alterum necessariò includat. Non enim est contemplatio, quæ non fit praxis & habeat suum opus; nec actio in genere talis quæ omnem contemplationem excludat.
units.tr: 89. There is no true difference, so that one part necessarily includes the other. For there is no contemplation which is not practice and has its own work; nor is there any action in general which excludes all contemplation.

units.la: 90 Immo non est omnino Ars, quam ipsi vocant Theoreticam, quæ suam non habeat Praxin, ad quam, in Theoria non acquiescens, e natura sua tendat, nec ulla, quam vocant Practicam, quæ discatur fine Theoria, aut in cuju Theoria auditor ejus, postquam eam perdidicit, acquiescere non possit, fi velit, ac sæpe etiam acquieverit.
units.tr: 90. Indeed, there is no art, which they call theoretical, that does not have its own practice, to which it naturally tends, not resting in theory; nor is there any so-called practical art which is learned without theory, or in whose theory its hearer, after he has learned it, cannot rest, if he wishes, and indeed often has rested.

units.la: 91. De Mathesi in confesso est; de Metaphysica aliquando publicè adverfarics quoque habuimus confitentes, absque quo licèt fuerit, de principaliffima ejus parte, doctrina scilicet, quæ agi git de Deo, sic omnino concludendum est, eam anam esse, & inutilem, nisi ad praxin dirigatur, mmo talem, quæ, Apostolo teste, ad Romanos v. 21. gravissimè à Deo puniatur. De Physica andem praxi quàm multorum opera testentur, ante indigitatum est.
units.tr: 91. About mathematics there is no dispute. About metaphysics, we have at times had public opponents who admitted it, but without which, however it may be, its most principal part, namely the doctrine which treats of God, must altogether be concluded to be vain and useless unless it is directed to practice. Indeed, it is such that, as the Apostle testifies (Rom. 1:21), it is most severely punished by God. About physics, that it has the same practice, as the works of many bear witness, has been pointed out before.

units.la: §2. His accedit, quod omnibus bene pensitas, pars Philosophiæ, practica ipsis, proprié ulla sit. Quodcunque enim in Ethicis, Oeconomicis, Politicis reperitur Catholicæ Veritatis præceptum, id ad Theologiam proprié spectat, quam amen à sua Philosophia, sic divisa, sive ab arbus suis, procul remotam volunt; de quo plurbus in progressu.
units.tr: §2. To this is added that, to all who weigh it well, no part of philosophy is properly practical. For whatever precept of catholic truth is found in ethics, economics, and politics properly pertains to theology, which, however, they wish to be far removed from their philosophy, thus divided, or from its branches; concerning which more will be said in the course of the work.

units.la: §3. Quo tollitur simul sista illa interpretatio vocis προϑέσεως pro actione virtuosa, quâ, ad itas redaêti, evadere semper satagunt. Cùm nihirum nulla sit aêtio virtuosa, quam Theologia on doceat, in quocunque tandem subjecto, sive ssa, sive simulacrum ejus, in, aut extra Ecclesiam conspiciatur.
units.tr: §3. By which that sophistical interpretation of the word prohairesis [προαίρεσις] as virtuous action is also removed, by which they always strive to escape, when they are driven back to it. For there is no virtuous action which theology does not teach, in whatever subject it is found, whether real or a semblance of it, inside or outside the Church.

units.la: §4. Qui verò exemplo & autoritate Ethnicorum excusare sese hîc voluerint, eos accusandos quisq; judiciofus merito sentiet. Quod enim illi in tenebris versantes scintillas honestatis in repertas, aut aliunde haustas, variis doctrinis ariè immiscuerint, id non illis, sed Imitatoriibus eorum, ex Scripturis Spiritu Sancto cooperante restiàs edoêtis, vitio verti potest.
units.tr: §4. But those who wish to excuse themselves here by the example and authority of the Gentiles, any judicious person will rightly feel they are to be accused. For what those men, dwelling in darkness, mixed into various doctrines as sparks of honesty found in themselves or drawn from elsewhere, this can be imputed not to them, but to their imitators, who are taught in the Scriptures with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: §5. Substituenda ergò alia verior, quæ talis sse potest, quâ ars alia generalis, alia specialis ocatur.
units.tr: §5. Therefore another, truer division must be substituted, by which one art is called general and another special.

units.la: §6. Cùm enim & objectum, & principia, & inis ejus tale sit, ut patet ex dictis, ipsam talem sse quis dubitabit, qui ex objecto, principiis & ne dividendam eam novit? Quod hic præmonium in subdivisionibus sequentibus repetendum.
units.tr: §6. For since both its object, its principles, and its end are such, as is clear from what has been said, who will doubt that it is itself such? Whoever knows it is to be divided by its object, principles, and end? This preface is to be repeated in the following subdivisions.

units.la: 97. Generalis iterum vel primaria, vel secundaria ; aut vel magis, vel minus talis est.
units.tr: 97. The general art is again either primary or secondary; or it is either more or less such.

units.la: 98. Primaria vel magis talis est Dialectica, Διαλεκτικὴ fine suo, sic vocata, Inventionem, & Dispositionem rationum præcipiendi, adæquatè tradens à Categoriis equidem, at non aliis, quàm quibus singulis argumentorum par vestiuntur, genuinè & ex natura sua instru&a Fallaciarum verò appendicem omnino repudians.
units.tr: 98. The primary, or more such, is Dialectic [Διαλεκτικὴ], so called from its end, which fully sets forth the invention and arrangement of the reasons for teaching; indeed, it is equipped with the Categories, but not with any other than those with which each part of the arguments is clothed, genuinely and according to its own nature; but it entirely rejects the appendix of fallacies.

units.la: 99. Secundariæ & minus tales sunt Grammatica & Rhetorica.
units.tr: 99. The secondary and less such are Grammar and Rhetoric.

units.la: 100. Grammatica à γράφω scribo dicitur, necdochicè, quia voce tam scriptâ, quàm prolatâ ad sensa animi prodenda uti consuevimus.
units.tr: 100. Grammar is called from write [γράφω], by synecdoche, because we are accustomed to use speech, both written and spoken, to express the thoughts of the mind.

units.la: 101. Hæc ad latinam linguam, quæ peregrinarum addiscendarum prima est, vernaculo cuiuscunque gentis idiomate tradenda ; ad reliquas vero in latinum sermonem, speciali bus & extraordinariis solis mutatis transferenda : Varietas enim illa methodi, & definitionum etiam communiter in singulis linguis multos multùm moratur.
units.tr: 101. These things are to be taught for the Latin language, which is the first of foreign tongues to be learned, in the vernacular idiom of each nation; for the rest, they are to be transferred into the Latin speech, with only special and extraordinary changes. For that variety of method and definitions, as commonly found in individual languages, keeps many people much delayed.

units.la: 102. Hujus præcepta, quia linguis, ut subjecto suo, aptanda, quæ pluribus irregularitatibus scatent, quia item ancillans tantùm est cum sua, usque adeo regularia & Legibus artium reliquarum accommodata tradi nequeunt.
units.tr: 102. Its precepts cannot be delivered so regularly and so adapted to the laws of the other arts, because they must be fitted to languages as to their subject, which abound in many irregularities; likewise because it serves only as a handmaid to its own subject.

units.la: 103. Rhetorica est ἀ ῥέω quod ab ἐρέω dico. In qua præcepta inventionis, & dispositionis heterogeneè repetuntur.
units.tr: 103. Rhetoric is from flow [ῥέω], which is from speak [ἐρέω]. In it the precepts of invention and arrangement are repeated in a mixed way.

units.la: 104. Hæ tres artes dicuntur Generales, & illæ quidem, magis, hæ, minus tales, ob rationes & tibus earum etiam sic dictis applicatas. Nempe quia cum reliquis artibus sic concrescunt, ut eæ sine arte & actu differendi cognoscij sine actu & arte loquendi communicari ; sine arte & actu dicendi ita commodè communicari nequeant.
units.tr: 104. These three arts are called General: the first two are general in a fuller sense, and these last in a lesser sense, on account of the reasons and uses of them that are applied in the so-called arts. For they grow together with the other arts in such a way that those cannot be known without the art and act of reasoning, nor communicated without the art and act of speaking, and neither can be conveniently communicated without the art and act of expressing oneself.

units.la: 105. Reliquntes tres artes, sunt Mathesis, Physica, Theologia, in præcedentibus nullum planè usum habentes, nec cum iis concrescentes. Hinc species.
units.tr: 105. The remaining three arts are Mathematics, Physics and Theology. They have no real use in the preceding arts and do not grow together with them. Hence the species.

units.la: 106. Mathesis à μαν̃θάνω disco, quòd hanc præ reliquis pueri olim discebant, explorandæ eorum indolis & ingenii ergo.
units.tr: 106. Mathematics is from μανθάνω, I learn, because in former times boys learned it before the others, in order to test their disposition and talent.

units.la: 107. Hujus vulgò partem aliam abstractam, aliam concretam constituunt. At omnibus bene pensitatis pars ejus concreta nulla est. Nam quicquid ad artem Physicam pertinet, aut ad nullam planè artem, sed ad hujus aut illius artis usum & facultatem; de qua postea.
units.tr: 107. Some commonly divide it into an abstract part and a concrete part. But on careful consideration it has no concrete part. For whatever belongs to the art of Physics belongs to no art at all, but to the use and faculty of this or that art, which will be discussed later.

units.la: 108. In Geometria tamen plerumque hodie rum quæ dicuntur concretæ Mathescos, principia sunt tradenda; inutiles demonstrationes recandæ, & praxis præcipuè spectanda.
units.tr: 108. Nevertheless, in Geometry, what are today called the concrete parts of Mathematics, principles must be taught, useless demonstrations must be avoided, and practice must be chiefly regarded.

units.la: 109. Physica est à φύσει natura, quam totam omnis Entis naturalis, tam in genere, quàm in specie, ac sic ipsorum etiam Spirituum, quoad catholicè potest, comprehendere & persequi debet.
units.tr: 109. Physics is from φύσις, nature. It ought to comprehend and pursue, as far as it can universally, the whole of every natural being, both in genus and in species, and so also the spirits themselves.

units.la: 110. Theologia ἀπὸ τῆς λογίων τῆς Θεοῦ eloquiis Dei dicitur, ut ex quibus singulariter ratione principiorum colligitur, unde & per doctrinam potiùs, quàm per artem definitur.
units.tr: 110. Theology is called from the oracles of God [τὰ λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ], the utterances of God, since from these it is gathered in a unique way by the reasoning of principles. For this reason it is defined as a doctrine rather than as an art.

units.la: 111. Hæc sola doctrinam catholicam 1. de Deo homogeneè tradit, non prout in se est; sic enim à nemine, nisi à seipso, cognoscitur; sed prout sese clariùs in libro Scripturæ, obscuriùs in libro naturæ nobis ad bene vivendum revelavit.
units.tr: 111. This alone teaches Catholic doctrine, first, concerning God, in a homogeneous way. It does not teach God as he is in himself, for in that way no one knows him except himself; it teaches him as he has revealed himself to us more clearly in the book of Scripture and more obscurely in the book of nature, for the sake of living well.

units.la: 112. Qui verò distinctionem faciunt doctrinæ de Deo, quatenus naturali, aut supernaturali lumine potest cognosci, eámq; quatenus supernaturali, &c. solam ad Theol. pertinere volunt,
units.tr: 112. Those, however, who make a distinction in the doctrine of God, insofar as it can be known by natural or by supernatural light, and who want the part that is known supernaturally, and so on, to belong to Theology alone,

units.la: illi thesi [septimâ] adversus Metaphysicam abunde refutati sunt, his summatim rationibus: 1. quòd scientiæ realis differentia non potest esse modus aut respectus rationis in objecto, sed necessariò aliquid reale, teste Scoto in prologo ad dist.
units.tr: have been thoroughly refuted against the seventh thesis on Metaphysics, for these summary reasons: (1) because a real difference of science cannot be a mode or a respect of reason in the object, but must necessarily be something real, as Scotus testifies in the prologue to the distinction.

units.la: 2. Quòd gradus cognitionis, qui per quatenus naturali lumine, &c. denotatur, non magis potest constituere speciem doctrinæ diversam, quàm quatenus ab homine rudi, à puero, à parùm sand aliquid cognosci potest. 3. Lumine naturali aliter de Deo nihil cognosci, quàm vel per effectus vel per argumentationem ab uno attributo ad aliud, quod idem etiam fiat lumine supernaturali. 4. Revelationem, seu lumen naturale esse quidem causam efficientem Theologiæ, sed non rationem formalem eandem specificantem, & ab aliis disciplinis distinguentem. 5. Quicquid veri & certi de Deo lumine naturali cognoscitur, id idem divinitùs revelatum, hoc est, lumine supernaturali cognoscitur; atque ideò, si id seorsim denuò tractetur, doctrinas saltem sine necessitate multiplicari.
units.tr: (2) The degree of knowledge denoted by "insofar as it is known by natural light" and so on cannot constitute a different species of doctrine any more than "insofar as it can be known by a rude man, a boy, or one little instructed" could. (3) By natural light nothing about God is known otherwise than either through effects or through argument from one attribute to another, and the same happens by supernatural light. (4) Revelation, or natural light, is indeed the efficient cause of Theology, but not the formal reason that specifies it and distinguishes it from other disciplines. (5) Whatever true and certain thing about God is known by natural light is also known as divinely revealed, that is, by supernatural light. Therefore, if it is treated again separately, doctrines are multiplied, at least without necessity.

units.la: 113. Hæc sola doctrinam catholicam 2. virtutum, seu honestatis, juris & æqui homogenee tradit, dum solam totam Dei voluntatem ad mores, voluntatem & vitam nostram dirigendum, revelatam, homogenee exhibet, quæ sola est illa ratio recta, si absoluta rectitudo spectatur, ut hic spectanda est, in qua sola, norma ac regula honestatis, juris & æqui, atque adeò virtutum, consensu sanorum omnium, constituitur.
units.tr: 113. This alone teaches Catholic doctrine, second, of virtue, or honesty, law and equity, in a homogeneous way, since it alone displays homogeneously the whole revealed will of God to direct our morals, our will and our life. This alone is that right reason, if absolute rectitude is considered, as it must be considered here; in it alone, by the agreement of all sound people, the norm and rule of honesty, law and equity, and so of the virtues, is established.

units.la: 114. Oeconomicæ ergò & Politicæ utilitas & necessitas ad Jurisprudentiam, licèt aliqua sit, præcipua tamen non est, sed Theologiæ. Hæc enim generales juris regulas primáq; principia & fundamenta omnia distinctissimè & perfectiùs suppeditat, illæ nonnisi quædam eorum, usibus fibus suis accommodata, eò secum devehunt.
units.tr: 114. Therefore the usefulness and necessity of Economics and Politics for Jurisprudence is some, but it is not the chief one; the chief one belongs to Theology. For Theology supplies most distinctly and perfectly the general rules of law and the first principles and foundations of all of them, whereas the other disciplines carry along with them only some of these, adapted to their own uses.

units.la: 115. Ethica vero utilitas & necessitas ad Jurisprudentiam plane nulla; cùm nihil proprium contineat praeter imperfectionem, reliquis omnibus ex Theologia mutuatis.
units.tr: 115. Ethics, however, has no usefulness or necessity at all for Jurisprudence, since it contains nothing of its own except imperfection, having borrowed everything else from Theology.

units.la: 116. Non obstantibus Ethicorum praetextibus sic saepe jam retextis, quorum praecipui sunt hi.
units.tr: 116. This is so despite the pretexts of the Ethicists, which have often been unravelled already, the chief of which are these.

units.la: 1. Beatitudinem civilem ac moralem à supernaturali & aeterna distinguunt. Cùm tamen 1. ipsa supernaturalis & aeterna beatitudo, respectu societatis civilis ac Politicae, in qua vivimus, considerata, civilis & moralis sit. 2. illa, quam dicunt civilem & moralem supernaturali contradistinctam, non naturalis, hoc est, ex natura corrupta proficiscens, sed supra eam, ex reliquiis naturae integrae per divinam gratiam, etiam in Ethnicis sapientioribus quodammodo firmatis & auctis, fluens, dici merito debeat. 3. prium bonum, beatitudo aut finis hominis, non fit multiplex. 4. non fit vera virtus, quae non ducat hominem ad suum finem, & summum bonum.
units.tr: (1) They distinguish civil and moral blessedness from supernatural and eternal blessedness. Yet (1) supernatural and eternal blessedness itself, considered with respect to the civil and political society in which we live, is civil and moral. (2) What they call civil and moral, set against the supernatural, ought rightly to be called not natural, that is, arising from corrupt nature, but flowing from above it, from the remnants of integral nature, somehow strengthened and increased by divine grace, even among the wiser pagans. (3) The one good, the blessedness or end of man, is not multiplied. (4) That is not true virtue which does not lead man to his end and highest good.

units.la: 2. Objectum aiunt Theologiae interiorem hominem esse, & pietatem; Ethicae mores externos & probitatem. Cùm tamen & hoc aeque fit Theologiae objectum, quae tam externam, quam internam obedientiam praecipit, etiam Keckermanno fatente, Canone 10. de fine Ethicae in praecogn. Ethic. & hominem ad imaginem Dei reformandum non minùs Ethica sibi vendicet, praecepta virtutum praescribendo, & à vitiis avocando, unde etiam prudentia regendi voluntatem & appetitum audire non detrectat.
units.tr: (2) They say that the object of Theology is the inner man and piety, and the object of Ethics external conduct and probity. Yet this too is equally an object of Theology, which enjoins external obedience as well as internal, as Keckermann also confesses in Canon 10, on the end of Ethics, in his Praecognita Ethica. Ethics claims no less for itself the task of reforming man to the image of God, by prescribing the precepts of the virtues and calling him away from vices; and so prudence does not shrink from governing the will and the appetite.

units.la: 3. Virtutes Ethicae terminis hujus vitae concludi, Theologicas ad futuram extendi addunt. At si 1. propterea statim aliquid cessaret esse Theologicum, quia terminis hujus vitae concluditur, multa verè Theologica cessarent esse theologica, ut praedicatio verbi, administratio Sacramentorum, &c. Deinde nunquam probare poterunt ullam virtutem in sua essentia cum hac vita cessaturam, licèt in certis quibusdam individuis cessatura sint quasdam virtutum simulac a. 4. Subjectum Ethicæ dicunt virum probum, bonum & honestum Theologiæ religiosum ac pium. Cui, præter illud quod ad rationem secundam dictum, huc etiam facit, quod ad priorem partem ipsi sibi aliàs respondent, quando docere Ethicam pie vivere affirmant: Quoad posteriorem, ad Titum 2. 12. manifestè Paulus referт, Theologiam etiam temperantèr & justè, hoc est probè & honestè vivere, docere. 5. Quid interest inter virtutes Ethicas & Theologicas (1.) Matthæi 5. 20. nec non cap.6, a 7. luculenter essendi. Ubi nihil aliud apparet, quàm quòd pro fine virtutum nemo privatam utilitatem & gloriam, sed honestatem solam sibi proponere debeat. Quod idem Ethicos de suis virtutibus dicere, plus quàm notum est, ut qui libertatem, divitias, honores, sanitatem, ab Ethico suo aliter spectari nolunt, quàm quatenus sunt adminiculum & instrumentum actiones virtutis commodiùs & facilius exercendi. Si verò hypocrisin & Pharisaismum, cuius præterea ibi fit mentio, Ethica tradat, quis, quæso, auditor ejus eritⁱ (2.) Ad Rom. 1. & 2. ubi nihil Ethicum conspicitur, nisi forte catalogum vitiorum sub finem primi capitis Ethicum dicere velint. At quâ fronte S. Scopus Apostoli illis binis capitibus est manifestum facere omnes homines esse transgressores legis divinæ, ac virtutum Theologicarum desertores.
units.tr: (3) They add that the ethical virtues are bounded by the limits of this life, while the theological virtues extend into the future. But (1) if something immediately ceased to be theological because it is bounded by the limits of this life, many things that are truly theological would cease to be theological, such as the preaching of the word, the administration of the sacraments, and so on. Next, they will never be able to prove that any virtue will cease in its essence with this life, although in certain individuals some virtues will cease as soon as... (4) They say that the subject of Ethics is the upright, good and honest man, and the subject of Theology the religious and pious man. To this, besides what has been said in answer to the second reason, the following also applies: as regards the first part, they themselves answer otherwise when they affirm that Ethics teaches living piously. As for the latter part, Paul clearly says in Titus 2:12 that Theology also teaches living soberly and justly, that is, uprightly and honestly. (5) What is the difference between ethical and theological virtues? (1.) Matthew 5:20 and also chapter 6 from verse 7 make this clear. There nothing else appears than that no one should propose to himself private advantage and glory as the end of the virtues, but honesty alone. The Ethicists say the same of their own virtues, which is more than well known: they do not want freedom, riches, honours or health to be regarded by their Ethics otherwise than insofar as they are an aid and instrument for exercising the actions of virtue more conveniently and easily. But if Ethics teaches hypocrisy and Pharisaism, which is also mentioned there, who, I ask, will be its hearer? (2.) Romans 1 and 2, where nothing ethical is seen, unless perhaps they wish to call the catalogue of vices at the end of the first chapter ethical.
