But with what face can the Apostle's purpose in those two chapters be shown to be that all men are transgressors of the divine law and deserters of the theological virtues?

units.la: 117. Hæ sex artes totum hominem perficiunt; Logica Intellectum; Theologia voluntatem; reliquis, Grammatica, Rhetorica, Mathesi, Physica, Locomotivam ejus in εὐπραξίαις suis ad amussim dirigentibus. 118 His
units.tr: 117. These six arts perfect the whole man: Logic perfects the intellect, Theology the will, and the rest, Grammar, Rhetoric, Mathematics and Physics, direct his locomotive faculty exactly in his actions [εὐπραξίαις]. 118. His

units.la: {y} Matthæi 5. 20.
units.tr: {y} Matthew 5. 20.

units.la: 118. His itaque sex artibus πωιδεῖας ac artium ψυχαλ◌ seu Encyclopædia perfectissimè complectur & absolvitur, non plures nec pauciores canciens. Quemadmodum id etiam, tum per remotionem earum artium, quas alii includere ipsi frustrà sategerunt, tum per objectorum & Legum artium verarum sufficientem enumerationem & attributionem, quibuscunque recte conveniunt, manifestum fecimus & in progressu faciemus.
units.tr: 118. Thus by these six arts the encyclopaedia of education [παιδείας] and of the soul [ψυχαγωγίας] is most fully embraced and completed, neither more nor fewer. We have shown this, and shall show it further in the course of the work, both by removing those arts which others have vainly laboured to include, and by a sufficient enumeration and assignment of the objects and laws of the true arts to whichever arts they rightly belong.

units.la: 119. Ac licet illorum quatuor præcognitorum, quæ, præter undecim scientias, quinque prudentias, & septem artes, Encyclopædiæ quidam intrudunt, nullam expressam introduxerimus mentionem; ex disiis tamen palàm est, Arthelogiam & Hexilogiam Technologiæ includi, ac sic cum ea circulo excludi: Didacticam verò ad totum circulum, necnon ad hanc ipsam Technologiam aut Technometriam, tanquam externum adjunctum se habere, & sic ab ipso circulo tanto longius removeri.
units.tr: 119. Although we have introduced no express mention of those four preliminary subjects which some insert into the encyclopaedia alongside eleven sciences, five prudences and seven arts, it is nevertheless plain from what has been said that Arthelogia and Hexilogia are included in Technologia, and so are excluded along with it from the circle. Didactica, however, stands to the whole circle, and also to Technologia itself or Technometria, as an external adjunct, and so is removed from the circle itself by that much further.

units.la: 120. Inter illas sex artes, Theologia, Logica & Grammatica de primatu certant. Theologia dignitate omnes reliquas antecedit; Logica generali necessitate & pro nostro tamen proficiendi modo Grammatica eisdem primas partes præripit, dignitate aliàs, ut ante monuimus, ultima futura.
units.tr: 120. Among those six arts, Theology, Logic and Grammar contend for the primacy. Theology surpasses all the others in dignity; Logic, by general necessity, and Grammar, by our manner of making progress, snatch the first place from them, though in dignity they are otherwise, as we have said before, to be last.

units.la: 121. Omnibus illis artibus cùm nemo unus ex hominibus omni modo possit uti, hinc earum usus atque adeò utendi ab artificibus acquisitæ facultates, in hoc vel illo vitæ genere, circa hoc vel illud objectum, ad hunc vel illum finem utiles in humana vita, certæ sunt. Quæ improprie & metonymicè artes, absolute & eminenter faculates solent appellari.
units.tr: 121. Since no one man can make use of all these arts in every way, their use follows, and so the faculties that artisans acquire by using them, in this or that way of life, concerning this or that object, for this or that end useful in human life, are fixed. These are improperly and by metonymy called arts, and absolutely and eminently are usually called faculties.

units.la: 122. Hæ ex artificum suorum, necnon ob-jecti
units.tr: 122. These arts, according to the dignity of their practitioners and of their object

units.la: jeđi & finis dignitate majori aut minori, in digniores,& minus dignas distinguuntur. Dignior et iterum in superiores, & inferiorem, quatenus scilicet illæ hanc adhuc aliquo antecellunt modo.
units.tr: The objects and ends are distinguished by greater or lesser dignity into more worthy and less worthy ones. The more worthy are again divided into superior and inferior, insofar as the superior ones excel the inferior in some respect.

units.la: 123. Facultates superiores sunt Theologica, Ecclefiæ Christi colligendæ & ædificandæ; Juridicæ, juridicendo & justitiæ administrandæ; Medicæ, sanitati hominum tuendæ apta nata.
units.tr: 123. The superior faculties are: the theological, for gathering and building up the Church of Christ; the juridical, for judging and administering justice; and the medical, born fit for preserving the health of human beings.

units.la: 124. Huc pertinet Jurifprudentia Corporeju- ris conclusa, & quæcunque alia scripta Legum civilium. Ea enim præter consuetudines & placita hominum, ψυχα, hoc est rationibus, quæ sunt vis & anima Legum, destituta, nihil aliud, quàm quorundam eximiorum Jurisperitorum facultatem in variis particularibus juris & æqui conclusionibus ex principiis catholicis eruendis, hoc est, Legibus specialibus constituendis, casibúsque variis dijudicandis, exercitam recenfent; ipsa principia catholica non tradunt licet quædam eorum ex Theologia, cui homogenea ea esse ostensum est, subinde per occasionem affumant. Unde novam ac distinctam aliquam artem & proprie dictam scientiam non conftituunt.
units.tr: 124. To this belongs the jurisprudence contained in the Body of Civil Law, and whatever other writings there are on the laws. For apart from the customs and decrees of human beings, these lack the soul [ψυχή], that is, the reasons, which are the force and life of the laws. Therefore they set forth nothing other than the skill of certain outstanding jurists, exercised in drawing various particular conclusions of law and equity from catholic principles, that is, in framing special laws and deciding various cases. They do not deliver the catholic principles themselves, though they sometimes take up some of them from Theology, to which these are shown to be akin, as occasion arises. Hence they do not constitute any new and distinct art, or science properly so called.

units.la: 125. Ex quo intelligimus, quàm immerito & indigne passim hodie Jurisconsulti, ne dicam, prudentes appellentur, qui solo Juris-Corpore contenti in juris nostri principiis tam parum sunt versati, ut ea ne supremis quidem libris degustasse, aut digitis attigisse videantur. Nam si scire leges non est verba earum tenere, sed vim ac potestatem, ut Celsus dicebat in l. scire leges 17. D. legibus, quis posset dicere se vim ac potestatem tenere Legis, cujus ignorat rationem? Aut quænam Juris ratio esse potest, quæ non ex juris principiis pendeat? Sunt verba Antonii Fabri Icti celeberrimi, non hic tantum, sed in sequentibus etiam merito meritò applicanda, mutatis mutandis.
units.tr: 125. From this we understand how undeservedly and unworthily nowadays the lawyers, not to say the prudent, are everywhere so called, who, content with the Body of Law alone, are so little versed in the principles of our law that they seem never to have tasted those principles even in the highest books, nor touched them with their fingers. For if to know the laws is not to hold their words, but their force and power, as Celsus said in the law "Scire leges" (D. de legibus, 17), who could say that he holds the force and power of a law whose reason he does not know? Or what reason of law can there be that does not depend on the principles of law? These are the words of the most celebrated jurist Antonius Faber, which should be rightly applied not only here but also in what follows, with the necessary changes made.

units.la: 126. Huc pertinet Medicina, seu scripta Medica qualiacunque, facultatem eximiorum Medicorum in particularibus conclusionibus Medicis ex principiis catholicis eruendis, hoc est, experimentis practicis faciendis, pharmacis variis praescribendis, exercitam, recensentia; ipsa vero principia medendi catholica non tradentia, sed pro occasione data ex arte Physica (in suo esse completo, non existere defectivo, considerata) repetentia; Atque adeò nullam novam distinctam artem constituentia.
units.tr: 126. To this belongs Medicine, or whatever medical writings there are, which set out the skill of outstanding physicians exercised in drawing particular medical conclusions from catholic principles, that is, in performing practical experiments and prescribing various remedies. These writings do not deliver the catholic principles of healing themselves, but take them up as occasion arises from the Physical art (considered in its complete being, not in its defective existence). And so they do not constitute any new and distinct art.

units.la: 127. Facultas inferior dicitur Philosophica, quia ἐστὶ τῆς σοφίας φίλων, hoc est eorum, qui ad ipsam Sophiam, quae proprie est facultatum superiorum, nondum pervenerunt, sed pervenire amantes; atque idcirco hac inferiore facultate acquisitâ viam quasi sibi sternunt.
units.tr: 127. The inferior faculty is called Philosophy, because it is "of the friends of wisdom" [ἐστὶ τῆς σοφίας φίλων], that is, of those who have not yet attained to Sophia itself, which properly belongs to the superior faculties, but who love to attain it. And so, having acquired this inferior faculty, they pave, as it were, a way for themselves.

units.la: 128. Hujus numerantur septem quasi partes, aut partiales facultates; Oratoria, sub qua Poetica qualiscunque; Cosmographia, in qua Astronomia & Geographia, seu utriusque globi usus; Optica; Musica; Architectonica; Oeconomica; Politica.
units.tr: 128. Seven, as it were, parts or partial faculties of this are counted: Oratory, under which is whatever Poetry there is; Cosmography, in which are Astronomy and Geography, or the use of either globe; Optics; Music; Architecture; Economics; Politics.

units.la: 129. Huc ergo pertinent Systemata illa Oratoria, Poetica, Cosmographica, Astronomica, Geographica, Optica, Musica, Architectonica, Oeconomica, Politica, facultatem eximiorum Philosophorum in particularibus conclusionibus Philosophicis, hoc est, Oratoriis, Poeticis, Cosmographicis, &c. accommodatione praeceptorum artium catholicorum, eruendis exercitam, recensentia; non nova praecepta catholica tradentia in artibus non tradita, aut saltem non tradenda, sed ea subinde pro occasionis ratione ex artibus repetentia; ac propterea nullas novas distinctasque artes, aut proprie dictas scientias, constituentia.
units.tr: 129. To this therefore belong those systems of Oratory, Poetry, Cosmography, Astronomy, Geography, Optics, Music, Architecture, Economics and Politics, which set out the skill of outstanding philosophers exercised in drawing particular philosophical conclusions, that is, oratorical, poetic, cosmographical, etc., by applying the precepts of the catholic arts. They do not deliver new catholic precepts in matters not handed down in the arts, or not to be handed down, but take them up as occasion requires from the arts. Therefore they constitute no new and distinct arts, or sciences properly so called.

units.la: 130. Lectio nihilominus, & cognitio eorum non parum conducit, tum ad Philosophiam, tum ad superiores facultates facilius & rectius acquirendas, inprimis vero ad Jurisprudentiam, Geographicæ cognitionis, quamvis non præcipua, magna tamen utilitas & necessitas est: quod nec in præcedentibus negare voluimus.
units.tr: 130. Nevertheless, the reading and knowledge of these contributes not a little both to Philosophy and to acquiring the superior faculties more easily and rightly; especially to Jurisprudence. Geographical knowledge, though not the chief, is nonetheless of great usefulness and necessity. This we did not wish to deny even in what has gone before.

units.la: 131. Facultates minus dignæ sunt variæ, nimirum, præter quatuor illas modo memoratas omnes reliquæ ab hominibus honestè & acquisitæ & exercitæ: Nulla siquidem harum ordinarie artificem suum in tanto, quanto illæ, dignitatis fastigio collocat, experientiâ reste.
units.tr: 131. The less dignified faculties are various: namely, apart from those four just mentioned, all the rest which are honourably acquired and exercised by human beings. For none of these ordinarily places its practitioner on so high a summit of dignity as those do, as experience rightly shows.

units.la: 132. Quamvis autem hæ facultates, eo quem diximus respectu minùs dignæ, aliisque respectibus sordidæ, questuosæ, illiberales, mechanicæ, manuales, & eminenter effectrices vocentur, quatenus scilicet pleræque earum communiter forte didi quæstûs causâ ab artificibus suis, quodam quasi illiberali, & servili modo acquiruntur, (unde esse potest, quòd apud veteres servis & peregrinis propriæ sint habitæ, ut Zabarella & alii annotant) ac in machinis manu potius quam ingenio efficiendis exercentur. In se tamen non ulla earum ingenuo ac libero homine indigna esse, multò minùs cuiquam sordere debet, aut cujusquam corpus animumque & mentem ad usus & actiones virtutis inutilem reddere potest.
units.tr: 132. Although these faculties are called less dignified in the respect we have mentioned, and in other respects sordid, mercenary, illiberal, mechanical, manual, and above all productive, inasmuch as most of them are commonly acquired by their practitioners for the sake of gain, in a certain illiberal and servile manner (whence it may be that among the ancients they were regarded as proper to slaves and foreigners, as Zabarella and others note), and are exercised in making machines by hand rather than by ingenuity. Yet in themselves none of them is unworthy of a free-born and noble man, much less ought any of them to be despised by anyone, nor can any of them render the body, soul and mind useless for the works and actions of virtue.

units.la: 133. Sunt enim artium, Mathefeos scilicet, & fere omnes physicæ, paucæ Grammaticæ, effectæ, ita ut ipsis quà talibus, nihil imputari queat, quod non eadem ratione ad artes ipsas, causas earum, derivetur. De artibus verò talia quæ prædicat, certè in prædicamento est absurdissimi hominis.
units.tr: 133. For the arts of mathematics, namely, and nearly all the physical arts, and a few of the grammatical, are productive, so that nothing can be imputed to them as such that cannot equally be traced back to the arts themselves, their causes. To predicate such things of the arts is certainly to be in the category of the most absurd of men.

units.la: 134. Immò contradictorium hoc est, quòd aliquid ad opera societatis, tam publicæ quam
units.tr: 134. Indeed it is a contradiction that something should be most necessary for promoting the works of society, both public and

units.la: privatæ, promovenda maximè necessarium sit, & corpus, animumque & mentem ad actiones virtutis inutilem reddat. Quandoquidem hoc tale peccatum aut peccati fomes est, ac idcirco neutiquam porest esse verè utile aut necessarium. Vel ergo minùs æqui harum facultatum æstimatores, ipsis ignominiæ illam maculam, vel necessitatem abstergant & utilitatem. Posterius cùm neque ausint, neque valeant; prius ergò.
units.tr: private, and yet render the body, soul and mind useless for the actions of virtue. For such a thing is either sin or the tinder of sin, and therefore can by no means be truly useful or necessary. Either, then, the less fair estimators of these faculties should wipe away from them the stain of disgrace, or the necessity and usefulness. Since they neither dare nor are able to do the latter, the former is the way.

units.la: 135. Sed Physicæ & Grammaticæ effecta sunt facultates hæ, non eatenus tantùm, quatenus ha ic illamve, ut ideam & exemplar suum, imitantur, operâ Mathematicos, quò minùs imitando aberrent, numerum, mensuram & pondus, id est, proportionem partium justam, in qua esse formæ est, examinantes: Sed etiam quatenus materiam operum suorum, & objectum exercitii sui principale ab alterutra earum mutuantur, ideò secundum eas commodissimè distinguenda.
units.tr: 135. But these faculties are productive in the sense that the Physical and Grammatical arts are, not only insofar as they imitate this or that as their idea and pattern, with the aid of mathematics, which by number, measure and weight, that is, the just proportion of the parts in which the being of a form consists, examines them lest they go astray in imitating; but also insofar as they borrow the matter of their works and their principal object of practice from one or other of those arts. Therefore they are most conveniently to be distinguished according to them.

units.la: 136. Sunt itaque facultates seu artes mechanicæ, aliæ Grammaticæ, circa res grammaticas, aliæ Physicæ, circa res Physicas versantes.
units.tr: 136. There are therefore arts, or mechanical skills, some grammatical, concerned with grammatical matters, and some physical, concerned with physical matters.

units.la: 137. Circa res grammaticas versantes sunt circa literas figuris, vel consuetis eleganter, seu calamo seu typo; vel insueris, seu propere & compendiose, seu tectè & occultè exprimendas.
units.tr: 137. Concerned with grammatical matters are the arts of expressing letters, either in the usual figures elegantly, whether with the pen or with type, or in unusual figures, whether quickly and concisely or secretly and hidden.

units.la: 138. Circa literas consuetis figuris eleganter calamo exprimendas est Calligraphia. Ad quam simul referendæ facultates Scribarum varii generis, Exceptorum, Amanuensium & similiūm, tanquam certæ quædam ejus propagines.
units.tr: 138. The art concerned with expressing letters elegantly with the pen, in the usual figures, is calligraphy. To this are also related the various kinds of scribes, copyists, amanuenses and the like, as certain offshoots of it.

units.la: 139. Circa easdem iisdem figuris exprimendas typo, est Typographia. Ex qua oritur Libraria, typis descripta; aut compingens, quod Bibliopegorum; aut recondita suis thecis servans, quod Bibliothecariorum.
units.tr: 139. The art concerned with expressing the same letters in the same figures with type is typography. From it arise bookselling, which deals in printed books, and either the binding of books, which is the work of bookbinders, or the keeping of books stored in their cases, which is the work of librarians.

units.la: 140. Circa literas insuetis figuris propere & com-
units.tr: 140. The art concerned with expressing letters quickly and com-

units.la: compendiosè exprimendas est Brachygraphia, novos & scriptu faciles characteres pro literis; tum singulis seporatim, tum pluribus voces crebrò seu terminantibus, seu integrantibus, conjunctim confingens, confictisq; utens.
units.tr: pendiously in unusual figures is brachygraphy, which devises new characters for letters that are easy to write, both single letters separately and, often, several letters joined together to form words, whether by ending or by integrating them, and which uses the characters so devised.

units.la: 141. Circa literas insuetis figuris occultè & tectè exprimendas est Ars Cyphrarum quam vocant, quâ duo pluresve ex compacto clam inter se scriptis ea communicant, quæ nulli alii lecta volunt. Quanquam hoc ipsum figuris etiam consuetis præstari potest, ad eum, quem Baro Verulamius l. 6. c. 1, de dignitate & augmentis scientiarum exponit, modum.
units.tr: 141. The art concerned with expressing letters secretly and hidden in unusual figures is what they call the art of ciphers, by which two or more people, writing to one another in secret by prior agreement, communicate those things which they wish to be read by no one else. Yet this can also be done with the usual figures, by the method which Lord Verulam sets out in book 6, chapter 1, of On the Dignity and Advancement of the Sciences.

units.la: 142. Omnibus hisce facultatibus Grammaticis subordinantur & inservit Chartopœia, & Pergamenopœia, chartas & membranas, quibus hodie litteræ inscribuntur, eis præparans.
units.tr: 142. Subordinate to all these grammatical skills and serving them is papermaking and parchmentmaking, which prepare the paper and parchment on which letters are today written.

units.la: 143. Circa Physicas materias sunt circa vel Elementa, Ignem, Aërem, Aquam, Terram; vel Elementata. Et utrinque iterum, vel circa ea ipsa, vel circa eorum qualitates.
units.tr: 143. Concerned with physical matters are the arts concerned either with the elements, fire, air, water and earth, or with compounds; and each of these again either with the elements themselves or with their qualities.

units.la: 144. Circa Ignem sunt circa eum artificiosè eliciendum, figendum, confervandum, projiciendum, aliis commodè communicandum &c. Quò pertinent omnes illæ artes bellicæ bombardarum, pulveris tormentarii, pyrobolidum, quatenus aliquo horum alióve modo circa ignem occupantur. Item artes luminum artificialium; nec non hypocaustorum, furnorum, & similium igni conservando commodéque communicando inservientium.
units.tr: 144. The arts concerned with fire deal with eliciting it artificially, fixing it, preserving it, projecting it, and communicating it conveniently to others, and so on. To these belong all those military arts of cannons, gunpowder and fireballs, insofar as they are occupied with fire in any of these or other ways. Likewise the arts of artificial lights, and of hypocausts, furnaces and similar things which serve to preserve fire and to convey its heat conveniently.

units.la: 145. Circa aerem, sunt circa eum concitandum, placandum, inficiendum, purgandum, & follibus spirandum.
units.tr: 145. The arts concerned with air deal with stirring it up, calming it, infecting it, purifying it, and moving it with bellows.

units.la: 146. Circa aquam sunt, circa eam in suis receptaculis per aggeres extructos continendam; ex loco in locum derivandam, sursum agendam; ininnandam; ad tempus quasi inhabitandam, quod est urinatorum; navigandam, unde ars nautica, quæ quatenus velis ventos colligit, etiam circa aerem occupata est.
units.tr: 146. The arts concerned with water deal with containing it in its receptacles by means of constructed embankments, conveying it from place to place, raising it upwards, and swimming in it; with dwelling in it for a time, as it were, which is the work of divers; and with sailing on it, whence comes the nautical art, which, insofar as it gathers the winds into its sails, is also occupied with air.

units.la: 147. Circa terram sunt circa eam arandam, occandam, fodiendam, aut aliis modis præparandam. In quibus est pars quædam Agricultura & Horticultura, facultas scil. aratoris, occatoris, fossoris, pastinatoris, &c.
units.tr: 147. The arts concerned with earth deal with ploughing it, harrowing it, digging it, or preparing it in other ways. Part of this is agriculture and horticulture, namely the skill of the ploughman, the harrower, the digger, the planter and so on.

units.la: 148. Circa elementorum qualitates sunt circa eas, vel primas, facultas calefaciendi, frigefaciendi, siccandi, humectandi; vel secundas, solidandi, liquefaciendi, attenuandi, condensandi, rarefaciendi.
units.tr: 148. The arts concerned with the qualities of the elements deal either with the primary qualities, the skill of heating, cooling, drying and moistening; or with the secondary ones: solidifying, liquefying, thinning, thickening and rarefying.

units.la: 149. Circa qualitates elementatorum sunt, circa Colorem, facultas Pictoria, Tinctoria; Sonum, Musica instrumentalis, quæ, pro instrumentorum varietate, varia, nimirum Chelyi, Psalterii, Organistæ, Lyricinis, Buccinatoris, Liticinis, Tubicinis, Citharædi, Panduri, Nablicinis, Tibicinis, Tympanistæ, Cornicinis, Utricularii, &c. Saporem, Culinaria, præcipue vero Cupedinaria; Odorem, facultas sufficiendi, & Coronaria quatenus herbas ad fragrantiam compingit.
units.tr: 149. The arts concerned with the qualities of compounds are these: concerning colour, the art of painting and dyeing; concerning sound, instrumental music, which varies with the variety of instruments, namely the players of the lyre, the psaltery, the organ, the lyre (lyricines), the trumpet, the lituus, the tuba, the cithara, the pandura, the harp, the flute, the drum, the horn, the bagpipe and so on; concerning taste, cookery, and especially confectionery; concerning smell, the art of perfuming, and garland-making insofar as it binds herbs together for fragrance.

units.la: 150. Circa elementata ipsa, sunt circa vel inanimata, Lapides, Metalla, Mineralia mediæ naturæ; vel animata.
units.tr: 150. The arts concerned with the compounds themselves deal either with the inanimate, stones, metals and minerals of intermediate nature; or with the animate.

units.la: 151. Circa lapides, sunt circa eos vel preciosos, facultas Gemmarii, Quadrigarii, Cælatoris gemmarum; vel viliores, tum naturales fodiendos, liquefaciendos & instar æris fundendos, dolandos, cælandos, quæ duo postrema sunt Lapidæ & Cælatoris; tum coctiles, facultas Lateraria, & consequenter Calciaria, Muraria.
units.tr: 151. The arts concerned with stones deal either with precious ones, the skill of the jeweller, the lapidary cutter and the engraver of gems; or with cheaper ones, both natural stones, which are to be dug up, melted and cast like bronze, hewn and carved (the last two belonging to the stonemason and the stone-carver), and baked stones, the skill of the brickmaker and consequently of the lime-burner and the mason.

units.la: 152. Circa metalla sunt, circa ea tam in genere fodienda, lavanda, exploranda, discernenda, excoquenda, polienda, quæ sunt Metallariorum in fodinis laborantium; quàm in specie circa aurum, argentum, aes, ferrum, cuprum, stannum, plumbum.
units.tr: 152. The arts concerned with metals deal with them both in general, digging, washing, testing, separating, smelting and polishing them, which is the work of miners labouring in the mines; and in particular, with gold, silver, bronze, iron, copper, tin and lead.

units.la: 153. Circa aurum & argentum sunt Bracteaaria; Aurifabrilis, in qua Inauratoria, Cœlatoria, Annularia, Monetaria.
units.tr: 153. The arts concerned with gold and silver are the goldbeater's art, and the goldsmith's, which includes gilding, engraving, ring-making and minting.

units.la: 154. Circa aes sunt fusoria aramentorum, campanarum, tormentorum, &c.
units.tr: 154. The arts concerned with bronze are the casting of vessels, bells, cannons and so on.

units.la: 155. Circa ferrum est ferrifabrilis qualiscunque, Claustrarii, Machaeropoei, Calcarificis, Loricarii, Armamentarii, Cultrarii, Falcificis, &c.
units.tr: 155. The arts concerned with iron are every kind of ironworking: locksmiths, knife-makers, spur-makers, armourers, the makers of weapons and tools, cutlers, sickle-makers and so on.

units.la: 156. Circa cuprum est Cuprifabrilis; Stannum, Stannaria; Plumbum, plumbaria.
units.tr: 156. The arts concerned with copper are coppersmithing; with tin, tinsmithing; with lead, plumbing.

units.la: 157. Circa minerialia media naturae sunt circa Salem excoquendum, praeparandum, Salaria; argillam, Figulina; Vitrum, Vitraria.
units.tr: 157. The arts concerned with minerals of intermediate nature deal with smelting and preparing salt, the salt-works; with clay, pottery; with glass, glassmaking.

units.la: 158. Circa animata sunt circa vel plantas, vel animalia. Et circa hæc vel rationalia, homines scilicet, vel bruta.
units.tr: 158. The arts concerned with animate things deal either with plants or with animals; and with these, either with rational beings, that is, humans, or with brute beasts.

units.la: 159. Circa plantas sunt circa Herbas primo Hortulani & Herbarii, tum Aromatarii, & aliquâ ratione etiam coqui & coronarii; Fruges seminandas & in spica curandas, Agricultura; metendas, Mefforia; colligandas, Colligatoria; Triturandas, Trituratoria; subigendas, Molitoria, Piftoria, Cerevisiaria; Vites, facultas Vinitoris, Putatoris, Pampinatoris, Vindemiatoris, Torculatoris; Arborea facultas Frondatoris, Infitoris, Pomarii quoad fructus, & omnis generis Lignifabrilis, Arcularii, Naupegi, Tornatoris, Vietoris, Carpentarii, Statuarii, Arcuarii, Carbonarii quoad lignum. Plantis annumeratur cetiam cannabis & linum; huc ergo pertinent quaevis circa illam hocve occupationes, nimirum, Restiaria, Linearia & similes.
units.tr: 159. The arts concerned with plants are these. Concerning herbs: first, the work of the gardener and herbalist, then of the apothecary, and in some sense also of the cook and the garland-maker. Grain, to be sown and tended in the ear, is agriculture; to be reaped is the work of the reaper; to be gathered, of the binder; to be threshed, of the thresher; to be ground, of the miller, the baker and the brewer. Vines: the skill of the vintner, the pruner, the tendril-cutter, the vintager and the wine-presser. Trees: the skill of the leaf-stripper, the grafter, the orchardist as regards fruit, and every kind of woodworker: the cabinet-maker, the shipwright, the turner, the wicker-worker, the carpenter, the sculptor, the arch-builder, and the charcoal-burner as regards wood. To plants are also reckoned hemp and flax; so whatever occupations concern these, namely rope-making, linen-making and similar trades, belong here.

units.la: 160. Circa animalia bruta sunt circa ea vel aeria, aves; vel aquatica, piscess; vel terrestria, pecudes, feras.
units.tr: 160. The arts concerned with brute animals deal with them either as aerial, birds; or aquatic, fish; or terrestrial, livestock and wild beasts.

units.la: 161. Circa aves sunt circa eas capiendas facultas Aucupum varii generis, Anatarii, Columbarii; servandas; condocefaciendas.
units.tr: 161. The arts concerned with birds are the skill of catching them, of various kinds: fowlers, duck-catchers, pigeon-keepers; and of keeping and training them.

units.la: 162. Circa pisces est facultas piscandi fundis, sagenis, tragulis, nassis, sportis ex cipulis, hamis aliisque instrumentis quae uno nomine dicitur Piscatoria; servandi item in Piscinis aut vivariis.
units.tr: 162. The art concerned with fish is the skill of fishing with nets, seine nets, trawls, traps, baskets made of wickerwork, hooks and other instruments, which is called by one name the art of fishing; likewise of keeping them in fishponds or fish-tanks.

units.la: 163. Circa pecudes sunt circa eas vel pascendas facultas Bubulci, Subulci, Opiliones, Caprarii; vel saginandas, facultas quâ sunt altilia, saginatoris, & mactandas facultas Lanionis; vel aliis usibus applicandas, quâ jumenta; quò pertinet facultas Equisonis, Agasonis, Mulionis, Aurigae, eorumque, qui his quasi subserviunt, ut jumenta; vel necessariis instruant, Ephippiarii, Scyto-tomiarii, Citellarii, qui ipsi Cerdones habent sibi subservientes; vel morbida curent, Veterinarii &c.
units.tr: 163. The arts concerned with livestock deal with them either as pasturage: the skill of the herdsman, the swineherd, the shepherd and the goatherd; or as fattening, the skill by which poultry are fattened, the fattener, and as slaughtering, the skill of the butcher; or as applied to other uses, as beasts of burden: this includes the skill of the horse-keeper, the groom, the muleteer, the driver, and those who serve these as it were, as the beasts do; or as furnishing necessities: the saddler, the harness-maker, the leather-cutter, who have the tanners as their subordinates; or as curing diseases: the veterinarians and so on.

units.la: 164. Circa feras, canibus, plagis, tendiculis, sepimentis, capiendas, inque vivariis servandas est, facultas Venatoris.
units.tr: 164. The art concerned with wild beasts, of catching them with dogs, snares, nets and fences, and of keeping them in enclosures, is the skill of the hunter.

units.la: 165. Circa hominem sunt circa corpus ejus, vel vestiendum quoad caput, facultas Pileonis; manus, Chirothecaria; pedes, Sutoria, tam Calceraria quàm Crepidaria, cui Cerdo etiam coria subministrat; quoad reliquum corpus, Pellionum, qui in locis quibusdam etiam caput & manus hominum vestiunt; Sartoris, eorumque omnium qui materias ei praeparant, ut Sericariorum, Globulariorum, Lanificum qualiumcunque, Discretoriorum, Concretoriorum seu Textorum, Fullonum & aliorum hujus generis; vel ad agilitatem exercendum, Luctatoria, Pugilatoria, facultas Currendi, Pilaria &c. vel sanandum, Chirurgica, Latomi, Vnguentarii, quae cum Pharmaceutica hue etiam praecipue pertinente, sunt Medicinae subministrae; vel purpurgandum, Balneatoria, Barbitonsoria.
units.tr: 165. The arts concerned with man deal with his body: clothing the head, the skill of the hatter; the hands, the glover's art; the feet, the shoemaker's art, both of the cobbler and of the sandal-maker, to whom the tanner also supplies hides; with the rest of the body, the furrier's art, who in some places also clothe the heads and hands of men; the tailor's art, and that of all those who prepare materials for him, such as silk-workers, ball-makers, makers of woollen cloth of every sort, carders, spinners or weavers, fullers, and others of this kind. With exercising agility: wrestling, boxing, the art of running, ball-playing and so on. With healing: surgery, the work of the stonecutter and the perfumer, which, together with pharmacy, which belongs here especially, are supplied to medicine. With cleansing: the bath-keeper's art and the barber's art.

units.la: 166. Hæ sunt pleraeque saltem si non omnes, facultates, quas homines ex artibus suo modo (alii videlicet cognitis & applicatis artium præceptis, alii traditione scriptâ, alii traditione per manus artificum) sibi acquirunt.
units.tr: 166. These are most, if not all, of the skills which men acquire from the arts, each in its own way (some, namely, from known and applied precepts of the arts, others from written tradition, others from tradition handed on by the hands of craftsmen).

units.la: 167. Verùm, ne quis inaniter aliquam harum pollentem se dicere, multúmque sæpe nocere possit, cùm prodesse debet, prudenter constitutum est, ut præcipuarum facultatum Candidatos quidam in eis eximii probent, approbent, & approbatos testimonio suo ornent.
units.tr: 167. But, so that no one may falsely claim to be proficient in any of these and do much harm when he ought to do good, it has been prudently established that certain distinguished men should examine candidates in the principal skills, approve them, and honour those approved with their testimony.

units.la: 168. Hinc gradus illi Academici: nimirum, qui facultate Philosophicâ, examine & tentamine prævio, excellens repertus est, Artium liberalium Magister, aut Philosophiæ Doctor; qui Medicâ, Doctor Medicinæ: qui Juridicâ, Doctor Juris prudentiæ; qui Theologicâ, Theologiæ Doctor ab ejusdem facultatis Doctoribus, in Academia aliqua præsidentibus, solemniter renunciatur, atque illam facultatem ubique locorum occasione datâ exercend, plenâ potestate ab ejusdem Academiæ supremo Magistratu donatur.
units.tr: 168. Hence those academic degrees: namely, whoever is found excellent in the faculty of philosophy, after a prior examination and trial, is declared Master of the Liberal Arts or Doctor of Philosophy; whoever is so in medicine, Doctor of Medicine; in law, Doctor of Law; in theology, Doctor of Theology, solemnly by the teachers of that same faculty presiding in some university; and, with an opportunity given, he is granted full authority to practise that faculty in any place, by the supreme magistracy of that same university.

units.la: 169. Hinc tyrocinium <bl>meisterstuck</bl> singulis Germaniæ opificibus faciendum, qui in privilegiato aliquo opificio liberè versari, necà tribulibus ejus opificii multari & impediri volunt.
units.tr: 169. Hence the apprenticeship, the masterpiece (meisterstück), which every German craftsman must make, who wish to practise freely in some privileged trade, and who would otherwise be hindered and obstructed by the fellow members of that trade.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.

units.la: ALIA TECHNOMETRIÆ Delineatio, per Quæstiones & Responsiones ad faciliore- m captum instituta ac proposita.
units.tr: ALIA TECHNOMETRIÆ Delineatio, per Quæstiones & Responsiones ad faciliorem captum instituta ac proposita.

units.la: 1. Quo apparatu dibes esse instructus, ut in Artibus peritus evadas?
units.tr: 1. What equipment must you have in order to become skilled in the arts?

units.la: Riplici apparatu; nempe ipsarum artium Præcognitione, Cognitione, & Recognitione.
units.tr: A threefold equipment: namely, foreknowledge of the arts themselves, knowledge of them, and recollection of them.

units.la: 2. Quid tibi generaliter præcognoscendum est ad Artes facilius discendas & adipiscendas?
units.tr: 2. What must you know in advance, in general, to learn and acquire the arts more easily?

units.la: Technometriam prænosse oportet.
units.tr: One must first know Technometria.

units.la: 3. Quid docet summatim Technometria?
units.tr: 3. What does Technometria teach in summary?

units.la: Omnium & singularium artium in genere Naturam & Usum.
units.tr: The nature and use of all the arts, both in general and in particular.

units.la: 4. In quo consistit Natura Artis?
units.tr: 4. In what does the nature of an art consist?

units.la: In ejus Definitione & Divisione.
units.tr: In its definition and division.

units.la: 5. Quomodo ergo definis Artem?
units.tr: 5. How, then, do you define art?

units.la: Ars est idea συνπαξίας regulis catholicis methodicè delineata.
units.tr: Art is the idea of good action [συμπραξία], methodically outlined by universal rules.

units.la: 6. Quid illa Artis definitio in genere in se comprehendit?
units.tr: 6. What does this definition of art contain in general?

units.la: Quatuor communia requisita proponit, quæ ad quamlibet artem constituendam sunt necessaria. Ejusmodi est, Genus, Differentia, Materia generis, & ejusdem Forma.
units.tr: It sets out four common requisites that are necessary for constituting any art. These are the genus, the differentia, the matter of the genus, and its form.

units.la: 7. Quid est commune Genus omnium artium? Est idea.
units.tr: 7. What is the common genus of all the arts? It is the idea.

units.la: 8. Quæ est communis differentia?
units.tr: 8. What is the common differentia?

units.la: Hæc ab objecto & Fine communi omnium artium est συνπαξίας divisa in suas partes & species, habénsque συνπαθόμενον ieu opus motu ipso factum sibi adjunctum.
units.tr: It is good action [συμπραξία], which is divided into its parts and species by the object and common end of all the arts, and which has as its accompaniment [συμπαθόμενον], that is, the work produced by the motion itself, joined to it.

units.la: 9. Quæ est materia ideæ?
units.tr: 9. What is the matter of the idea?

units.la: Sunt regulæ catholicæ, id est, veritissimæ, justissimæ, sapientissimæ.
units.tr: It consists of universal rules, that is, most true, most just, and most wise.

units.la: 10. Quomodo & unde fiunt hujusmodi regulæ?
units.tr: 10. How and from what are such rules made?

units.la: Fiunt juxta tres leges, Veritatis, Justitiæ, & sapientiæ: idque ex principiis cuilibet speciei συπραξίας (singularibus.
units.tr: They are made according to three laws: of truth, of justice, and of wisdom. And this is done from the principles singular to each species of good action [συμπραξία].

units.la: 11. Unde inveniuntur & quibus adminiculis colliguntur ista artium principia singularia?
units.tr: 11. From where are these singular principles of the arts discovered, and by what aids are they gathered?

units.la: Inveniuntur ex rebus, sive creatis, sive factis. Quælibet enim res, in quantum est subjectum adæquatum artium, in ipsa principia communia resolubilis est à mente nostra; nempe, Affectionem, Appellationem, ornatam Distinctionem, Sanctitatem, Naturam, & Finem sive bonitatem. Ex his postea omnia singularia artium principia per Sensum, Observationem, Inductionem & Experientiam colliguntur.
units.tr: They are discovered from things, whether created or made. For any thing, insofar as it is an adequate subject of the arts, can be resolved by our mind into its common principles, namely: affection, appellation, adorned distinction, holiness, nature, and end or goodness. From these, all the singular principles of the arts are afterwards gathered through sense, observation, induction, and experience.

units.la: 12. Quis est usus regularum catholicarum sic conformatarum?
units.tr: 12. What is the use of universal rules formed in this way?

units.la: Hæ efficiunt in mente nostra tres habitus; nempe, Intelligentiam principiorum inventorum; eorundem inter se conjungendorum scientiam; & aliorum ex aliis deductorum Sapientiam.
units.tr: They produce in our mind three habits: namely, understanding of the principles discovered, knowledge of how these are to be joined with one another, and wisdom concerning the things deduced from others.

units.la: 13. Quanam est idea συνπαξίας forma?
units.tr: 13. What is the form of the idea of good action [συμπραξία]?

units.la: Methodica ejus delineatio, quæ quartum parit mentis habitum; scilicet, prudentiam. Et horum demum simul omnium quatuor habituum inter se ordine naturæ in συνπαξίας colligatio & concursus proprie dicitur Ars.
units.tr: Its methodical outline, which gives birth to a fourth habit of the mind, namely prudence. And finally, the joining and concurrence of all four of these habits together, in good action [συμπραξία], in the order of nature, is properly called art.

units.la: 14. Sed quoniam hæc omnia haberi mihi inaudita & obscura [sunt], ea singulatim plenius explica: & primo Definitum, quod est Ars, ambiguum esse videtur.
units.tr: 14. But since all of this is strange and obscure to me, explain each part more fully. And first, the term defined, which is art, seems ambiguous.

units.la: Etsi vocabulum Artis varia variis significet (ut ad quaest. 19, 20, & 21. notabimus) in qua tamen significatione à nobis accipiatur, manifestum est.
units.tr: Although the word Ars signifies various things in various ways (as we shall note at questions 19, 20, and 21), it is evident in which sense we take it here.

units.la: 15. Unde dicitur Ars?
units.tr: 15. Whence is the word art derived?

units.la: Latinis venit ab Arce; quoniam instar munitissimæ arcis omnes errores ἐνστρεφὰξίας, id est, bonæ Actionis arcet: vel ab Artu; quia sicut artus sunt corporis robur, sic præcepta Artium eandem conservant & integrant, adeò ut si unum illorum enervetur, cum eo reliqua omnia, atque ipsa Ars ruat necesse est.
units.tr: In Latin it comes from arx, a citadel, since, like a very strong citadel, it keeps off all errors of good conduct [ἐνστρεφὰξίας], that is, of good action. Or it comes from artus, a joint or limb, since just as the limbs are the strength of the body, so the precepts of the arts preserve and complete it. So much so that if one of these is weakened, all the rest, and art itself, must necessarily collapse with it.

units.la: 16. Quid est idea in definitione? Idea est formula seu exemplaris scientia in mente Artificis, ante actionem ad actionem efformata, ut eam repræsentet & repræsentando regat.
units.tr: 16. What is the idea in the definition? An idea is a formula or exemplar knowledge, formed in the mind of the artificer before the action, for the purpose of representing the action and governing it by that representation.

units.la: 17. Declara hoc planius.
units.tr: 17. Explain this more clearly.

units.la: Omnis scilicet non ex casu agens, primò propter formam agit; quod fieri nequit nisi eam habeat per similitudinem in se præ-existentem, nimirum vel secundum Esse naturale, si fit agens naturaliter; vel secundum Esse intelligibile, si sit agens ex consilio, qualiter ex arte agitur: atque illa forma similitudo vocatur Idea: ut similitudo domus in mente Architecti præexistens vocatur idea domus, quam acturus inspicit, ut ad eam operationem suam insequentem aptet.
units.tr: Every agent that does not act by chance acts first for the sake of a form, which it cannot do unless it has that form through a likeness existing beforehand in itself. This is either in natural being, if it acts naturally, or in intelligible being, if it acts by deliberate choice, as is the case when one acts by art. This formal likeness is called an Idea. For example, the likeness of a house, existing beforehand in the mind of the architect, is called the idea of a house, which he, about to act, looks upon so that he may fit his subsequent operation to it.

units.la: 18. Cur Artis Genus Ideam facit?
units.tr: 18. Why does the genus of art make it an idea?

units.la: Quia idea generalem artis essentiam (quæ est repræsentare & regere bonam actionem) propriissimè & proximè exprimit, omnia, quæ de ea veriùs dicuntur, comprehendens, & omni cmnino arti conveniens.
units.tr: Because the idea most properly and most closely expresses the general essence of art (which is to represent and govern good action), embracing all the things that can be said of it more truly, and agreeing with every art without exception.

units.la: 19. Annon alii Artis Genus rectius statuunt habitum ex mente Aristotelis, qui Artem definit, quòd sit habitus opus post se relinquens? Habitus quidem Ars quoque dici potest, vel quia habetur, vel quia habentem fe habilem & potentem ad operandum facit: verùm cùm neutrum horum Artis essentiam constituat, sed utrumque eam constitutam sequatur, illud ut Adjunctum, istud ut effectum; ideirco Habitus Genus artis minùs convenienter statuitur.
units.tr: 19. Do not others more rightly set down habit as the genus of art, following Aristotle, who defines art as a habit leaving behind a work? Habit indeed may also be called art, either because it is possessed or because it makes the one who has it fit and able to act. But since neither of these constitutes the essence of art, but both follow upon it once it has been constituted, the one as an accident and the other as an effect, therefore habit is less suitably set as the genus of art.

units.la: 20. Quid ergò judicas de Doctrina, Disciplina, Facultate, Libro aut Systemate, quæ nonnulli Artis Genera faciunt?
units.tr: 20. What, then, do you judge of doctrine, discipline, faculty, book, or system, which some make into genera of art?

units.la: Ars dici potest Doctrina, quatenus docetur: Disciplina, quatenus discitur: Facultas, quatenus faciles ad agendum reddit: Liber aut Systema, quatenus literis pluribus inter se compositis, olim libro aut cortici inscriptis, calamo aut typis exprimitur. At neq; hæc primò de Artis effentia sunt, sed eam in & per homines, sive constituendam antecedunt, sive constitutam consequuntur.
units.tr: Art can be called doctrine insofar as it is taught; discipline insofar as it is learned; faculty insofar as it makes people ready to act; book or system insofar as it is expressed in several letters arranged together, once inscribed on a book or bark, and by pen or print. But these are not primarily of the essence of art; rather they go before it, or follow it once constituted, in and through human beings.

units.la: 21. An forte Virtus melius dicitur Ars?
units.tr: 21. Or is perhaps virtue better called art?

units.la: Virtus dici nequit, nisi quatenus vel doctrina virtutis est pars cujusdam artis, vel rei cujuslibet scientia Græcis virtus dicitur, quia illa ad actionem virtuosam reftiùs exercendam non parùm conducit: Unde etiam intellectuales virtutes vulgò appellatæ. Sed quamvis hæc etymi fortassis sufficiens ratio fit illis, qui, sive ἀρετή, sive ab אריה arah, id est, fortis fuit, (à quo ipsa vox ἀρετή) deducunt Artis vocem: nobis tamen Generis aut essentiæ generalis ratio esse haud potest.
units.tr: Virtue cannot be called art, except insofar as the teaching of virtue is part of some art, or insofar as virtue is the name the Greeks give to the knowledge of any thing, because this contributes not a little to exercising virtuous action more correctly. Hence also what are commonly called the intellectual virtues. But although this may perhaps be a sufficient etymological reason for those who derive the word art either from [ἀρετή], or from the Hebrew arah [אריה], that is, was strong (from which the word [ἀρετή] itself comes), yet for us it cannot be a reason for the genus or the general essence.

units.la: 22. Quodnam est idea objectum & Finis?
units.tr: 22. What are the object and end of the idea?

units.la: Est συμπαξία, id est, bona actio. Objectum est, quatenus circa hanc repræsentandam versatur. Finis verò, quatenus ad eam repræsentandam dirigendam tendit.
units.tr: It is good action [συμπαξία], that is, good action. The object is that with which it is concerned in representing this. The end, however, is that toward which it tends in order to represent and direct this.

units.la: 23. Atqui ab aliis mens & voluntas Objectum artis, artis, & utriusque rectio vel directio Finis ejusdem statuitur.
units.tr: 23. But others hold that the mind and will are the object of art, and that the rule or direction of both is its end.

units.la: Id minus accurate fieri ipsorum addita verba produnt, quibus mentem in cognitione, voluntatem in actione dirigi aiunt. Hinc enim palam est, cognitionem & actionem ab arte primario dirigi & objective: mentem vero & voluntatem nonnisi secundario & subjective, quatenus operationes artis, hoc est, cognitio & actio in iis fundantur. Quod postremum nec nos inficiamur. At rectio & directio non tam Finis artis est, quam pars essentiae ejus generalis, ideae scilicet in repraesentando & regendo absolute constitutae.
units.tr: The added words of these writers show that this is less accurate: they say the mind is directed in knowing, and the will in acting. For from this it is plain that knowing and acting are directed by art primarily and objectively, whereas the mind and will are directed only secondarily and subjectively, insofar as the operations of art, that is, knowing and acting, are founded in them. We do not deny this last point. But rule and direction are not so much the end of art as part of its general essence, namely of the idea, which is constituted absolutely in representing and governing.

units.la: 24. Cur εὐτεξίαν Finem omnibus artibus communem facit, cum vulgo Philosophia (quam vocant) Practica solum finem illum adscribant?
units.tr: 24. Why do you make well-orderedness [εὐταξία] the end common to all arts, when the so-called Practical Philosophy commonly ascribes that end alone to itself?

units.la: Certe illos, decipit fida illa interpretatio vocis εὐτεξίως pro actione virtuosa, qua ad incitas redacti evadere semper satagunt: cum nimirum nulla sit actio virtuosa quam Theologia non doceat, in quocunque tandem subjecto, sive ipsa, sive simulacrum ejus, in aut extra Ecclesiam, conspiciatur. Sed de his in divisione artium.
units.tr: Those people are certainly deceived by that faithful interpretation of the word well-ordered [εὐτεξίως] as virtuous action, by which they always strive to make themselves seem to be the equals of the most excellent. For there is no virtuous action that Theology does not teach, in whatever subject it may be seen, whether in the Church or outside it, whether itself or its likeness. But more on these matters under the division of the arts.

units.la: 25. Quid vero est εὐτεξία in definitione?
units.tr: 25. What, then, is well-orderedness [εὐταξία] in the definition?

units.la: Est regularis agentis in agendo motus. Tunc enim bene agere dicimur, cum propriis propositae rei regulis convenienter, non uspiam ab eis vel minimum aberrando, agimus.
units.tr: It is the motion of the agent, regulated in acting. For we are said to act well when we act in agreement with the proper rules of the thing proposed, never deviating from them even in the slightest.

units.la: 26. Num hujus εὐτεξίας aptitudinem Ars omnibus illis, quibus inest, secum affert?
units.tr: 26. Does art bring with it, to all those in whom it is present, the aptitude for this well-orderedness [εὐταξία]?

units.la: Omnino ex natura sua.
units.tr: Altogether, by its nature.

units.la: 27. Unde igitur fit, quod hujus aptitudinis usus in hominibus non usquam adeo perfectus est?
units.tr: 27. Whence then does it happen that the use of this aptitude is nowhere so perfect in human beings?

units.la: Id fit tum ob ipsam artium in eis imperfectionem; tum ob imbecillitatem virium humanarum ad agendum requisitarum: sed tamen εὐτεξία finis artis esse non definit.
units.tr: This happens partly because of the imperfection of the arts themselves, and partly because of the weakness of the human powers required for acting. Yet euexia [εὐεξία] does not cease to be the end of art.

units.la: 28. Annon hæc συνεσταλκία ullo modo dividitur? Imo dividitur in suas partes & species.
units.tr: 28. Is this synestalkia [συνεσταλκία] not divided in any way? Indeed it is divided into its parts and kinds.

units.la: 29. At cum omnis Artis συνεσταλκία, sit imitatio sapientiæ divinæ creaturis impressa, quæ dividi non potest, quemodo tu συνεσταλκίαν legitimè dividesi?
units.tr: 29. But since all the synestalkia of an art is an imitation of divine wisdom impressed on creatures, which cannot be divided, how do you legitimately divide synestalkia?

units.la: Quamvis hæc συνεσταλκία, ut & idea ejus, ac ars ipsa in exercitio Dei existens, sit actus unicè unus & simplicissimus; quia tamen opus exercitum, id est, res omnes creatæ sunt concretæ & divisibiles, ipsa quoque artis συνεσταλκία, quasi ex refractione radiorum multiplicatur ac dividitur, & in illa multiplicitate percipitur à rationis oculo & exercetur.
units.tr: Although this synestalkia, like its idea and the art itself existing in God's exercise, is an act that is wholly one and most simple, yet because the work carried out, that is, all created things, are concrete and divisible, the synestalkia of art itself is, as if by the refraction of rays, multiplied and divided. In that multiplicity it is perceived by the eye of reason and exercised.

units.la: 30. Quot sunt igitur συνεσταλκίας partes integrantes?
units.tr: 30. How many integral parts, then, does synestalkia have?

units.la: Duæ: Genesis & Analysis. Quæ adeò strictè reciprocæ sunt, ut regulariter primò ubicunque alterutra earum definit aut incipit, ibi altera incipiat vel desinat: deinde eadem vestigia utraq; premat.
units.tr: Two: Genesis and Analysis. These are so strictly reciprocal that, as a rule, wherever one of them ends or begins, the other begins or ends there in turn; and then both tread the same footsteps.

units.la: 31. Quid est Genesis?
units.tr: 31. What is Genesis?

units.la: Est progressus regularis à simplicibus ad composita, hæc ex illis constituendo.
units.tr: It is a regular progress from simples to composites, constituting the latter from the former.

units.la: 32. Quid est Analysis?
units.tr: 32. What is Analysis?

units.la: Est regressus regularis à compositis ad simplicia, illa in hæc resolvendo.
units.tr: It is a regular regress from composites to simples, resolving the former into the latter.

units.la: 33. Quorsum refert Genesin illam quæ ad Analysin requiritur, & peculiari nomine Imitatio dicitur?
units.tr: 33. To what purpose is that Genesis which is required for Analysis, and is called by the special name Imitation?

units.la: Hæc proprie non est alterius loci quoad generalem suam naturam. Quemadmodum ipsa Genesis & Analysis in genere alibi quàm hic de arte in genere doceri nequit: siquidem Geneseos & Analyseos specialis doctrinam quælibet ars ut prosequitur, itâ cum exordio suo orditur.
units.tr: This does not properly belong to another place as regards its general nature. Just as Genesis and Analysis in general cannot be taught anywhere other than here, where art in general is treated; for each art, as it pursues the special doctrine of Genesis and Analysis, begins with its own beginning.

units.la: 34. Quot sunt species συνεσταλκίας?
units.tr: 34. How many kinds of synestalkia are there?

units.la: Sex: quarum tres sunt magis vel minùs generales: aliæ autem magis vel minùs speciales.
units.tr: Six: of these, three are more or less general, and the others more or less special.

units.la: 35. At sic videris mihi ςυμπραξίαν tanquam Genus & Speciem viiosè diviiere?
units.tr: 35. But you seem to me to divide symparaxia wrongly, as genus and species?

units.la: Non dico in Genus & speciem, quasi generalis συμπραξία effet Genus specialis ἀδ πραξίας, ut communis generis : led generalem & jpsciałem dico quoad usum suum.
units.tr: I do not say it is divided into genus and species, as if the general symparaxia were a genus of a special praxia, like a common genus. I call it general and special with regard to its use.

units.la: 36. Quaest maiis-generalis ἀδ πραξίας?
units.tr: 36. What is the most general praxia?

units.la: Est bene differere Ciceroni, hoc est, rationes rerum bene invenire & bene disponere.
units.tr: It is "to discourse well" in Cicero's sense, that is, to find well the reasons of things and to arrange them well.

units.la: Hæc συμπραξία cum omnibus aliis ἀδ πραξί- αῖς, & cum seipsa in usu concrescit; & quidem ex absoluta necessitate, ita ut reliquæ sine ea esse aut exerceri non possint. Hinc recte vocatur πολιτικωτάτη, id est, universalissima.
units.tr: This symparaxia grows together with all the other praxiae, and with itself, in use; and indeed of absolute necessity, so that the others cannot exist or be exercised without it. Hence it is rightly called most political [πολιτικωτάτη], that is, most universal.

units.la: 37. Quaenam sunt minus-generales ἀδ πραξίαι: Bene-loqui & bene dicere: Quae usum suum habent cum reliquis ἀδ πραξίαις concrescentem, at nonnisi ex hypothetica necessitate (quatenus scilicet illæ ab aliquo cognitæ aliis sunt communicandæ) & idcirco priorem illam usus generalitate non æquant. Illius quippe cognitio seu imago ab homine recepta, has duas ἀδ ςυμπραξίας secundarias & sibi ancillantes parit, quibus hæc ab homine ad hominem deferri possit. Atqui sic hæ illi, ad ipsius in hominibus saltem melius esse, subserviunt.
units.tr: 37. What are the less general praxiae? To speak well and to say well. These have their use growing together with the other praxiae, but only from hypothetical necessity (namely, insofar as what someone has come to know must be communicated to others). For this reason they do not equal the former in the generality of their use. For the knowledge, or the image of it received by a man, gives birth to these two secondary symparaxiae, which serve it, and by which it can be conveyed from man to man. And thus these serve the former, at least for the better being of man.

units.la: 38. Quae est ergo minus-specialis ἀδ συμπραξίας?
units.tr: 38. What, then, is the least special symparaxia?

units.la: Bene-mensurare: quia hæc cum ἀδ πραξίᾳ bene-naturandi ex parte tantum, h. e. quoad dimensiones corporum concrescit.
units.tr: To measure well, because this grows together with the praxia of to be well-natured only in part, that is, as regards the dimensions of bodies.

units.la: 39. Quae est magis-specialis ἀδ πραξία?
units.tr: 39. What is the more special praxia?

units.la: Bene naturare & bene-vivere: quia scilicet cum nulla ἀδ πραξίᾳ nulla ex parte in usu concrescit.
units.tr: To be well-natured and to live well, because, namely, it grows together in use with no praxia in any part.

units.la: 40. Cum vero omnem motum necessario & immediate sequatur res aliqua ipso motu factı? An proinde cujuslibet artis qualemcunque motum scilicet cet ἀδ'προξίαν, opus motu ipso factum sequitur.
units.tr: 40. But since something made by the motion itself always and necessarily follows every motion, does the work made by the motion itself therefore follow any motion whatever of any art, that is, of any praxia?

units.la: Omnino habent singuiarum disciplinarum ἐντεχνίαν προξίαι sua ὑπερδιατὰ φύσεα: quemadmodum in inductione fit manifestum. Nam differere, sex ars differendi relinquit post se argumenta inventa & dispositta; Loqui, orationem congruam; Dicere, orationem ornatam; Mensurare, mensuras; Naturare, naturas; Vivere, vitam. Unde etiam ex Aristotelis mente omnis disciplina erit ars; quia omnis disciplina est (ut explicatum) habitus opus potest se relinquens.
units.tr: Certainly the individual disciplines' technical praxiae have their own results beyond nature, as is made plain by induction. For to discourse, the art of discourse leaves behind arguments found and arranged; to speak, a fitting speech; to say, an adorned speech; to measure, measurements; to be well-natured, natures; to live, a life. Whence also, according to the mind of Aristotle, every discipline will be an art, since every discipline is (as explained) a habit that leaves behind a work.

units.la: 41. At vero alii opus externum & in sensus inciduns ab Arte velistum volunt, ex sententia Aristotelis; qui multis in locis ποιηστικὸν id significare solent.
units.tr: 41. But others, following Aristotle's opinion, want an art to be an external work falling under the senses, for he is accustomed to use poiētikon to signify this in many places.

units.la: Nos quidem cujusdam, imo plerarumque artium (etiam nostrarum) opus in sensus incurrere non diffitemur cum Aristotele: At hinc quod omne omnis artis opus in sensus incurrere debeat, aut quod ποιητικὸν opus in sensus incurrens solum modo significet, nulla omnino est consequentia.
units.tr: We indeed do not deny with Aristotle that the work of some, indeed of most arts (including our own), falls under the senses. But from this there is no consequence at all that every work of every art must fall under the senses, or that poiētikon signifies only a work falling under the senses.

units.la: 42. Quot sunt ἐντεχνίαι προπριετάτες!
units.tr: 42. How many are the primary technical relations [ἐντεχνίαι προπριετάτες]?

units.la: Duae: Usus & Abstractio. Usu quidem omnium artium ἐντεχνίαι conglutinantur; atque adeo ars prior, & praeceptum prius posteriori inservit. Verum speculatione abstrahuntur & separantur a se invicem (quemadmodum eorum ἐντεχνίαι, harum que praecepta sunt distincta) & reducitur unumquodque ad suam propriam artem.
units.tr: Two: Use and Abstraction. By use the technical elements of all the arts are cemented together, and so the prior art and precept serve the posterior. But by speculation they are abstracted and separated from one another (just as their technical elements, and the precepts of these, are distinct), and each is reduced to its own proper art.

units.la: 43. Quid prodest tam accurata operum artium ad propriam cujusque artem reductio?
units.tr: 43. What is the benefit of so exact a reduction of the works of the arts to each one's proper art?

units.la: Hujusmodi reductio naturalem rei constitutionem resolvit, claréque nobis exhibet quae sit natura ejus rei; verbi gratia, cum περιτλόμενον iSTud: Homo est fanum (in quo exemplo communis & confusus est usus distinctorum περιτλομένων, Logicae, Grammaticae, Rhetoricae, Mathematicæ, Physicæ, Theologiæ) resolvo, ita, ut in eo suum cuilibet arti tribuatur, adque eam traducatur; tum ostendo quicquid ad istius operis naturam constituendam, & à nobis cognoscendam requiritur. Quemadmodum in artium delineatione fieri consequens jam est, ut ob oculos ponamus.
units.tr: Such a reduction resolves the natural constitution of the thing and clearly shows us what the nature of that thing is. For example, when I resolve this proposition, "Man is a rational animal" (in which example the use of distinct propositions is common and confused: logical, grammatical, rhetorical, mathematical, physical, theological), so that in it each part is assigned to its own art and carried over to that art, then I show whatever is required for constituting the nature of that work and for our knowing it. As is now the consequence in the delineation of the arts, we set this before our eyes.

units.la: 44. Quomodo delineata est idea hæc ἐντετύπωσις? Delineata est non uno sed plurimis delineamentis: Non uno quippe, sed pluribus adtibus singulæ ὑπογραφαὶ absolutæ à Deo concipiuntur (ut supra quæst. 29.) & ab homine absolvuntur.
units.tr: 44. How is this idea delineated [ἐντετύπωσις]? It is delineated not by one outline but by many. For each of the absolute outlines is conceived by God not in one act but in several (as above, question 29), and is completed by man.

units.la: 45. Quibus nominibus appellantur hæc delineamenta? Quia ὑπογραφὴ suam fideliter & absque fuco repræsentant, dicuntur Axiomata fide digna: quia regunt ὑπογραφὴν insequentem, dicuntur Regulæ: quia regunt percipiendo instar edictorum Prætoriorum, dicuntur Præcepta: quia fecundùm ea, & actuum & actorum judicium & examen fit, κατηγορία five Canones: quia περὶ τῶν προβλημάτων projecta in iisdem videntur & apparent, Problemata, Theoremata.
units.tr: 45. By what names are these outlines called? Because they faithfully represent their own outline without deceit, they are called trustworthy axioms. Because they govern the outline that follows, they are called rules. Because they govern by being perceived, like the edicts of the praetor, they are called precepts. Because according to them the judgement and examination of acts and deeds is made, they are called katēgoriai or canons. Because the things projected in them appear and become visible with respect to problems [perì tōn problēmátōn], they are called problems and theorems.

units.la: 46. Quare in definitione Regulas vocare maluisti? Quia vox Regulæ de Ideæ prima effentia est, & vim artis maximè notam maximè exprimit.
units.tr: 46. Why did you prefer to call them rules in your definition? Because the word "rule" concerns the first essence of the idea, and most fully expresses the force of art.

units.la: 47. Quales debent ista Regulæ esse? Hæ regulæ cûm primitûs fuerint ac sint in Deo verissimo, justissimo, sapientissimo, non possunt non esse verissimæ, justissimæ, sapientissimæ, id est, juxta legem ... Catholicæ. Quinimo cûm certò & infallibiliter debeant regere, (quò rectè respiciunt illi qui ab arce artem dictam volunt) non ex parte saltem veræ, id est, dubiæ, multò minus injustæ aut insipientes ullâ ratione esse possunt. Hinc delineatam hanc Ideam regulis Catholicis diximus.
units.tr: 47. What sort of rules ought these to be? Since these rules were originally, and are, in the most true, most just, most wise God, they cannot but be most true, most just, most wise, that is, according to the Catholic law... Moreover, since they must rule certainly and infallibly (as those who want the art so named from the citadel rightly look for), they cannot in any way be partly true and partly doubtful, much less unjust or unwise. Hence we have called this delineated idea by Catholic rules.

units.la: 48. Quomodo igitur Verissimæ erunt regulæ?
units.tr: 48. How, then, will the rules be most true?

units.la: Si earum principia legi veritatis κατὰ πνευμα sint consona, id est, talia, ut cùm inter se axiomatice componuntur, consequens de omni antecedente verum sit. Quæ enim ἀξιώματα non de omni antecedente consequens enunciant, pro diversitate assumti antecedentis tam falsa quam vera sunt; Ac sic per se & in se neque vera, neque falsa.
units.tr: If their principles are consonant with the law of truth according to the Spirit [κατὰ πνεῦμα], that is, such that when they are combined with one another axiomatically, the consequent is true of every antecedent. For axioms which do not state a consequent that is true of every antecedent are, according to the variety of the antecedent assumed, both false and true; and thus in themselves are neither true nor false.

units.la: 49. Quid sunt principia regularum verissimarum?
units.tr: 49. What are the principles of the most true rules?

units.la: Nihil aliud sunt quàm singularia illa singularum artium.
units.tr: They are nothing other than those particular principles of the individual arts.

units.la: 50. Quomodo vocatur huiusmodi principiorum inventio?
units.tr: 50. How is the discovery of principles of this kind called?

units.la: Vocatur Intelligentia. Qui enim quod in singulis est singulare, percipit, hunc intelligentem dicere consuevimus.
units.tr: It is called intelligence. For we customarily call one who perceives what is particular in each thing an intelligent person.

units.la: 51. Quid differt hac Intelligentia in Deo & in homine?
units.tr: 51. How does this intelligence differ in God and in man?

units.la: Hæc intelligentia in Deo est Archetypa, in homine Ectypa. Quippe cum Deo ab æterno immediatè insit, nullatenus advenieus aut imprefsa, verè ut est in ipso, est principium & omnis & primi typi; se scilicet exprimens per quandam refractionem in rebus creatis & gubernatis, quæ sunt intelligentiæ humanæ typus, ex quo ea colligitur.
units.tr: In God this intelligence is archetypal; in man it is ectypal. For since it is present in God immediately from eternity, never arriving or impressed from without, it is truly as it is in him, and is the principle of every type and of the first type; expressing itself, namely, by a certain refraction in created and governed things, which are the type of human intelligence, from which it is gathered.

units.la: 52. Annon Ars hominis etiam Archetypa dicenda est, eò quòd quarundam verum & sic alicujus typi causa & principium est?
units.tr: 52. Should the art of man not also be called archetypal, since it is in a certain sense the cause and principle of some type?

units.la: Est quidem principium per imitationem, cùm tamen principium, neque primi, neque omnis typi sit, ut Intelligentia aut Ars Dei, sed ipsa, qualiscunqne fuerit, typum aliquem pro suo
units.tr: It is indeed a principle by way of imitation; yet since it is not the principle of the first type or of every type, as the intelligence or art of God is, but is itself, whatever its quality, some type of its own kind...

units.la: Principia Logicae verae ex ejus subjecti, videlicet Ri ipsamque Logicae essentiae
units.tr: The Principles of True Logic, drawn from its subject, namely the Reason, and from the essence of Logic itself

units.la: Per Logicam intuemur, quicquid Rationis sive affectionis { essentia / existentia } 1. esse in sua 2. subsistere / comparari absolute prout rem in sese indicant: Quid sit nimirum in sua non sit: ubi enim intuiti fuerimus
units.tr: Through Logic we perceive whatever belongs to Reason or to affection {essence / existence} 1. to be in its own nature, 2. to subsist / to be compared absolutely, as they show the thing in itself. That is, what a thing is, and what it is not; for once we have perceived

units.la: comparare: postquam enim contemplati sumus quid sit & non sit, comparamus jam cum aliis rebus primitivae, quas intuemur vel una aliqua simplici affectione vel essentiali vel complementali, ut vocis seu nominis rei cognatio, ad aliquid denominatio plurium simplicium Affectionum combinatione, ut est naturae rei communitas cum aliis rebus, hab consideratione videmus rem singularitas, qua consistit in sese Inventionem: Indicium; & est Dispositio, qua affectiones rerum inventas ad usum congrue & naturaliter inter se disponimus, idque vel primario, ad judicium de illis ferendum, quae sint ac proponantur secundario, ad recte judicatas memoria retinet
units.tr: compare: for after we have considered what a thing is and is not, we now compare it with other things. We perceive the thing's primitive features, either by a single simple affection, essential or complemental, such as the kinship of a word or name to something; or by the denomination of something from a combination of several simple affections, such as the community of a thing's nature with other things. By this consideration we see the singularity of the thing, by which it stands on its own: that is Invention, the discovery of its marks. And there is Disposition, by which we arrange the affections of things, once discovered, fittingly and naturally for use. This is done primarily so that we may pass judgment on them, which are or are to be proposed, and secondarily so that the memory may retain them once rightly judged.

units.la: extra Fabricam rei post absolutam aliorum omnium in natura rei contemplationem, & est simplex rei affectio, qua de ejus natura attestatio vel Clara, per se ac sua Obscura & dubiae, de
units.tr: outside the fabric of a thing, after the complete contemplation of all other things in nature. It is a simple affection of the thing, by which testimony about its nature is given, either clear, through itself and its own, or obscure and doubtful, concerning

units.la: Lines of the scan cut off on the right side.
units.tr: Lines of the scan cut off on the right side.

units.la: ationis, naturali circa Res usu, collecta; m constituentia.
units.tr: ation, gathered from the natural use of things; constituting.

units.la: s ullo modo circa ens quodcunque versatur. tia entia stentia elemento vel ornamento mus quicquid ad rei con- omnibus aliis rebus leviore emus rem non esse aliam dissensione vel graviore ferre tantum ab sui nihilo vel negatione. d res in Gradu (quantitate) & reperimus eam vel aequalem, inaequalem , vel in Natura sua (qualitate) vel similem, dissimilem lia nomina
units.tr: ...in any way concerns any being whatever ... beings ... element or ornament ... whatever pertains to the constitution of a thing ... lighter to all other things ... agreement or greater ... to bear only from its own nothing or negation. ... a thing in degree (quantity), and we find it either equal, unequal, or in its nature (quality) either similar or dissimilar ... names.

units.la: c autem integrum, esse, vel genus. contentum in suis membris, speciebus. Distributio Totius in partes: Generis in species.
units.tr: ...whole, being, or genus, contained in its members, species. Distribution of the whole into parts; of the genus into species.

units.la: : ab aliis omnibus rebus remota, propriî materiâ scilicet & forma constituti Perfecta.
units.tr: ...removed from all other things, constituted by its own proper matter and form: Perfect.

units.la: : secundariâ consideratione rem circumscripti quasi limites quoulqz pertingant Imperfecta.
units.tr: ...by a secondary consideration, the thing is bounded as if by limits, up to which it extends: Imperfect.

units.la: n extra, sursum deorsumq; & ad
units.tr: ...outside, upward, downward, and to ...

units.la: m ejus penitus quasi pervasimus
units.tr: ...of it, as if we had thoroughly penetrated ...

units.la: nus essentiae illius fines, qui vel perhibetur. accipitur. Testimonium.
units.tr: ...of that essence, which is either asserted ... is received. Testimony.

units.la: uce manifestæ, judicium (sententia) de iis statim fertur Axioma.
units.tr: ...from things manifest, a judgment (sentence) about them is at once pronounced: Axiom.

units.la: iis amplius deliberatur per discursum mentis ope cerebrae alicujus asse- ctum post talem earum dispositionem certum de iisdem judicium fer- Syllogismus. manifesta
units.tr: ...they are further deliberated by discursus of the mind, with the aid of some reasoning faculty; after such an arrangement of them, a certain judgment about them is pronounced: Syllogism.

units.la: adum juxta ordinem naturae suae debitum Methodus.
units.tr: ...according to the order of its nature, which is due: Method.

units.la: Definitio.
units.tr: Definition.

units.la: Principia Logicae
units.tr: Principles of Logic

units.la: [illegible, ~20 letters]
units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: Pars I. Logicae [?] [illegible, ~12 letters] principio habuerit; idcirco Ectypa potiùs quàm Archetypa dicitur.
units.tr: Part I of Logic [?] [illegible] has had its principle; for this reason it is called Ectypa rather than Archetypa.

units.la: 53. Quid vocas Typum, in quo omnis ars resplendet, & ex quo ab homine principia ejus, quæ Intelligentiam humanam ficiunt, colliguntur?
units.tr: 53. What do you call the Type in which all art shines forth, and from which man gathers the principles that make up human understanding?

units.la: Voco res primariò quidem à Deo creatas & gubernatas, secundariò verò ab homine similiter factas aut fictas. Hinc Græci artem τέχνην vocant, à τεύχομαι Fabrico; quia nempe fabricæ rei imprimitur, & ex ea tanquam typo suo elucet.
units.tr: I call the things primarily created and governed by God, and secondarily those similarly made or fashioned by man. Hence the Greeks call art [τέχνην], from [τεύχομαι] to fabricate, because it is impressed upon the thing fabricated and shines forth from it as from its type.

units.la: 54. Quomodo hæ res aliter appellantur?
units.tr: 54. In what other ways are these things called?

units.la: Quatenus sunt, dicuntur Ens, hoc est, si resolvas, quod est; quatenus finguntur esse, seu possibiliter, Ens fictum possibile; seu impossibiliter, Ens fictum impossibile. Quamvis id quod fingitur esse etiam Non-ens dicatur, quatenus non est verè: & quoque Ens rationis pura aut ratiocinantis, quatenus in sola ratione aut intellectu alicujus est & existit. Quemadmodum aliàs, quicquid non est, Non-ens dicitur; & si itá non sit, ut id esse plane repugnet, Non-ens negativum; si itá, ut aliquando esse possit, Non-ens potentiale; si itá, ut esse aliquando debuerit, dicitur Non-ens privativum.
units.tr: Insofar as they are, they are called Being, that is, if you resolve it, that which is; insofar as they are feigned to be, or possibly, fictive possible being; or impossibly, fictive impossible being. Although that which is feigned to be is also called non-being, insofar as it is not truly; and also being of reason pure or of the reasoner, insofar as it exists only in the reason or understanding of someone. Otherwise, whatever is not is called non-being; and if it is such that its being is plainly contradictory, negative non-being; if such that it could sometime be, potential non-being; if such that it ought at some time to have been, it is called privative non-being.

units.la: 55. Declara igitur mihi quomodo in Typo rerum artes appareant?
units.tr: 55. Then explain to me how the arts appear in the Type of things?

units.la: Typus hic, quem res ipsas aut Ens ipsum diximus esse, ex omnium artium principiis concretus est, quæ tum circa eum, tum in eo, apparent ac refulgent.
units.tr: This Type, which we have said is the things themselves or Being itself, is compounded from the principles of all the arts, which appear and shine both around it and within it.

units.la: 56. Quid circa Typum undique, & ex omni ejus parte fulget?
units.tr: 56. What shines around the Type on every side and from every part of it?

units.la: Ratio, relatio aut affectio rerum mutua, ut mediante eâ res ipsæ ad intellectum nostrum deferantur, qui quicquid percipit, non aliter quàm sub ratione aut affectione quadam percipit. Hinc differendi principia oriuntur.
units.tr: Reason, relation, or the mutual affection of things, so that through it things themselves are brought to our understanding, which perceives whatever it perceives only under some reason or affection. Hence the principles of reasoning arise.

units.la: 57. Quanam cum ratione & in ea radicaliter quoque conspiciuntur?
units.tr: 57. In what reason and in what way are these also seen radically?

units.la: Appellationes rerum seu verba tam pura quàm ornata (utpote quæ utraque à ratione seu affectione aliquâ rei desumuntur) quod mediantibus iis res ab homine ad hominem deferantur. Hinc principia loquendi & dicendi.
units.tr: The appellations of things, or words, both plain and ornate (since both are drawn from some reason or affection of the thing), by means of which things are conveyed from one man to another. Hence the principles of speaking and saying.

units.la: 58. Quid in Typo videtur?
units.tr: 58. What is seen in the Type?
