units.la: Videtur 1. Quantum; quia res omnes primò materiatæ sunt, ut sic primò statim à Deo differant & propterea quantæ. Hinc principia mensurandi: 2. Natura; quia res secundò à se invicem distinctæ, ac potissimum quidem per formam, quæ præcipuè rerum Natura est. Hinc principia naturandi. 3. Finis, qui est bonitas illa universalis, Gloria scilicet Dei, quæ in omnibus rebus spectatur, & ad quam eædem omnes spectant, ad eandem instar sagittæ alicujus directæ. Hinc principia vivendi.
units.tr: There is seen (1) Quantity, because all things are primarily materialized, and thus first of all differ from God and are therefore quantified. Hence the principles of measuring. (2) Nature, because things are secondarily distinct from one another, and chiefly through form, which is especially the nature of things. Hence the principles of natures. (3) End, which is that universal goodness, namely the glory of God, which is observed in all things and to which all of them look, like an arrow directed to a mark. Hence the principles of living.

units.la: 59. Num omnia hæc principia Typus rerum creatarum nobis referunt?
units.tr: 59. Do all these principles the Type of created things bring back to us?

units.la: Initio quidem perfectissimè referebat homini adhuc in Integritatis statu constituto facilè obvia: at postquam homo lapsus est, bonitas tum reliquarum creaturarum, quæ propter hominem vanitati & maledictioni subjectæ suat, tum ipsius hominis in cujus conscientia præcipuè elucebat, (erat enim cordi ipsius inscripta) itá obscurata & obtenebrata est, ut non nisi paucissima & corruptiffima quidem ejus principia supersint nobis ibidem conspicienda.
units.tr: At the beginning it certainly brought them back most perfectly to man, still established in the state of integrity, and easily at hand. But after man fell, the goodness both of the remaining creatures, which are subjected to vanity and curse because of man, and of man himself, in whose conscience it chiefly shone forth (for it was written upon his heart), was so obscured and darkened that only a very few and very corrupt traces of its principles remain for us to behold there.

units.la: 60. Unde igitur Bonitatis principia percipere possumus?
units.tr: 60. Whence, then, can we perceive the principles of goodness?

units.la: Benignè Deus ac sapienter hæc nobis consuluit, dum deficiente ea in parte rerum typo Scripturas substituit; in quibus bonitatis, hoc est, honestatis, pietatis, justi & æqui principia, ultra vestigia illa, quæ in rebus ipsis seu creaturis adumbrantur, perfectissimè revelavit, ut bene vivendo ad Deum adscendamus.
units.tr: God, kindly and wisely, has provided these for us, when, the Type of things failing in that part, He substituted the Scriptures; in which He has most perfectly revealed the principles of goodness, that is, of honesty, piety, and of what is just and fair, beyond those traces that are shadowed forth in the things themselves or in creatures, so that by living well we may ascend to God.

units.la: 61. An etiam reliqua principia præter bonitatem Typus rerum obscurè referant?
units.tr: 61. Does the Type of things also refer obscurely to the remaining principles besides goodness?

units.la: Imo perfectè adhuc satis refert, sed non nisi indefessâ Analysi interiora ejus penetrantibus, intimè videnda & colligenda. Quin nec bonitatis principia in sacris scripturis revelata, quis intimè cognoverit & perspecta habebit, ni factâ etiam ipsarum Scripturarum Analysi dexterâ, apertis simul à Spiritu Sancto oculis mentis ejus; quod postremum hic quidem summè & absolutè necessarium; ibi verò, ad reliqua nimirum indaganda non parùm utile.
units.tr: Indeed it still refers to them quite fully enough, but only to those who penetrate its inner parts by tireless analysis, so that they must be seen and gathered inwardly. Nor will anyone know the principles of goodness revealed in the Holy Scriptures intimately, nor have them thoroughly perceived, unless he also makes a skilful analysis of the Scriptures themselves, with the eyes of his mind opened at the same time by the Holy Spirit. The latter is here absolutely and supremely necessary, whereas there it is, of course, not a little useful for investigating the remaining things.

units.la: 62. Quomodo fit Sacræ Scripturæ ac rerum Analysis?
units.tr: 62. How is the analysis of Holy Scripture and of things carried out?

units.la: Iflius perficitur Logicæ præceptis ritè applicatis: Harum inchoatur sensu, omnia sive in se, sive ratione effectorum apparentia & sensibilia, sine alterius interventu, apprehendente; Provehitur observatione, sensu percepta, eorumque inchoatam cognitionem sedulò notante & retinente; Perficitur inductione, sensu sæpe percepta, & observatione retentâ inter se ferìò comparante, & certi quid inde concludente; Confirmatur experientiâ, conclusâ diu multúmque volvente, revolvente, ac quâvis occasione datâ accuratè ac solidè examinante.
units.tr: The analysis of the former is completed by rightly applying the precepts of Logic. The analysis of the latter begins with sense: the apprehending of all things, whether in themselves or as effects, that appear and are perceptible, without the intervention of anything else. It advances by observation: what has been perceived by the senses, carefully noting and retaining the incipient knowledge of them. It is completed by induction: frequently perceived by the senses and retained by observation, comparing them with one another, and concluding something certain from them. It is confirmed by experience: rolling over and over and turning again what has been concluded, and examining it carefully and soundly on every occasion given.

units.la: 63. Num quatuor ista adminicula sunt necessaria ad colligenda animum verissima principia?
units.tr: 63. Are these four aids necessary for gathering the most true principles into the mind?

units.la: Omnino. Eorum enim tantus neglectus in singulis disciplinis (maximè in Physicis) primus & præcipuus fons est errorum, defectuum ac controversiarum studiis literarum in eo statu permanentibus nunquam finiendarum.
units.tr: Entirely so. Such neglect of these principles in the individual disciplines (chiefly in physics) is the first and principal source of errors, defects and controversies, which in studies of letters that remain in that condition are never brought to an end.

units.la: 64. Non ergo doctorum sententiis innixi possumus in afferendis dogmatis Philosophicis? Possumus; verum caute.
units.tr: 64. Therefore can we not rely on the opinions of teachers in setting out philosophical doctrines? We can, but with caution.

units.la: 1. Scriptis sive veterum sive recentiorum quorundam vix accuratis non itaque superstitiose inniti amur, ut sacrilegium ab iis recedendo nos commissuros credamus: quamvis manifesta per alios ante dictis mediis exquisita, & explorata veritas id summe suadeat. Quaerentes quippe prius quid, quam quid dixerit.
units.tr: 1. We should not lean superstitiously on the writings of the ancients or of certain recent authors, which are scarcely accurate, as if we would commit sacrilege by departing from them. Truth, sought out and tested by the means mentioned before and made plain by others, strongly urges this. We should ask first what is said, before who said it.

units.la: 2. Veterum hoc in genere scriptis licet suus debeatur respectus & honos; scripta tamen recentiorum (caeteris paribus) iis prae-non-postponi debent: Cum oculi plus videant, quam oculus, dies diem doceat, cogitationes secundae primis sint meliores.
units.tr: 2. Some respect and honour is due to the writings of the ancients in this matter. Nevertheless, the writings of recent authors (other things being equal) ought to be preferred to them, since eyes see more than a single eye, day teaches day, and second thoughts are better than first ones.

units.la: 3. Ethnicorum etiam scripta aestimari debent: At magis Christianorum, ut quorum oculos divina gratia magis aperros esse magis confitentur est: Psal. 119. v. 51, 52.
units.tr: 3. The writings of the heathen too ought to be valued, but those of Christians more, since they confess that divine grace has opened their eyes more widely: Ps. 119. vv. 51, 52.

units.la: 4. Inter ipsos Christianos cujuscunque aetatis Scriptores discrimen faciendum est. Nempe opera per cacoethes scribendi & philautiam enixa non tanti sunt habenda, quanti ex sincero veritatis amore ab amicis Dei probitate vitae se demonstrantibus profecta.
units.tr: 4. A distinction must be made among Christian writers of any age. Works produced by an itch for writing and self-love are not to be held in as much esteem as those that come from a sincere love of truth and from friends of God who show their uprightness of life.

units.la: 65. Quid vero censes de auctoritatibus hominum adhibendis in rebus Theologicis & Juridicis?
units.tr: 65. What then do you think about using the authority of men in theological and juridical matters?

units.la: In Theologia, Jurisprudentia, si ullorum sententiis adhaerere liceat in re valde obscura, Christianorum potius quam Ethnicorum, piorum quam impiorum etiam plurimorum adhaerendum est. Sic tamen, ullius mancipia nescimus, sed veritatem ducentem, & ab hallucinationibus superiorum nostrorum (ut qui homines ad imaginem Adami etiam geniti sunt) avocantem liberé & animosé sequamur, omnia probantes, tes, quod bonum est retinentes: amicus Plato, amicus Aristoteles, at magis amica Veritas.
units.tr: In theology and jurisprudence, if it is permitted to adhere to the opinions of anyone in a very obscure matter, we should adhere to Christians rather than heathens, and to the pious rather than the impious, and indeed to very many of them. Yet we must not become the slaves of anyone. We should follow freely and boldly the truth that leads us, and calls us back from the delusions of our superiors (who, as men, were also born in the image of Adam), "proving all things, holding fast that which is good" (1 Thess. 5:21). Plato is a friend, Aristotle is a friend, but truth is a greater friend.

units.la: 66. Hastenus audivi regularum verissimarum constitutionem: dic porro, quomodo fiunt regulæ justissimæ.
units.tr: 66. So far I have heard the constitution of the most true rules; now tell me how the most just rules are made.

units.la: Principia verissima si juxta legem Justitiæ ⁠ὡς τὸ αὐτὸ homogeneè seu essentialiter componantur, fiunt regulæ Justissimæ. Ubi enim unicuique suum tribuitur, ibi justissimè agitur.
units.tr: If the most true principles are composed homogeneously, or essentially, according to the law of Justice [ὡς τὸ αὐτὸ, as the same], they become the most just rules. For where each thing is given its due, there justice is done most fully.

units.la: 67. Quomodo vocatur Judicium horum principiorum ita compositorum?
units.tr: 67. What is the judgement of these principles so composed called?

units.la: Vocatur Scientia. Causas quippe & essentias rerum nosse (quod tum ante compositionem in componente requiritur, & ex compositione in verè eam cognoscente exsugit) prima, verissimáque Scientia est.
units.tr: It is called Science. For to know the causes and essences of things (which is required in the one composing before the composition, and is drawn from the composition in the one who truly knows it) is the first and truest science.

units.la: 68. Quis tandem est usus Legis Sapientiæ ⁠Ϙολὺ σοφίαν ⁠ʕ
units.tr: 68. What then is the use of the Law of Wisdom?

units.la: Principia verissima homogeneè composita si juxta Legem Sapientiæ adæquatè & reciprocè diducantur, fient regulæ sapientissimæ. Quæ enim justo nec latius, nec angustiùs extenduntur, ea sapientissimè extensa merito dicuntur. Talium etiam principiorum judicium, est Sapientia.
units.tr: If the principles composed homogeneously are unfolded adequately and reciprocally according to the Law of Wisdom, they become the most wise rules. For those rules which are extended neither more broadly nor more narrowly than the just requires are rightly said to be most wisely extended. The judgement of such principles is also Wisdom.

units.la: 69. Num hic, quem indicasti, usus trium istarum Legum est, ut in omnibus & singulis disciplinis, quoad omnes & singulas regulas essentiales observari debeant?
units.tr: 69. Is this, which you have indicated, the use of these three laws: that in every discipline, and with regard to each and every essential rule, they ought to be observed?

units.la: Omnino debent, at non conjunctim, verùm disjunctim, itâ ut Lex posterior includat priorem; sed non vicissim. Alioquin nisi in his regulæ congruant, vitiosæ jure habentur. Commorationes autem, seu commentationes ex parte quidem ab ipsis eximuntur, at nonnisi justis de causis, & paucissimæ sunt admittendæ.
units.tr: They ought indeed to be observed, but not jointly; rather, severally, so that the later law includes the earlier, but not conversely. Otherwise, unless the rules agree in these respects, they are rightly held to be faulty. Digressions, or commentaries, are indeed in part exempted from these, but only for just reasons, and very few are to be admitted.

units.la: 70. Quid denique requiritur ad Ideam hanc, ut artis naturam perfectè compleat?
units.tr: 70. What finally is required for this Idea to perfectly complete the nature of an art?

units.la: Si idea hæc αὐτοτελὲς regulis hisce catholicis constans methodicè delineetur juxta Legem Methodi, Prudentia inde exurgit, quæ Intelligentiæ, Scientiæ, Sapientiæ, adjuncta, completam reddit Artem.
units.tr: If this idea, self-complete [αὐτοτελὲς], consisting of these universal rules, is methodically outlined according to the Law of Method, Prudence arises from it. Joined to Understanding, Science and Wisdom, it makes the Art complete.

units.la: 71. Num hæc est genuina horum vulgò duplorum mentis Habituum natura & sic turpigo?
units.tr: 71. Is this the genuine nature of these two habits of mind, commonly so called, and is this how they are constituted?

units.la: Hæc certè, ut videlicet (ceu ex dictis apparuit) itâ necessariò in omni Arte colligentur, quòd eorum qualicunque deficiente, ipsa Idea deficiat, & ad artis completionem justam non deveniat.
units.tr: Certainly this is so: as has appeared from what was said, they must necessarily be gathered together in every Art, so that if any one of them is lacking, the Idea itself is lacking and does not attain to the proper completion of the art.

units.la: 72. Annon ergò vitiosè quidam Disciplinæ alicui sive scientiam, sive Sapientiam, sive Prudentiam detrahunt?
units.tr: 72. Do some people therefore wrongly deprive a discipline of science, or wisdom, or prudence?

units.la: Illi catenus eam laude suâ spoliant, ut sive heterogenea, sive inadæquata, sive amethodica ejus præcepta tacitè & per interpretationem dicant.
units.tr: They strip it of its praise to the extent that, tacitly and by interpretation, they declare its precepts to be either heterogeneous, or inadequate, or unmethodical.

units.la: 73. Hucusque Naturam & Essentiam seu Definitionem Artis servestigavimus. Nunc mihi edissere, quid sentis de ejus Divisione in Theoreticam & Practicam?
units.tr: 73. So far we have investigated the nature, essence or definition of art. Now explain to me what you think of its division into theoretical and practical.

units.la: Ista Divisio vulgò quidem recepta, verùm multis modis vitiosa, ideóque repudianda est.
units.tr: This division, though commonly accepted, is faulty in many ways and therefore must be rejected.

units.la: 74. Quomodo hoc probas?
units.tr: 74. How do you prove this?

units.la: Quia est sine ulla vera differentia, itâ ut unum ejus membrum necessariò includat alterum. Non enim est contemplatio quæ non sit praxis & habeat suum opus, nec actio in genere talis est quæ omnem contemplationem excludat. Imò non est omnino ars, quam ipsi vocant Theoreticam, quæ suam non habeat Praxim, ad quam, in Theoria non acquiescens, ex natura sua tendat: nec quam vocat Practicam, quæ discatur sine Theoria, aut in cujus Praxi auditor ejus, postquam eam perdidicit, acquiescere non potest si velit, ac sæpe etiam æquiverit; quod suprà (quæst. 40) inculcavimus.
units.tr: Because there is no true difference in it, so that one member necessarily includes the other. For there is no contemplation which is not also practice and has its own work, nor is there any action in general which excludes all contemplation. Indeed there is no art, which they call theoretical, that does not have its own practice, to which it tends by its nature and in which it does not rest in theory. Nor is there any art called practical that can be learned without theory, or in whose practice a learner, once he has learned it, cannot rest if he wishes, and often has in fact rested; which we urged above (question 40).

units.la: 75. Quid dicis de Mathesi, Metaphysica & Physica: annon sunt hæ pure Theoreticæ?
units.tr: 75. What do you say of mathematics, metaphysics and physics: are not these purely theoretical?

units.la: De Mathesi in confessio est, eam esse satis practicam. De Metaphysica constat etiam, eam habere Praxin, quoad generales terminos, qui ad Logicam reducuntur. Absque quo licet fit, de principalissima ejus parte quæ agit de Deo, sic omnino concludendum est, eam esse vanam & inutilem, nisi ad praxin dirigatur; imò talem, quæ Apostolo teste Rom. 1. v. 21. gravissimè à Deo puniatur. De Physica tandem praxi & agricolarum & hortulanorum & opificum, & aliorum quamplurimorum opera per imitationem naturata abundè testantur.
units.tr: As for mathematics, it is agreed that it is quite practical. Of metaphysics it is also established that it has a practice, as regards its general terms, which are reduced to Logic. Apart from this, as to its most principal part, which treats of God, we must conclude entirely that it is vain and useless unless it is directed to practice; indeed, it is such that, as the Apostle witnesses, it is most severely punished by God (Rom. 1. v. 21). As for physics, finally, the practice of farmers, gardeners, craftsmen and very many others, through the imitation of nature, abundantly bears witness.

units.la: 76. Quânam aliâ ratione probas non esse veram Artis divisionem in Theoreticam & Practicam?
units.tr: 76. By what other reason do you prove that the division of art into theoretical and practical is not a true one?

units.la: Id ex eo patet, quòd omnibus bene perspectis pars Philosophiæ Practica proprie nulla sit. Quodcunque enim in Ethicis, Oeconomicis, Politicis reperitur catholicum veritatis præceptum, id ad Theologiam proprie spectat, quam tamen à Philosophia, sic divisa, sive ab artibus suis, dictæ Divisionis patroni procul remotam volunt; de quo pluribus in progressu (quæst 88. 94.) Quod autem de interpretatione vocis Praxeos afferunt, suprà (quæst. 24.) refutatum est.
units.tr: This is clear from the fact that, when everything is well examined, there is properly no practical part of philosophy. For whatever universal precept of truth is found in ethics, economics and politics properly belongs to theology. Yet the advocates of the said division wish theology to be far removed from philosophy so divided, or from its arts; on this more will be said in the course of the work (questions 88, 94). And what they say about the interpretation of the word praxis has been refuted above (question 24).

units.la: 77. Atqui ista Artis divisio ab Aristot. & aliis antiquis Philosophis approbata fuit?
units.tr: 77. But was this division of the arts approved by Aristotle and the other ancient philosophers?

units.la: Qui exemplo & authoritate Ethnicorum excusare sese hic voluerint, eos accusatos quisque judiciosus merito sentiet. Quòd enim illi in tenebris versantes, scintillas honestatis in se reperitas, aut aliunde haustas, variis doctrinis variè immisceuerint, id non illis, sed Imitatoribus eorum, ex Scripturis Spiritu Sancto cooperante rectius edoctis, vitio verti potest.
units.tr: Those who wish to excuse themselves here by the example and authority of the heathen will, as every judicious reader will rightly feel, be accused. For when they, living in darkness, mingled various doctrines with sparks of honesty found in themselves or drawn from elsewhere, the fault lies not with them but with their imitators, who were more rightly taught from the Scriptures with the Holy Spirit's cooperation.

units.la: 78. Quænam ergo verior est Artis Divisio? Ea talis esse potest; quâ ars alia generalis; alia specialis vocatur; & utraque primaria seu magis, vel secundaria seu minùs talis est.
units.tr: 78. What division of the arts, then, is the truer? It may be this: one art is called general, another special, and each is either primary or more so, or secondary or less so.

units.la: 79. Unde constat hujus Divisionis veritas? Cum enim & Objectum (quæst. 35. 36. 37.) & Finis (ibid.) & Principia (quæst. 56. 57. 58.) artis talia sunt, ut patet ex dictis; ipsam talem esse quis dubitabit, qui ex objecto fine & principiis dividendam eam novit.
units.tr: 79. How is the truth of this division established? Since the object (questions 35, 36, 37), the end (ibid.), and the principles (questions 56, 57, 58) of an art are such as is clear from what has been said, who will doubt that the division itself is such, when he knows that it must be made according to object, end and principles?

units.la: 80. Quæ est primaria vel magis generalis ars? Logica, à λογίζεσθαι fine suo sic vocata, Inventionem (scilicet & Dispositionem rationum præcisè sumtarum adæquatè tradens, Categoriis equidem, at non aliis quam quibus singula argumentorum paria vestiuntur, genuinè & ex natura sua, instructa; Fallaciarum verò appendicem omnino repudians. Sed hæc & similia alia controversa seorsim descepabimus.
units.tr: 80. Which art is the primary or most general? Logic, so called from λογίζεσθαι [to reckon] after its end. It sets out invention and arrangement of arguments taken precisely, and it does so fully and genuinely, drawing from their own nature the categories, but not any others than those with which the individual pairs of arguments are clothed. It entirely rejects the appendix of fallacies. But these and similar other controversial matters we shall discuss separately.

units.la: 81. Quæ sunt secundaria & minùs generales artes? Duæ sunt: nimirum, Grammatica, à γράφω scribo, dicitur Synecdochice, quia voce tam scripta quam prolata ad sensa animi prodenda uti consuevimus; quæ ad Latinam linguam, quæ peregrinarum addiscendarum prima est, vernaculo cujusvis gentis idiomate tradenda: Ad reliquas verò addiscendas in Latinum sermonem (sed specialibus & extraordinariis solis mutatis) transferenda, ut eo citius ac feliciùs discantur.
units.tr: 81. Which are the secondary and less general arts? There are two: namely, Grammar, called from γράφω [to write], since we customarily use speech, both written and spoken, to express the thoughts of the mind. Grammar is to be taught in the vernacular of each nation, for the Latin tongue, which is the first to be learned of foreign tongues. The rest are to be taught in Latin, though only special and extraordinary matters are to be changed, so that they may be learned more quickly and successfully.

units.la: 82. An Grammatica æquè ac aliarum artium præcepta tribus legibus artium possint conformari? Hujus præcepta, quia linguis ut subjecto suo aptanda, quæ pluribus irregularitatibus scatent, quia item ancillans tantum est cum socia sua (Rhetorica) idcirco usque adeo regularia & legibus artium reliquarum accommodata tradi nequeunt.
units.tr: 82. Can the precepts of Grammar be brought into conformity with the three laws of the arts, as those of the other arts are? Its precepts cannot be handed down so regularly, or adapted to the laws of the other arts, because they are fitted to their subject, languages, which abound in many irregularities; and because it is merely a handmaid to its companion, Rhetoric.

units.la: 83. Quanam est altera minus generalis Ars s Rhetorica, à ῥέω, quod ab ἐρέω dico venit. In qua præcepta Logicæ inventionis & dispositionis heterogeneè repetuntur.
units.tr: 83. What is the other, less general art? Rhetoric, from ῥέω [to flow], which comes from ἐρέω [to speak]. In it the precepts of logical invention and arrangement are repeated in a mixed way.

units.la: 84. Quare hæ tres Artes dicuntur generales, & Logica quidem magis, Grammatica vero & Rhetorica minus tales s Ob rationes astibus earum etiam sic distis applicatas. Nempe, quia cum specialibus artibus sic concrescunt, ut eæ sine arte & astu disserendi cognosci; sine arte & astu loquendi communicari; sine arte & astu dicendi commodè communicari nequeant.
units.tr: 84. Why are these three arts called general, Logic more so, but Grammar and Rhetoric less so? Because they are applied to the arts of the same kind, called by their own skill. Namely, because they grow together with the special arts in such a way that these cannot be known without the art and skill of reasoning, cannot be communicated without the art and skill of speaking, and cannot be communicated conveniently without the art and skill of expressing.

units.la: 85 Quæ sunt speciales artes s Tres sunt; nempe, Mathesis à μαθεῖν disco, quia hanc præ reliquis pueri olim discebant, explorandæ eorum indolis & ingenii ergò.
units.tr: 85. What are the special arts? There are three, namely, Mathematics, from μαθεῖν [to learn], because boys in former times learned it before the rest, for the sake of testing their disposition and talent.

units.la: 86. Quot sunt partes Mathefeos s Hujus vulgò partem aliam abstractam à Physica (ut est Geometria & Arithmetica) aliam concretam cum illa (ut Cosmographia, Astronomia, Geographia, Optica, Musica,) constituunt: At omnibus bene pensitatis pars ejus concreta nulla est. Nam quicquid in ea tradi solet, aut ad artem Physicam pertinet, aut ad nullam plane artem, sed ad hujus vel illius artis usum & facultatem; de qua postea.
units.tr: 86. How many parts does Mathematics have? Commonly one part is set apart from Physics, abstract (as are Geometry and Arithmetic), and another concrete, joined with it (such as Cosmography, Astronomy, Geography, Optics, Music). But when everything is weighed properly, it has no concrete part. For whatever is usually taught in it belongs either to the art of Physics, or to no art at all, but to the use and faculty of this or that art; of which later.

units.la: In Geometria tamen plerorúmque horum, quæ dicuntur concretæ Mathefeos, principia sunt tradenda; inutiles demonstrationes resecandæ, & Praxis præcipuè spectanda.
units.tr: Yet in Geometry the principles of most of those things called the concrete part of Mathematics must be taught; useless demonstrations are to be pruned away, and practice especially regarded.

units.la: 87. Quæ est secunda ars specialis s Physica, à φύσις natura, quam totam, omnis Entis naturalis, tam in genere, quam in specie, naturam, ac sic ipsorum etiam spirituum, quoad catholicè potest, comprehendere & perlequi debet.
units.tr: 87. What is the second special art? Physics, from φύσις [nature]. It ought to comprehend and survey, as far as it can universally, the whole nature of every natural being, both in general and in particular, and so also of the spirits themselves.

units.la: 88 Quae est tertia specialis ars?
units.tr: 88. What is the third special art?

units.la: Theologia, θεολογία, ab eloquiis Dei, dicitur, utpote ex quibus singulariter ratio. ne principiorum colligitur. Unde & per Doctrinam potius, quam per Artem definitur. Hæc sola doctrina catholicam, tam de Deo clarius in scriptura, obscuriùs in natura, nobis ad benevivendum revelato, quàm de virtutibus sive honestate, justo & æquo, perfectissimè & homogeneè tradit.
units.tr: Theology, θεολογία [theologia], is called from the oracles of God [ab eloquiis Dei], since from them alone the reasons of its principles are gathered. Hence it is defined as a doctrine rather than as an art. This doctrine alone delivers most perfectly and homogeneously the universal teaching, both about God, more clearly in Scripture and more obscurely in nature, which has been revealed to us for living well, and about virtues or honesty, the just and the equitable.

units.la: 89. Quomodo Sex illarum artium comprehensionem vocas?
units.tr: 89. What do you call the comprehension of these six arts?

units.la: Harum omnium artium pro subordinatione finium circularis comprehensio, quæ res emanant ab Ente primo, & ad ipsum denuo redeunt Encyclopædia nominatur, & earundem omnium conjunctio Pansophia est.
units.tr: The circular comprehension of all these arts, by the subordination of their ends, from which things emanate from the first Being and return again to it, is called the Encyclopaedia; and the union of all of them is Pansophia.

units.la: 90. Num ergo his sex artibus συνδέσμος artium κυκλῳ seu Encyclopædia arqs Pansophia perfectissimè completur, non plures nec pauciores sapiens
units.tr: 90. Is the bond of the arts, the circle, or Encyclopaedia, or Pansophia, most perfectly completed by these six arts, neither more nor fewer, as a wise man would say?

units.la: Omnino: Hæ enim totum hominem perficiunt; Logica intellectum seu rationem; Theologia, voluntatem & affectus; Grammatica, Rhetorica, Mathesis & Physica loco motivam ejus ad amussim dirigentibus. Deinde id etiam, tum per remotionem earum artium, quas alii ipsi includere frustra sategerunt; tum per objectorum ac legum artium verarum sufficientem enumerationem & attributionem, quibuscunque rectè conveniunt, manifestum fecimus, & in progressu faciemus, (quæst. 94, 97, 101. ad 134.)
units.tr: Certainly. For these arts perfect the whole man: Logic perfects the intellect or reason; Theology the will and affections; Grammar, Rhetoric, Mathematics and Physics, which direct its movement exactly. We have shown this further, both by removing those arts which others have vainly tried to include, and by a sufficient enumeration and attribution of the objects and laws of true arts, to which they rightly belong; and we shall show it further in the course of the work (questions 94, 97, 101 to 134).

units.la: Quod verò attinet ad quatuor illa Præcognita, quæ, præter undecim Scientias quinque Prudentias (ut vocant) & septem Artes, Encyclopædiæ quidam intrudunt: Archilogia certè & Hexilogia, ceu ex dictis palàm est, Technologiæ includuntur; ac sic cum ea circulo excluduntur: Didactica autem ad totum circulum, necnon ad hanc ipsam Technologiam, id est, Technometriam, tanquam externum adjunctum se habet; & sic ab ipso circulo tanto longius removetur.
units.tr: As for those four Preliminaries which some introduce into the Encyclopaedia, besides eleven Sciences, five Prudences (as they call them) and seven Arts: Archilogy and Hexilogy, as is plain from what has been said, are certainly included in Technology, and so are excluded together with it from the circle. Didactics, however, stands related to the whole circle, and also to this same Technology, that is, Technometry, as an external adjunct; and so it is removed much further from the circle itself.

units.la: 91. Quænam inter illas sex artes de primatu certant?
units.tr: 91. Which of those six arts contend for primacy?

units.la: Theologia, Logica, Grammatica.
units.tr: Theology, Logic, Grammar.

units.la: Theologia dignitate omnes reliquas antecedit; Logica generali necessitate; Pro nostro tamen proficiendi modo Grammatica eisdem partes primas præripit, dignitate aliàs (ut ante monuimus) ultima futura.
units.tr: Theology surpasses all the rest in dignity; Logic in general necessity; yet for our manner of making progress Grammar seizes the first place for itself, though otherwise it will be last in dignity, as we warned before.

units.la: 92. Num omnibus illis artibus unus aliquis ex hominibus omnimodo potest uti?
units.tr: 92. Can any one man use all those arts in every way?

units.la: Neutiquam; atque ideo earum usus, & utendi ab Artificibus acquisitæ facultates, in hoc vel illo vitæ genere, circa hoc vel illud objectum, ad hunc vel illum finem, utiles in humana vita certè sunt. Quæ improprie & Metonymicè Artes, absolutè & eminenter Facultates solent appellari.
units.tr: By no means; and therefore their uses, and the faculties acquired by artisans through using them, are certainly useful in human life, in this or that kind of life, concerning this or that object, for this or that end. These are commonly called Arts improperly and by metonymy, and Faculties absolutely and eminently.

units.la: 93. Quomodo artium Facultates distinguuntur. Hæ ex Artificum suorum, necnon objecti & finis dignitate majore vel minore, in digniores & minus dignas distinguuntur. Digniores iterum in superiores & inferiorem; quatenus scilicet illæ hanc adhuc aliquo antecellunt modo.
units.tr: 93. How are the faculties of the arts distinguished? They are distinguished, according to the greater or lesser dignity of their artisans, and also of their object and end, into more worthy and less worthy. The more worthy are again divided into superior and inferior, insofar as the former surpass the latter in some way.

units.la: 94. Quanam sunt Facultates Superiores?
units.tr: 94. What are the superior faculties?

units.la: Sunt tres: Theologica, Juridica, Medica; Theologica Ecclesiæ Christi colligendæ & ædificandæ; Juridica juridicendo & justitiæ administrandæ juxta Catholica principia justi & æqui in Theologia tradita (unde novam ac distinctam aliquam artem à Theologia non constituit) stituit) Medica sanitati hominum tuendæ ac restituendæ, apta nata; principia medendi catholica non tradens, sed pro occasione data ex arte Physica (in suo esse completo, non existere defectivo considerata) repetens, atque adeo nullam novam ac distinctam ab ea artem constituens.
units.tr: There are three: Theological, Juridical, Medical. The Theological faculty is for gathering and building up the Church of Christ. The Juridical faculty is for judging and administering justice according to the catholic principles of the just and the equitable delivered in Theology; hence it does not constitute any new and distinct art from Theology. The Medical faculty is fitted by nature to preserve and restore the health of men; it does not deliver catholic principles of healing, but, as the occasion arises, draws them from the art of Physics (considered in its complete being, not in its defective existence), and so it constitutes no new and distinct art from it.

units.la: 95. Quomodo vocatur Facultas inferior?
units.tr: 95. What is the lower faculty called?

units.la: Vocatur Philosophica, quia est τῷ τῆς σοφίας φίλων, hoc est, eorum qui ad ipsam Sophiam, quæ proprie est facultatum superiorum, nondum pervenerunt, sed pervenire amant; atque ideo hac inferiori facultate acquisita viam sibi quasi sternunt.
units.tr: It is called Philosophical, because it belongs to those who are lovers of wisdom [τῷ τῆς σοφίας φίλων], that is, of those who have not yet reached Sophia herself, which properly belongs to the higher faculties, but who love to reach her. By acquiring this lower faculty they thus pave a way for themselves.

units.la: 96. Quot sunt partes Facultatis Philosophicæ?
units.tr: 96. How many parts does the Philosophical Faculty have?

units.la: Hujus numerantur septem quasi partes, aut partiales facultates: Oratoria, sub qua Poësis qualiscunque; Cosmographia, in qua Astronomia & Geographia seu utriusque globi usus; Optica, Musica, Architectonica; Oeconomica, Politica.
units.tr: Seven parts, or partial faculties, are counted: Oratory, under which falls poetry of whatever kind; Cosmography, which includes Astronomy and Geography, or the use of both globes; Optics; Music; Architecture; Economics; and Politics.

units.la: 97. Annon Facultates ista pro attributis proprie dictis vulgo habentur?
units.tr: 97. Are these faculties not commonly held to be attributes properly so called?

units.la: Itá quidem, sed imperitè: Oratoria enim & Poetica sunt facultates Rhetoricæ artis; Cosmographia cum Astronomia & Geographia, itemque Optica, Musica, & Architectonica sunt diversorum membrorum artis Physicæ facultates: Oeconomica denique & Politica sunt facultates Theologiæ: ac propterea nullas novas distinctaque artes constituunt.
units.tr: They are so held, but wrongly. For Oratory and Poetics are faculties of the art of Rhetoric; Cosmography with Astronomy and Geography, likewise Optics, Music and Architecture, are faculties of different parts of the art of Physics; and finally Economics and Politics are faculties of Theology. Therefore they do not constitute new and distinct arts.

units.la: 98. Quæ sunt Facultates minus dignæ?
units.tr: 98. Which are the less worthy faculties?

units.la: Eæ sunt variæ; nimirum præter quatuor illas modò memoratas, omnes reliquæ ab hominibus & acquisitæ & exercitæ.
units.tr: These are various: namely, apart from the four just mentioned, all the rest, which are both acquired and practised by human beings.

units.la: 99. Quare sic vocantur?
units.tr: 99. Why are they so called?

units.la: Nulla siquidem harum ordinariè Artificem suum in tanto, quanto illæ, dignitatis faltigio collocat, experientiâ teste.
units.tr: Since, as experience bears witness, none of these ordinarily places its practitioner on so high a pinnacle of dignity as those do.

units.la: 100. Quomodo hæ Facultates aliàs appellantur Sordidæ, quæstuosæ, illiberales, mechanicæ, manuales, & eminenter effectrices vocantur, quatenus scilicet pleræque earum communiter fordidi quæstus causâ ab artificibus suis, quodam quasi illiberali & servili modo acquiruntur, (unde esse potest quod apud veteres servis & peregrinis propriæ sunt habitæ) atqs machinis manu potiùs quàm ingenio efficiendis exercentur. In se tamen non ulla earum ingenuo ac libero homine indigna esse, multo minùs sordere debet, aut cujusquam corpus, animúmque & mentem ad usus & actiones virtutis inutilem reddere poterit, cùm ad societatem tam privatam quàm publicam promovendam maximè necessariæ sint.
units.tr: 100. Why are these faculties also called sordid, mercenary, illiberal, mechanical, manual, and especially productive? Namely, because most of them are commonly acquired by their practitioners for the sake of base gain, in a certain illiberal and servile manner (whence it may be that among the ancients they were regarded as proper to slaves and foreigners), and are practised with machines and hands rather than with the intellect. Yet in themselves none of them is unworthy of a free-born man, and much less should any of them be thought base, nor can any of them render the body, soul and mind useless for the uses and actions of virtue, since they are most necessary for promoting society, both private and public.

units.la: 101. Ex quibus igitur artibus, & quomodo oriuntur hæ facultates?
units.tr: 101. From which arts, then, and how do these faculties arise?

units.la: Sunt MathesEos ope ferè omnes Physicæ, pauce Grammaticæ Effectæ, non eatenus tantùm, quatenus hanc illâmve, ut exemplar sit, imitantur, operâ MathesEos, quo minùs imitando aberrent, Numerum, Mensuram & Pondus, id est, proportionem partium justam, in qua esse formæ est, examinantes: sed etiam quatenus materiam operum suorum, & objectum exercitii principale ab alterutra earum mutuantur. Ideóque secundum istas artes commodissimè sic distingui debent facultates Mechanicæ, quòd aliæ sunt Grammaticæ circa res Grammaticas; aliæ Physicæ circa res Physicas versantes.
units.tr: By means of mathematics almost all are Physical, and a few are Grammatical and Productive. This is not only in so far as they imitate this or that model, using mathematics so that they may err less in imitating, by examining number, measure and weight, that is, the just proportion of the parts, in which the form of a thing consists; but also in so far as they borrow the material of their works and their principal object of practice from one or other of these arts. Therefore, according to these arts, the mechanical faculties ought to be distinguished most conveniently in this way: some are Grammatical, concerned with grammatical matters; others Physical, concerned with physical matters.

units.la: 102. Quanam sunt facultates circa res Grammaticas versantes?
units.tr: 102. What are the faculties concerned with grammatical matters?

units.la: Eæ sunt circa literas, figuris; vel consuetis eleganter, sive calamo, sive typo; vel insuetis, seu properè & compendiosè, seu tectè & occultè, exprimendas.
units.tr: They are concerned with letters and characters, to be expressed either in the customary way, gracefully, with a pen or with type; or in unusual ways, either swiftly and concisely, or secretly and covertly.

units.la: 103. Qua facultas versatur circa literas consuetis sueris figuris eleganter calamo exprimendas?
units.tr: 103. Which faculty is concerned with letters in the customary characters, to be expressed gracefully with the pen?

units.la: Calligraphia; ad quam simul referendae sunt facultates scribarum varii generis, nempe, Excerptorum, Amanuensium, & similium tanquam certae quaedam ejus propagines.
units.tr: Calligraphy; to which are to be referred at the same time the faculties of scribes of various kinds, namely, of copyists of excerpts, amanuenses and the like, as certain offshoots of it.

units.la: 104. Quae versatur circa easdem iisdem figuris consuetis typo exprimendas?
units.tr: 104. Which is concerned with the same letters in the same customary characters, to be expressed by type?

units.la: Typographia; ex qua oritur Libraria typis descripta; aut compingens, quod Bibliopegorum; aut fervans suis thecis recondita, quod Bibliothecariorum officium.
units.tr: Typography; from which arises the book trade, which is practised in printed form; or binding, which is the office of bookbinders; or keeping books stored away in their cases, which is the office of librarians.

units.la: 105. Quae facultas versatur circa literas inconsuetis figuris propere & compendiose exprimendas?
units.tr: 105. Which faculty is concerned with letters in unusual characters, to be expressed swiftly and concisely?

units.la: Brachygraphia, novos & scriptu faciles characteres, pro literis, tum singulis separatim, tum pluribus, voces crebro seu terminantibus, seu integrantibus conjunctim, confingens, conficiisve utens.
units.tr: Brachygraphy, which devises or uses new characters easy to write, for letters, both single and several together, for words frequently recurring, whether ending or integrating, joined together.

units.la: 106. Quae versatur circa easdem iisdem figuris occulte & tecte exprimendas?
units.tr: 106. Which is concerned with the same letters in the same characters, to be expressed secretly and covertly?

units.la: Ciphraria, qua duo pluresve ex compacto clam inter se scriptis ea communicant, quae nulli alii lecta volunt. Huc pertinet Characteristica, hoc ipsum literis etiam consuetis praestans.
units.tr: Cryptography, by which two or more people, by agreement, write secretly to one another so as to communicate things they wish to be read by no one else. To this belongs Characteristica, which accomplishes this even with ordinary letters.

units.la: 107. Annon sunt alia facultates Grammaticae?
units.tr: 107. Are there other grammatical faculties?

units.la: Omnibus hisce recensitis facultatibus Grammaticis subordinatur & inservit Chartopoeia & Pergamenopoeia, chartas & membranas, quibus hodie literae inscribuntur, eis praeparans.
units.tr: Papermaking and parchment-making are subordinate to, and serve, all the grammatical faculties just enumerated, preparing for them the paper and parchment on which letters are today inscribed.

units.la: 108. Quanam sunt facultates circa Physicam materiam versantes?
units.tr: 108. What are the faculties concerned with physical matter?

units.la: Eae sunt circa vel Elementa, Aerem, Ignem, Aquam, Terram; vel Elementata. Et utrinque iterum vel circa ea ipsa, vel circa eorum qualitates.
units.tr: They are concerned either with the Elements, air, fire, water, earth; or with elemented things. And on either side they are again concerned either with the elements themselves or with their qualities.

units.la: 109. Quae versatur circa Ignem?
units.tr: 109. Which faculty is concerned with fire?

units.la: In genere Pyrotechnia: in specie circa eum artificiosè eliciendum, fingendum, confervandum, aliis commodè projiciendum, communicandum, &c. versantur omnes illæ facultates bellicæ, Bombardarum, Pulveris tormentarii, Pyrobolidum, quatenus aliquo horum, aliove modo circa ignem occupantur. Item facultates Luminum artifi ialium; necnon hypocaustorum, fumorum, & similium igni confervando commodéque communicando intervientium.
units.tr: In general, Pyrotechnics. In particular, all those military faculties are concerned with fire, artfully eliciting, shaping, preserving, conveniently projecting and communicating it, etc.: cannons, gunpowder, fireworks, in so far as they are occupied with fire by one or other of these means. Likewise the faculties of artificial lights, and of hypocausts, smokes and the like, which intervene in preserving and conveniently communicating fire.

units.la: 110. Quæ versantur circa Aërem?
units.tr: 110. Which are concerned with air?

units.la: Aërotechnia, circa eum concitandum, placandum, inficiendum, purgandum, & follibus spirandum versans.
units.tr: Aerotechnics, which is concerned with stirring up, calming, tainting, purifying air, and with breathing it by bellows.

units.la: 111. Quænam sunt facultates circa Aquam versantes?
units.tr: 111. What faculties are concerned with water?

units.la: In genere est Hydrographia: in specie sunt, circa eam in suis repagulis per aggeres extructos continendam; per aquæ receptaria ex loco in locum derivandam, sursum agendam, Hydrogogia; innandam, Natatoria; ad tempus quasi inhabitandam, Urinatoria; navigandam, Navigatoria, unde Nautica, quæ, quatenus velis ventos colligit, etiam circa aërem occupata est.
units.tr: In general, Hydrography. In particular, there are: those concerned with containing water in its channels by means of constructed embankments; Hydrogogy, which concerns deriving water from place to place through water-conduits, and raising it upward; Swimming; Diving, which concerns living in the water for a time, as it were; and Navigation, which concerns sailing on water. Hence Nautical science, which, in so far as it gathers winds with sails, is also occupied with air.

units.la: 112. Quæ facultates versentur circa Terram?
units.tr: 112. Which faculties are concerned with earth?

units.la: Eæ sunt vel circa terram arandam, Aratoria; vel occandam, Occatoria; vel fodiendam, Fossoria; aut aliis modis præparandam, &c.
units.tr: They are concerned either with ploughing the earth, Ploughing; or harrowing it, Harrowing; or digging it, Digging; or preparing it in other ways, etc.

units.la: 113. Quæ facultates versentur circa Elementorum qualitates?
units.tr: 113. Which faculties are concerned with the qualities of the elements?

units.la: Eæ sunt circa Qualitates vel primas; ut Calefactoria, Frigefactoria, Siccatoria, Humectatoria, vel secundas, Solidatoria, Liquefactoria, Attenuatoria, Condensatoria, Rarefactoria, &c.
units.tr: They are concerned with the qualities, either primary, such as heating, cooling, drying, moistening; or secondary, such as solidifying, liquefying, attenuating, condensing, rarefying, etc.

units.la: 114. Quæ versantur circa qualitates Elementatorum?
units.tr: 114. Which are concerned with the qualities of elemented things?

units.la: Eæ sunt vel circa colorem, vel sonum, vel saporem, vel odorem.
units.tr: They are concerned either with colour, or sound, or taste, or smell.

units.la: 115. Quæ sunt circa colorem § Pictoria, Tinctoria, Fucatoria. 116. Quæ sunt circa sonum?
units.tr: 115. Which arts are concerned with colour? §Pictoria, Tinctoria, Fucatoria.

units.la: Circa eum solùm est Musica instrumentalis, quæ pro Instrumentorum varietate, varia; nempe Chelycina, Psaltricina, Organicina, Lyricina, Cytharædicina, Panduricina, Nablicina, Tibicina, Tympanicina, Cornicina, Utricularicina, &c. circa sonum cum saltatione est Saltatoria.
units.tr: Concerned with sound alone is instrumental music, which varies with the variety of instruments: namely Chelycina, Psaltricina, Organicina, Lyricina, Cytharædicina, Panduricina, Nablicina, Tibicina, Tympanicina, Cornicina, Utricularicina, etc. Concerned with sound together with dancing is Saltatoria.

units.la: 117. Quæ sunt circa saporem & odorem §
units.tr: 117. Which arts are concerned with taste and smell? §

units.la: Circa Saporem est Culinaria, præcipuè verò Cupedinaria: circa Odorem sunt Suffitoria, & Coronaria, quatenus herbas ad fragrantiam compingit.
units.tr: Concerned with taste are cookery and, above all, confectionery. Concerned with smell are the makers of incense and of garlands, insofar as they put herbs together for fragrance.

units.la: 118. Quæ facultates versantur circa Elementata §
units.tr: 118. Which arts are concerned with the elements and what is compounded from them? §

units.la: Ex sunt vel circa inanimata, Lapides, Metalla, Mineralia mediæ naturæ; vel circa animata.
units.tr: They are concerned either with inanimate things, stones, metals, and minerals of intermediate nature, or with animate things.

units.la: 119. Quæ versantur circa Lapides?
units.tr: 119. Which arts are concerned with stones?

units.la: Circa eos sunt, vel pretiosos, Gemmaria, Quadrigaria, Gemmiculatoria; vel viliores, eòsque naturales, Effoditoria, Liquefactoria, & instar æris Fusoria, Dolatoria seu Lapicidæ, & Cœlatoria; tum cotiles, Lateraria, Figulina, Calcearia seu Cœmentaria, Muraria.
units.tr: Concerned with them are either those dealing with precious stones: gem-cutters, quarriers of gems, and makers of small jewels; or those dealing with cheaper stones, and these in their natural state: diggers, smelters, and, like bronze-founders, casters, stonemasons or hewers, and carvers; then those dealing with rough stones: brickmakers, potters, lime-burners or mortar-makers, and wallers.

units.la: 120. Quæ versantur circa Metalla §
units.tr: 120. Which arts are concerned with metals? §

units.la: Ex in genere sunt Metallariorum in fodinis laborantium, ut Fossaria, Lavatoria, Exploratoria, Discretoria, Excoctoria, Politoria. In specie autem sunt vel circa aurum & argentum, ut, Bractearia, Aurifabrilis, in qua Inauratoria, Cœlatoria, Annularia, Monetaria; vel circa æs, ut Fusoria æramentorum, Campanarum, Tormentorum, &c. vel circa ferrum, ut Ferrifabrilis qualiscunque, Claustraria, Machæropolia, Calcarialia, Loricaria, Armamentaria, Cultraria, Falcearia, &c. vel circa stannum, Stannaria; vel denique circa Plumbum, Plumbaria; vel circa cuprum, Cupraria.
units.tr: In general, there are the metal-workers who labour in the mines, such as diggers, washers, assayers, separators, smelters, and polishers. In particular, some are concerned with gold and silver: goldbeaters, and the goldsmith's trade, within which are gilders, carvers, ring-makers, and moneyers; others with bronze: founders of utensils, bells, cannon, etc.; others with iron: any kind of ironsmith, locksmiths, sword-makers, spur-makers, armourers, the makers of weapons, knife-makers, scythe-makers, etc.; others with tin: tinsmiths; finally others with lead: plumbers; or with copper: coppersmiths.

units.la: 121. Quae versantur circa mineralia media natura §
units.tr: 121. Which arts are concerned with minerals of intermediate nature? §

units.la: Eae sunt vel circa salem excoquendum, praeparandum, Salaria; vel circa argillam, Figulina; vel circa vitrum, Vitraria.
units.tr: They are concerned either with salt to be boiled down and prepared: saltworkers; or with clay: potters; or with glass: glassmakers.

units.la: 122. Quae versantur circa res animatas §
units.tr: 122. Which arts are concerned with living things? §

units.la: Eae sunt vel circa plantas, vel animalia, tam rationalia, nempe homines, quàm bruta. Circa plantas iterum sunt, circa herbas, fruges, vites, arbores, ligna.
units.tr: They are concerned either with plants or with animals, both rational, namely humans, and brute beasts. Concerned again with plants are those dealing with herbs, grain, vines, trees, and wood.

units.la: 123. Quae versantur circa herbas §
units.tr: 123. Which arts are concerned with herbs? §

units.la: Hortularia, Herbaria, Aromataria, & aliqua ratione facultas Coqui & Coronarii.
units.tr: Gardeners, herbalists, spice-dealers, and, in a certain sense, the cook's and the garland-maker's art.

units.la: 124. Quae versantur circa fruges §
units.tr: 124. Which arts are concerned with grain? §

units.la: Circa eas, seminandas & in spica curandas, Agricultura; metendas, Messoria; colligandas, Colligatoria; triturandas Trituratoria; subigendas, Molitoria seu Molendinaria, Pistoria, Cerevisiaria.
units.tr: Concerned with it, in sowing it and tending it in the ear, is agriculture; in reaping it, the reaping trade; in binding it, the binding trade; in threshing it, the threshing trade; in grinding it, the milling trade, or the miller's work, the baker's trade, and the brewer's trade.

units.la: 125. Quae versantur circa Vites §
units.tr: 125. Which arts are concerned with vines? §

units.la: Vinitoria, Putatoria, Pampinatoria, Vindemiatoria. Torculatoria.
units.tr: Wine-making, pruning, stripping of leaves, and grape-harvesting; wine-pressing.

units.la: 126. Quae versantur circa Arbores & Ligna?
units.tr: 126. Which arts are concerned with trees and wood?

units.la: Frondatoria, Infitoria, Pomaria quoad fructus; & omnis generis Lignifabrilis, Arcularia, Naupegica, Tornatoria, Victoria, Statuaria, Arcuaria, Carbonaria quoad lignum. Plantis annumerentur etiam cannabis & linum. Huc ergo pertinent quaevis circa illam hoc ve occupationes, nimirum Restiaria, Linearia, & similes.
units.tr: Lopping, grafting, and fruit-growing as regards fruit; and every kind of woodworking: cabinet-making, shipbuilding, turning, carving, statue-making, arch-building, and charcoal-burning as regards the wood. Hemp and flax are also counted among plants. To this therefore belong any occupations of this kind concerned with them, namely ropemaking, linen-weaving, and similar trades.

units.la: 127. Quae facultates versantur circa animalia bruta.
units.tr: 127. What arts are concerned with brute animals?

units.la: Hae sunt vel circa aerea, Aves; vel aquatica, Pisces; vel terrestria, Pecudes, Feras.
units.tr: These are concerned either with airborne creatures, birds; or with aquatic creatures, fish; or with terrestrial creatures, cattle and wild beasts.

units.la: 128. Quae versantur circa Aves § Eæ sunt circa eas vel capiendas, Aucupiaria varii generis, ut Anataria, Columbaria; vel servandas & condocefaciendas.
units.tr: 128. Which arts are concerned with birds? § They are concerned with them either in catching them, the fowling of various kinds, such as duck-catching and dove-catching; or in keeping them and training them.

units.la: 129. Quæ versatur circa Piscès?
units.tr: 129. Which art is concerned with fish?

units.la: Facultas vel piscandi fundis, sagenis, tragulâ, nassis, sportis & scapulis, hamis, aliisve instrumentis; quæ uno nomine dicitur Piscatoria: vel servandi in piscinis aut Vivariis, unde Piscinaria, Vivaria.
units.tr: The skill of fishing with nets, seine-nets, trawls, traps, baskets, and hooks, or with other instruments, which in one word is called Piscatoria; or of keeping them in fishponds or fish-tanks, whence Piscinaria and Vivaria.

units.la: 130. Quæ versantur circa pecudes?
units.tr: 130. Which arts are concerned with cattle?

units.la: Circa eas iunt vel pascendas, Bubolica, Subolica, Opilionaria, Capraria; vel saginandas & mactandas, Saginaria, Lanionia; vel aliis usibus applicandas, quà jumenta; scilicet Equisonia, Agasonia, Mulionia, Aurigaria. Huc pertinent etiam facultates, quæ his subservdiunt, ut jumenta vel necessariis instruant, nimirum Ephippiaria, Scytomiaria, Clitellaria; vel morbida jumenta curent, ut Veterinaria, &c.
units.tr: Concerned with them are either the pasturing of them: herding oxen, herding swine, shepherding, and goatherding; or the fattening and slaughtering of them: butchery and meat-trade; or applying them to other uses, as beasts of burden: horse-tending, stable-keeping, mule-driving, and carting. To this also belong the arts which serve these, such as those which equip the beasts with what they need: saddlery, harness-making, and pack-saddle making; or those which treat sick beasts: veterinary medicine, etc.

units.la: 131. Quæ versantur circa Feras?
units.tr: 131. Which arts are concerned with wild beasts?

units.la: Circa eas canibus, plagis, tendiculis, sepimentis capiendas, inque vivariis servandas est facultas Venatoria.
units.tr: Concerned with catching them with dogs, snares, nets, and enclosures, and with keeping them in tanks, is the art of hunting.

units.la: 132. Quænam versantur circa Hominem?
units.tr: 132. Which arts are concerned with man?

units.la: Eæ sunt circa corpus ejus vel vestiendum, vel ad agilitatem exercendum, vel sanandum, vel purgandum.
units.tr: They are concerned with his body, either for clothing it, or for exercising it for agility, or for healing it, or for cleansing it.

units.la: 133. Quæ versantur circa corpus hominis ve- stiendum?
units.tr: 133. Which arts are concerned with clothing the human body?

units.la: Quoad caput, Pileonaria; quoad manus, Chirothecaria; quoad pedes, Sutoria, tam Calcearia, quàm Crepidaria, cui Cerdo etiam coria subministrat, unde Coriaria. Quoad reliquum corpus sunt facultas Pellionaria, quæ apud nos & in locis quibusdam etiam caput & manus hominum vestit; facultas Sartoria & aliæ omnes, quæ materias corpori præparant, ut Sericaria, GloGlobularia, Lanificiaria qualiscunque, Difcretoria, Concretoria seu Textoria, Fullonia, & aliæ hujus generis.
units.tr: As regards the head, hat-making; as regards the hands, glove-making; as regards the feet, shoemaking, both the shoemaker's trade and the sandal-maker's, to which the tanner also supplies hides, whence the leather-worker. As regards the rest of the body there is the furrier's trade, which among us and in certain places also clothes the head and hands of people; the tailor's trade, and all the others which prepare materials for the body: silk-working, the making of beads, any kind of wool-working, carding, combing or weaving, fulling, and others of this kind.

units.la: 134. Quænam sunt reliquæ facultates circa cor- pus hominis ¶
units.tr: 134. What other arts are concerned with the human body? ¶

units.la: Circa illud ad agilitatem exercendum sunt, Luctatoria, Pugilatoria, Cursoria, Pilaria, Saltatoria, &c. Circa fanandum sunt, Chirurgica, Latomica, Unguenraria, Pharmaceutica, quæ Medicinæ subministrant. Circa purgandum denique sunt, Balneatoria, Barbitonsoria.
units.tr: Concerned with exercising it for agility are wrestling, boxing, running, ball-playing, dancing, etc. Concerned with healing are surgery, stone-cutting, the ointment-making, and pharmacy, which supply medicine. Concerned finally with cleansing are bath-keeping and barbering.

units.la: 135. Sunt ne præterea aliæ facultates ex arti- bus ortæ ¶
units.tr: 135. Are there, besides these, other faculties arising from the arts?

units.la: Hæ sunt pleræque saltem, si non omnes facultates, quas homines ex artibus suo modo, alii videlicet cognitis & applicatis artium præceptis, alii traditione scriptâ, alii traditione per manus artificum, sibi acquirunt.
units.tr: These are at least most, if not all, of the faculties which men acquire for themselves from the arts in their own way: some by knowledge and application of the precepts of the arts, others by written tradition, others by tradition through the hands of craftsmen.

units.la: 136. Postquam aliquam harum facultatum quis- quam sibi acquisivit, quo jure illâ utitur ¶
units.tr: 136. After someone has acquired one of these faculties, by what right does he use it?

units.la: Ne quis aliquâ harum pollentem inaniter se diceret, multúmque sæpe nocere possit cum prodesse debeat, prudenter constitutum est, ut præcipuarum facultatum Candidatos quidam in iis eximii probent, approbent, & approbatos testimonio suo, vel Gradu Academico (si sint Facultatis dignioris Candidati) vel Tyrocinio aliquo (si facultatis Mechanicæ erit) ornent.
units.tr: So that no one may vainly call himself proficient in any of them, and so that he may not harm many people when he ought to help them, it has been wisely arranged that certain examiners test the candidates in the chief faculties, approve those who are found fit, and honour the approved either with their testimony, or with an academic degree (if they are candidates of the higher faculty), or with some apprenticeship (if the faculty is mechanical).

units.la: 137. Quinam sunt Gradus illi Academici, quibus facultatis dignioris Candidati ornari solent ¶
units.tr: 137. What are those academic degrees with which candidates of the higher faculties are customarily honoured?

units.la: Nimirum, qui facultate Philosophica, examine & tentamine prævio Excellens repertus est, Artium liberalium Magister, aut Philosophiæ Doctor; qui Medicâ, Doctor Medicinæ; qui Juridicâ Doctor Jurisprudentiæ; qui Theologicâ, Theologiæ Doctor, ab ejusdem Facultatis Doctoribus in Academia aliqua præsidentibus, solenniter pronunciatur, atque illam facultatem ubique locorum occasione data exercendi plena potestate, ab ejusdem Academiae supremo Magistratu, donatur,
units.tr: Namely, one who is found excellent in the philosophical faculty, after a prior examination and trial, is solemnly pronounced Master of Liberal Arts or Doctor of Philosophy; one in medicine, Doctor of Medicine; one in law, Doctor of Jurisprudence; one in theology, Doctor of Theology, by the doctors of that same faculty presiding in some university; and he is granted, by the supreme magistrate of that same university, full power to exercise that faculty anywhere, when the occasion arises.

units.la: 138. Quod est illud Tyrocinium, quo facultatis minus dignioris Candidati ornantur ?
units.tr: 138. What is that apprenticeship with which candidates of the less honoured faculties are honoured?

units.la: Tyrocinium illud, (ein Meisterstuck) in facultate unaquaque opificum, lingua Germanica Meisterstuck appellatur; Aliis autem artificibus alio nomine venit secundum nationes suas & ordines proprios: quod singulis fere Germaniae opificibus faciendum; qui in privilegiato opificio liberè versari, nec à tribulibus ejus facultatis multari & impediri volunt.
units.tr: That apprenticeship (ein Meisterstück, a masterpiece) in each craft is called in the German language Meisterstück; other craftsmen have another name for it according to their nations and their own guilds. This is to be done by almost every craftsman in Germany who wishes to work freely in his privileged trade and not to be fined or hindered by the fellow members of that craft.

units.tr: Thesis I.

units.la: ARs est regularis institutio rei, in existentia & operatione, ad suum finem.
units.tr: Art is the regular arrangement of a thing, in its existence and operation, toward its end.

units.la: 2. Ad eam requiruntur, Intellectus principiorum, quæ ad eam rem sunt necessaria ; eorundem inter fe conjungendorum Scientia; aliorum ex aliis deductio per Sapientiam ; omnium ad usum applicandorum Prudentia, & executio ipsa, quæ proprie dicitur Ars ; & fi ab alio alteri tradatur, Doctrina vel Disciplina.
units.tr: 2. For it are required: understanding of the principles necessary for the thing; knowledge of these principles joined together with one another; the deduction of some from others by wisdom; the application of all to use by prudence; and the execution itself, which is properly called art. If it is handed on from one person to another, it is called teaching or discipline.

units.la: 3. Ars hæc quadruplicem habet exiftentiam, 1. In Idea, 2. In actu exercito, 3. In opere ejus effecto, & 4. In pictura vel imagine ejus expressa.
units.tr: 3. This art has a fourfold existence: (1) in idea; (2) in exercised action; (3) in its effected work; and (4) in its picture or expressed image.

units.la: 4. Idea artis primo, perfecte & eminenter, est in ente Primo, à quo reliqua emanant, id est, in Deo. Est etiam ex parte in rationali creatura, cui Deus & oculum dedit ad eam percipiendam, & eam ipsam pro suo modulo communicavit, per sensum, observationem, & experientiam.
units.tr: 4. The idea of art exists first, perfectly and eminently, in the First Being, from whom all other things emanate, that is, in God. It also exists in part in the rational creature, to whom God gave an eye to perceive it and communicated it, according to its measure, through sense, observation and experience.

units.la: 5. Actus primo est in rerum creatione, & creatarum directione ad finem, sed Ars est etiam in hominis actionibus per imitationem.
units.tr: 5. The act exists first in the creation of things and their direction to their end. But art is also in human actions, through imitation.

units.la: 6 Opus primo est in rebus ipsis creatis, & earum statu, sed est etiam in rebus ab homine simili modo concinnatis, hujus est usus conjunctus & speculatio separata
units.tr: 6. The work exists first in created things themselves and their state, but it is also in things fashioned by man in a similar way. Of these, the use is joined to them and the speculation is separate.

units.la: 7 Imago est effigies illa, quae vel in rationalis creaturae speculatione existit, vel in ejus delineatione, quae ponitur in libro, constans ex praeceptis perfectissimis ad certae rei συντεταξιαν concinnatis.
units.tr: 7. The image is that likeness which exists either in the contemplation of the rational creature or in its outline, set down in a book, consisting of the most perfect precepts arranged for the ordering [συντεταξία] of a certain matter.

units.la: 8 Haec imago ex rei artificio colligitur per Analyfin ejus in principia prima. in Ideam postea convertitur a creatura rationali, quae etiam similem structuram exprimit quae Genesis nominatur.
units.tr: 8. This image is gathered from the workmanship of the thing by its analysis into first principles. It is afterwards turned into an idea by the rational creature, which also expresses a similar structure, called Genesis.

units.la: 9 Ars prout in Deo est, licet virtute multiplex, actu tamen simplex est & una; sed in rebus creatis, quae omnes sunt concretae (quasi ex refractione radiorum) multiplex evadit: & in illa multiplicitate a rationis oculo recipitur, & exercetur.
units.tr: 9. Art, as it is in God, though manifold in power, is nevertheless simple and one in act. But in created things, which are all concrete (as if from the refraction of rays), it becomes manifold; and in that multiplicity it is received and exercised by the eye of reason.

units.la: 10 In rebus creatis distinctè considerantur ens ipsum reale, & ratio ejus: inter quae priorem ex natura locum habet ratio, quae non solum vim habet in re jam facta dirigenda, & in omni ejus parte: sed etiam in ejus effectione, & in suimet ipsius reflexione.
units.tr: 10. In created things the real being itself and its reason are considered distinctly. Of these, reason has the prior place by nature, since it has power not only to direct the thing already made, and every part of it, but also in its making and in its own reflection.

units.la: 11 Rationis Ars est Dialectica.
units.tr: 11. The art of reason is Dialectic.

units.la: 12 Hujus artis imago ab homine recepta duas alias artes secundarias & sibi ancillantes parit, quibus ab homine ad hominem deferri possit, Grammaticam & Rhetoricam.
units.tr: 12. The image of this art, received by man, gives birth to two other secondary arts that serve it, by which it can be conveyed from man to man: Grammar and Rhetoric.

units.la: 13 Istæ tres artes sunt generales, quia in omnibus rebus & artibus usum habent
units.tr: 13. These three arts are general, because they have use in all things and arts.

units.la: 14 In ipso Ente reali est, limitatio per quantitatem, actus per naturam, & finis quæ bonitas appellatur.
units.tr: 14. In the real being itself there is limitation through quantity, action through nature, and an end which is called goodness.

units.la: 15 Quantitatis artes sunt Mathematice, Naturæ Physica, Bonitatis Theologia: sed Theologiæ non nisi tenuia principia in rebus creatis insunt, aut ex ipsis colligi possunt: quoniam irrationales creaturæ, quamvis Deum versus tendunt, qui est primum & summum bonum, ad ipsum tamen non attingunt. Homini igitur doctrina seu revelatione divina opus est, ultra vestigia illa bonitatis quæ in creaturis adumbrantur, ut bene vivendo ad Deum ascendat.
units.tr: 15. The arts of quantity are mathematics, of nature physics, and of goodness theology. But to theology only slight principles inhere in created things, or can be gathered from them, since irrational creatures, although they tend toward God, who is the first and highest good, nevertheless do not attain to him. Man therefore needs teaching or divine revelation, beyond those traces of goodness which are shadowed forth in creatures, so that by living well he may ascend to God.

units.la: 16 Harum omnium artium comprehensio, qua res emanant ab ente primo, & ad ipsum denuo redeunt, Encyclopædia nominatur: cujus catenæ circularis primus annulus est Dialectica, & ultimus Theologia.
units.tr: 16. The comprehension of all these arts, by which things emanate from the First Being and return to it again, is called Encyclopaedia; of this circular chain the first link is Dialectic, and the last Theology.

units.la: THESIS I.
units.tr: THESIS I.

units.la: DIalectica est ars bene differendi; id est, rationes rerum bene discernendi, & inter se componendi.
units.tr: Dialectic is the art of reasoning well, that is, of discerning the reasons of things well and of arranging them among themselves.

units.la: 2. Rationes rerum vel simpliciter & seorsim considerantur, vel conjunctim & compositæ: Dialecticæ igitur duæ sunt partes, Inventio & Disposicio.
units.tr: 2. The reasons of things are considered either simply and separately, or jointly and in combination. Dialectic therefore has two parts: Invention and Disposition.

units.la: 3. Inventio est prima pars hujus artis qua simplices rationes investigantur: singulæ enim inventionis regulæ sunt totidem viæ ac normæ rationes rerum discernendi.
units.tr: 3. Invention is the first part of this art, by which simple reasons are investigated. For each rule of invention is, as it were, a way and a norm for discerning the reasons of things.

units.la: 4. Simplices istæ rationes dicuntur argumenta, quia affectum vel aptitudinem habent ad aliud aliquid arguendum: id est respectu, vel habitudine feruntur ad aliud aliquid: & eum à quo recte intelliguntur ad cogitationem illius secum ferunt.
units.tr: 4. These simple reasons are called arguments, because they have an affection or aptitude for arguing something else: that is, they are directed by a relation or connection to something else, and they carry with them, for anyone who rightly understands them, the thought of that other thing.

units.la: 5. Argumentorum alia in se vim habent arguendi, quia sunt in ipso artificio rei; atque adeo possunt ab artifice beneficio artis investigari; aliud vero non habet in se,sed ad se assumit aliunde,quia est extra artificium rei & ab artifice commodato tenetur:illud argumenti genus dicitur Artificiale, hoc autem Inartificiale.
units.tr: 5. Of arguments, some have in themselves the power of arguing, because they lie in the very nature of the thing, and so can be discovered by the skilled person through the help of art. Others do not have this in themselves but take it from elsewhere, because they lie outside the nature of the thing and are held on loan from the skilled person. The first kind of argument is called artificial, the second inartificial.

units.la: 6. Inter Argumenta artificialia, quaedam primitus afficiuntur ad arguendum, id est, vim illam a se & primario habent, quae dicuntur Prima: quaedam vero secundario afficiuntur ad arguendum, & Orta vocantur, quae vim illam quam habent referunt acceptam ad priora.
units.tr: 6. Among artificial arguments, some are primarily disposed to argue, that is, they have that power from themselves and in the first place; these are called primary. Others are disposed to argue only secondarily, and are called derived; they refer the power they have back to earlier arguments from which they received it.

units.la: 7. Argumenta prima vel simpliciter & absolute inter se referuntur & inde dicuntur Simplicia seu Absoluta: vel ita referuntur, ut aestimatio inde utriusque fiat, atque ideo Comparata dicuntur.
units.tr: 7. Primary arguments are related to one another either simply and absolutely, and so are called simple or absolute; or they are related in such a way that each is valued by means of the other, and so they are called compared.

units.la: 8. Argumentorum simplicium affectio, vel est amica quaedam consensio, qualis intercedere solet ubi una res ad alterius essentiam, effectionem, vel complementum aliquod concurrit; vel est disjungens quaedam vel dissocians alienatio; illa sunt Consentanea, haec Dissentanea.
units.tr: 8. The relation of simple arguments is either a kind of friendly agreement, such as usually obtains when one thing contributes to the essence, production, or some completion of another; or it is a kind of separating and dissociating estrangement. The former are consentaneous, the latter dissentaneous.

units.la: 9. Consentaneorum alia arctius inter se conspirant, ita ut alterum ab altero pendeat quoad essentiam, effectionem & cognitionem, atque ideo dicuntur absoluta vel simpliciter Consentanea, Causa nempe & Effectum; alia vero levius & remissius ita ut nulla intercedat communio essentiæ, sed unum requiratur tantum ad alterius bene esse; & inde vocantur modo quodam Consentanea, Subjectum (scil. & Adjunctum.
units.tr: 9. Of consentaneous arguments, some are joined more closely, so that one depends on the other in essence, production and knowledge; and these are called absolute or simply consentaneous, namely cause and effect. Others are joined more loosely and slackly, so that there is no shared essence, but only one thing is required for the well-being of the other; and these are called consentaneous in a certain manner: subject (and adjunct.

units.la: 10 Causa est quæ vim adfert ad rei productionem, à causa enim vis proficiscitur, quæ conferens aliquid ad rei constitutionem, in re ipsa hæret: res igitur suum esse habet à causa per hanc vim; unde sequitur, accuratam scientiam rei, non posse haberi nisi per cognitionem illarum causarum, quarum vires ac virtutes concurrunt ad eam constituendam: atque hæc eadem est ratio, cur inter omnia Argumenta primum locum teneat: quia (scil. affectionem primam & primariam habet in artificio rei.
units.tr: 10. A cause is that which brings force to the production of a thing. For force proceeds from the cause, and, contributing something to the constitution of the thing, it clings to the thing itself. A thing therefore has its being from the cause through this force. From this it follows that an accurate knowledge of a thing cannot be had except through knowledge of those causes whose powers and virtues concur to constitute it. And this is the reason why cause holds the first place among all arguments: because (namely) it has the first and primary affection in the artifice of the thing.

units.la: 11 Causarum quædam simul incipiunt operari ad existentiam rei, ut Efficiens & Materia: quædam ab iis inceptum peragunt, & rem ipsam simul existere faciunt, ut Forma & Finis.
units.tr: 11. Some causes begin to work together toward the existence of a thing, such as the efficient and the matter. Others carry on what these have begun and bring the thing itself into existence together, such as the form and the end.

units.la: 12 Efficiens est causa à qua motus vel operatio ad rem incipit & perficitur. Quoniam vero originem præbet ipsi motui, non potest in motu vel re motu facta contineri; sed vim suam tantum iis commodare solet.
units.tr: 12. The efficient is the cause from which motion or operation begins and is completed in the thing. But since it provides the origin of the motion itself, it cannot be contained within the motion or within the thing moved; it usually only lends its power to them.

units.la: 13 Quamvis Causarum in reali earum natura tot sint species quot sunt earum exempla, nulla tamen ex quatuor Causis veras habet species, in Logica notione; nihil enim inter illas & rem intercedit, sed proximæ causæ sunt rei existentis. Efficiens ergo non habet veras species.
units.tr: 13. Although, in the real nature of things, there are as many kinds of causes as there are examples of them, none of the four causes has true kinds in the logical sense. For nothing intervenes between them and the thing, but they are the proximate causes of the existing thing. Therefore the efficient has no true kinds.

units.la: 14 Distinguitur nihilominus modi​s quibusdam; quorum illa est natura, ut eidem efficienti possint convenire: cjus tamen affectionem in arguendo effecto, multum variant.
units.tr: 14. Nevertheless it is distinguished by certain modes. The nature of these is that they can belong to the same efficient, although they vary greatly in how they bear on the reasoning about the effect.

units.la: 15 Varii modi efficientis apparent, aut in effecto, quod vel facit ut sit, & dicitur procreans, vel ut porro sit, & confervans nominatur; aut in adjunctis, quia sine vel aliis ejusdem generis & ordinis rem quampiam dat effectam, & dicitur folitaria, vel cum aliis, quæ dici potest concausa, ubi vel pares vires adferunt, vel una præit, & dicitur principalis, aliæ subsequuntur, & adjuvantes vel ministræ dicuntur; quorum etiam peculiaris quidam modus est in instrumentis quæ infimum locum habent, quia non tam sua vi agunt ad effectum producendum, quam se præbent ut aliena vi agantur, aut deniq; in ipsa vi seu facultate agendi, quæ vel est interna, unde efficiens dicitur per se, sive natura tura five consilio agat: vel externa, unde efficiens dicitur per accidens; five neccffitat coacta agat, five fortuna errans à suo scopo
units.tr: 15. The various modes of the efficient appear either in relation to the effect, which either brings it about that the effect exists, and is called creating, or sustains it so that it continues to exist, and is named conserving; or in relation to adjuncts. An efficient is called solitary when it produces some thing without others of the same kind and order; it is called concausal when it acts together with others, which happens either when they contribute equal powers, or when one goes first and is called principal, while the others follow and are called helping or ministering. A special mode of this is found in instruments, which hold the lowest place, because they do not act so much by their own power to produce the effect as present themselves to be moved by another's power. Finally, the modes arise from the power or faculty of acting itself, which is either internal, whence the efficient is called through itself, whether it acts by nature or by counsel; or external, whence the efficient is called through accident, whether it acts under compelled necessity, or wanders from its aim by chance.

units.la: 16. Materia paratur, disponitur, atque adeo movetur ab efficiente ad formam recipiendam: proxime igitur ad efficientem accedit ordine, & formam antecedit ut principium potentiæ & perpessionis. Ingreditur in rem non vi sola sed & realitate sua partem essentiæ constituens interne: est igitur causa ex qua res est, tanquam ex fundamento ædificii totius, quæ etiam formæ existentia & actio solent corroborari.
