Nullis modis distinguitur, quia licet vis variis modis ab efficiente conferri potest, ipsa tamen realitas materiæ non nisi realiter communicatur. Distinctio illa in primam & secundam, &c. non est Logica, quia variam notionem rationem realitatis materiæ non continet, sed ordinem solum materialium principiorum quæ non sunt hujus disciplinæ.
units.tr: 16. Matter is prepared and disposed, and so is moved by the efficient to receive the form. It is therefore nearest to the efficient in order, and precedes the form as the principle of potency and passivity. It enters into the thing not by power alone but also by its own reality, constituting a part of the essence inwardly. It is therefore the cause out of which the thing is, as the foundation of a whole building; and the existence and action of the form are usually strengthened by it. It is not divided into any modes, because although power can be conferred on it by the efficient in various ways, the reality of the matter itself is communicated only really. That division into first and second, etc., is not logical, because it does not contain a varied notion of the reality of matter, but only the order of the material principles, which do not belong to this discipline.

units.la: 17 Forma permeat totam materiam, & esse illud proprium confert quod res habet, ultra illam communem naturam quam habet à materia. Variæ res possunt eandem efficientem & eandem materiam habere, sed non eandem formam. hinc Forma est causa per quam res est id quod est.
units.tr: 17. Form pervades the whole matter and confers that proper being which the thing has beyond the common nature it has from matter. Different things can have the same efficient and the same matter, but not the same form. Hence form is the cause through which a thing is what it is.

units.la: 18 Forma tria habet officia, 1. Determinate rem constituere, unde forma vocatur. 2. Essentialiter eam distinguere, unde appellatur differentia. 3. Efficere operationes & actiones quarum est principium, unde actus nominatur.
units.tr: 18. Form has three offices: (1) to constitute the thing determinately, whence it is called form; (2) to distinguish it essentially, whence it is called difference; (3) to produce the operations and actions of which it is the principle, whence it is named act.

units.la: 19 Finis exurgit ex conjunctione materiæ & formæ,& est illa bonitas vel persectio rei qua elt ad operationem & usum apta.
units.tr: 19. The end arises from the joining of matter and form, and it is that goodness or perfection of a thing by which it is apt for operation and use.

units.la: 20 Bonitas hæc in efficientis intentione,est adjuvans causa; usus ad quem tendit, est effectum; res vel persona cui inservit in usu,est objectum:ad hæc tamen omnia propter affinitatem, finis nomen solet applicari:bonitas vel aptitudo ad usum est proprie finalis causa;appetitio ejus impellens efficientem,est finis intentionis; usus est secundarius finis cujus; res vel persona ad quam petat est finis cui.& in his omnibus generibus,unus aliquando finis operis dicitur;& alius operantis: sed scopus operantis à natura operis alienus, per accidens, tantum finis dicitur operationis.
units.tr: 20. This goodness, in the intention of the efficient, is the helping cause; the use to which it tends is the effect; the thing or person it serves in use is the object. Yet because of their affinity, the name end is usually applied to all of these. Goodness or aptitude for use is properly the final cause; the desire for it which drives the efficient is the end of intention; use is the secondary end of which; the thing or person toward which one aims is the end to which. And in all these kinds, one is sometimes called the end of the work and another the end of the agent; but the aim of the agent, being foreign to the nature of the work, is called the end of the operation only by accident.

units.la: 21 Quamvis causæ distinctæ sint essentia & definitione, res tamen quæ vi causarum fit unicam habet naturam, quæ licet arguatur à singulis causis, tamen ab efficiente ut à principio quod primam vim exerit ad ejus productionem, nomen habet effecti.
units.tr: 21. Although causes are distinct in essence and definition, the thing that comes about by the force of the causes has one nature. Although this nature is inferred from each of the causes, it takes the name of effect from the efficient, as from the principle that exerts the first force toward its production.

units.la: 22 Effectum e causis existit.existere vero plus aliquid in se habet quam esse: atq; adeo dicitur esse ab efficiente, ut effectum, ex materia,ut materiatum; per formam,ut formatum; & propter finem,ut finitum; non autem existere nisi ex causis omnibus.
units.tr: 22. The effect exists from its causes. But to exist has something more in itself than to be: and so it is said to be from the efficient as effect, from the matter as made of matter, through the form as formed, and for the end as finished; but it does not exist except from all its causes.

units.la: 23 Esse rei fluit a qualibet causa:essentia a materia & forma,quæ idcirco dicuntur causæ essentiales: existentia pendet ab omnibus causis simul concurrentibus ad esse & essentiam rei completam: subsistentia connotat etiam adjuncta, & consistentia membra.
units.tr: Being of a thing flows from any cause. Essence flows from matter and form, which for this reason are called essential causes. Existence depends on all the causes concurring together to the being and complete essence of the thing. Subsistence also implies adjuncts, and consistence implies the parts.

units.la: 24 Effectum duos habet gradus (quorum unus est alterius causa) motum procreationis aut conservationis, & rem motu factam, sive procreatam, sive etiam conservatam.
units.tr: An effect has two stages, one of which is the cause of the other: the motion of production or of conservation, and the thing made by motion, whether produced or also conserved.

units.la: 25 Rei jam effectæ & e causis existenti,accedit semper aliquid ab essentia & causis ita distinctum ut ad modum ejus pertineat solum, vel ad bene esse, & accidentale ejus complementum; hinc fluunt notiones subjecti & adjuncti.
units.tr: Once a thing has been effected and exists from its causes, there always attaches to it something distinct from its essence and causes, which pertains only to its mode, or to its well-being and accidental completion. From this arise the notions of subject and adjunct.

units.la: 26 Subjectum natura præcedit ut substratum quid, cui adjunctum est adventitium quid præter essentiam accedens. quæ unica subjecti ratio tam simplex est, & invariabilis, ut quamvis discrimen latum sit inter receptaculum & obiectum, nec non inter recipiens in se ac ad se, & obiectum materiale ac formale, &c. tamen verae species non dantur subjecti, nec modorum differentiae nisi aut mancae aut alienae.
units.tr: The subject precedes by nature as a kind of substratum, to which is attached an adventitious thing that comes in addition to the essence. This single account of the subject is so simple and invariable that, although there is a wide difference between receptacle and object, and also between what receives within itself and what receives toward itself, and between material and formal object, and so on, yet no true species of subject are given, nor differences of modes, except defective or alien ones.

units.la: 27 Adjunctum illud est quod rei ex causis existenti, vel substratae adjungitur: sive sit receptum sive occupatum, sive inhaerens sive adhaerens, sive proprium sive commune.
units.tr: The adjunct is that which is added to a thing existing from its causes, or to a substratum: whether it is received or occupied, inhering or adhering, proper or common.

units.la: 28 In iis argumentis consentaneis, categoria est eorum omnium quae unum vel idem dicuntur, vel communis locus continens primos & simplices fontes omnis unitatis vel identitatis: quae enim dici solent eadem genere sunt eadem materia & forma communi, sed non ultima; eadem (ut loquuntur) specie sunt eadem ultima forma communi; eadem numero eandem habent formam singularem; eadem tempore idem habent adjunctum; eadem loco idem subjectum.
units.tr: In these consentaneous arguments, category is that of all the things that are said to be one or the same, or a common place containing the first and simple sources of all unity or identity. For things that are commonly said to be the same in genus are the same in common matter and form, but not in the ultimate form; things the same (as they say) in species are the same in the ultimate common form; things the same in number have the same singular form; things the same in time have the same adjunct; things the same in place have the same subject.

units.la: 29 Ex iisdem etiam fontibus oritur secundario dissociatio rerum inter se: quae enim non sunt eadem causis, effectus, subjectis, vel adjunctis, illa dissociantur, vel dissentiunt inter se; idque levius aut gravius pro ratione distantiae quam habent ab unitate. in omnibus autem binis rebus est & consensio & dissensio; consensio per affirmationem unitatis, dissensio vero per negationem ejusdem.
units.tr: From these same sources there arises, secondarily, the dissociation of things from one another. For things that are not the same in causes, effects, subjects, or adjuncts are dissociated, or disagree with one another, more lightly or more gravely according to the degree of distance they have from unity. In every pair of things there is both consent and dissent: consent through the affirmation of unity, dissent through the negation of the same.

units.la: 30 Cum Dissentaneorum ratio in dis‑ sociatione aut divisione consistat, & eo‑ rum unum in sua propria natura non pen‑ deat ab altero qua Dissentaneum est, quoad esse, existere, vel sciri, idcirco sunt æqualis luminis & æqualium utrinque virium in arguendo; quapropter etiam uno nomine, unaque definitione per singulas species continentur. quæ omnia longe aliter se habent in consentaneis. in ipsa tamen na‑ turali accommodatione qua eorum asse&tio exercetur, illustrant sese mutuo vi ipsius dissensionis.
units.tr: Since the account of dissentients consists in dissociation or division, and neither of them, in its own nature, depends on the other as far as being, existing or being known goes, therefore they have equal light and equal forces on both sides in arguing. For this reason too they are contained under one name and one definition through each of their species. All these things stand quite otherwise in consentients. Yet in the very natural adjustment by which their assertion is exercised, they illuminate one another by the force of the dissension itself.

units.la: 3 1 Dissociatio rerum duplici gradu fit: quædam enim ita dissociantur ut possint consociari, quoniam externe tantum dissentiunt & sola ratione; vel respectu alicujus argumentalis affectionis, in qua convenire possent ex natura sua: & hæc appellantur diversa, quia quasi divertunt & secedunt paululum à se invicem sine alienatione constante: Quædam autem ita dissociantur, ut non possint consociari vel conjungi, quoniâ interne etiâ dissentiunt, ac reali natura sua, id est, ipsa materia vel forma: & hæc vocantur opposita, quia non divertunt solum unum ab altero, sed& alienationem talem inter fe exercent, ut positio unius obsistat cæterorum vel alterius positioni, in eadem re, secundum eundem respectum, partem, eodem tempore.
units.tr: Dissociation of things takes place in a twofold degree. Some things are so dissociated that they can be associated, since they differ only externally and in reason alone, or in respect of some argumentative affection in which by their nature they could agree. These are called diverse, because they turn aside and withdraw a little from one another without any lasting alienation. Others are so dissociated that they cannot be associated or joined, because they differ also internally, in their real nature, that is, in matter or form itself. These are called opposed, because they not only turn one away from the other but also exercise such alienation between themselves that the position of one stands against the position of the other, in the same thing, in the same respect, part, and time.

units.la: 3 2 Opposita semper debent ita considerari ut lex illa observetur, eidem secundum idem, ad idem, & eodem tempore. alias non differentiunt re: sic autem considerata, tam realem habent differsionem, ut unius affirmatione cogitata & statuta, alterius negatio cogitetur & statuatur necessario, contraqjuno negate cogitato, alterius alicujus affirmatio statuatur. quæ simul affirmatur, aut simul negatur, non sunt opposita
units.tr: Opposites must always be considered under the law that is observed: of the same, in the same respect, toward the same, and at the same time. Otherwise they do not differ in reality. So considered, they have such a real difference that when the affirmation of one is thought and posited, the negation of the other is necessarily thought and posited, and conversely, when the negation of one is thought, the affirmation of some other is posited. Things that are affirmed together, or denied together, are not opposites.

units.la: 3 3 Eorum quæ re differentiunt quædam longius à se invicem distant, & remotiore solo genere continentur, atque adeo leviorem habent oppositionem; non fit enim directe per proximas formas propter illam separationem, unde etiam disparata dicuntur, quasi disserata, quorum unum multis pariter vel eadem ratione poteft opponi, quia per illam distantiam remotam locus datur interventui multorum; & nihil est quod separatur ab una sola re: quædam continentur sub proximo genere & sub eo pugnant
units.tr: Of things that differ in reality, some lie further from one another and are contained under a more remote genus alone, and so have a weaker opposition. For this opposition does not come about directly through proximate forms, because of that separation. Hence they are called disparate, as if disparted. One of them can be opposed in the same way to many things at once, because through that remote distance room is given for many to intervene, and nothing is separated by one thing alone. Some things are contained under a proximate genus and fight within it,

units.la: quasi cominus contra se invicem per suas proximas formas, unde Contraria dicuntur, quae duobus plura non sunt, quia licet unum a pluribus aeque separari possit, non potest tamen ferri in plura ita ut recto quasi intuitu vel facie ad faciem se invicem petant; neque proximis formis opponi possunt quae pariter opponuntur aliis remotis.
units.tr: as if at close quarters against one another through their proximate forms. Hence they are called contraries, and there are not more than two of them. For although one thing can be equally separated from several, it cannot be carried toward several in such a way that they seek each other with a direct look, face to face. Nor can things that are opposed equally to other, remote things be opposed by proximate forms.

units.la: 34 Contraria est rei positio tum positioni alterius cum illo pugnantis, tum etiam ejusdem rei negationi : illa sunt contraria affirmativa, haec negativa.
units.tr: A contrary is the positing of a thing, both in relation to the positing of another thing that fights with it, and also in relation to the negation of the same thing. The former are affirmative contraries, the latter negative ones.

units.la: 35 Contraria affirmativa vel ita opponuntur inter se ut consensionem summam habeant dissensionis suae quasi fundamentum substratum, qua unum ad alterum referitur; vel pure & directe pugnant unum adversus alterum : illa dicuntur relata, haec adversa.
units.tr: Affirmative contraries are opposed to one another in one of two ways: either they have the greatest agreement in their dissension, a common substratum to which each is referred to the other; or they fight purely and directly, one against the other. The former are called relatives, the latter adverse.

units.la: 36 Relata cum ita considerantur ut oppositionis lex (de attributione eidem,&c.) observetur, tum sunt contraria propter contrarium utrinque situm; cum vero considerantur ut duæ res inter se mutuo afsectæ, tunc maximum habent consensum, ut mutuam coexistentiam causantia.
units.tr: When relatives are considered under the law of opposition (of attribution to the same, and so on), they are contraries because they are placed on opposite sides. But when they are considered as two things mutually affected toward each other, they then have the greatest agreement, as causing one another's coexistence.

units.la: 37 Tota natura unius relati ( qua talis ) fluit ab affectione alternante qua spectat
units.tr: The whole nature of one relative (as such) flows from the alternating affection by which it looks toward another and is looked upon by it,

units.la: ber suas dicun- ia licet fit,non recto e invi- oppo- r aliis posi- tum a sunt oppo- mam men- erum nt u- rela- t on-
units.tr: ...called their own ... although it is done, not directly ... in opposition ... placed to others ... are opposed ... relative ...

units.la: pectat alterum & ab illo spectatur, ita ut unum alterius (per mutuas quasi vicissitudines) causa sit & effectum, duæ sunt partes omnis relationis; quarum unafluit ab uno termino, & altera ab altero, ac in oppositum fertur, ex quibus una affectio mutua coalescit.
units.tr: ...so that one is, by a kind of mutual alternation, the cause and effect of the other. There are two parts of every relation: one flows from one term and the other from the other, and each is carried toward the opposite, and from these one mutual affection coalesces.

units.la: 38 In relatis igitur quoad ipsam assectionem alternantem totam non est prius & posterius, sed simul sunt natura: quia unum non magis alterius est causa vel ef- sectum, quam alterum est ejus.
units.tr: In relatives, therefore, as regards the whole alternating affection itself, there is no prior and posterior; they are simultaneous in nature, because one is no more the cause or effect of the other than the other is of it.

units.la: 39 Quoniam vero essentia unius fluit ab altero, non tantum æque manifesta sunt, ut omnia Dissentanea; sed etiam ut causæ ratio postulat, scientia unius oritur semper ex alterius cognitione.
units.tr: Since, however, the essence of one flows from the other, they are not only as manifest as all dissentients are, but also, as the account of cause requires, the knowledge of one always arises from the knowledge of the other.

units.la: 40 Adversa nullam consentaneam afsectionem habent admixtam (ut relata) sed perpetuo pugnant quocunque modo considerantur,idque in linea directa quasi ex diametro.
units.tr: Adverse things have no consentient affection mixed into them (as relatives do), but always fight in whatever way they are considered, and that in a direct line, as it were along a diameter.

units.la: 41 Adversa omnia ( qua talia,) sunt immediata. cum enim opponuntur mediis,non sunt adversa sed disparata.virtus media opponitur adversegeneri vitiorum extremorum, sive nominato sive innominato ; extremis ipsis tantum disparate. sic liberalitas adversatur illiberalitati sumptæ generatim, avaritiæ autem & effusioni speciatim confideratis opponitur tantum disparate.
units.tr: Adverse things, as such, are all immediate. For when they are opposed through intermediaries, they are not adverse but disparate. A middle virtue is opposed as adverse to the genus of extreme vices, whether named or unnamed, but only disparately to the extremes themselves. Thus liberality is adverse to illiberality taken generically, but is opposed only disparately to avarice and prodigality considered specifically.

units.la: 42 In contrariis negantibus non sunt duæ res positæ, ut in affirmantibus, sed affirmatio & negatio unius ac ejusdem.
units.tr: In contraries that deny there are not two things posited, as in affirming ones, but the affirmation and negation of one and the same thing.

units.la: 43 Hæc autem negatio vel est infinita quæ negat illam rem ubique, ac potest affirmari de qualibet alia re præter illam quam negat, & tum sunt contradicentia vel negat eam tantum in illo subjecto, in quo pernaturam potest inesse, & tum sunt privantia; unde sequitur privantia maxime omnium dissentire: quia privatio tollit rem cum inimicitia tam adversa ut nihil aliud in ejus locum relinquat, quod contradictio non facit.
units.tr: This negation is either infinite, which denies that thing everywhere and can be affirmed of any other thing except the one it denies, and then they are contradictories; or it denies the thing only in that subject in which by its nature it could be present, and then they are privatives. Whence it follows that privatives differ most of all, because privation removes the thing with such hostile opposition that it leaves nothing else in its place, which contradiction does not do.

units.la: 44 Ut ad consentanea omnes modi identitatis, sic ad ista dissentanea simplices omnes differentiæ modi debent referri.
units.tr: 44 Just as all modes of identity are referred to consentanea (things that agree), so all simple modes of difference must be referred to these dissentanea (things that disagree).

units.la: 45 Res ex causis existentes adjunctis ornatæ, & à cæteris rebus disjunctæ, inter se committi solent, ut eorum æstimatio fiat secundum aliquod tertium in quo consentiunt vel dissentiunt: unde comparata dicuntur, & res ipsæ, & rationes illæ in quibus conferuntur.
units.tr: 45 Things that exist through causes, are furnished with adjuncts, and are separated from other things are usually set against one another, so that their estimation is made by some third thing in which they agree or disagree. For this reason both the things and the grounds on which they are compared are called comparata.

units.la: 46 Comparatorum unum non est natura sua notius altero (quæ consentaneorum est ratio) tio) neque luminis æqualis quoad res fas (ut omnia dissentanea)nedum ut ef-
units.tr: 46 One of the comparata is not by its own nature better known than the other (this is the principle of things that agree), nor is it of equal clarity in respect of the things (as with all things that disagree), let alone does the essential account of one depend on knowledge of the other through equal reciprocity, as in relation.

units.la: ntialis unius ratio pendeat ab alterius ognitione per alternationem æqualem ut in relatu) sed comparationis vi quasi bra æstimatio utriusq; quoad rationem qua comparantur æque nota fit utrinue. quamvis ex rerum natura ante exlorata alterum altero alicui notius esse let. Quemadmodum autem in rei ponere ac valore æstimando aliquando gnum appositum vel impressum satis abetur, sæpe tamen ad bilancem vocaur, & ipsa in una lance locata, opponiur in altera pondus idoneum ad libranum : sic se res habet in collatione raionum.
units.tr: 47 Rather, by the force of comparison, the estimate of each becomes equally known with respect to the ground on which they are compared, although by the nature of things one may be better known to someone than the other beforehand. Just as, when estimating the weight and value of a thing, a stamp applied or impressed is sometimes enough, yet it is often taken to the scales: the thing itself is placed in one pan and a suitable weight is set in the other to balance it, so it is with the comparison of reasons.

units.la: 47 Duo igitur sunt modi comparationis, aliquando enim implicite fit & sæpe per notam aliquam brevem, unam vel plures: aliquando explicatius in partibus disjunctis, quarum una propositio dicitur, argumentum ut plurimum complexa, alera redditio nominatur, rem argutam continens maxima ex parte; quamvis ea it aliquando explicationis ratio ut red-ditionis nota tribuatur argumento, & propositionis rei argutæ, ut in illis majorum formis, non solum sed etiam.
units.tr: 48 There are therefore two modes of comparison. Sometimes it is implicit and is often expressed by one or more short marks. Sometimes it is more explicit, in separate parts, one of which is called the propositio, usually a complex argument, and the other called the redditio, containing for the most part the subtle matter. Yet there is sometimes such a manner of explanation that the mark of the redditio is given to the argument and that of the propositio to the subtle matter, as in those forms of the majorum type, non solum sed etiam.

units.la: 48 Hoc etiam est proprium comparatorum, ut eorum unum si fingatur, non alterum tantum fictum arguat (quod omnium argumentorum commune est) sed verum alterum.
units.tr: 49 It is also peculiar to comparata that if one of them is assumed, it does not merely show the other to be assumed (which is common to all arguments), but shows the other to be true.

units.la: 49 Instituitur autem omnis comparatio vel in gradu seu mensura, quae est quantitas logica, & tum est paritas vel imparitas; vel in ipsa natura terminorum, quae est qualitas logica, & tum est similitudo vel dissimilitudo.
units.tr: 50 Every comparison is set up either in degree or measure, which is the logical quantitas, and then it is paritas (equality) or imparitas (inequality); or in the very nature of the terms, which is the logical qualitas, and then it is similitudo (likeness) or dissimilitudo (unlikeness).

units.la: 50 Paria sunt, quae una mensura sive regula sive mente concepta mensurantur: ita ut aequilibrium faciant inter pendendum.
units.tr: 51 Paria (equals) are those which are measured by one measure or rule, whether actual or conceived in the mind, so that they balance one another when weighed.

units.la: 51 Si ad unam mensuram non conveniant, tum sunt imparia: illud cujus mensura excedit majus, & cujus exceditur minus.
units.tr: 52 If they do not agree under one measure, they are imparia (unequal): that whose measure exceeds is the majus (greater), and that which is exceeded is the minus (lesser).

units.la: 52 Similia sunt, quæ eandem habent naturam, vel essentialem vel adjunctam. quoniam vero eadem natura proprie non potest esse duplex, vel simul in duabus rebus, idcirco hæc identitas est in proportione tantum, qua una res habet illam naturæ rationem pro sua portione, & altera etiam pro sua.
units.tr: 53 Similia (like things) are those which have the same nature, either essential or adjunct. But since the same nature cannot properly be double, or be present at once in two things, this identity lies only in proportio (proportion): one thing has that nature in its own proportion, and the other likewise in its own.

units.la: 53 In explicata similitudine termini aliquando quatuor sunt re ipsa distinct, & tum similitudo disjuncta dicitur: aliquando quatuor uando vero non re sed ratione tantum unt quatuor distincti, & tum continua nominatur, quia proportio continuatur per repetitionem secundi.
units.tr: 54 When the terms of an explicit likeness are four things really distinct, the likeness is called disjuncta (disjoined). When there are four terms, but distinct only in reason and not in fact, it is called continua (continued), because the proportion is continued by the repetition of the second term.

units.la: 54 Quorum natura non est eadem in proportione, sed diversa, illa sunt dissimilia. eædem igitur res quæ absolute consideratæ sunt diversa, comparate spectatæ sunt dissimilia.
units.tr: 55 Things whose nature is not the same in proportion, but different, are dissimilia (unlike). Thus the same things which, considered absolutely, are diversa (diverse), are dissimilia when viewed in comparison.

units.la: Hactenus de Argumentis primis.
units.tr: Hitherto concerning the primary arguments.

units.la: 55 Orta, ex primis tanquam ex radiibus exsurgunt: quibusdam etiam eandem vim habent arguendi, sed secundario & symbolice, id est comprehensive & notarum instar.
units.tr: 56 Orta (derived things) arise from the prima (primary things) as from roots. Some of them also have the same force in arguing, but secondarily and symbolically, that is, comprehensively and in the manner of marks.

units.la: 56 Horum autem alia simplicem habent ortum, ex uno aliquo primo, ut Conjugata & Notatio: alia compositum ex plurium combinatione, ut Distributio & Definitio.
units.tr: 57 Of these, some have a simple origin from one primary thing, such as Conjugata (cognates) and Notatio (notation); others have a compound origin from the combination of several, such as Distributio (distribution) and Definitio (definition).

units.la: 57 In conjugatis est deductio nominum quæ eodem jugo vel nexu continentur: quorum unum comprehendit naturam absolutam vel abstractam, aliud naturam dependentem vel concretam, & tertium naturam activam, una cum ejus modo a prioribus fluente.
units.tr: 58 In conjugata there is the derivation of names that are held together under one yoke or bond: one of them comprehends an absolute or abstract nature, another a dependent or concrete nature, and a third an active nature, together with its mode flowing from the former.

units.la: 58 In notatione ratio redditur cur talis res tali nota designetur.
units.tr: 59 In notatio, an account is given of why such a thing is designated by such a mark.

units.la: §9 Sequuntur illa orta quæ comprehendunt prima magis tecte, magisque composita ratione, ita tamen necessaria ut constituant perpetuam reciprocationem non axiomaticæ tantum veritatis, quam sapientiæ. lex in omnibus præceptis artium requirit; nec mutuæ solum relationis qualis reperitur in omni argumentorum pari; sed communis essentiæ quæ est harum rationum propria, quæ realem rerum naturam notat.
units.tr: §9 Next come those orta which comprehend the prima more covertly and by a more composite reasoning, yet so necessary that they establish a perpetual reciprocatio, not only of axiomatic truth, which the wisdom of every art requires in its precepts, nor only of mutual relation such as is found in every pair of arguments, but of a common essence proper to these reasons, which marks the real nature of things.

units.la: §o Cujusvis autem rei natura spectatur vel ut communis est pluribus, vel ut in se consistit ab aliis remota: illa docet in distributione, hæc in definitione: illa enim tributionem indicat communem, hæc fines seu finitionem statuit propriam.
units.tr: §o Now the nature of anything is viewed either as it is common to several things, or as it subsists in itself, apart from others. The former teaches in distributio, the latter in definitio: for the one indicates a common division, the latter sets out the bounds, or proper limitation.

units.la: 61 Distributio duo continet, viz. commune aliquid, unde totum; & communun pluribus, unde partes.Totū continet partes communitate unius formæ; partes divisæ consideratæ distinguunt totum (quæ proprie dicitur distributio) & collective summptæ constituunt totum, quæ est inductio.
units.tr: 61 Distributio contains two things, namely something common, whence the totum (whole), and what is common to several, whence the partes (parts). The whole contains its parts by the commonality of one form. Parts considered as divided distinguish the whole (which is properly called distributio), and taken collectively they constitute the whole, which is inductio (induction).

units.la: 62 Necesse autem est ut partes consentiant in eo quod commune habent, & differant vel differant in eo quod sunt plura; unde est quod partes consentire debent cum toto, inter se autem dissentire, & quo magis hoc fit,eo fit accuratior distributio, maxime autem consentiunt cum proximo toto, & sub eo maxime dissentiunt per contrarietatem; quæ propria est ratio principatus illius quem Dichotomia obtinet in distribuendo.
units.tr: 62 It is necessary that the partes agree in what they have in common, and differ in what makes them many. Hence the parts must agree with the whole, but differ among themselves; and the more this is so, the more exact the distributio. They agree most with the nearest whole, and within it differ most by contrariety. This is the proper ground of the primacy which the Dichotomy holds in distributing.

units.la: 63 Pendet natura distributionis magis ex affectione partium ad totum, quam ex illa quam habent inter se: atque adeo non ex dissentaneis, sed ex consentaneis distinctiones distributionis petuntur.
units.tr: 63 The nature of distributio depends more on the relation of the partes to the totum than on the relation they have to one another. Therefore the distinctions of distributio are sought not from things that disagree, but from things that agree.

units.la: 64 Quando igitur plures causæ distinguuntur inter se in affectione ad unum affectum, vel plura effecta in affectione ad unam causam, vel plura subjecta in afsectione ad unum adjunctum, vel plura adjuncta in affectione ad unum subjectum, tum pro ratione illarum distinctarum rerum distributio dicitur esse ex Causis, Effectis, Subjectis, Adjunctis.
units.tr: 64 When, therefore, several causes are distinguished from one another in their relation to one effect, or several effects in their relation to one cause, or several subjects in their relation to one adjunct, or several adjuncts in their relation to one subject, then the distribution is said to be made, according to the nature of those distinct things, into Causes, Effects, Subjects, Adjuncts.

units.la: 65 Quia vero essentialis consensio est proprie inter causam & effectum, & in eo genere excellunt istæ distributiones quæ sunt integri in membra, aut generis in species, in istis igitur solis exquisita ratio totius & partium apparet.
units.tr: 65 But since essential agreement is properly found between cause and effect, and in that kind the distributions excel which divide a whole into its members, or a genus into its species, the exact reason of whole and parts appears in these alone.

units.la: 66 In distributione integri in membra, membra sunt causæ singulares, tectæ, ac inter se compactæ, ac in unum redactæ, sed ita ut actu continentur ab integro cu[illegible, ~2 letters] dant essentiam, & in quo existunt: materia igitur & forma integri conflatur ex[illegible, ~2 letters] materia & forma omnium membrorum.
units.tr: 66 In the distributio integri in membra (division of a whole into its members), the members are singular causes, hidden, compacted with one another and reduced into one, yet in such a way that they are actually contained by the whole, and give it its essence, and in which it exists. Thus the matter and form of the whole are made up of the matter and form of all the members.

units.la: 67 In distributione generis in species, genus est nota causarum essentialium communium: existit igitur in singulis speciebus dans illis essentiam, & in omnibus communicans illis eandem essentiam: tota igitur essentia generis est in singulis speciebus; sed tota communitas vel totum genus proprie non nisi in cunctis.
units.tr: 67 In the distributio generis in species (division of a genus into species), the genus is the mark of the common essential causes. It therefore exists in each of the species, giving them their essence, and communicates the same essence to all of them. The whole essence of the genus is therefore in each species; but the whole commonality, or the whole genus, properly exists only in all of them together.

units.la: 68 Nota causarum communium primarum est genus generalissimum, nihil enim habet prius, mediarum nota est subalternum genus: specierum eadem est ratio nam nota effecti medii est species subalterna, infimi vero est infima vel specialissima.
units.tr: 68 The mark of the primary common causes is the genus generalissimum (highest genus), for it has nothing prior to it. The mark of the intermediate causes is the subalternum genus (subaltern genus). The same holds for the species: the mark of an intermediate effect is the species subalterna (subaltern species), and that of the lowest is the infima or specialissima (lowest species).

units.la: 69 Definitio explicat naturam propriam rei definitae, idque vel a causis tantum essentialibus communibus, quae generi comprehenduntur, & propria insuper forma si queat haberi, vel ab aliis etiam argumentis reciprocis. illa definitio est perfecta, haec imperfecta vel descriptio.
units.tr: 69 Definitio explains the proper nature of the thing defined, either from the common essential causes alone, which are comprehended under the genus, together with its proper form if this can be had, or also from other reciprocal arguments. The former definition is perfecta (perfect), the latter imperfecta or a descriptio (description).

units.la: 70 Extra artificium rei nihil arguere potest; nisi proficiscatur ab eo qui novit artificium, & offendit quod novit. hoc autem a quacunq; persona quocunq; modo fiat unius generis est, & testimonium vocatur:
units.tr: 70 Nothing outside the art of a thing can prove anything, unless it comes from someone who knows the art and reports what he knows. Whatever kind of person does this, in whatever way, is a kind of evidence and is called testimony.

units.la: 71 Testimonium igitur ipsum in se consideratum, (id est, affirmatio seu negatio estantis de re testata) nihil habet artis aut virtutis arguendi, sed fulciri debet argumentis artificialibus; tantum autem valet quantum & notitiæ & simplicis veracitatis in teste apparet. aliud majorem, aliud minorem, aliud nullam vim habet.
units.tr: 71 Testimony, considered in itself (that is, the affirmation or denial of something by a witness about the matter attested), has no power of proof from art or skill, but must be supported by artificial arguments. Its weight is as great as the witness's knowledge and plain truthfulness appear to be. Some testimony has great weight, some little, and some none.

units.la: 72 Reciprocatio est cum rei propositæ artificialia argumenta spectantur & adruntur, ad testimonii ac testis veracitatem arguendam.
units.tr: 72 Reciprocation is when the artificial arguments concerning the proposed matter are examined and applied, in order to prove the truthfulness of the testimony and of the witness.

units.la: ARgumenta jam inventa debent ad [?]um inter se disponi. Hæc igitur Dispositio est Logicæ pars altera.
units.tr: Arguments once discovered must be arranged among themselves in order. This arrangement is therefore the second part of Logic.

units.la: 74 Dispositio autem argumentorum [?]ventorum, vel eo tendit ut judicium de fiat, quod ex dispositione naturaliter manat, quasi ex flore; vel ut memoria [?]int retineri: hi enim tres actus ratio-[?]s sunt, invenire, judicare, & memoria inere, quibus tres interni sensus inferint, phantasia, cogitativa facultas & memoria sensitiva: secunda igitur logicæ rectissime dividitur in Judicium & Methodum.
units.tr: 74 The arrangement of the discovered arguments aims either at a judgment about the matter, which arises naturally from the arrangement as from its flower, or at the arguments being kept in memory. For these are the three acts of reason: to discover, to judge, and to remember, which correspond to the three inner senses: the imagination, the cogitative faculty, and the sensitive memory. So the second part of logic is rightly divided into Judgment and Method.

units.la: 75 Quod judicio subjicitur vel clarum & per se vel sua luce manifestum, vel obscu-
units.tr: 75 What is subjected to judgment is either clear, and manifest of itself or by its own light, or obscure

units.la: obscurum & dubium: de manifestis judi[?] cium statim fertur cum proponuntur, d[?] dubiis amplius deliberatur & discursu[?] mentis habetur: unde judicium accuratis[?] sime dividitur in Axiomaticum & Dianoe[?] eticum.
units.tr: and doubtful. Judgment is passed at once on manifest matters when they are put forward; doubtful matters are considered further and reached by the discursive working of the mind. Hence judgment is most accurately divided into Axiomatic and Dianoetic.

units.la: 76 Axioma proprie notat eam senten[?] tiam, quæ omnium approbatione digní[?] putatur (vox enim existimationem & di[?] gnitatem sonat;& non male vertitur pro[?] nunciatum honorarium) cum igitur & illu[?] complectatur quod Enunciatum, Enuncia[?] tio, Pronunciatum, Pronunciatio,&c. & [?] mul etiam indicet, quænam sententiæ e[?] hac doctrina judicentur, illæ nempe qu[?] non indigent approbatione, sed per se fid[?] dignæ sunt; idcirco aptissima vox est qu[?] huic dispositionis parti accommodatur.
units.tr: 76 Axiom properly denotes a proposition that is thought worthy of the approval of all. (The word means esteem and dignity, and it is fairly translated honourable pronouncement.) Since it also comprehends what are called Enunciatum, Enunciatio, Pronunciatum, Pronunciatio, and so on, and at the same time indicates which propositions in this doctrine are to be judged, namely those that need no approval but are worthy of trust in themselves, it is therefore the most fitting word for this part of the arrangement.

units.la: 77 Cum axioma semper lucem claram[?] præ se ferat, proponit tantum vel decla[?] rat argumenta illa quæ vinculo aliquo in[?] ter se connectuntur; neque probat quid[?] quam sed judicat rem esse, vel non ess[?] id est, declarat & exponit.
units.tr: 77 Since an axiom always carries its own clear light, it only puts forward or declares those arguments that are connected with one another by some bond. It does not prove anything, but judges that a thing is or is not, that is, it declares and sets it out.

units.la: 78 In hac autem dispositione argu[?] menta vel componuntur inter se vincul[?] affirmato & tum axioma dicitur affirma[?] tum, vel à se invicem dividuntur vincul[?] negato, & tum dicitur negatum. quod [?] iden[?] idem axioma & affirmetur & negetur tum est contradiction.
units.tr: 78 In this arrangement, arguments are either joined to one another by an affirming bond, and then the axiom is called affirmative; or they are separated from one another by a denying bond, and then it is called negative. When the same axiom is both affirmed and denied, it is a contradiction.

units.la: 79 Si componantur res in natura compositæ, vel dividantur res in natura divisæ, tum axioma est verum: si vero componantur res in natura divisæ, aut compositæ dividantur, tunc est falsum.
units.tr: 79 If things that are composed in nature are joined, or things divided in nature are separated, then the axiom is true. If, however, things divided in nature are joined, or things composed are separated, then it is false.

units.la: 80 Si quæ componuntur murabiliter conveniant, axioma est contingens, & judicium ejus est opinio, per opinionem autem non debet intelligi vacillans & dubia rerum perceptio, nedum assensus retentio & suspensio, quomodo in usu vulgari sæpe usurpatur, sed notio, ex contingenti mutabilique rerum in axiomate dispositarum natura, in mente cum assensu concepta: quæ sæpe est certa, præsertim de præteritis & futuris, quibus etiam adhæret quædam necessitas, ratione contrarietatis facti & non facti; sed hæc est alterius axiomatis proprie, non ejusdem.
units.tr: 80 If things joined together agree in a changeable way, the axiom is contingent, and its judgment is opinion. By opinion we should not understand a wavering and doubtful perception of things, still less the holding and suspending of assent, as it is often used in common speech; rather it is a notion, conceived in the mind with assent, arising from the contingent and changeable nature of the things arranged in the axiom. This is often certain, especially concerning past and future things, to which a certain necessity also adheres, by reason of the contrariety of what is and what is not; but this belongs properly to another axiom, not to the same one.

units.la: 81 Si quæ componuntur immutabiliter conveniant, nec esse aliter possint ex natura sua, tum axioma est necessarium.
units.tr: 81 If things joined together agree unchangeably, and cannot be otherwise by their own nature, then the axiom is necessary.

units.la: 82 Necessitas veritatis hoc in loco debet intelligi illa quæ est axiomatis propria: præter quam duæ sunt aliæ necessitates Logicæ, quarum una est coactionis in efficiendi modo, & altera consequentia in syllogismo. B
units.tr: 82 The necessity of truth here must be understood as that which is proper to the axiom. Besides this there are two other logical necessities: one is of constraint in the mode of effecting, and the other is of consequence in the syllogism.

units.la: 83 Hujus necessitatis tres habentur gra‑ dus, qui notis honorariis designantur, primus est χτῇ παντὸς, quo requiritur ut axioma sit omnino, ubique, & semper verum, excludens & falsa commenta, & contingentia, quæque sunt ex parte tantum vera; quæ ideo lex dicitur veritatis. Secundus est καθ' αὑτὸ, quo requiritur insuper ut partes axiomatis inter se sint essentiales, idque per se, non per aliud, excludens omnia adventitia, ut cuique rei tribuat quod essentiæ suæ debetur; quæ ideo lex dicitur justitiæ. Tertius est καθόλου πρῶτον, quo requiritur adhuc, ut partes inter se conveniant, primo & æqualiter vel reciproce, (sic ut aliud in eo genere prius enunciari non possit, nec illud de alio) excludens confusiones & tautologias, quæ ideo dicitur lex sapientiæ.
units.tr: 83 There are three degrees of this necessity, marked by honorary signs. The first is kath' pantos [κατὰ παντός], by which it is required that the axiom be wholly, everywhere, and always true, excluding false inventions, contingent statements, and whatever is true only in part. For this reason it is called the law of truth. The second is kath' hauto [καθ' αὑτό], by which it is further required that the parts of the axiom be essential to one another, and that they be so of themselves and not through something else, excluding everything accidental, so that each thing is given what is due to its essence. For this reason it is called the law of justice. The third is kathholou proton [καθόλου πρῶτον], by which it is further required that the parts agree with one another primarily and equally or reciprocally (so that one thing in that genus cannot be stated earlier than another, nor that one said of the other), excluding confusions and tautologies. For this reason it is called the law of wisdom.

units.la: 84 Hæ tres leges debent observari in omnibus artium præceptis; neque ulli axiomati conveniunt omnes, nisi præceptum sit alicujus artis,neque ulli, nisi per accommodationem talis præcepti,vel deductionem ex illo.
units.tr: 84 These three laws must be observed in all precepts of the arts. Not all of them agree with every axiom, unless the precept belongs to some art, and none agrees with any axiom except by the adaptation of such a precept or by deduction from it.

units.la: 85 Hujusmodi axiomatum judicium est prima verissimaque scientia, deductio aliorum axiomatum ex illis est sapientia humana.
units.tr: 85 The judgment of axioms of this kind is the first and most certain science; the deduction of other axioms from these is human wisdom.

units.la: Tales fuerunt communes axiomatis af- sectiones, sequuntur species.
units.tr: Such were the common affections of the axiom; its species follow.

units.la: 86 In axiomatica dispositione vel unicus directus & simplex actus mentis est, quasi una linea recta duo argumenta complectens (quo modo omnia argumenta praeter plenas comparationes & distributiones disponi possunt) & tum axioma dicitur simplex; vel compositus, quasi linea curva faciens quandam circuitionem, & tum axioma dicitur compositum.
units.tr: 86 In axiomatic arrangement there is either a single, direct and simple act of the mind, like a straight line embracing two arguments (in which way all arguments, except full comparisons and distributions, can be arranged), and then the axiom is called simple; or a compound act, like a curved line making a certain circuit, and then the axiom is called compound.

units.la: 87 Simplicis axiomatis vinculum vel forma est in verbo; verbum autem grammaticum non debet hic intelligi (quamvis eo etiam exprimi soleat vinculum una cum consequente vel ejus parte) sed logica verbi vis mente concepta; qua argumenta disposita inter se conglutinantur & axioma totum viget ac animatur.
units.tr: 87 The bond or form of a simple axiom lies in the verb. Here the verb is not to be understood grammatically (although the bond is usually expressed by it together with the consequent or part of it), but as the logical force of the verb conceived in the mind, by which the arguments set out are glued together and the whole axiom is given life and vigour.

units.la: 88 Mens differentis simpliciter enunciando, vel spectat totum illud in communi cui aliquid attribuit, & axioma est generale, ubi & consequens & modus attribuendi debent esse communes: vel partem ejus tantum & quasi species, quod efficit axioma speciale, in quo pars illa vel incerte ac dubie notatur, quod axioma particulare constituit; vel singulariter, & proprie designatur, quod est axioma proprium. 89 Generali affirmato, quoniam includit totum antecedens, contradicitur aliquo modo per exclusionem totius; sed non immediate nec efficaciter ad constantem divisionem veri à falso, nisi per exclusionem partis alicujus, quod maxime directe fit per axioma particulare oppositum, particulare unum oppositum alteri non contradictionem facit sed distributionem: non enim idem subjectum necessario designant; atque adeo non affirmatur & negatur idem illa ratione: sed ubi pars incerta affirmatur, ut contradictio fiat, totum debet negari per axioma generale, & sic e contra. tunc autem semper dividitur verum à falso, ita ut verum ab una parte stet, ac falsum ab altera.
units.tr: 88 In simply enunciating a difference, the mind either regards the whole in common to which it attributes something, and the axiom is general, where both the consequent and the mode of attribution must be common; or it regards only a part of that whole, as it were a species, which makes a special axiom, in which that part is marked vaguely and doubtfully, and this constitutes a particular axiom; or it is designated singly and properly, which is a proper axiom. 89 A general affirmative, since it includes the whole antecedent, is contradicted in some way by the exclusion of the whole; but not immediately, nor effectively for the constant division of true from false, except by the exclusion of some part, which is done most directly by the opposite particular axiom. One particular opposed to another makes not a contradiction but a distribution, for they do not necessarily designate the same subject; and so the same thing is not affirmed and denied in that respect. But where an indefinite part is affirmed, for a contradiction to occur the whole must be denied by a general axiom, and so conversely. Then indeed the true is always divided from the false, so that the true stands on one side and the false on the other.

units.la: Hactenus de Axiomate Simplici.
units.tr: Thus far on the Simple Axiom.

units.la: 90 Quando argumenta duobus plurib in eodem axiomate disponuntur, vel duorum disposicio multiplex est & circumducta, tum vinculum non potest esse verbum unum, sed conjunctio plurium, quae maxima ex parte grammaticis conjunctionibus, aliquando voculis etiam relativis notatur; hoc igitur axiomatis genus compositum vocatur, ubi conjunctioni adhaeret affirmatio, negatio, & contradictio, quae dividit semper verum à falso.
units.tr: 90 When arguments are arranged in one axiom in two or more ways, or the arrangement of the two is multiple and circuitous, then the bond cannot be a single verb but a conjunction of several, which for the most part is marked by grammatical conjunctions and sometimes even by relative particles. This kind of axiom is therefore called compound, where affirmation, negation and contradiction attach to the conjunction, which always divides the true from the false.

units.la: 91 Conjunctio vero aut sensum conjungit, una cum verbis, aut verba sola conjungit, sensum vero disjungit: fi sensum conjungat, axioma dicitur congregativum; fi vero verba tantum, fegregativum.
units.tr: 91 A conjunction either joins the sense together with the words, or joins only the words and disjoins the sense. If it joins the sense, the axiom is called congregative; if only the words, segregative.

units.la: 92 Quæ sensum conjungit vel id necefsario facit, partem unam alligans alteri quasi attrahente nexu, quod axioma est connexum: vel non necessario, & fine dependentia ulla partes inter fe collateraliter tenentur quasi jugo vel copula æquali, quod genus axiomatis dicitur copulatum.
units.tr: 92 That which joins the sense, or does so necessarily, binding one part to another with a kind of drawing bond, is a connected axiom. That which does not do so necessarily, and where the parts are held together side by side without any dependence, as if by an equal yoke or coupling, is the kind of axiom called copulated.

units.la: 93 In axiomate copulato illa præcipue & maxime proprie conjunguntur quæ vel solent vel possunt separari (ut Cæsar doctus fuit & pugnax) cujus dispositionis vel vinculi nota vel est conjunctio grammatica copulativa (ut, ac, &, etiam, item, nec non, quoque, que, atque, itemq; neque) vel adverbia cum conjunctionibus conjuncta, (ut, simul, una, pariter, &c.) vel denique relationum illarum particulæ, quæ pertinent ad plenas comparationes, five sint qualitatis five quantitatis.
units.tr: 93 In a copulated axiom those things are conjoined especially and most properly which either usually or can be separated (as Caesar was learned and warlike). The mark of this arrangement or bond is either the copulative grammatical conjunction (ac, &, etiam, item, nec non, quoque, que, atque, itemque, neque), or adverbs joined with conjunctions (simul, una, pariter, etc.), or finally those particles of relation which pertain to full comparisons, whether of quality or of quantity.

units.la: 94 Tota vis axiomatis copulati est in ipsa copulatione: verum igitur non est dicendum, nisi in copulatione partes omnes veræ sint: falsum vero fi vel una fit falsa. æque igitur contradicitur copulato per
units.tr: 94 The whole force of a copulated axiom lies in the copulation itself. Therefore it must be said to be true only if all the parts of the copulation are true, and false if even one is false. A copulated axiom is thus contradicted equally by the exclusion of one part and by the removal of all of them.

units.la: unius partis exclusionem, ac per omniu[?] remotionem: imo talis remotio non c[?] copulationis vel copulati axiomatis, f[?] partium negatio, quæ non semper divid[?] verum à falso.
units.tr: Indeed such a removal is not a negation of the copulation or of the copulated axiom, but a negation of the parts, which does not always divide the true from the false.

units.la: 95 In connexo axiomate disponunt[?] illa, quæ inter se concatenatione quadar[?] cohærent, continua vel contigua serie, qu[?] unum alterum potest se trahit aut infe[?] quadam necessitate. exprimitur hæc illa[?] tio per conjunctionem connexivam si, si[?] &c. vel per relationem consequentiæ, cu[?] hoc, tum etiam illud.
units.tr: 95 In a connected axiom are arranged those things which cohere with one another by a certain chaining, in a continuous or contiguous series, so that one can draw or, as it were, infer the other by a certain necessity. This relation is expressed by the connective conjunction if, if, etc., or by the relation of consequence, since this, therefore also that.

units.la: 96 Connexionis necessitas hic spect[?] tur sola: quæ potest esse vera ex partibu[?] falsis, quemadmodum & falsa ex partibu[?] veris, quoniam ex vero nil nisi verum, ne[?] tamen ex quolibet quidlibet sequitur a[?] pendet, contradictio igitur est per quam[?] libet consequentiæ negationem.
units.tr: 96 Only the necessity of the connection is considered here. It can be true from false parts, just as it can be false from true parts, since from the true nothing but the true follows, yet from anything whatever it does not follow that anything at all does. The contradiction of such a connection is therefore by the denial of any consequence.

units.la: Hæc de Congregativo Axiomate.
units.tr: These things concerning the Congregative Axiom.

units.la: 97 Conjunctiones segregativæ vel segre[?] gant non necessario, ea quæ solent vel pos[?] sunt convenire discernentes, unde axioma dicitur discretum, præcipue ac proprie con[?] tinens diversa: vel necessario, ea quæ non[?] possunt convenire per disjunctionem sepa[?] rantes, unde axioma dicitur disjunctum, præcipue ac proprie oppositta disponens.
units.tr: 97 Segregative conjunctions either separate without necessity, distinguishing things that usually or possibly agree, whence an axiom is called discrete, chiefly and properly containing diverse things; or they separate with necessity, joining by disjunction things that cannot agree, whence an axiom is called disjunct, chiefly and properly setting out opposites.

units.la: 98 Discretæ conjunctionis vel fejunctionis notæ sunt, autem, ast, at, interea, interim, ut, vero, verum, nunc, tamen, e: fi, tamen fi, quamvis, extraquam, pro erquam.
units.tr: 98 The marks of discrete conjunction or disjunction are but, however, yet, meanwhile, in the meantime, as, indeed, true, now, nevertheless, and; even if, nevertheless if, although, except that, except.

units.la: 99 Discretio fit proprie per unius partis affirmationem (realem vel fictam) & alterius negationem : quæ ambæ debent esse veræ in vero discreto ; cum autem hoc modo segreget ea quæ videri potuerint conjuncta, in distinguendo præcipue adhibetur, & contradicit copulato connexoque, vel potius contradictionis eorum est consectarium.
units.tr: 99 Discretion properly takes place through the affirmation of one part (real or feigned) and the negation of the other; both of these must be true in a true discrete axiom. Since it separates in this way things that might seem conjoined, it is chiefly used in distinguishing, and it contradicts the copulative and connective, or rather is a consequence of their contradiction.

units.la: 100 Disjunctum axioma sic appellatur ἀπὸ ἐξολής, quia necessariam disjunctionem per se ferre solet, potest autem disjunctum axioma esse necessariæ veritatis, ex partibus non necessariis, & non necessariæ, ex parte aliqua necessaria. hujus enim axiomatis veritas pendet ex necessaria partium disjunctione; sicut veritas connexi ex earum simili connexione.
units.tr: 100 A disjunct axiom is so called from [ἀπὸ ἐξολής], because it usually carries a necessary disjunction within itself. A disjunct axiom may, however, be of necessary truth while its parts are not necessary, and of non-necessary truth if some part is necessary. For the truth of this axiom depends on the necessary disjunction of its parts, just as the truth of a connective depends on their similar connection.

units.la: 101 Hic significatur unum esse verum & non nisi unum : quia non est legitime disjunctum axioma, si ullæ partes inter se conveniant, nec verum, si numeratio non sit plena: ex hac autem enumeratione plena, argumenta disposita rationem habent oppositionis immediatæ.
units.tr: 101 This signifies that only one is true, and no more than one. For it is not properly a disjunct axiom if any of its parts agree with one another, nor is it true if the enumeration is not complete. From this complete enumeration, the arguments so arranged have the character of immediate opposition.

units.la: 102 In distributione generis in species fi ratio habeatur consensionis quæ est inter totum & partes, axioma est copulatum: sed prout spectatur partium inter se diffensio, axioma est disjunctum.
units.tr: 102 In the division of a genus into species, if account is taken of the agreement between the whole and its parts, the axiom is copulative; but as the disagreement of the parts among themselves is regarded, the axiom is disjunct.

units.la: Hactenus de Judicio Noetico, sequitur de Dianoetico.
units.tr: So far on the Noetic Judgment; what follows concerns the Dianoetic.

units.la: 103 Cum veritas aut falsitas axiomatis non est per se clara, sed obscura vel dubia, sive in se, sive ipsi cui fides ejus est facienda, tum quæstio fit: circa quam exercet se mens hominis cursitando, vel transmittendo se ab uno ad aliud, ut faciat rem claram, aut inferat ei lucem; hæc est dianoetica ratio syllogismi.
units.tr: 103 When the truth or falsity of an axiom is not self-evident, but obscure or doubtful, either in itself or to the one to whom its credibility must be given, then a question arises. The mind of man exercises itself upon this question by running about, or by passing from one thing to another, so that it may make the matter clear or bring light to it. This is the dianoetic reasoning of the syllogism.

units.la: 104 Illatio syllogismi semper est necessaria vi dispositionis, quamvis nulla sæpe pars ejus in se considerata necessario sit vera: hæc est necessitas consequentiæ, & necessitas ex suppositione vel hypothesi.
units.tr: 104 The inference of a syllogism is always necessary by the force of its arrangement, although often no part of it, considered in itself, is necessarily true. This is the necessity of consequence, and necessity from supposition or hypothesis.

units.la: 105 Quæstio inferenda continet semper argumenta duo; de quibus non liquet utrum conjungenda sint an potius disjungenda. hoc ut appareat tertium aliquod argumentum adhiberi debet, quod cum illis duobus dispositum illorum concordiam aut discordiam palam efficere possit: tria igitur sunt argumenta in omni syllogismo non pauciora, neque plura possunt esse: quia tum inferrent etiam plura, non unum illud quod in dubium vocatur: unum tamen argumentum variis terminis contineri potest: sicut etiam argumenta varia sub uno termino sæpe latent, qui variam habet significationem.
units.tr: 105 The question to be inferred always contains two arguments, about which it is not clear whether they should be joined or rather disjoined. For this to appear, a third argument must be brought in, which, arranged with those two, can make plain their agreement or disagreement. There are therefore three arguments in every syllogism, no fewer and no more; for otherwise they would infer more than the one thing that is called into doubt. Yet one argument may be contained in various terms, just as various arguments often lie hidden under one term, which has several meanings.

units.la: 1. 6 Tertium argumentum disponendum est cum utraque parte quæstionis, ut lucem & vim adferat illi dispositioni ac affectioni, quam habent inter se. disponitur imprimis cum consequente (saltem) ejus parte, quæ præcipue constituit quæstionem; & illa dispositio præponitur tanquam fundamentum ratiocinationis, unde propositio vocatur; ex qua assumitur tertium argumentum, & vel per se, vel cum antecedente parte quæstionis secundo in loco disponitur, quæ pars idcirco assumtio nominatur: ex quibus infertur quæstio ipsa, ratiocinationem totam claudens, unde conclusio dicitur.
units.tr: 106 The third argument must be arranged with each part of the question, so as to bring light and force to the relation and affinity which they have with one another. It is arranged first with the consequent (at least) of the question, the part which chiefly constitutes the question; and this arrangement is placed first as the foundation of the reasoning, whence it is called the proposition. From it the third argument is taken, and either by itself or together with the antecedent part of the question it is arranged in the second place, and this part is therefore named the assumption. From these the question itself is inferred, closing the whole reasoning, whence it is called the conclusion.

units.la: 107 Partium harum deest aliquando una, ut in enthymemate, ad illas etiam aliæ nonnunquam accedunt, ut in syllogismorum implicatis formis, Sorite & Dilemmate; sed revocari semper debet ratiocinationis vis ad unicam syllogismi formam: præter quam nulla est alia dispositio, cujus vi, necessario consequentia vel conclusio efficiatur.
units.tr: 107 Sometimes one of these parts is lacking, as in the enthymeme; at other times others are also added, as in the complex forms of syllogisms, the Sorites and the Dilemma. But the force of the reasoning must always be reduced to the single form of the syllogism, beyond which there is no other arrangement by whose force a consequence or conclusion is necessarily produced.

units.la: 108 Dispositio quæstionis cum argumento tertio, est vel plane simplex & per partes consequentis nempe in propositione & antecedentis in assumptione, cujus rationis syllogismus est simplex: vel composita, totius nempe quæstionis in propositione, quæ ratio est compositi syllogismi.
units.tr: 108 The arrangement of the question with the third argument is either wholly simple, namely through the parts of the consequent in the proposition and of the antecedent in the assumption, and this kind of reasoning is the syllogism that is simple; or compound, namely of the whole question in the proposition, which is the principle of the compound syllogism.

units.la: 109 Si tertium argumentum in simplici syllogismo conlentiat cum utraqueparte quæstionis, tum syllogismus debet omnibus partibus affirmari: si cum consequente sola tum sola propositio, si cum antecedente sola, tum sola assumptio affirmatur & pars reliqua una cum conclusione negatur; quæ enim in aliquo tertio conveniunt, conveniunt etiam inter se, & quæ in eodem tertio dissentiunt, dissentiunt etiam inter se. ex utraque antecedentis parte negata nullus conficitur syllogismus: quoniam illud quod dissentit ab utraque parte quæstionis, neque consensionem neque dissensionem eorum inter se ostendere potest: similis est ratio utriusque particularis, nullam enim connexionem habent, sed scopas dissolutas & quatuor argumenta.
units.tr: 109 If, in a simple syllogism, the third argument agrees with each part of the question, then the syllogism must be affirmed in all its parts. If it agrees with the consequent alone, then only the proposition is affirmed; if with the antecedent alone, then only the assumption is affirmed, and the remaining part is denied together with the conclusion. For things which agree in some third thing agree also with one another, and those which disagree in the same third thing disagree also with one another. When the antecedent is denied on either side, no syllogism is formed, since what disagrees with either part of the question cannot show either agreement or disagreement between them. The reasoning is similar for each particular case: they have no connection, but are loose twigs and four arguments.

units.la: 110 In simplici dispositione prima illatio est quasi à specie ad genus & dicitur syllogismus contractus, quia tali forma semper argu- & per sitio- cujus mpo- opofi- ni. mplici quæ- nibus per fere occurrit ; in quo tertium argumentum est species vel quasi species prioris termini in quæstione: atque ideo præcedit in utraque parte; est enim angustior utroq; termino: ideo etiam assumptio affirmatur, in qua antecedens pars quæstionis tribuitur tertio argumento tanquam speciei suæ : idcirco etiam conclusio est particularis,quia species non infert secum genus nisi ex parte, vel particulariter ut pars ejus.
units.tr: 110 In the simple arrangement the first inference is, as it were, from species to genus, and is called the contracted syllogism, because it almost always occurs in such a form. In it the third argument is a species, or quasi-species, of the first term in the question, and therefore it precedes in each part, for it is narrower than either term. Hence also the assumption is affirmed, in which the antecedent part of the question is attributed to the third argument as to its species. For this reason the conclusion is also particular, because a species brings the genus with it only in part, or particularly, as its part.

units.la: 111 Secunda illatio est quasi à genere ad speciem, & vocatur primus explicatus; argumentum enim est quiddam consusius quam vel consequens vel antecedens; atque ideo sequitur in utraque parte; ideo etiam concludit semper negative, quia consensio generalis non efficit consensionem specialem, sed dissensio generalis dissensionem efficit specialem.
units.tr: 111 The second inference is, as it were, from genus to species, and is called the first explicated. For the argument is somewhat more confused than either the consequent or the antecedent, and therefore it follows in each part. For the same reason it always concludes negatively, because a general agreement does not produce a special agreement, but a general disagreement produces a special disagreement.

units.la: 112 Tertia illatio est quasi ab affectione medii alicujus inter genus & speciem, ad affectionem eorum inter se, & dicitur explicatus secundus; in quo argumentum tertium est angustius quid, & quasi species consequentis, atque ideo praecedit in propositione, & latius quid vel quasi genus antecedentis, atque ideo sequitur in assumptione: quia consensio medii cum superio-
units.tr: 112 The third inference is, as it were, from the affection of some middle between genus and species to their affection towards each other, and is called the second explicated. In it the third argument is narrower, and as it were a species of the consequent, and therefore it precedes in the proposition; and it is broader, or as it were a genus of the antecedent, and therefore it follows in the assumption, because agreement of the middle with the superior term does not make it agree with the inferior,

units.la: re non efficit illud cum inferiore confentire, nisi idem etiam cum inferiore confentiatjneq; dissensio ejus ab inferiore,& consensio cum superiore, facit ut illa inter fe dissentiant, ut animal, homo, equus.
units.tr: unless the same also agrees with the inferior; nor does its disagreement with the inferior, together with its agreement with the superior, make those two disagree with each other, as in animal, man, horse.

units.la: 113 In istis explicatis quoniam consequens pars quaestionis habet rationem vel generis vel speciei ad tertium argumentum,& ejus vi debet applicari ad antecedentem, ideo propositio debet esse generalis; vel propria quæ ad generalis rationem accedit: conclusio autem est vel specialis vel propria, si antecedentis alterutra pars talis fuerit: quia medium nullum affectionem extremorum inter se ostendere potest ulterius quam afficitur ipsum erga utrumque.
units.tr: 113 In these explicated forms, since the consequent part of the question has the character of genus or species in relation to the third argument, and by its force must be applied to the antecedent, the proposition must therefore be general, or proper, which approaches the character of the general. The conclusion, however, is either special or proper, if either part of the antecedent is of that kind, because the middle can show the affection of the extremes towards each other no further than it is affected towards each of them.

units.la: Sic fuit Syllogismus Simplex.
units.tr: Thus was the Simple Syllogism.

units.la: 114 In compohta syllogismi dispositione quaestio & argumentum simul ingrediuntur propositionem: necesse ergo est, ut tota vis illationis in eadem comprehendatur: hoc vero fieri non potest in simplici axiomate, nec proprie in negato; quare syllogismi compositi propositio debet esse affirmata & composita.
units.tr: 114 In the composite arrangement of a syllogism, the question and the argument both enter the proposition. It is therefore necessary that the whole force of the inference be contained in it. This cannot happen in a simple axiom, nor properly in a negated one. Hence the proposition of a composite syllogism must be affirmative and compound.

units.la: 115 Ex propositione vel assumitur tertium argumentum, ut concludatur quaestio: vel tollitur tertium argumentum in assumptione ut tollatur quæstio in conclusione: tollere autem est contradictionem ponere maxime directam.
units.tr: 115 From the proposition, either the middle term is assumed, so that the question is concluded, or the middle term is removed in the assumption, so that the question is removed in the conclusion. To remove is to posit the most direct contradiction.

units.la: 116 Requiritur etiam ut necessitas sit in illatione: hæc vero non proprie inest axiomati copulato, aut discreto, illud enim congregat, hoc segregat non necessario: in connexo autem necessaria est connexio; & in disjuncto est necessaria disjunctio: syllogismi igitur compositi propositio est aut connexa aut disjuncta, atq; adeo syllogismus ipse vel connexus vel disjunctus.
units.tr: 116 Necessity is also required in the inference. This does not properly belong to a copulative or disjunctive axiom, for the former joins and the latter separates without necessity. In a connected axiom the connection must be necessary, and in a disjunctive axiom the disjunction must be necessary. Therefore the proposition of a composite syllogism is either connected or disjunctive, and so the syllogism itself is either connected or disjunctive.

units.la: 117 In axiomate connexo quia consequens semper perhibetur verum idq; non absolute & simpliciter, sed ex suppositione antecedentis; idcirco non sequitur ratio, à remotione antecedentis ad remotionem consequentis, aut à positione consequentis ad positionem antecedentis; ex falso enim verum sequi potest: sed à positione antecedentis ad positionem consequentis, qui est connexus primus; & à remotione consequentis ad remotionem antecedentis, qui est connexus secundus, quia ex vero nil nisi verum sequitur.
units.tr: 117 In a connected axiom, the consequent is always held to be true, and not absolutely or simply, but on the supposition of the antecedent. Therefore no inference follows from the removal of the antecedent to the removal of the consequent, or from the positing of the consequent to the positing of the antecedent, for from a falsehood a truth may follow. But an inference does follow from the positing of the antecedent to the positing of the consequent, which is the first connected form; and from the removal of the consequent to the removal of the antecedent, which is the second connected form, because nothing but truth follows from truth.

units.la: 118 In disjuncto axiomate, quia necessitas non est ex suppositione aliqua sed absoluta; ideo valet hic illatio à remotione unius (sive antecedentis sive consequentis) ad positionem alterius, qui est disjunctus primus, & a positione unius ad remotionem alterius, qui est disjunctus secundus: ratio prioris est quia in axiomate disjuncto significatur unum esse verum: ratio alterius est, quia unicum.
units.tr: 118 In a disjunctive axiom, since the necessity is not based on some supposition but is absolute, the inference holds from the removal of one part (whether antecedent or consequent) to the positing of the other, which is the first disjunctive form, and from the positing of one part to the removal of the other, which is the second disjunctive form. The reason for the first is that a disjunctive axiom signifies that one part is true; the reason for the second is that only one can be true.

units.la: 119 Post Judicium sequitur Methodus; memoria enim non recte tenentur, nec ad memoriam recte disponuntur, de quibus prius non recte judicatur.
units.tr: 119 After Judgment comes Method, for things about which we have not judged rightly are not rightly retained in the memory, nor rightly arranged for memory.

units.la: 120 Ad methodū igitur tam inventio quā judicium concurrunt: & hac ratione methodus ultimo in loco docetur & exercetur.
units.tr: 120 Therefore both invention and judgment contribute to method, and for this reason method is taught and practised in the last place.

units.la: 121 Dispositio est axiomatum proprie, non argumentorum, nisi qua in axiomatis includuntur; neque syllogismorum, nisi quatenus axiomatis inserviunt.
units.tr: 121 Arrangement properly concerns axioms, not arguments, except insofar as they are contained in axioms; nor does it concern syllogisms, except insofar as they serve the axioms.

units.la: 122 Hæc axiomata debent semper esse homogenea, id est, ad eundem finem, & ad idem objectum sub eadem communi ratione spectantia.
units.tr: 122 These axioms must always be homogeneous, that is, they must bear on the same end and the same object under the same common aspect.

units.la: 123 Inter illa methodus observat ordinem prioris ac posterioris.
units.tr: 123 Among these, method observes the order of prior and posterior.

units.la: 124 Prius axioma cum posteriore conjungitur in methodo vi conjunctionis axiomaticæ, vel expressæ vel implicitæ.
units.tr: 124 In method, a prior axiom is joined with a posterior one by the force of an axiomatic conjunction, either expressed or implied.

units.la: 125 Prius in methodo est, quod clarius est, & lucem adfert prærequisitam ad sequentium intellectum. Tale autem est, quod prius est natura. 126 Prius & clarius natura, est vel causa respectu effecti, vel subjectum respectu adjuncti, vel commune respectu minus communis.
units.tr: 125 In method the prior is what is clearer and brings the light required for understanding what follows. Such is what is prior by nature. 126 What is prior and clearer by nature is either a cause with respect to its effect, or a subject with respect to its adjunct, or the common with respect to the less common.

units.la: 127 Cum autem progressio naturæ fit ab intentione finis, per media, ad assequutionem finis intenti; sic etiam artificiosa progressio est à fine & officio totius indicato per partes, ad finis & totius persectionem.
units.tr: 127 Since the progress of nature proceeds from the intention of an end, through means, to the attainment of the intended end, so too the artificial progress proceeds from the end and purpose of the whole, indicated through the parts, to the perfection of the ends and of the whole.

units.la: 128 Resolutio igitur & compositio non sunt duæ methodi, sed duæ actiones, quæ possunt in uno axiomate exerceri, & in hac unica methodo quodammodo observantur ambæ.
units.tr: 128 Resolution and composition, therefore, are not two methods but two actions, which can both be carried out in a single axiom; and in this one method both are in a sense observed.

units.la: 129 Cum scopus differentis non est simpliciter docere, sed delectare, movere, decipere, tum cryptis hujus methodi est adhibenda, transponendo, egrediendo, commorando, & omnia ad consilium dicentis, & auditorum ingenium prudenter accommodando.
units.tr: 129 Since the aim of a teacher is not simply to teach but also to delight, move and persuade, the tricks of this method must be employed: transposing, digressing, lingering, and prudently adapting everything to the purpose of the speaker and the disposition of the hearers.

units.la: PEr Logicam hunc in modum exercitam, intuemur quicquid rationis ullo modo circa ens quodcunque versatur. Occurrunt enim primo simplicia rationis, deinde eorum dispositio: simplicia illa vel sunt in ipso artificio & fabrica rei
units.tr: SINCE Logic is practised in this manner, we perceive whatever belongs to reason in any way concerning any being. For first the simple items of reason present themselves, and then their arrangement. Those simple items are either within the very craft and structure of the thing,
