units.la: vel extra illam. primo artificium rei nof[?] fe oportet priusquam testimonium de ill[?] vel accipiamus vel perhibeamus. sim[?] plicia in artificio rerum sunt vel prima[?] ria, vel secundaria quæ ex illis oriuntur[?] Illa primo intuemur ut sunt in sese, ante[?] quam comparamus cum aliis. & in sese[?] prius quid sint,quam quid non sint. qui[?] sint,tam in effentia & existentia,quam i[?] subsistentia, complementis & ornamen[?] tis. ubi sic intuiti fumus quicquid ad re[?] consummationem spe&at, inde videmu[?] non esse rem aliam, sed differre ab omni[?] bus; ab aliis leviore dissensione, ab alii[?] majore: neque tantum ab aliis rebus dif[?] ferre, sed etiam à nihilo, vel negation[?] fui. Post contemplationem hanc, qu[?] consideravimus quid res fit, & quid no[?] fit,comparamus eam cum aliis vel in gra[?] du, vel in natura sua, & reperimus æqua[?] lem, vel inæqualem, similem vel diffimi[?] lem. Cum sic intuiti fumus illa qu[?] prima sunt in artificio rei, fecundari[?] quadam consideratione ad ea deflec&imu[?] quæ ab iis oriuntur:contemplantes deno[?] minationem rei, ab argumento aliqu[?] essentiali vel complementali,una cum no[?] minis ejus ad alia cognatione: deind[?] communitatem illam, quam eadem re[?] habet in consentiendo cum multis : quomodo effectum unum fit respectu multarum causarum, vel una causa respectu multorum effectorum, vel unum adjunctum respectu multorum subjectorum, vel unum deniq; subjectum refp. ctu multorum adjunctorum.Hac autem in confideratione, videmus rem esse integrum, constans in suis membris, quæ nihil aliud sunt nisi symbola, seu comprehensiones causarum:deinde ut speciem certi generis, quod continet easdem speciei causas, quas membra continent integri, sed alio modo. Postremo postquam prima & secundaria contemplatione rem sumus intuiti, tam intra quam extra, sursum deorsumque, & ad latus speculando, & naturam ejus penitus quasi pervasimus ac penetravimus, um limitamus illam, & certa definitione fines essentiæ circumducimus: eosque vel proprios designamus materia scilicet & forma, in definitione perfecta: vel quasi circumscriptione linearum quousque pertingant ostendimus in descriptione. Post horum omnium contemplationem, tum de rei natura vel perhibere testimonium vel accipere licet secure.
units.tr: or outside it. First, we must know the craft of the thing before we either accept or give testimony about it. Simple items within the craft of things are either primary or secondary, the secondary arising from the primary. We regard the primary items first as they are in themselves, before we compare them with others, and in themselves we consider what they are before what they are not, and what they are in essence, in existence, in subsistence, and in their complements and ornaments. Having thus considered everything that pertains to the completion of the thing, we see from this that it is not another thing but differs from all others, some by a slighter difference, some by a greater; and that it differs not only from other things but even from nothing, or from its own negation. After this contemplation, in which we have considered what the thing is and what it is not, we compare it with others, either in degree or in nature, and find it equal or unequal, similar or dissimilar. Having thus considered the primary items of the craft of the thing, we turn by a secondary consideration to those that arise from them: contemplating the naming of the thing from some essential or complementary argument, together with its affinity to other names; then that community which the same thing has in agreeing with many things: how one effect is related to many causes, or one cause to many effects, or one adjunct to many subjects, or finally one subject to many adjuncts. In this consideration we see that the thing is a whole, consisting of its members, which are nothing other than the symbols or comprehensions of causes; then that it is a species of a certain genus, which contains the same causes of the species that its members contain as parts of the whole, but in another way. Lastly, after we have beheld the thing by primary and secondary contemplation, both within and without, above and below, and looking at its sides, and have as it were thoroughly traversed and penetrated its nature, we limit it and by a certain definition circumscribe the boundaries of its essence; and we designate these boundaries either as proper, namely matter and form, in a perfect definition, or we show, as it were by drawing lines around it, how far they extend, in a description. After all these things have been contemplated, it is then permitted to give or to receive testimony about the nature of the thing with confidence.

units.la: Hæc simplicia rationis postquam inventa fuerint, congruenter naturæ suæ dispo-
units.tr: Once these simple items of reason have been found, we arrange them in a manner congruent with their nature,

units.la: disponimus: idq; vel primario ad judicium vel secundario ad memoriam. Ad judicium tentandum disponuntur argu menta prout sua propria luce apparent; i in re manifesta sententia statim fertur sive illa conjungantur, sive disjungantur sive simpliciter, sive compositè hoc fiat si vero in dubio res versetur, tum ad lu cem & fidem faciendam, auxilium petitur à tertio aliquo argumento, quod cum illis disponitur, vel singulatim,ut in sim plici syllogismo,ut lumen singulis admoveatur; vel conjunctim, ut in compositi Post quam rerum coagitationem,certum judicium fertur tanquam de re manifest
units.tr: and we do this either primarily for judgment or secondarily for memory. For testing judgment, arguments are arranged as they appear in their own light. In a matter that is plain, a verdict is pronounced at once, whether the terms are joined or separated, and whether simply or in composite form. But if the matter is in doubt, then to produce light and conviction, aid is sought from some third argument, which is arranged with the others either singly, as in a simple syllogism, so that light is brought to each, or jointly, as in a composite one. After the agitation of the matter, a certain judgment is pronounced as if on a manifest thing.

units.la: Secundaria disposition ad memoriam e in methodo: qua disponuntur argumenti axiomatis inclusa, & vel per se, vel op aliorum judicata,eo ordine quem haber in sua natura.
units.tr: The secondary arrangement, for memory, is in method: in it the axioms contained in the arguments are arranged, either by themselves or as judged by others, in the order they have in their nature.

units.la: Videntes igitur Logicæ virtutes, sed lo studeamus oculum rationis nostræ pe hanc propriam ejus regulam direktur habere, & exerceamus nosmet ipsos a hanc rationem, ut omnia in omnibus d stinste contemplari, certo judicare, s constanter meminisse possimus.
units.tr: Therefore, seeing the virtues of Logic, let us strive to have the eye of our reason directed by this its proper rule, and let us exercise ourselves in this reason, so that we may be able to contemplate all things distinctly in all things, to judge with certainty, and to remember constantly.

units.la: FAllax consuetudo ( Amice Lector) modernos Philosophos ita dementat, ut contradicere antiquis scriptoribus ipsis religi͏�µ sit: etiam (quod magis mirere) in rebus à veritate maxime alienis. Verum enimvero cum justi viri & liberalis ingenii sit, veritatem ab omni injuria vindicare: Endantur tibi arma, quibus acies Metaphysicorum dissipetur, ac vera Philosophia (unicuique arti tribuendo, quod suum est) libertati suæ restituatur. Vale ac fruere, & postquam lumen veritatis tibi affulserit, mentem sophisticis tenebris involvi ne finito.
units.tr: A deceptive habit (friendly reader) so drives the modern philosophers out of their minds that it is a scruple for them to contradict the ancient writers, even (what you may wonder at more) in matters most remote from the truth. But since it belongs to a just and generous mind to defend truth against every wrong, let weapons be put on you by which the battle line of the Metaphysicians may be scattered, and true philosophy (giving each art what is its own) may be restored to its liberty. Farewell and enjoy yourself, and once the light of truth has shone upon you, do not allow your mind to be wrapped in sophistical shadows.

units.la: THESIS. I.
units.tr: THESIS. I.

units.la: GRave vitium est oculorum, quando ita hallucinantur, ut ea quæ simplicia sunt, pro geminis aut pluribus cernant. Sed gravior est hallucinatio mentis, quæ in plerisque perperam philosophantibus reperitur, dum unam simplicem doctrinam, duplicem, triplicem, & aliquando feptuplicem sibi & aliis repræsentant.
units.tr: It is a serious defect of the eyes when they so hallucinate that they see single things as double or multiple. But a hallucination of the mind is more serious, and it is found in most who philosophize badly, when they present to themselves and to others one simple doctrine as two, three, and sometimes even seven.

units.la: II. Vitium hoc in una eademq; disciplina cum admittitur (utpote si generis & speciei doctrina quinquies in logica tractetur, quod Peripateticis est solenne) tædium & nauseam parit intelligenti lectori. Magis tamen est noxium & intolerabile, quado integras disciplinas, variæ quæ non sunt, varias facit, ex qua hallucinatione Metaphysica tota dependet atq; consistit.
units.tr: II. When this fault is admitted within a single discipline (for example, when the doctrine of genus and species is treated five times in logic, as is customary among the Peripatetics), it breeds boredom and nausea in the intelligent reader. It is more harmful and intolerable, however, when they make distinct disciplines out of what are not distinct, and it is on this hallucination that all of Metaphysics depends and rests.

units.la: III. Quamvis autem incertæ fictionis nomen sit Metaphysica, quia necdum constat inter horum sacrorum mystas, quænam ex istis septem sententiis, quasde objecto ejus refert & exponit Suarez, disput. 1. sit recipienda, certa tamen præsumptio omnium fere Metaphysicorum est, quod polliceantur suis lectoribus naturalem quandam Theologiam, aliam plane ab illa, quam supernaturali revelatione traditam habemus in sacra scriptura: quod in Ethnicis philosophis non est mirandum, sed neutiquam ferendum inter Christianos, qui Theologiam in Scripturis traditam suis omnibus partibus consummatam agnoscunt.
units.tr: III. Although Metaphysics is a name for an uncertain fiction, since it is still not settled among these initiates of the sacred mysteries which of the seven opinions that Suárez sets out and explains in Disputation 1, concerning its object, should be accepted, there is nonetheless a fairly certain presumption among almost all Metaphysicians: that they promise their readers a certain natural theology, wholly different from that which we have handed down by supernatural revelation in Sacred Scripture. This is not surprising in the pagan philosophers, but it is in no way to be tolerated among Christians, who acknowledge that the theology delivered in the Scriptures is complete in all its parts.

units.la: IV. Si de hac Theologia judicium ferendum sit, prout ab Aristotele (Metaphysicorum Papa) docetur, impietatis crimini subduci nullo modo potest; quia rerum humanarum non tantum providentiam, sed & scientiam Deo auferens, Metaphys. 12. & necessitatem naturalem in volendo & agendo ipsi tribuens, fatente ipso Suarez disput. 30. sec. 16. & futurorum omnium contingentium veritatem determinatam negans (quod idem Suarez, disp. 19. sec. 10. agnoscit) fundamentum religionis penitus evertit. Cui impiae sententiae (magna saltem ex parte) tribuendum videtur, quod quamvis ex schola Platonis ad Ecclesiam primitivam transfierint olim praestantissimi quique viri (Justinus, Origines, Augustinus &c.) vix unus tamen potest nominari, qui peripateticam antea professus philosophiam, fidei Christianae veritatem postea recepit. Adeo verum est, quod alicubi Melanchton habet: Non sapit (Christus palato Aristotelicis argutius infesto.
units.tr: IV. If we are to pass judgement on this theology, as Aristotle (the Pope of the Metaphysicians) teaches it, it cannot in any way be excused from the crime of impiety. For it takes away from God not only providence but also knowledge of human affairs (Metaphysics 12), and it ascribes to him natural necessity in willing and acting, as Suárez himself admits (Disp. 30, sec. 16), and it denies a determinate truth of all future contingent things (which Suárez too acknowledges, Disp. 19, sec. 10). In this way it utterly overthrows the foundation of religion. To this impious opinion (at least in large part) seems to be due the fact that, although the most distinguished men once passed from the school of Plato to the early Church (Justin, Origen, Augustine, and others), scarcely one can be named who, having previously professed Peripatetic philosophy, afterwards received the truth of the Christian faith. So true is that remark of Melanchthon somewhere: Christ does not savour of the palate that is too subtly hostile to Aristotelians.

units.la: V. Sed ut hoc largiamur, spectandam esse Metaphysicam prout jam à Christianis correcta est & limata, adhuc tamen arguendam eam dicimus praesumptionis imprimis adversus Theologiam Christianam, quatenus Dei & rerum divinarum tractationem arrogat sibi, & postea vanitatis, quatenus neque divini neque humani quidquam, id est, nihil omnino habet, quod dicere possit suum, aut sui proprium, aut circa quod suo jure occupetur.
units.tr: V. But even if we grant that Metaphysics is to be considered as it has now been corrected and polished by Christians, we still say that it must be challenged, first, for presumption against the Christian theology, inasmuch as it claims for itself the treatment of God and divine things; and second, for vanity, inasmuch as it has nothing at all, neither divine nor human, that it can call its own, or its proper possession, or that it can occupy by its own right.

units.la: VI. Contemplatio Dei (ait Suarez, disp. 1 sec. 5. n. 44. & sec. 6. num. 32.) proprius actus & praecipuus finis est Metaphysicae, in quo naturalis hominis beatitudo consistit. Sed 1. haec fictitia beatitudo taliis est, ut cum damnatorum hominum & ipsius Diaboli miseria consistere simul possit; Diabolus enim est summus Metaphysicus.
units.tr: VI. The contemplation of God (says Suárez, Disp. 1, sec. 5, n. 44, and sec. 6, n. 32) is the proper act and chief end of Metaphysics, in which the natural happiness of man consists. But, first, this fictitious happiness is of such a kind that it can coexist with the misery of damned men and of the Devil himself; for the Devil is the supreme Metaphysician.

units.la: 2. Si naturalis beatitudo hominis in actu proprio Metaphysicae consistat, tum Metaphysica perficit naturam hominis, quod fieri non potest nisi omnes defectus, obliquitates, & perturbationes naturales tollat, & justitiam afferat originalem & universalem.
units.tr: Second, if the natural happiness of man consists in the proper act of Metaphysics, then Metaphysics perfects the nature of man. This cannot happen unless it removes all natural defects, crookedness, and disturbances, and brings original and universal justice.

units.la: 3. Si beatitudo consisteret in concontemplatione, tum intellectuales virtutes majoris essent perfectionis, quam morales. 4. Si contemplatio Dei beatificaret, esset actus Metaphysicæ proprius, tum Metaphysica esset vitæ spiritualis & æternæ doctrina; ita ut non differret à Theologia Christiana, nisi gradu & modo. Hæc autem omnia & singula sunt perquam absurda.
units.tr: Third, if happiness consisted in contemplation shared with others, then the intellectual virtues would be of greater perfection than the moral virtues. Fourth, if the contemplation of God made one blessed, and were the proper act of Metaphysics, then Metaphysics would be the doctrine of spiritual and eternal life, so that it would differ from Christian theology only in degree and manner. But all of these, taken singly and together, are exceedingly absurd.

units.la: VII. Metaphysicam de Deo & rebus divinis tractare dicunt, quatenus possunt cognosci lumine naturali: Theologiam vero Christianam de eisdem agere, quatenus per divinam revelationem cognoscantur: illam tantum esse theoreticam, hanc etiam practicam.
units.tr: VII. They say that Metaphysics treats of God and divine things insofar as they can be known by the natural light, while Christian theology treats of the same things insofar as they are known through divine revelation; that the former is only theoretical, but the latter is also practical.

units.la: Adversus quas distinctiunculas hæc habemus dicenda. 1. hæc est generalis nota Metaphysicæ vanitatis, quod ipsamet confiteatur se nihil tractare absolute, sed tantum sub hoc aut illo respectu & modo idem explicare, quod alibi vel absolute vel sub alio respectu & modo tractatur. Scientiæ enim realis differentia specifica non potest esse modus aut respectus rationis in objecto, sed debet necessario esse aliquid reale. Hoc bene observat Scotus in prologo ad dist. Scientia non constituitur subjectum suum sub ratione reali, non est realis. Absolutum & respectivum non
units.tr: Against these little distinctions we have the following to say. First, this is the general mark of Metaphysical vanity: that it itself confesses it treats nothing absolutely, but only explains under this or that respect and manner the same thing which is treated elsewhere either absolutely or under another respect and manner. For the specific difference of a real science cannot be a mode or respect of reason in the object, but must necessarily be something real. Scotus observes this well in the prologue to his Distinctions: A science is not constituted by its subject under a real aspect; it is not real. The absolute and the relative do not

units.la: faciunt unum conceptum per se sed per accidens tantum. 2. Limitatio illa, quatenus possunt cognosci lumine naturali, denotat gradum tantum cognitionis, atque adeo non magis constituit speciem doctrinae, quam quatenus cognosci possunt a puero, ab homine rudi, parum sano, &c. magis & minus non variant speciem. Logica artificialis & naturalis non sunt duae Logicae, nec charitas viae & patriae, duae charitates.
units.tr: make one concept per se, but only per accidens. Second, that limitation insofar as they can be known by the natural light denotes only a degree of knowledge, and therefore constitutes no more a species of doctrine than insofar as they can be known by a child, by a rude man, by one of little sense, etc. Greater and less do not vary the species. Artificial logic and natural logic are not two logics, nor are the love of the road and the love of the homeland two loves.

units.la: 3. Lumine naturali nihil potest a priori cognosci de Deo, sed vel per effectus vel per argumentationem ab uno attributo ad aliud. teste Zuarez disp. 30. in prin. horum autem modorum prior, si Metaphysicus sit & non Theologicus, tum metaphysice tantum non Theologice dixit David: Caeli enarrant gloriam Dei: & Paulus, Ipsius invisibilia jam inde a condito mundo ex iis quae fecit mente perspecta videntur.
units.tr: Third, by the natural light nothing can be known a priori about God, but only through effects or through argument from one attribute to another, as Suárez testifies (Disp. 30, at the beginning). If the first of these methods belongs to a Metaphysician and not a theologian, then David spoke only metaphysically, and not theologically, when he said: The heavens declare the glory of God; and Paul, His invisible things have been clearly seen from the creation of the world, being understood through the things that are made.

units.la: Posterior autem modus ut a Theologia removeatur, oportet ut Metaphysici intercedicant Theologis usu rationis, quasi ignis & aquae, caeterarum omnium disciplinarum. 4. Revelatio est quidem causa efficiens Theologiae sacrae, sed non est ratio formalis eandem speciem constans, & ab aliis disciplinis essentialiter distinguens: Si enim alicui extra ordinem revelaret Deus Mathematicam, aut ipsam Metaphysicam, non idcirco suam speciem exueret & in aliam transfiret, sed eadem plane maneret, quæ jam est cum acquiritur naturali ratione. Lex Dei moralis per Mosen revelata, eadem plane est cum ea quæ in cordibus hominum dicitur inscripta, Rom. 2. 15. Æterna Dei potentia & divinitas, sive hominibus a Deo manifestata, Rom. 1. 19, 20. sive per homines revelata, sicut una & eadem res est, sic etiam unius ejusdemque disciplinæ. 5. Nihil est veri & certi de Deo & rebus divinis lumine naturali notum, quod non cognoscatur etiam ex divina revelatione, & eo nomine tractari debeat in Theologia sacra: quia ad perfectionem scientiæ spectat (ut Zuarez disp. 1. observat) integre atque complete subjectum suum considerare. nulla igitur necessitas adigit, ut quædam divina in alia disciplina tractentur, neque est philosophi, vel entia vel disciplinas absque necessitate multiplicare. 6. Ex eo ipso evinci potest Metaphysicam esse disciplinam imaginativam, quod fateatur se esse meram speculativam. Nulla etenim vera est scientia, quæ non eo tendit ut scientem dirigat in aliqua praxi. 7 Quicquid cognosci potest de Deo, illud sua natura ducit hominem ad Deum rite colendum. Apostolus ipse hoc diserte testatur de naturali cognitione Dei per effectus, quam sibi vendicant Metaphysici, quasi mancipio & nexu suam. Propterea quod cum Deum noverint, tamen ut Deum non glorificaverunt, neque gratias ei egerunt. Rom. 1. 21. Dignum est igitur omnii approbatione quod pohit Scotus in prologo ante citato: De Deo nulla potest esse scientia speculativa, necessario enim notitia ejus conformis est praxi aptitudinaliter. Et haec una forsan est causa, cur Metaphysici homines tam irreverenter saepe garriant de Deo & rebus divinis, quia professio ipsorum est nihil curare praxin, Dictat enim Theologia practica (ut Guilielmus Parisiensis loquitur) non tantum cavendum esse nobis, ne falsi aliquid dicamus vel sentiamus de Deo creatore benedicto, sed etiam timorate, & reverenter, & circumspectius examinatissimisque sermonibus loquendum esse nobis de ipso, qui nec speciem ullam nec suspicionem erroris habeant.
units.tr: The second method, however, if it is to be removed from theology, requires that the Metaphysicians should stand apart from the theologians in their use of reason, as fire and water stand apart, and from all other disciplines. Fourth, revelation is indeed the efficient cause of sacred theology, but it is not the formal reason that constitutes the same species and essentially distinguishes it from other disciplines. For if God were to reveal to someone, outside the ordinary way, mathematics or Metaphysics itself, it would not on that account put off its species and pass into another, but would remain entirely the same as it already is when acquired by natural reason. The moral law of God revealed through Moses is entirely the same as that which is said to be written in the hearts of men (Rom. 2.15); the eternal power and divinity of God, whether manifested to men by God (Rom. 1.19, 20) or delivered through men, is one and the same thing, and so it belongs to one and the same discipline. Fifth, nothing true and certain about God and divine things is known by the natural light that is not also known from divine revelation, and that should not therefore be treated in sacred theology, because it belongs to the perfection of a science (as Suárez observes, Disp. 1) to consider its subject wholly and completely. There is therefore no necessity compelling that certain divine things be treated in another discipline, nor is it the business of a philosopher to multiply beings or disciplines without necessity. Sixth, from this very point it can be shown that Metaphysics is an imaginary discipline, since it admits that it is purely speculative. For no science is true which does not tend to direct the one who knows it toward some practice. Seventh, whatever can be known about God, by its very nature leads man to worship God rightly. The Apostle himself testifies this plainly about the natural knowledge of God through effects, which Metaphysicians claim for themselves as if it were their property by purchase and bond: Because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God, nor gave thanks to him. (Rom. 1.21). Therefore what Scotus says in the prologue cited above deserves all approval: There can be no speculative science of God, for the knowledge of him is necessarily conformed to practice in its aptitude. And perhaps this is one cause why Metaphysicians so often chatter irreverently about God and divine things: their profession is to care nothing for practice. For practical theology (as William of Paris puts it) dictates not only that we must take care not to say or think anything false about God the blessed Creator, but also that we must speak of him fearfully and reverently and more cautiously, with most carefully examined words, which have neither any appearance nor any suspicion of error.

units.la: Theologia metaphysicæ hunc in modum profligata, sequitur ut ejusdem vanitas in cæteris ca- pitibus breviter indicetur.
units.tr: Since metaphysics has been overthrown in this way, its vanity in the remaining chapters is now briefly pointed out.

units.la: VIII. Versatur (ut aiunt) circa ens, quatenus est ens reale. Ens autem vel summitur ut participium, & sic idem notat quod actu existens, vel ut nomen, & sic notat essentiam rei. Essentia autem est natura cujusque rei quæ per definitionem explicatur. Suarez disp. 2. Quibus verbis, hic neotericorum omnium, qui hujus sectæ sunt, Patriarcha clare satis testatur, doctrinam hanc totam de ente quatenus est ens ad illam disciplinam pertinere, cujus est natura, essentiæ, & definitionis doctrinam generalem explicare, id est, ad logicam. Non temere igitur Suarez disp. 1. 1. præmonuit, Metaphysicam singularem quandam connexionem habere cum Dialectica.
units.tr: VIII. It is concerned (as they say) with being, insofar as it is real being. Being, however, is taken either as a participle, and then it means what actually exists, or as a noun, and then it signifies the essence of a thing. Essence is the nature of each thing, which is explained by definition. Suarez, disp. 2. In these words the patriarch of all the modern writers of this school bears clear witness that this whole doctrine of being, insofar as it is being, belongs to that discipline whose task is to explain the general doctrine of nature, essence and definition, that is, to logic. Suarez therefore did not without reason warn, in disp. 1, that metaphysics has a certain peculiar connection with dialectic.

units.la: IX. Tres sunt passiones vel affectiones Entis, ait Suarez disp. 3. Unum, verum, bonum. Quod neq; verum est, quia aliæ fingi possunt affectiones æque propriæ entis omnis atq; istæ, ut durabile, ubi, potens, differens, collatum, antecedens, consequens, &c. neque pertinent affectiones illæ ad Metaphysicam, sed Logicam, sicut statim apparebit.
units.tr: IX. There are three passions or affections of being, says Suarez, disp. 3: one, true, good. This is not true, because other affections just as proper to every being can be imagined, such as durable, located, powerful, differing, compared, prior, posterior, etc. Nor do those affections belong to metaphysics but to logic, as will immediately appear.

units.la: X. Tam sublimia quidem subinde loquuntur de affectionibus istis transcendentalibus, ut omnem rationem infra se relinquant. Unū tradunt cui non opponitur multiplex, verum cui non opponitur falsum, & bonum cui non opponitur malum. Sic Suarez disp. 4. unum ut importat negationem multitudinis seu plurium, non intrat rationem formalem unius transcendentis. & disp. 9. in rebus extra intellectum non est propria aut rigorosa falsitas, & disp. 11. num. 20. bonum & malum secundum communes rationes non habent perfectam & completam oppositionem.
units.tr: X. Indeed, they sometimes speak so loftily of these transcendental affections that they leave all reason far beneath them. They teach that the one is that to which the many is not opposed, the true is that to which the false is not opposed, and the good is that to which evil is not opposed. So Suarez, disp. 4: the one, as it implies the negation of multitude or of many, does not enter into the formal notion of the transcendental one; and disp. 9: in things outside the intellect there is no proper or strict falsity; and disp. 11, no. 20: good and evil, according to common notions, do not have a perfect and complete opposition.

units.la: XI. Sed tamen ad se redeuntes unum docent esse, quod habet certam & determinatam & indivisam entitatem, convenire enti ex vi solius entitatis, ejus adjuncta negatione. disp. 4. f. 3. n. 8. disp 5. f. 1. n. 4. Cum igitur certae & determinatae entitatis ratio nihil aliud sit quam ejus definitio, sequitur unitatem istam transcendentalem esse mere logicae considerationis. Quamvis autem unitatis hujus ratio in definitione explicetur, ejus tamen principium (sicut & definitionis) petendum est ex entitatis & essentiae constitutivis causis. Accuratissime igitur observatur à P. Ramo logicae cap. 10. ad finem: Omnes modos unitatis ad consentaneorum argumentorum categoriam tanquam ad simplices fontes referri debere, & distinctionum modos ad categoriam dissentaneorum.
units.tr: XI. Yet, returning to themselves, they teach that the one is that which has a certain, determinate and undivided entity, which belongs to being from the force of its entity alone, with the negation added. Disp. 4, f. 3, no. 8; disp. 5, f. 1, no. 4. Since, then, the notion of a certain and determinate entity is nothing other than its definition, it follows that this transcendental unity belongs to logical consideration alone. Although the notion of this unity is explained in the definition, its principle, however (as also that of the definition), must be sought from the constitutive causes of entity and essence. Ramus observes this most accurately in his Logic, chapter 10, near the end: All modes of unity ought to be referred to the category of agreeing arguments as to their simple sources, and the modes of distinction to the category of disagreeing ones.

units.la: XII. Veritatem omnem in significando ad Dialecticam pertinere, disertis verbis faretur Suarez disp. 8. Et veritatem cognitionem esse in judicio: Veritatem etiam in essendo vel transcendentalem explicari posse per modum vel aptitudinalis vel actualis conformitatis ad illud judicium vel intellectum cognoscentem, quatenus unaquæque res apta nata est verâ sui æstimationem conferre respectu intellectus, & à veritate cognitionis translatum esse nomen veri ad significandâ proprietatem cujuslibet entis realis, quæ etiam ex communi omnium consensu consistit in conformitate inter rem & intellectum, sive sit intellectus ad rem, sive rei ad intellectū. Ex quibus omnibus manifeste sequitur (quod etiam Contarenus primæ philosoph. lib. 3 agnoscit) veritatem omnē proprie loquendo esse in compositione & divisione intellectus, i.e. in affirmatione & negatione axiomatica, quæ ad logicam ab omnibus referuntur. Suarez etiam disp. 10. s. 1. n. 19. fatetur, veritatem esse conditionem consequentem vel concomitantem objectum intellectus potius, quam formaliter illud consistuentem tuentem uentem: quod contra effet, si res essent vere per se, ante judicium intellectus.
units.tr: XII. Suarez, disp. 8, plainly admits that all truth in signifying pertains to dialectic. And truth of cognition lies in judgment. Truth in being, or transcendental truth, can also be explained by way of either aptitudinal or actual conformity to that judgment or to the knowing intellect, insofar as each thing, fitted and born to yield its true estimate with respect to the intellect, and the name of truth has been transferred from the truth of cognition to signify the property of any real being, which also, by the common consent of all, consists in conformity between thing and intellect, whether it is the intellect's conformity to the thing or the thing's to the intellect. From all these things it clearly follows (as Contarenus also acknowledges in the third book of his First Philosophy) that all truth, properly speaking, lies in the composition and division of the intellect, that is, in axiomatic affirmation and negation, which everyone refers to logic. Suarez also admits in disp. 10, sect. 1, no. 19, that truth is a condition following upon or accompanying the object of the intellect, rather than formally constituting it; which would be otherwise if things were true in themselves, before the judgment of the intellect.

units.la: XIII. Bonum absolute sumptum (ait Suarez disp. 10.) nihil aliud est quam perfectum, quam ens ipsum. Bonum alicui vel alicui conveniens est passio entis. Ex quibus constat (addit ipsemet Suarez sect. 2.) bonum importare habitudinem causae finalis, & rationem finis. Nihil clarius dici potest ad Logicam rationem boni declarandam.
units.tr: XIII. The good taken absolutely (says Suarez, disp. 10) is nothing other than the perfect, which is being itself. The good, belonging to someone or something, is an affection of being. From these things it is evident (Suarez himself adds, sect. 2) that the good implies the relation of a final cause and the character of an end. Nothing clearer can be said to explain the logical notion of the good.

units.la: XIV. Praeter ens, qua ens, & istas proprietates (ut appellantur) entis, Metaphysica nihil omnino tractandum habet, nisi velit de omnibus rebus & earum specialibus proprietatibus considerare, & hac ratione omnes alias scientias devorare, quod nonnullis Metaphysicis aequum & justum habetur, apud Suarez disput. 1. f. 2. n. 2. nam media illa via Suarezii (qui vult ens a Metaphysica considerari, non ut omnino praecisum sed etiam ut totum potentiale, prout includit aliquo modo inferiora, atque adeo aliquas inferiorum rerum proprietates, sed non omnes) haec inquam via gratis insistitur a quibusdam contra omnem rationem. Fatetur enim Suarez disp. 1. f. 2. n. 14. uxta principium illud ex quo quaedam rationes inferiores tractantur, alias etiam tractari debere, de quibus nihil potest in Metaneorum argumentorum categoriam tanquam ad simplices fontes referri debere, & distinctionum modos ad categoriam differ-entium.
units.tr: XIV. Apart from being as being, and those properties (as they are called) of being, metaphysics has absolutely nothing to treat, unless it wishes to consider all things and their special properties, and in this way to devour all the other sciences. Some metaphysicians hold this to be fair and just, according to Suarez, disp. 1, f. 2, no. 2. For that middle way of Suarez (who wishes being to be considered by metaphysics not as wholly abstracted but as wholly potential, insofar as it includes in some way the inferior things, and so some but not all of the properties of inferior things), this way, I say, is pursued in vain by some, against all reason. For Suarez admits, disp. 1, f. 2, no. 14, that according to the principle by which some inferior notions are treated, others too ought to be treated, of which nothing can properly be said in metaphysics; such as the common notion of living, knowing, understanding, etc.

units.la: XII. Veritatem omnem in significando ad Dialecticam pertinere, disertis verbis fatetur Suarez disp. 8. Et veritatem cognitionis esse in judicio: Veritatem etiam in essendo vel transcendentalem explicari posse per modum vel aptitudinalis vel actualis conformitatis ad illud judicium vel intellectum cognoscentem, quatenus unaquaeque res apta nata est vera sui aestimationem conferre respectu intellectus, & a veritate cognitionis translatum esse nomen veri ad significandam proprietatem cujuslibet entis realis, quae etiam ex communi omnium consensu consistit in conformitate inter rem & intellectum, sive sit intellectus ad rem, sive rei ad intellectum.
units.tr: XII. Suarez, disp. 8, plainly admits that all truth in signifying pertains to dialectic. And truth of cognition lies in judgment. Truth in being, or transcendental truth, can also be explained by way of either aptitudinal or actual conformity to that judgment or to the knowing intellect, insofar as each thing, fitted and born to yield its true estimate with respect to the intellect, and the name of truth has been transferred from the truth of cognition to signify the property of any real being, which also, by the common consent of all, consists in conformity between thing and intellect, whether it is the intellect's conformity to the thing or the thing's to the intellect.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus manifeste sequitur (quod etiam Contarenus primae philosophi lib. 3 agnoscit) veritatem omne proprie loquendo esse in compositione & divisione intellectus, i.e. in affirmatione & negatione axiomatica, quae ad logicam ab omnibus referuntur. Suarez etiam disp. 10. sect. 1. n. 19. fatetur, veritatem esse conditionem consequentem vel concomitantem objectum intellectus potius, quam formaliter illud constituentem. uentem: quod contra effet, si res essent ve- æ per se, ante judicium intellectus.
units.tr: From all these things it clearly follows (as Contarenus also acknowledges in the third book of his First Philosophy) that all truth, properly speaking, lies in the composition and division of the intellect, that is, in axiomatic affirmation and negation, which everyone refers to logic. Suarez also admits in disp. 10, sect. 1, no. 19, that truth is a condition following upon or accompanying the object of the intellect, rather than formally constituting it. following: which would be otherwise if things were true in themselves, before the judgment of the intellect.

units.la: XIII. Bonum absolute sumptum (ait Suarez disp. 10.) nihil aliud est quam persectum, quam ens ipsum. Bonum alteri vel alicui conveniens est passio entis. Ex quibus constat (addit ipsemet Suarez sect. 2.) bonum importare habitudinem causæ finalis, & rationem finis. Nihil clarius dici potest ad Logicam rationem boni declarandam. XIV. Præter ens, qua ens, & istas proprietates (ut appellantur) entis, Metaphysica nihil omnino tractandum habet, nisi velit de omnibus rebus & earum specialibus proprietatibus considerare, & hac ratione omnes alias scientias devorare, quod nonnullis Metaphysicis æquum & justum habetur, apud Suarez disput. 1. f. 2. n. 2. nam media illa via Suarezii (qui vult ens a Metaphysica considerari, non ut omnino præcisum sed etiam ut totum potentiale, prout includit aliquo modo inferiora, atque adeo aliquas inferiorum rerum proprietates, sed non omnes) hæc inquam via gratis insistitur a quibusdam contra omnem rationem. Fatetur enim Suarez disp. 1. f. 2. n. 14. uxta principium illud ex quo quædam rationes inferiores tractantur, alias etiam tractari debere, de quibus nihil potest in MeMetaphysica dici convenienter; ut communis ratio viventis, cognoscentis, intelligentis, &c.
units.tr: XIII. The good taken absolutely (says Suarez, disp. 10) is nothing other than the perfect, which is being itself. The good belonging to another or to someone is an affection of being. From these things it is evident (Suarez himself adds, sect. 2) that the good implies the relation of a final cause and the character of an end. Nothing clearer can be said to explain the logical notion of the good. XIV. Apart from being as being, and those properties (as they are called) of being, metaphysics has absolutely nothing to treat, unless it wishes to consider all things and their special properties, and in this way to devour all the other sciences. Some metaphysicians hold this to be fair and just, according to Suarez, disp. 1, f. 2, no. 2. For that middle way of Suarez (who wishes being to be considered by metaphysics not as wholly abstracted but as wholly potential, insofar as it includes in some way the inferior things, and so some but not all of the properties of inferior things), this way, I say, is pursued in vain by some, against all reason. For Suarez admits, disp. 1, f. 2, no. 14, that according to the principle by which some inferior notions are treated, others too ought to be treated, of which nothing can properly be said in metaphysics; such as the common notion of living, knowing, understanding, etc.

units.la: XV. Ratio causæ,& specierum,ac modorum ejus in omni Logica ( quamvis Metaphysicis hominibus conscripta )plene solet tractari. Neque ulla reddi potest ratio quare unius rei eædem definitiones, distributiones, & proprietatum explicationes in duabus aut pluribus tradantur disciplinis. Res ipsæ quæ sunt causæ,fparsim in omnibus artibus docentur. Relationem & habitudinem causæ ad suum essectum, Logicæ considerationis esse nemo Logicus negabit. Causationem autem vel causalitatem & influxum ipsum, quod est proprium fundamentum relationis,realem ab ipsa distinctionem habere negat Suarez, difp. 47. f. 3.
units.tr: XV. The notion of cause, with its species and modes, is customarily treated fully in every Logic, although it was written by Metaphysicians. Nor can any reason be given why the same definitions, divisions and explanations of the properties of one thing should be delivered in two or more disciplines. The things that are causes are taught scattered through all the arts. No logician will deny that the relation and respect of a cause to its effect belong to logical consideration. But Suarez, disp. 47, sect. 3, denies that causation or causality, and the influx itself, which is the proper foundation of the relation, has a real distinction from the relation.

units.la: XVI. Entis finiti ratio definitione explicatur: infiniti autem entis perfectionem, fc. totam omnium finitorum in continentis eminenter ( sicut Suarez nonnem illam exponit difp.28.f.1.11.18.) Theologia sola proponit:
units.tr: XVI. The notion of finite being is explained by definition. Only Theology sets forth the perfection of infinite being, namely that of the whole of all finite things contained eminently in it (as Suarez himself expounds that notion in disp. 28, sect. 1, nn. 11 and 18).

units.la: XVII. Esse effentia & existentia entis creati in communi & abstracta sua ratione,Logica causarum doctrina accurate satis exponit.
units.tr: XVII. The logical doctrine of causes expounds quite accurately enough the being, essence and existence of created being in its common and abstract notion.

units.la: XVIII. De suppositc in divina natura
units.tr: XVIII. On the supposit in the divine nature

units.la: ex principiis naturalibus fere nihil dici posse fatetur Suarez, disp. 34. sect. 1. In natura creata, suppositi vel personæ doctrina ad eandem scientiam spectat cum natura intellectuali, & ipsa anima rationali, cuius considerationem à Metaphysica ad Physicam remittit Suarez, disp. 1. sect. 2. n. 18.
units.tr: Suarez admits that almost nothing can be said about it from natural principles. In created nature, the doctrine of the supposit or person belongs to the same science as the intellectual nature and the rational soul itself, whose consideration Suarez refers from Metaphysics to Physics (disp. 1, sect. 2, n. 18).

units.la: XIX. Decem illa genera, vel prædicamenta, in quæ forte fortuna potius quam certa ratione dividunt Peripatetici ens creatum, utrum ad Logicam an Metaphysicam, vel quomodo ad utramque spectat, penes ipsos prædicamentales Philosophos agitatur adhuc lis magna. Sed integris arbitris facile apparebit unam & eandem rem non posse esse variorum integrorum membrum, & decem ista tam heterogenea capita ad nullam unam disciplinam pertinere: sed substantiam creatam absolute spectatam, una cum qualitate sua esse Physicæ considerationis; Quantitatem simili ratione objectum proprium Mathesios; relationem esse Logicum argumentum; actionem pertinere ad effectum; passionem ad subjectum; ubi ad subjectum & habitum, quando ad Adjunctum Logicum.
units.tr: XIX. Those ten genera, or categories, into which the Peripatetics divide created being, by chance rather than by sound reasoning, are still the subject of a great dispute among the categorical philosophers themselves: whether they belong to Logic or to Metaphysics, or how they belong to either. But to unprejudiced judges it will easily appear that one and the same thing cannot be a member of several wholes, and that these ten heterogeneous heads belong to no single discipline. Rather, created substance considered absolutely, together with its quality, belongs to physical consideration; quantity, in a similar way, is the proper object of mathematics; relation is a logical subject; action belongs to the effect; passion to the subject; where it belongs to the subject and to habit, when to the logical adjunct.

units.la: Ergo
units.tr: Therefore

units.la: Revera Commentarius ille qui dicitur τὰ μετὰ τὰ φυσικά ad docendum vel discendum nihil habet compendii. Plutarch. in Alexand. Theologiam vero, quam Aristoteles in Metaphysica docet, impietatem omnium impietatum maxime detestabilem & execrabilem esse confirmo; flagitiumque inexpiabile statuo, in Christianis quibusdam scholasticis, etiam (quod magis mirere) purioris Theologiæ studiosis, confirmare publicatis scriptis, Metaphysicam Aristotelis Christianæ religionis tanquam columnam quandam esse. Petrus Ramus in præfat. ad Scholas Metaph. Hisce adjungimus illud Nicolai Beraldi Anno 1516. Qui sophisticis nugis, & frivolis argutiis dediti, non rebus ipsis, sed rerum umbris falsisque imaginibus inhærent, longe falluntur, totaque (quod dicitur) errant via. Non enim studiosorum ingenia exacuunt captiunculæ istæ, & tricæ spinosæ, (ut plerisque persuasum est) sed mentis succum omnem exhauriunt, adeoque à pietatis studio abduxere nonnullos.
units.tr: Indeed, that commentary which is called "the things after the natural things" [τὰ μετὰ τὰ φυσικά] has no brevity for teaching or learning. Plutarch, in the life of Alexander. But I affirm that the theology which Aristotle teaches in the Metaphysics is the most detestable and accursed of all impieties; and I declare it an inexpiable crime that certain Christian scholastics, even (which you may marvel at more) those devoted to purer theology, should maintain in published writings that the Metaphysics of Aristotle is a kind of pillar of the Christian religion. Peter Ramus, in the preface to the Metaphysics Schools. To these we add the saying of Nicolaus Beraldus, 1516: Those who are devoted to sophistical trifles and frivolous subtleties cling not to the things themselves but to the shadows of things and false images; they are greatly mistaken and wander, as the saying goes, completely off the road. For those little captious tricks and thorny snares do not sharpen the wits of students, as most have been persuaded, but drain all the juice of the mind, and so have drawn some away from the pursuit of piety.

units.la: Disputatio Theologica, De Perfectione SS. Scriptura.
units.tr: Disputation on Theology, On the Perfection of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Thesis I.
units.tr: Thesis I.

units.la: PErfectio Sacrae Scripturae est, ejus omnimoda sufficientia in tradenda tota voluntate divina, qua spectat ad bene beatéque vivendum.
units.tr: The perfection of Holy Scripture is its complete sufficiency in delivering the whole divine will, insofar as it concerns living well and blessedly.

units.la: II. Quia autem haec perfectio vel sufficientia prout absolutè sonat, tam qualitativum, quàm quantitatum est, sive tam extensivam, quàm extensivam plenitudinem sufficientiae notat; nos imprasentiarum de extensiva aut quantitativa perfectione sus acturi.
units.tr: II. But since this perfection or sufficiency, taken absolutely, is both qualitative and quantitative, that is, it denotes both an intensive sufficiency and an extensive fullness of sufficiency, we shall for the present treat only of the extensive or quantitative perfection.

units.la: III. Possumus autem hanc perfectionem Sacrae Scripturae concipere, tum qua in se perfecta, tum qua talis est respectu directionis atque institutionis nostrae. Est ea perfecta in se, 1. quia nihil addi vel potest debet, ac proinde est undequaque perfecta, Psal. 19. vers. 8. Doctrina Jehovae integra est restituens animam, Deut. 9. v. 2, nec dite ad verbum illud quod ego praecipio vobis, vobis, neq; detrahite de eo, Apoc.22.v.18, 19. Vnâ teflor euivs audienti verba prophetiæ hujus: si quis adjecerit ad hæc, &c. Prov. 30.6. nè adjicito ad verba ejus, ut non corripiat te, & efficiarus mendax.
units.tr: III. We may conceive this perfection of Holy Scripture both as it is perfect in itself and as it is such with respect to our direction and instruction. It is perfect in itself: (1) because nothing can or ought to be added to it, and therefore it is perfect in every way. Psalm 19:8: "The teaching of the LORD is whole, restoring the soul." Deut. 4:2: "You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take away from it." Rev. 22:18, 19: "I testify to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to these things, etc." Prov. 30:6: "Do not add to his words, lest he rebuke you and you be found a liar."

units.la: IV. Exinde etiam secundò perfectio ipsius Scripturæ patet,quòd non alium autorem quàm ipsum sapientissimum Deum (à quo nihil nisi perfectum, aut saltem sufficiens ad illum finem cui destinatur provenire potest) immediatè habeat. Hinc illud adeò tritum in prophetiis particulatibus, eloquium Jehovæ, quod æque locum habet in aliis omnibus particulis Scripturæ, 2 Pet. 1. v. 20.
units.tr: IV. Secondly, the perfection of Scripture itself is evident from this, that it has as its immediate author none other than the most wise God himself (from whom nothing but what is perfect, or at least sufficient for the end to which it is directed, can come). Hence that commonplace about the particular prophecies, "the utterance of the LORD," which holds equally for all other parts of Scripture: 2 Pet. 1:20.

units.la: V. Huic veritati non adversatur, quod verbum Dei scriptis fuerit mandatum per amanuenses humanos. Utebatur enim ipsis Deus tanquam instrumentis aut nuntiis publicis in revelanda propria voluntate, Jer. 1. 9. Extendens Jehova manum suam ad os meum, dixit, Ecce indo verba mea in ore tuo. Fiebat tamen illud gradatim, sicut ipsius summæ sapientiæ maxime consentaneum fuit, cum suavi illa verbum attemperatione, quæ maximè conveniebat personæ & conditioni scribentis.
units.tr: V. This truth is not undermined by the fact that the word of God was committed to writing through human scribes. For God used them as instruments or public messengers in revealing his own will, Jer. 1:9: "The LORD stretched out his hand and touched my mouth, and said, Behold, I have put my words in your mouth." Yet this was done gradually, as was most fitting to supreme wisdom, with that gentle adaptation of the word which best suited the person and condition of the writer.

units.la: VI. Ulterius etiam tertiò, Scriptura perfectio elucet ex titulis perfectionem notantibus, ut quod sit, Pfal. 19 v. 9, 10. Testimonium verax, mandatum rectum, ipsa veritas, &c. Rom. 1. 2. Scriptura sancta. Deut. 32. 47. Vita, sapientia, & prudentia ante oculos populorum, 4. 6. 2. Pet. 1. v. 19. Lucerna splendens in obscuro loco. Prov. 30. 5. Scutum recipientibus se ad ipsum, & c.
units.tr: VI. Thirdly, the perfection of Scripture further shines forth from the titles that denote perfection, such as: Ps. 19:9, 10: "the true testimony, the right commandment, the truth itself, etc."; Rom. 1:2: "the holy Scriptures"; Deut. 32:47: "life, wisdom, and prudence before the eyes of the peoples"; Deut. 4:6; 2 Pet. 1:19: "a lamp shining in a dark place"; Prov. 30:5: "a shield to those who take refuge in him, etc."

units.la: VII. Hactenus fuit perfectio Scripturae
units.tr: VII. So far the perfection of Scripture

units.la: in se considerata, sequitur ejusdem persectio, respectu directionis atque institutionis ostra. Respectu nostri dicitur perfecta tum copiam ac sufficientiam omnium praeceptorum in ea contentorum, quae aliquâ altem ratione ad nostram in hac vita, & singulis ejus actionibus (quatenus Deum, nos ipsos, aut proximum spectant) directionem pertinere possunt; tum etiam respectu efsectorum quae in nobis per verbum Sp. Sanctus operatur. Prior illa perfectio Regularis potest nuncupari.
units.tr: considered in itself; there follows its perfection with respect to our direction and instruction. With respect to us it is called perfect both in the abundance and sufficiency of all the precepts contained in it, which can pertain at least in some way to our direction in this life and in each of its actions (insofar as they concern God, ourselves, or our neighbour); and also with respect to the effects which the Holy Spirit works in us through the word. The former may be called the regular perfection.

units.la: VIII. Siquidem est Scriptura totalis non partialis Regula seu canon vivendi, & hoc de natura canonis ut nullam additionem aut detractionem admittat quia tamen Mensura (ut omnibus notum,) debet esse adaequate proportionata rei mensurandae. IX. Hinc necessario evincitur 1. (quoniam Scriptura pro subjecto vitam habet informandam, Pfal. 1. 19. v. 9, Joan. 6. 68. A 3 Joan.5.39.) eam undequaq; sufficientem esse ad eam cum omnibus actionibus persecte dirigendam. Quod & insuper ex notis hisce Scripturae locis plus quam manifestum evadit, Prov.6. 20,21,22,23. &
units.tr: VIII. For Scripture is the total, not the partial, rule or canon of living; and while this belongs to the nature of a canon, that it admits neither addition nor subtraction, nevertheless a measure (as is known to all) ought to be adequately proportioned to the thing measured. IX. From this it is necessarily shown, first (since Scripture has life as its subject to be formed, Ps. 119:9; John 6:68; John 5:39), that it is wholly sufficient to direct every action perfectly. This becomes more than plain also from these well-known passages of Scripture: Prov. 6:20–23, and

units.la: 2. Tim.3. 16,17. Psal. 119. v. 9. & 105. Psal.19. v.9. Deut. 6. 6,7,8,9, &c. Verba quae ego praecipio tibi hodie, acute ingeres filiis tuis, ac loqueris de eis cum sedes domi tuae, & cum ambulas per viam, cum cubas ac cum surgis, &c. Vid. significatur omnino, nullam actionem esse cujus directio non sit petenda ex verbo Dei.
units.tr: 2 Tim. 3:16, 17; Ps. 119:9; Ps. 105; Ps. 19:9; Deut. 6:6–9, etc.: "These words that I command you today shall be on your heart; you shall teach them diligently to your sons, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, when you lie down and when you rise, etc." Clearly this signifies that there is no action whose direction is not to be sought from the word of God.

units.la: X. Non desunt tamen multi, qui huic veritati temerario ausu sese opponant; ut sunt omnes illi qui huic verbo aliquid addere, vel detrahere studeant. Addere quidem conantur omnes illi, qui traditionibus <bl>παραδόσεις</bl>, nullum in Scriptura fundamentum habentibus, eandem, aut similem plane autoritatem, cum Scriptura, tribuunt, quales quidem sunt & Judaeorum Rabbini, & Pontificiorum Doctores.
units.tr: X. Yet there are not lacking many who rashly set themselves against this truth; such as all those who strive either to add to this word or to take away from it. Indeed, all those add who ascribe to traditions, which have no foundation in Scripture (παραδόσεις), the same or plainly similar authority as to Scripture; of this kind are both the rabbis of the Jews and the teachers of the Papists.

units.la: XI. Rabbini quidem, dum cabbalam (quam appellant) ejusdem esse autoritatis contendunt cum lege Mosaica, utpote quae eundem (ut illi quidem fabulantur) autorem agnoscat: Horum errorem notasse suffecerit cum ulteriori refutatione non indigeat.
units.tr: XI. The rabbis, indeed, while they contend that the Cabbala (as they call it) has the same authority as the Mosaic law, since it acknowledges (as they indeed fable) the same author: it will suffice to have noted this error, which does not need further refutation.

units.la: XII. Hisce tamen (ut & hoc obiter moneamus) suo modo suffragari videntur omnes illi qui statuunt sine Rabbinorum commentariis non posse nos pervenire ad solidum Divini eloquii sensum. Fatemur quidem & nos eos usui esse posse ad majorem S. linguae intelligentiam, quod ad verborum proprietates & significationes attinet; ad Scripturae vero genuinum sensum eruendum tantum abesse ut prosint, ut etiam (immane quantum!) officiant. Si modo verum sit (quod orientalium linguarum peritissimi pro me observarunt): Lege unum Joh. Rainold. in censura lib. Apocryph. lect. 149, citabit ille plures, illos manifestis fabulis contra mentem Scripturae confictis scatere. Non est igitur, quod facem ab illis accendamus, qui perfusi sunt spiritu soporis alti, ut loquitur Propheta, Iesa. 29. 10. Rom. 11. 8.
units.tr: XII. Yet these men (let us also remark this in passing) seem in their own way to lend support to all those who maintain that without the commentaries of the rabbis we cannot arrive at the solid sense of the divine utterance. We too admit that they may be of use for a greater understanding of the sacred tongue, as far as the proper meanings and significations of words are concerned; but for drawing out the genuine sense of Scripture they are so far from helping that they even hinder (how enormously!). That is, if it is true (as the most skilled in the oriental languages have observed on my behalf): read John Reynolds, in his censure of the Apocrypha, lecture 149; he will cite many of them, overflowing with obvious fables invented against the mind of Scripture. There is therefore no reason for us to kindle a torch from those "who have been poured over with the spirit of deep sleep," as the Prophet says, Isa. 29:10; Rom. 11:8.

units.la: XIII. Unicum est quod aliqua cum specie objici videtur, nimirum, Rabbinos magnam lucem nobis praebere ad explicationem caeremoniarum & rituum observatorum tempore legis in Ecclesia Mosaica. Ad quod tamen facilis est responsio. Primo omnes istas caeremonias a Mose ipso adeo accurate esse perscriptas ut ulterior earum explicatio non sit quaerenda. Fuit il-
units.tr: XIII. There is one objection which seems to have some appearance, namely, that the rabbis provide us with great light for explaining the ceremonies and rites observed in the time of the law in the Mosaic Church. To this, however, the answer is easy. First, all those ceremonies were set down by Moses himself so accurately that no further explanation of them need be sought. He was

units.la: le fidelis in totâ domo Dei, nihil omnino in ceremoniali lege tradenda omisit, omnes ad lebetes (quibus cinerem excipiebant) ad fuscinulas, ad forcipes usque recensuit. Exod. 27. v 3. Si quid postea additum fuerit, Judaicæ tribuendum superstitioni: in mandatis habuerunt ne ab exemplari recederent. Secundò verissimum est (adstipulantibus Doctoribus (nullibi Rabbinos magis delirasse, quam in multiplicandis ceremoniis, quod etiam Evangelistæ sæpissimè notarunt. Math. 15. 2. Marc. 7. 1, 2, 4. Tertio, ipsi Rabbini nihil de talibus rebus habuerunt, præter incertos rumores, quos à suis fabularum patribus acceperunt (qui potentosis quibusdam deliriis, & anilibus fabulis in totum sese dederunt.) vix enim exstant scripta ulla antiquorum Rabbinorum qui non fuerunt hostes Christi, & eo nomine maledicti, & expositi efficaciæ errorum ac mendaciorum.
units.tr: faithful in all the house of God; he omitted absolutely nothing in delivering the ceremonial law, and listed everything down to the pots (into which they received the ashes), the fire-forks, and the tongs. Exod. 27:3. If anything was added afterwards, it must be attributed to Jewish superstition; they were under command not to depart from the pattern. Secondly, it is most true (with the teachers agreeing) that nowhere have the rabbis raved more than in multiplying ceremonies, which the Evangelists also very often noted. Matt. 15:2; Mark 7:1, 2, 4. Thirdly, the rabbis themselves had nothing about such matters except uncertain rumours, which they received from the fathers of their fables (who gave themselves wholly over to certain powerful delusions and old wives' tales). For hardly any writings of the ancient rabbis survive which were not enemies of Christ, and on that account cursed, and exposed to the efficacy of errors and lies.

units.la: XIV. Ex hisce etiam liquet secundò, quid de traditionibus Papisticis sit sententi- endum, ac quantopere de via errent illi, dum statuant in Scripturis non contineri totam doctrinam, sive de fide, sive de moribus, sed insuper requiri etiam verbum Dei non scriptum, quale quidem (quod sciam
units.tr: XIV. From these things it is also clear, secondly, what we should think of Papist traditions, and how far they go astray in holding that the whole doctrine, whether of faith or of morals, is not contained in Scripture, and that an unwritten word of God is also required, from which conclusions about matters disputed in the Church must be drawn. Such a word, as far as I know, no longer exists.

units.la: am) jam non exstat, ex quo conclusiones de rebus in Ecclesia controversis deducendæ sint.
units.tr: Such a word, as far as I know, no longer exists, from which conclusions about matters disputed in the Church are to be drawn.

units.la: XV. Huic illorum perniciosissimo errori quod prætexant non inveniunt, nisi contra quædam Scripturæ testimonia (ut Joh. 16.21,25. 1.Cor.11.2. 2.Thess.3.6.) quibus quidem locis nihil continetur, quod vel minima specie pro ipsis facere possit, non agitur enim illis in locis de traditionibus non scriptis (quales Pontificii fingunt) sed vel de iis quæ postea scriptæ fuerunt, vel de iis quæ pro illa sola temporis ratione necessariæ fuerunt, vel denique de iis, quæ æque incertæ sunt Pontificiis ac nobis.
units.tr: XV. For this most pernicious error of theirs, which they put forward as a pretext, they find no support except in certain passages of Scripture (such as John 16:21, 25; 1 Cor. 11:2; 2 Thess. 3:6). Yet in none of these places is anything contained that could lend even the slightest appearance of support to them. These passages do not treat of unwritten traditions (of the kind the Papists invent), but either of things that were afterwards written down, or of things that were necessary only for the circumstances of that time, or finally of things that are equally uncertain to the Papists and to us.

units.la: XVI. Quales vero pleraque traditiones Papistarum sint, nemini obscurum est, ut Apostolicarum traditionum nomine obtrudantur simplicioribus, quale quiddam & olim tentarunt eorum parentes, teste Apost. 2. Thess. 2.v.2. Ne cito à mente dimoveamini, neque per spiritum neque per Epistolam tanquam per nos scriptam. Sin autem larva ipsis detrahatur, apparebit Apostolum genuinas illarum notas tradidisse, Col. 2. v.20. ut appareat ex illorum præceptis, Ne Esitaris neque Tetigeris. Quarum rerum non
units.tr: XVI. What sort of traditions the Papists' most of them are is obvious to everyone: they are foisted on simpler folk under the name of apostolic traditions. Their forebears once tried something of this sort as well, as 2 Thess. 2:2 attests: "Do not be quickly shaken in mind, neither by spirit, nor by letter, as if written by us." But if the mask is stripped from them, it will appear that the Apostle has given the genuine marks of these traditions at Col. 2:20, so that it is clear from their precepts: "Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch."

units.la: Lavit sivit nos esse ignaros idem Apostolus, 1. Tim. 4. v. 1, 2, 3. &c. diserte prædixit Spiritus fore, &c. Quid? ut posterioribus temporibus quidam desciscant a fide attenti spiritibus deceptoribus, ac doctrinis dæmoniorum, prohibentium contrahere matrimonium, jubentium abstinere a cibis, quos condidit Deus ad participationem cum gratiorum actione.
units.tr: Nor did the same Apostle leave us ignorant of these matters. In 1 Tim. 4:1–3 and following he plainly foretold that the Spirit would say that in later times some would fall away from the faith, giving heed to deceiving spirits and doctrines of demons, forbidding marriage and commanding abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving.

units.la: XVII. Cavendum tamen imprimis,ne dum traditiones non scriptas jure & ex præscripto Dei rejiciamus (Esai. 29. 13. Matth. 15. 9. Gal. 1. v. 7, 8. Col. 2. v. 20. 1. Tim. 1. v. 9.) omnes qualescunque scripturarum interpretationes pro traditionibus habeamus. Illæ enim perfectioni sacrarum literarum nihil detrahunt, sed modo tantum differunt a verbo Dei. Sunt enim & continent verbum Dei quod attinet ad sententiam, seu doctrinam ipsam; non tamen quoad verba quæ adhibentur ex hominum deliberatione. Adde quod tantum abest ut perfectioni Scripturarum quippiam detrahant, ut eam saltem quoad nos, per modum declarationis ac expositionis perfectiorem reddant. Illud fit, quia ex ipsa Scriptura, ope generalium artium Grammaticæ, Logicæ, & Rhetoricæ, tales explicationes eliciuntur. olus, dixit ribus tendeatriquos gra. s,ne ex 13. 20. crionii sa-
units.tr: XVII. Yet above all we must take care that, while we rightly and by God's command reject unwritten traditions (Isa. 29:13; Matt. 15:9; Gal. 1:7–8; Col. 2:20; 1 Tim. 1:9), we do not count as traditions all manner of interpretations of Scripture. For these detract nothing from the perfection of the holy letters; they differ from the word of God only in mode. For they are and contain the word of God as far as the sense or doctrine itself is concerned, though not as regards the words, which are chosen by human deliberation. Add that these interpretations are so far from detracting anything from the perfection of Scripture that they render it, at least for us, more perfect, by way of declaration and exposition. This happens because such explanations are drawn out of Scripture itself, by means of the general arts of grammar, logic and rhetoric. [illegible in the scan]

units.la: XVIII. Tertiò, ex hisce omnibus consequitur, neque istos Philosophos commodè posse excusari, qui sustinent (salva perfectione Scripturæ) defendere aliquam datri scientiam de Deo, aut bonis moribus, quæ ex S. Scriptura non sit petenda, aut secundum eam reformanda.
units.tr: XVIII. Thirdly, from all these things it follows that those philosophers cannot fairly be excused who maintain that (with the perfection of Scripture preserved) some knowledge of God, or of good morals, can be defended which is not to be sought from Holy Scripture or reformed according to it.

units.la: XIX. Horum illi nugas suas divendunt sub nomine Theologiæ naturalis, & Metaphysicorum titulo superbiunt. Hi morales Philosophi censentur. Egregiè scil. Rabbini habent suum קבלה & Pontificii suas traditiones, Metaphysici suam Theologiam. Hisce quidem opinionibus refutandis facile possum superseders: respondeant tamen Metaphysici, mont eatam; ntur quod rum uoad itioa ex ium ales II.
units.tr: XIX. These men sell their trifles under the name of natural theology and boast of the title of Metaphysicians; these are reckoned moral philosophers. Admirably, forsooth, the rabbis have their qabbalah, the Papists their traditions, and the Metaphysicians their theology. I could easily set aside the refutation of these opinions; yet let the Metaphysicians answer [the remainder is illegible in the scan].

units.la: XX. Primò, Utrum Theologia naturalis ex Scriptura non possit peti, quae naturam nostram errantem dirigit? Secundò, An si naturaliter cognoscere, sit cognoscere per effecta in sensus incurrentia ? utrum effecta Dei in creatione, conservatione, & gubernatione mundi nobis in Scripturis non sint revelata? nondum ita frontem perfricuerunt ut hoc negent, in cujus contemplatione saepissime versatur Israelitarum psaltes.ut Psal.8.v.9,5.Psal.147.v.8,9,16, 17, 18. 107.23,24,25. &c. Tertio, An non argumentatio ab uno ad aliud concessa sit Theologiæ (artium ac disciplinarum perfectissimæ) ac cuilibet alii morali aut naturali disciplinæ?
units.tr: XX. First: Can natural theology not be drawn from Scripture, which directs our erring nature? Secondly: If to know naturally is to know through effects that fall under the senses, are not God's effects in the creation, preservation and governance of the world revealed to us in Scripture? They have not yet so hardened their brow as to deny this, since the psalmist of Israel is so often occupied in contemplating it, as in Psal. 8:9, 5; Psal. 147:8, 9, 16, 17, 18; 107:23, 24, 25, etc. Thirdly: Is not the argument from one thing to another granted to theology (the most perfect of arts and disciplines) and to any other moral or natural discipline?

units.la: XXI. Non procul ergo est ab impietate eorum sententia, qui non verentur asserre hanc solam scientiam veram Dei cognitionem tradere, ejusque naturam (quantum quidem hominibus licet) explicare, & se mirari quo jure possit quis graviores Theologiæ controversias, hoc præsidio destitutus, non tantum profiteri, sed vel serio attingere; doctrinam cœlitus de lapsu non minus inniti primæ philosophiæ, quam vastam molem solido fundamento.
units.tr: XXI. Therefore their opinion is not far from impiety, those who do not hesitate to assert that this alone is the true knowledge of God, that it sets forth his nature (as far as is permitted to men), and that they marvel by what right anyone, destitute of this safeguard, can not only undertake but even seriously touch upon the weightier controversies of theology; that the doctrine of the fall, delivered from heaven, rests no less on first philosophy than a vast mass rests on a solid foundation.

units.la: XXII. Porrò effecta Sp. Sancti (ut incepimus dicere I Thess. 7.) quæ in nobis per verbum existunt, idem verbum quoad nos perfectum reddunt. Tenendum enim hoc unicum solummodo esse ordinarium instrumentum operationum Sp. Sancti, quas omnes concinnè complectitur Apostolus Rom. 1. cum ait Evangelium esse τὴν δύναμιν παντὶ τῷ πιστεύοντι εἰς σωτηρίαν. Totū ergo nostræ salutis opus in applicatione Mediationis Christi in fide, conversione, justificatione, &c. unicæ Sp. Sancti operationi per verbum tribuendum est. Effecta autem Spiritus Sancti quæ verbum ipsum magis proprie spectant, hæc sunt præcipua. pua. I. Quod nos eatenus beatos ejus possessione efficiat in hac vita, quatenus ullius mortalis natura fit capax, Psal. 1. v. 1. Beatus est vir ille cujus oblectatio est in lege Jehovæ. Quæ beatitudo, 2. nobis realiter communicatur, 1. In Illuminatione oculorum per verbum Psal 119. v. 130. Auditus verborum tuorum illuminat oculos prudentiâ, instruit simplices. Confer cum verf. 98, 99. &c. 2 Pet. 1. 19. 2. Tim. 3. 15. &c.
units.tr: XXII. Moreover, the effects of the Holy Spirit (as we began to say, 1 Thess. 7) which exist in us through the word make the same word perfect as far as we are concerned. For we must hold that this is the one and only ordinary instrument of the operations of the Holy Spirit, all of which the Apostle neatly embraces in Rom. 1, when he says that the gospel is "the power of God unto salvation for everyone who believes" [τὴν δύναμιν παντὶ τῷ πιστεύοντι εἰς σωτηρίαν]. The whole work of our salvation, therefore, in the application of the mediation of Christ in faith, conversion, justification, etc., is to be ascribed to the one operation of the Holy Spirit through the word. The effects of the Holy Spirit which pertain more properly to the word itself are these, the principal ones: 1. That it makes us blessed in this life, by its possession, so far as the nature of any mortal is capable of it: Psal. 1:1, "Blessed is the man whose delight is in the law of Jehovah." This blessedness is communicated to us really, 2. first, in the illumination of the eyes through the word: Psal. 119:130, "The opening of your words gives light; it gives understanding to the simple." Compare verses 98, 99, etc.; 2 Pet. 1:19; 2 Tim. 3:15, etc.

units.la: 2. In penetratione ad animas & conscientias nostras, quâ fit ut fervido ac flammanti desiderio feramur ad mandatorum Dei executionem, Psal. 119. v. 131. Os meum diffundo & anhelo, quia præceptorum tuorum cupidus sum. Psal. 42. v. 2. Sicut cervus clocitat aspirans ad alveos aquarum, sic anima mea clocitat aspirans ad te, Deus.
units.tr: 2. In the penetration into our souls and consciences, by which we are carried with a fervent and flaming desire to the execution of God's commandments: Psal. 119:131, "I open my mouth and pant, for I long for your precepts." Psal. 42:2, "As the deer pants after the water brooks, so my soul pants after you, O God."

units.la: 3. In suppeditatione talium virium, quibus instructi confidenter possimus currere in stadio mandatorum Dei. Eph. 6. 15. calceatis pedibus præparatione Evangelii.
units.tr: 3. In the supplying of such strength, by which, being equipped, we may run confidently in the course of God's commandments: Eph. 6:15, "having your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel."

units.la: 4. Renovatione omnium animi & corporis facultatum, summâ claritate ac luce, ita ut ablato (quasi) velo ad finem Legis & Evangelii respiciamus, nempe Iesum Christum ἀκρογωνιαῖον ἀπόστολον ἡμῶν καὶ ἀρχιερέα. 5. Tandem perductione ad extremum spei nostræ communicationem videlicet gloriosam osam cum Patre, Filio, & Sp. Sancto, 1. Joh. 1. v. 2,3. Quod vidimus & audivimus id annunciamus, ut communionem habeat nobiscum, & communio nostra est cum Patre & Filio ejus Iesu Christo.
units.tr: 4. In the renewal of all the faculties of mind and body, with the greatest clarity and light, so that, the veil (as it were) being taken away, we look to the end of the Law and the Gospel, namely Jesus Christ, "the apostle and high priest of our confession" [ἀκρογωνιαῖον ἀπόστολον ἡμῶν καὶ ἀρχιερέα]. 5. Finally, by leading us to the goal of our hope, namely the glorious fellowship with the Father, Son and Holy Spirit: 1 John 1:2, 3, "What we have seen and heard we proclaim to you, so that you may have fellowship with us; and our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ."

units.la: XXIII. Hæc effecta Scripturæ cum per fe sic fatis sint manifesta, fidelium propria experientia, & interna Sp. Sancti teftificatione tamen illustriora reddentur, fi doctrina de Deo aut moribus in Scripturis tradita, in comparationem ducatur cum doctrina Philosophica, five illa fit Theoretica in Metaphysica, five Practica in Ethica. Metaphysicam enim quod attinet, 1. Præterquam quod nihil de rebus divinis fui peculii habeat, illud quicquid est (quod certe minimum est) tantum eo tendit (testantibus eorum patronis) ut nos in speculationem rerum divinarum adducat: quam non esse separandum à praxi, & vera Theologia & fana ratio docet. 2. Metaphysica necesse habet nobis tradere Deum fine Patre, Deum fine Redemptore aut Sanctificatore. Quantum vel Turcica Theologia tradiderit. Quo respectu non adeo absurdum erit dicere, Metaphysicam nobis tradere Deum fine Deo. Si quid tamen laudis Metaphysica fit tribuendum, illud erit, quod inanes quosdam portentofarum di-ftin&iftinctionum fumos invexerit, ad obscurandam simplicem veritatem.
units.tr: XXIII. Although these effects of Scripture are sufficiently manifest in themselves, they will be made clearer still by the personal experience of the faithful and by the inward testimony of the Holy Spirit, if the doctrine concerning God or morals delivered in Scripture is set beside philosophical doctrine, whether it be theoretical, in metaphysics, or practical, in ethics. As far as metaphysics is concerned: first, apart from having nothing of its own concerning divine things, whatever it has (which is certainly very little) tends only (as its patrons attest) to lead us into the contemplation of divine things; yet sound reason and true theology teach that this must not be separated from practice. Secondly, metaphysics is bound to deliver to us God without a Father, God without a Redeemer or Sanctifier; as much as even Turkish theology has delivered. In this respect it will not be too absurd to say that metaphysics gives us God without God. If, however, any praise is to be given to metaphysics, it will be this: that it has introduced certain empty puffs of monstrous distinctions, to obscure the simple truth.

units.la: XXIV. Ethica Philosophia. Primò, Civilitatem tantum quandam morum externorum in sua perfectione requirit; non penetrat ipsa cordis penetralia; quemadmodum Ethica Christiana in Scripturis tradita. 2. Moralis Philosophia non rapit hominem extra semetipsum; sed tantum invitat ad bona nostra recognoscenda, quibus inaniter confisi ad felicitatem contendamus; unde fit (ut observat Calv.) quod inani fiducia homo intumescat, & superbia infletur. Theologia nobis inspiciendam proponit paupertatem, ignominiam, turpitudinem, imbecillitatem nostram. 3. Philosophia illa nobis subsistendum esse docet in nuda virtutum actione, nulla habita ratione principii aut finis omnium actionum, fidei nempe, aut gloriae divinae. Unde factum est ut non nemo Theologorum dixerit, virtutes Ethnicorum nihil esse, quam splendida peccata.
units.tr: XXIV. Ethical philosophy. First, it requires only a certain civility of outward conduct for its perfection. It does not penetrate the innermost recesses of the heart, as Christian ethics is delivered in the Scriptures. 2. Moral philosophy does not carry a man outside himself. It only invites him to recognise his own goods, and trusting in these in vain, he strives after happiness. Hence it comes (as Calvin observes) that man swells with empty confidence and is puffed up with pride. Theology sets before us for inspection our poverty, shame, baseness, weakness. 3. That philosophy teaches us to rest in the bare practice of the virtues, with no regard to the principle or the end of all actions, namely faith or the glory of God. Whence it has come about that not a few theologians have said that the virtues of the heathen are nothing but splendid sins.

units.la: XXV. Longè alias proprietates practici philosophi suae morum doctrinae solent tribuere: quae tamen in solidum morum doctrinae in Scripturis traditae conveniunt. Dicunt ex gr. Ethicae finem esse legi naturae & rationi rectae congruenter vivere.
units.tr: XXV. Practical philosophers usually attribute quite different properties to their doctrine of morals, yet these agree entirely with the doctrine of morals delivered in the Scriptures. They say, for example, that the end of ethics is to live in accordance with the law of nature and right reason.

units.la: Id est, (ut ego interpretor) congruenter Decalogo, seu legi naturæ in hominum cordibus scriptæ, quæ fine dubio in Scripturis est explicata.
units.tr: That is, (as I interpret it) to live in accordance with the Decalogue, or with the law of nature written in men's hearts, which is without doubt explained in the Scriptures.

units.la: 2. Tradunt subjectum Ethicæ esse moderari hominum actiones & passiones; non repugno, modo eâdem æquitate & mihi concedant, Scripturam esse omnium Actionum nostrarum (cujuscunque tandem generis sint, quatenus vitam nostram respiciunt) unicam, regulam ac normam. 3. Ethicam volunt tradere omnium actionum humanarum, qua tales, vera principia, id est, principia sine fundamento, actiones sine fide. Præterea quicquid tandem tradunt de istiusmodi principiis, illud plerunque solent ex Physicis describere, Tautologiâ satis onerosâ. 4. Policetur eadem etiam nobis felicitatem; plumbeam aut ligneam credo: Sola Theologia veram describit. 5. Ultimò Ethicam (ajunt tradere omnium civilium virtutum naturas ac descriptiones. Quod etsi falsum sit, cogentur tamen vel inviti concedere, Scripturam illas ipsas virtutes, & multò plures tradere. Quod ut pateat, obiter percurramus omnium Aristotelicarum virtutum formulas.
units.tr: 2. They hold that the subject of ethics is the regulation of human actions and passions.
