I do not object, provided that with the same fairness they grant me that Scripture is the one rule and norm of all our actions (of whatever kind they may be, so far as they concern our life). 3. They want ethics to deliver the true principles of all human actions as such, that is, principles without foundation, actions without faith. Moreover, whatever they deliver about such principles, they usually take from the physicists, with rather burdensome tautology. 4. The same philosophy promises us happiness; leaden or wooden, I suppose. Only theology describes it truly. 5. Finally, ethics (they say) delivers the natures and descriptions of all the civil virtues. Even if this is false, they will be forced, though unwillingly, to concede that Scripture delivers those very virtues, and many more. To make this clear, let us briefly run through the formulas of all the Aristotelian virtues.

units.la: XXVI. Aristoteles igitur & qui ipsum πόλις sequuntur, has decem virtutum for-
units.tr: XXVI. Aristotle therefore, and those who follow him [πόλις], have these ten formulas of the virtues.

units.la: formulas habent. 1. Fortitudinem. 2. Temperantiam. 3. Liberalitatem, magnificentiam. 4. Magnanimitatem. 5. Mansuetudinem, clementiam. 6. Affabilitatem. 7. Veracitatem. 8. Comitatem. 9. Verecundiam, nemefin. 10 Justitiam. Quarum 1, 3, 4. prout ab Aristotele describuntur, omnibus nequaquam conveniunt, non nisi bellicosis, divitibus, aut ambitiosis. 6, 7, 8, 9. ab ipso Arist, pro virtutibus proprie dictis vix videntur censeri. Has igitur virtutes omnes, & multò plures, si manifestissimis Scripturæ testimoniis non evicero in Sacro codice exstare, digitum tollam. Cū igitur omniū prædicatarū virtutū infinita exstent in Scripturis doctrinalia exempla (ex quibus ad imitationem nostra praecepta sint exstruenda) nemo debebit ægre ferre, quod in subjecta Scripturarū enumeratione exemplapræceptis intermiscentur.
units.tr: 1. Courage. 2. Temperance. 3. Liberality, magnificence. 4. Magnanimity. 5. Gentleness, clemency. 6. Affability. 7. Truthfulness. 8. Courtesy. 9. Modesty, nemesis. 10. Justice. Of these, 1, 3 and 4, as Aristotle describes them, do not suit everyone at all, but only the warlike, the rich, or the ambitious. 6, 7, 8 and 9 are hardly to be counted by Aristotle himself as virtues properly so called. I shall therefore not lift a finger unless I prove from the clearest testimonies of Scripture that all these virtues, and many more, are found in the sacred code. Since, then, there are countless doctrinal examples of all the virtues named in the Scriptures (from which our precepts are to be built up by imitation), no one should be troubled that in the following enumeration of Scripture, examples are mingled with precepts.

units.la: XXVII. 1 De fortitudine ejusque extremis.]
units.tr: XXVII. 1. Of courage and its extremes.

units.la: Fortitudinis bellicæ (cujus naturam præcipue Aristoteles describit) tot sunt exempla in Scripturis, quot prælia ac bella à sancto populo fuerunt gesta. Eminent autem inter cætera exempla Gideonis, Baraci, Sampsonis, Davidis, & comitum ejus, quorum Catalogum vide 2,Sam.23.v. 8.&c. De fortitudine & causis ejus secundum dum objeƈti sui latitudinem, considerentur sequentes loci. Heb. 11. 33, 34, 35, 36, 37, &c. Gen. 14. 14, 15. Psal. 18. 32, 34, 35, 37. 38, 39, 40, 42. Psal. 60. 11, 12, 13. 1. Sam. 17. 45. Deut. 20. 3, 4, 8. Prov. 3. 22, 23, 24, 25. Isai. 51. 7. Psal. 23. 4. & 27. 1, 2, 3. & 18. 2. & 46. 1, 2, 3. Isai 41. à verf. 10, ad 16. Timiditas. Prov. 28. 1. cap. 29. 25. & 10. 9, 14, 15. cap. 1. 27. Isa. 43. verf. 1, 2, 5, 6, 7. Psal. 48. 5. Psal. 142. 6, 7. Ex hac fortitudine effectum est quod Theologia plures habuerit martyres, quam Philosophia sectatores.
units.tr: Of warlike courage (whose nature Aristotle chiefly describes) there are as many examples in Scripture as there were battles and wars waged by the holy people. Among the other examples stand out those of Gideon, Barak, Samson, David and his companions, whose catalogue see at 2 Sam. 23. 8 etc. Concerning courage and its causes, according to the breadth of its object, the following passages may be considered. Heb. 11. 33, 34, 35, 36, 37, etc. Gen. 14. 14, 15. Psal. 18. 32, 34, 35, 37, 38, 39, 40, 42. Psal. 60. 11, 12, 13. 1 Sam. 17. 45. Deut. 20. 3, 4, 8. Prov. 3. 22, 23, 24, 25. Isai. 51. 7. Psal. 23. 4, and 27. 1, 2, 3, and 18. 2, and 46. 1, 2, 3. Isai. 41 from verse 10 to 16. Timidity. Prov. 28. 1; chap. 29. 25; and 10. 9, 14, 15; chap. 1. 27. Isa. 43. verses 1, 2, 5, 6, 7. Psal. 48. 5. Psal. 142. 6, 7. From this courage it has resulted that Theology has had more martyrs than Philosophy has had followers.

units.la: 2. De temperantia & extremis] Temperantiam Aristotelici volunt esse mediocritatem in appetendis & utendis voluptatibus quae pertinent ad tactum aut gustum. Quoniam igitur sic ipsius placet (etiamsi ejus objectum multo latius extendatur) nos in congerendis Scripturae locis illud praecipuè spectabimus. Rom. 13. 13, 14. Prov. 23. 1, 2, 3. Luc. 21. 34. 1 Thes. 5. 7, 8. Illustratur autem haec materia praecipuè ab oppositis vitiis, Ebrietate videlicet, Prov. 23. verf. 29, 30, 31, 32, 34, 35. cap. 20. 1. & v. 21. 1. Pet. 4. 34. Isai. 5. v. 11, 12. Hos. 8. 5. Illicitis & immodicis cupiditatibus in venere, Prov. 5. 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23. &c. & cap. 6. à verf. 24. ad finem usque DeDenique huc pertinent acerrimae conciones Prophetarum in Luxuriem populi Israelitici.
units.tr: 2. Of temperance and its extremes. The Aristotelians hold temperance to be the mean in desiring and using those pleasures which pertain to touch or taste. Since this is their view (even though its object extends much more widely), we shall in gathering Scripture passages attend chiefly to this. Rom. 13. 13, 14. Prov. 23. 1, 2, 3. Luke 21. 34. 1 Thess. 5. 7, 8. This matter is illustrated chiefly from the opposed vices, namely drunkenness: Prov. 23. verses 29, 30, 31, 32, 34, 35; chap. 20. 1; and verse 21. 1 Pet. 4. 3. Isai. 5. verses 11, 12. Hos. 8. 5. Illicit and immoderate desires in sex: Prov. 5. 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, etc., and chap. 6 from verse 24 to the end. Finally, to this belong the most fierce sermons of the Prophets against the luxury of the Israelite people.

units.la: 3. De liberalitate & extremis.] Liberalitas summa fuit imperata Legibus illis Mosaicis, quibus agitur de colligendis fructibus, &c. Sed porro etiam mandatur, describitur, & illustratur his & similibus locis, Prov. 11.24.29. Psal. 105. 9. Eccles. 11. 1,2,6. Prov. 3. v. 3,4,27,28, Jac. 2. 5,16. 2.Cor. 8. per totum caput Rom. 12,13. huc pertinet locus de Eleemosynis: Magnificentia cum modus tantum quidam Liberalitatis sit, qui spectat donorum copiam illis omnibus Scripturae locis possit illustrari, quibus admonemur ad copiosam donorum largitionem: Verum cum Aristoteles hic praecipuam mentionem faciat dedicationum Deorum, heroumque & magnarum exstructionum, &c. Perpenduntur sumptus populi Judaici in exstruendo templo & similibus operibus, Exod. 35. per totum caput. 1. Chron. 23.
units.tr: 3. Of liberality and its extremes. Great liberality was enjoined by those Mosaic laws which deal with gathering the fruits, etc. But further, it is also commanded, described and illustrated by these and similar passages: Prov. 11. 24, 29. Psal. 105. 9. Eccles. 11. 1, 2, 6. Prov. 3. verses 3, 4, 27, 28. Jas. 2. 5, 16. 2 Cor. 8, throughout the whole chapter. Rom. 12, 13. To this belongs the passage on alms. Magnificence, since it is only a certain mode of liberality which regards the abundance of gifts, can be illustrated by all those Scripture passages in which we are urged to generous giving. But since Aristotle here makes especial mention of dedications to the gods, heroes and great buildings, etc., the expenditures of the Jewish people in building the temple and similar works are weighed: Exod. 35, throughout the whole chapter. 1 Chron. 23.

units.la: 2. Hezrae 2. verf. 68, 69.
units.tr: 2. Ezra 2. verses 68, 69.

units.la: 3 De Magnanimitate.] Neminem mirum videri debet quod in convehendis Scripturae locis breviores hic simus. Quoniam Aristoteles sub titulo Magnanimi pharisaicum factum videtur introducere. Facit enim Magnanimum aliorum [illegible, ~12 letters] καλ-λαφεγν- πνόν[?]
units.tr: 3. Of magnanimity. No one should think it strange that in assembling the Scripture passages here we are briefer. For Aristotle, under the title of the magnanimous man, seems to introduce something Pharisaic; for he makes the magnanimous man a despiser of others [illegible] [καλ-λαφεγν-πνόν]

units.la: πνεύμα̣ Cui illud unum suffecerit oppositum, Prov. 16. v. 19. Melius est submissum esse cum manuetis, quàm partiri spolia cum superbis, Magnanimitatis tamen (quae confiteri perhibetur in congruenti moderatione affectuum, in suscipiendis honoribus & eorum repulsam ferendo) non desunt exempla è Scripturis, Exempli gratia in Iosepho Gen. 41. 41, &c. Mosè Hebr. 11. v. 24, 25, 26. Davide, Daniele, Nehemia, &c.
units.tr: [πνεύμα] To this one opposite suffices: Prov. 16. 19. It is better to be of a lowly spirit with the meek than to divide the spoil with the proud. Yet examples of magnanimity (which is said to consist in a fitting moderation of the affections, in accepting honours and in bearing their refusal) are not lacking in Scripture. For instance, in Joseph, Gen. 41. 41, etc.; Moses, Heb. 11. 24, 25, 26; David, Daniel, Nehemiah, etc.

units.la: 5. Mansuetudo] Ea versatur in ira aliorumque ex ira affectuum moderatione, ut liquet ex Prov. 14.29. cap.15.18. cap.16. 31. Eccl. 8.8,9. Prov. 19. 11. Zachar. 2.2. Matth. 5.44. Rom. 12.18,19. 1. Pet. 3. v. 8,9, &c.
units.tr: 5. Gentleness. It is concerned with the moderation of anger and of the other passions arising from anger, as is clear from Prov. 14. 29; chap. 15. 18; chap. 16. 31. Eccl. 8. 8, 9. Prov. 19. 11. Zach. 2. 2. Matt. 5. 44. Rom. 12. 18, 19. 1 Pet. 3. 8, 9, etc.

units.la: 6. De affabilitate. 7. Veracitate, & Comitate.] Tres hae virtutes praecipue spectant conversationem civilem in colloquiis & congressibus, idcirco illas una conjungemus. Affabilitatis proprium esse volunt, ut quoscunque compellemus cum significatione humanitatis, habità tamen ratione dignitatis personarum, officii, &c. aliosque cum facilitate ad colloquium admittamus, vocatur à nonnullis συνωρίσ; hac virtus, ut & Comitas; praecipue apparet, in humanissimis fidelium sub veteri & novo testamento colloquiis, congressibus, salutationibus, &c. quare non opus erit laboriosâ Scripturarum congerie. Præsertim cum ex hominum naturali constitutione dependeant.
units.tr: 6. Of affability. 7. Of truthfulness and courtesy. These three virtues chiefly concern civil conversation in talks and meetings, so we shall join them together. Affability is said to be the quality by which we address whomever we meet with a sign of humanity (yet having regard to the dignity of persons, their office, etc.), and admit others to conversation with ease; by some it is called [συνωρίς]. This virtue, like courtesy, appears chiefly in the most humane conversations, meetings and greetings of the faithful under the Old and New Testament, etc. So there will be no need for a laborious gathering of Scriptures, especially since these virtues depend on the natural constitution of men.

units.la: 7. Veracitas cum extremis.] Ea nobis expresse in parte affirmativa noni præcepti præcipitur, aliisq; insuper locus commendatur, describitur quoque, ut Prov. 3.4. cap. 12.17, 18. Zach 8.16,17. Eph. 4.25. Prov. 12,21, 22. Psal. 15.2. illustratur maximè ab oppositus, ut falsitate, Prov. 12. v. 5. 9. 28.23. cap. 15.18. Adulat. Prov. 26.22. cap. 18.8. cap. 20.19. cap. 27.14. 28.23. 29.5. cap. 16. 24,25,26, ἀλαζονείας, Prov. 25.14. cap. 12.9. cap. 20.6. cap. 25.27. c. 27.2.
units.tr: 7. Truthfulness and its extremes. In the affirmative part of the ninth commandment this is expressly enjoined on us, and other places commend it to us as well. It is also described, as in Prov. 3.4. cap. 12.17, 18. Zach 8.16,17. Eph. 4.25. Prov. 12,21, 22. Psal. 15.2. It is illustrated chiefly by its opposites, as falsehood, Prov. 12. v. 5. 9. 28.23. cap. 15.18. Flattery, Prov. 26.22. cap. 18.8. cap. 20.19. cap. 27.14. 28.23. 29.5. cap. 16. 24, 25, 26. boastfulness [ἀλαζονείας], Prov. 25.14. cap. 12.9. cap. 20.6. cap. 25.27. c. 27.2.

units.la: 8. De affectibus virtuti affinibus Verecundia, & Nemesi.] Verecundia est timere dedecus ex facto turpi, & rubore suffundi post dedecus aliquod admissum, juvenum propria secundum Aristotelem. Contra 1. Tim. 2. v. 9. Heb. 12.8.
units.tr: 8. Of affections related to virtue: shamefastness and nemesis. Shamefastness is fear of disgrace arising from a shameful deed, and a blush suffusing one after some disgrace has been committed; according to Aristotle it is a characteristic of the young. Against 1. Tim. 2. v. 9. Heb. 12.8.

units.la: 9. Nemesis.] Est justa indignatio ob honores aut commoda tributa indignis, negata dignis. Hic tenenda illa Regula est, Prov. 19.22. Psal. 37.1,2. ipsa virtus Prov. 26.1. Eccles. 10. v. 2, 3, 4. exempla, Salvatoris, Marc. 3. v. 4,5. Mosis Exod. 11. v. 8. Num. 16. 14,15. Jonathanis, 1. Sam. 20. v. 33, 34. Davidis, Psal. 119. v. 136. 139. Pauli, Gal. 5. v. 12.
units.tr: 9. Nemesis. It is a righteous indignation at honours or benefits given to the unworthy and withheld from the worthy. Here that rule must be kept: Prov. 19.22. Psal. 37.1, 2. the virtue itself Prov. 26.1. Eccles. 10. v. 2, 3, 4. Examples: of the Saviour, Mark 3. v. 4, 5. of Moses, Exod. 11. v. 8. Num. 16. 14, 15. of Jonathan, 1 Sam. 20. v. 33, 34. of David, Psal. 119. v. 136. 139. of Paul, Gal. 5. v. 12.

units.la: 10. Justitia.] Justitia tam distributiva quàm commutativa elucet in constitutione politiæ Israelitieæ. Continetur parte affirmativa octavi præcepti. Vindicativa apparet in severissimis Dei judiciis.De commutativa & distrib. Prov. 11.1.c. 16. 11. c.21.3 c.21.28.c.28 10,11. c.29. 4. c. 31. 8,9. Rom.13.7,8. Rom.12.v.10. Lev.19. 36. alii[que locis infinitis.
units.tr: 10. Justice. Justice, both distributive and commutative, shines forth in the constitution of the Israelite commonwealth. It is contained in the affirmative part of the eighth commandment. Vindictive justice appears in God's most severe judgments. On commutative and distributive justice see Prov. 11.1. c. 16. 11. c. 21.3. c. 21.28. c. 28. 10, 11. c. 29. 4. c. 31. 8, 9. Rom. 13.7, 8. Rom. 12. v. 10. Lev. 19. 36. and in other countless places.

units.la: XXVIII. Sit igitur nube testium probatum omnes practicas virtutes (dianoeticas enim & semivirtutes de industria omisimus, utpote quæ non habent accuratam virtutis rationem)Ariftotelis in Scripturis reperiri. Nemini (qui vel supremis labris Ethicam Christianam deguftarit) obscurum esse poterit, innumera alia virtutum nomina Ariftotelicis esse Apocrypha.
units.tr: XXVIII. Let it therefore be proved, by a cloud of witnesses, that all the practical virtues of Aristotle are to be found in the Scriptures (for we have deliberately omitted the dianoetic virtues and the semi-virtues, since they do not have an exact account of virtue). To no one who has tasted Christian ethics even with the tip of his lips can it be unclear that countless other names of virtues are apocryphal for the Aristotelians.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: FINIS.

units.la: GUILIELMI AMESII THESES LOGICÆ.
units.tr: The Logical Theses of William Ames.

units.la: Thesis I.
units.tr: Thesis I.

units.la: Intellectus, scientia, sapientia & ars non differunt reipsa, sed solâ ratione, prout de disciplinâ aliqua prædicantur.
units.tr: Understanding, science, wisdom and art do not differ in reality, but only in the way they are predicated of some discipline.

units.la: 2. Ars primariò & maximè proprie est in rebus.
units.tr: 2. Art is primarily and most properly in things.

units.la: 3. Ars constare debet ex præceptis scientificis.
units.tr: 3. Art must consist of scientific precepts.

units.la: 4 Artium omnium prima & maximè universalis est Dialectica.
units.tr: 4. Of all the arts, the first and most universal is Dialectic.

units.la: 5. Dialectica dicitur universalis ars, non tantum quia objectum ejus est ubiq; sed etiam quia usum habet in rebus omnibus.
units.tr: 5. Dialectic is called a universal art not only because its object is everywhere, but also because it has its use in all things.

units.la: 6. Proprium formale objectum Dialecticæ est ratio.
units.tr: 6. The proper formal object of Dialectic is reason.

units.la: 7. Ens & non-ens sunt objectum Dialecticæ materiale, quatenus nempe ratio est in Ente, & non-ente, Ratio est in ente suâ natura, in non-ente per fictionem.
units.tr: 7. Being and non-being are the material object of Dialectic, insofar as reason is found in being and in non-being. Reason is in being by its nature; in non-being it is there by fiction.

units.la: 8. Ratio illa quæ est proprium objectum &tum Logicæ non est ratio humana, sed ratio rerum, id est, respectus & habitudines rerum, quas habent inter se.
units.tr: 8. The reason which is the proper object of Logic is not human reason but the reason of things, that is, the relations and connections which things have among themselves.

units.la: 10 Ratio tamen humana perficitur per Logicam, quia nihil percipit, nisi sub ratione Logica, atq; adeo quo melius rationem illam Logicam percipit, eo persectius res ipsas percipiet.
units.tr: 10. Human reason is nevertheless perfected through Logic, because it perceives nothing except under a logical reason; and so the better it grasps that logical reason, the more perfectly it will perceive the things themselves.

units.la: 11 Finis Logicæ adæquatus, neque est Syllogismus, neque Demonstratio, neque cognitio veritatis, sed bene differere.
units.tr: 11. The adequate end of Logic is neither the syllogism, nor demonstration, nor the knowledge of truth, but to reason well.

units.la: 12 Bene differere est rationes rerum recte discernere, & inter se disponere.
units.tr: 12. To reason well is to discern the reasons of things rightly and to arrange them among themselves.

units.la: 13 Discernere rationes, est invenire, & easdem disponere, est dispositio. Dialecticæ igitur duæ sunt partes; Inventio & Dispositio.
units.tr: 13. To discern reasons is to invent them, and to arrange them is disposition. Dialectic therefore has two parts: Invention and Disposition.

units.la: 14 Notiones omnes Logicæ non sunt notiones secundæ: quædam etiam sunt primæ, ut causa, effectum, subjectum, adjunctum & similia.
units.tr: 14. Not all notions of Logic are second notions; some are also first, such as cause, effect, subject, adjunct and the like.

units.la: 15 Istæ notiones Logicæ non magis sunt à mente vel in mente humana, quàm notiones Physicæ & Mathematicæ.
units.tr: 15. These logical notions are no more from or in the human mind than the notions of Physics and Mathematics are.

units.la: 16 Notiones istæ rectius dicuntur argumenta, quam vel termini, vel conceptus vel καταγορήματα vel aliud quidvis.
units.tr: 16. These notions are more correctly called arguments than either terms, or concepts, or categoremata [καταγορήματα], or anything else whatever.

units.la: 17 Argumenta, quà talia, non percipiuntur à brutis.
units.tr: 17. Arguments, as such, are not perceived by brute animals.

units.la: 18 Argumentum proprie non est res, aut vox, sed ratio rerum & vocum.
units.tr: 18. An argument is properly not a thing or a word, but the reason of things and words.

units.la: 19 In unaquaque re omnia fere argumenta possunt reperiri.
units.tr: 19. In any given thing almost all arguments can be found.

units.la: 20 Mutatâ affectione, mutatur argumentum; multiplicatâ affectione multiplicatur argumentum.
units.tr: 20. When the affection changes, the argument changes; when the affection is multiplied, the argument is multiplied.

units.la: 21 Argumentum non arguit actu, nisi in Dispositione.
units.tr: 21. An argument does not argue actually except in Disposition.

units.la: 22 Illud quod arguitur, quia arguitur non est argumentum, sed aliquid, vel thema.
units.tr: 22. That which is argued, insofar as it is argued, is not the argument but something else, or the theme.

units.la: 23 Quicquid tamen arguitur, consequenter affectum est ad illud arguendum, à quo antea arguebatur.
units.tr: 23. Whatever is argued, however, is consequently affected for the purpose of being argued by that by which it was argued before.

units.la: 24 Causa est omnium argumentorum prima.
units.tr: 24. Cause is the first of all arguments.

units.la: 25 De ratione causæ nullibi agendum est, præterquam in Logica.
units.tr: 25. The nature of cause is to be treated nowhere except in Logic.

units.la: 26 Causa est principium & essendi & cognoscendi.
units.tr: 26. Cause is the principle both of being and of knowing.

units.la: 27 Causa inferendi potest appellari etiam aliud quodlibet argumentum.
units.tr: 27. Any other argument whatsoever may also be called a cause of inference.

units.la: 28 Omnis causa naturâ prior est suo effecto, & etiam prior dignitate, quatenus nempe effectum ab ipsa dependet.
units.tr: 28. Every cause is prior to its effect by nature, and also prior in dignity, insofar as the effect depends upon it.

units.la: 29 Essentia causæ consistit in vi, virtute, & facultate producendi effectum.
units.tr: 29. The essence of a cause consists in the force, power and faculty of producing an effect.

units.la: 30 Mera igitur occasio non est causa.
units.tr: 30. Mere occasion therefore is not a cause.

units.la: 31. Negs
units.tr: 31. Nor

units.la: 31 Neq; causa est, quicquid necessarió prærequiritur ad exsistentiam, quod vulgò dicitur causa sine qua non.
units.tr: 31. Nor is a cause whatever is necessarily presupposed for existence, which is commonly called the cause without which not.

units.la: 32 Quoniam vis causæ ingreditur in effectum, idcirco verè dicitur, qualis causa, tale causatum, respectu scil. illius virtutis quam accipit à causa.
units.tr: 32. Since the force of a cause enters into the effect, it is rightly said that such as the cause, such is the caused, namely with respect to that power which it receives from the cause.

units.la: 33 Vis causæ est potentia activa, vel porestas.
units.tr: 33. The force of a cause is an active potency, or power.

units.la: 34 Cum illa potentia adest, & non exeritur, tum causa tantum est potentia & cùm exeritur, causa est actu.
units.tr: 34. When that potency is present and is not exerted, the cause is only a potency; when it is exerted, the cause is actual.

units.la: 35 Causarum genera non sunt plura quàm quatuor: Efficiens, Materia, Forma, & Finis.
units.tr: 35. There are no more kinds of causes than four: efficient, matter, form and end.

units.la: 36 Efficiens & materia quia simul incipiunt operari, unum genus causæ constituunt.
units.tr: 36. Efficient and matter, because they begin to act together, constitute one kind of cause.

units.la: 37 Forma & finis quia non ante rem existunt, aut agunt, sed simul cum re, id circo alterum genus constituunt.
units.tr: 37. Form and end, because they do not exist or act before the thing but together with it, therefore constitute the other kind.

units.la: 38 Efficiens est prima causa, quia primum principium totius operationis confert; & cæteræ causæ pendent aliquo modo ab efficiente.
units.tr: 38. The efficient is the first cause, because it confers the first principle of the whole operation; and the other causes depend in some way on the efficient.

units.la: 39 Efficiens causa non potest distribuin veras species Logicas.
units.tr: 39. The efficient cause cannot be divided into true Logical species.

units.la: 40 Modi efficientis causæ sunt tantùm adjuncta, non formæ essentiales. 41 Causa exemplaris refertur ad efficientem, tanquam adjuvans ad principalem.
units.tr: 40. The modes of the efficient cause are only adjuncts, not essential forms. 41. The exemplary cause is referred to the efficient, as an assistant to the principal.

units.la: 42 Causa quæ dicitur moralis, agens (scil. suadendo, pertinet ad efficientem causam adjuvantem.
units.tr: 42. The cause called moral, acting (namely by persuading), belongs to the efficient cause as an assisting cause.

units.la: 43 Finis proprie est in intentione, eodem pertinet.
units.tr: 43. The end properly lies in intention, and belongs to the same.

units.la: 44 Omnis causa per accidens reducitur ad causam aliquam per se.
units.tr: 44. Every incidental cause is reduced to some cause per se.

units.la: 45 Causa per accidens agit, & suâ vi agit, sed non principaliter suâ vi, quoad effectum determinatum.
units.tr: 45. An incidental cause acts, and acts by its own force, but not principally by its own force with respect to a determinate effect.

units.la: 46 Non solum causa voluntaria, sed etiam naturalis potest cogi, & potest agere fortunâ.
units.tr: 46. Not only a voluntary cause but also a natural cause can be compelled, and can act by chance.

units.la: 47 Materia non tantum patitur, sed etiam patiendo agit.
units.tr: 47. Matter not only suffers but, in suffering, also acts.

units.la: 48 Ita tamen agit, ut per se fit indifferens ad hoc aut illud agendum.
units.tr: 48. It acts, however, in such a way that by itself it is indifferent to acting in this way or that.

units.la: 49 Causalitas materiæ consistit in constituendo rem imperfectè & inchoatè.
units.tr: 49. The causality of matter consists in constituting a thing imperfectly and in a rudimentary way.

units.la: 50 Materia respectu efficientis est obiectum; respectu formæ est quasi subjectum.
units.tr: 50. With respect to the efficient, matter is the object; with respect to form it is, as it were, the subject.

units.la: 51 Omnis creatura habet materiam ex qua constat.
units.tr: 51. Every creature has the matter of which it consists.

units.la: 52 Forma non proprie informat materiam, sed totum compositum, vel rem effectam.
units.tr: 52. Form does not properly inform matter, but the whole compound, or the thing effected.

units.la: §3 Causalitas formæ consistit in constituendo rem perfectè; in certo gradu & specie entis eam constituendo.
units.tr: 53. The causality of form consists in constituting a thing perfectly, constituting it at a certain grade and species of being.

units.la: §4 Forma est essentialis cujusque rei differentia.
units.tr: 54. Form is the essential difference of each thing.

units.la: §5 Posità formâ, ponitur formatum.
units.tr: 55. Once the form is posited, the thing formed is posited.

units.la: §6 Unius rei una tantùm est forma.
units.tr: 56. Each thing has only one form.

units.la: §7 Materia & forma, sunt causæ essentiales rei, id est, essentiam rei constituentes.
units.tr: 57. Matter and form are the essential causes of a thing, that is, they constitute the essence of the thing.

units.la: §8 Præcipua pars essentiæ est forma.
units.tr: 58. The chief part of an essence is form.

units.la: §9 Actio convenit rei propter formam; passio propter materiam, vel ratione formæ & ratione materiæ.
units.tr: 59. Action belongs to a thing on account of its form; passion on account of its matter, or by reason of both form and matter.

units.la: §o Finis & bonum convertuntur.
units.tr: 60. End and good are convertible.

units.la: §1 Propria causandi ratio in fine, est quod perficit, absolvit, vel finit rem.
units.tr: 61. The proper manner of causing in the end is that it perfects, completes, or finishes the thing.

units.la: §2 Finis, qui dicitur cui, est objectum illud, quod in effectione rei spectatur, cujus usui res destinatur.
units.tr: 62. The end, which is called that for which, is the object which is looked to in the making of the thing, and for whose use the thing is destined.

units.la: §3 Usus seu operatio solet appellari finis, sed proprie est effectum.
units.tr: 63. Use or operation is commonly called the end, but properly it is the effect.

units.la: §4 Finis est aptitudo rei ad usum, cui suâ naturâ inservit.
units.tr: 64. The end is the fitness of a thing for the use to which by its nature it serves.

units.la: §5 Nihil igitur existit, quin proprie loquendo habeat suum finem, primum & proximum.
units.tr: 65. Nothing therefore exists which, properly speaking, does not have its own end, first and proximate.

units.la: §6 Effectum, Materiatum, Formatum, & Finitum non differunt re ipsâ, sed sola ratione.
units.tr: 66. Effect, matter-made, form-made and end-made do not differ in reality, but only in reason.

units.la: §7 Fini
units.tr: 67. Of the end

units.la: 67 Fieri vel effectio proprie est à causa efficiente: esse vel entitas à singulis caufis: essentia à materia & forma: exsistentia ab omnibus causis.
units.tr: 67. Coming to be, or effection, properly belongs to the efficient cause; being, or entity, belongs to each of the causes; essence belongs to matter and form; existence belongs to all the causes.

units.la: 68 Omne effectum completum exsistit ex quatuor causis.
units.tr: 68. Every complete effect exists from four causes.

units.la: 69 Exsistentia cujusque rei non distinguitur ab essentia nisi ut modus rei à re.
units.tr: 69. The existence of each thing is not distinguished from its essence except as the mode of a thing from the thing.

units.la: 70 In omni operatione completa, est & motus & res motu facta.
units.tr: 70. In every complete operation there is both motion and the thing made by motion.

units.la: 71 Omnis actio est motus, & omne opus est res motu facta.
units.tr: 71. Every action is motion, and every work is a thing made by motion.

units.la: 72 Distinctio igitur artium in θεωρητικὰς & ποιητικὰς nou est accurata.
units.tr: 72. The division of the arts into theoretical [θεωρητικάς] and poetical [ποιητικάς] is therefore not exact.

units.la: 73 Motus generaliter sumptus pertinet ad Logicam, & nihil aliud est quàm primus effecti modus.
units.tr: 73. Motion, taken generally, belongs to Logic, and is nothing other than the first mode of the effect.

units.la: 74 Actio provenit ab efficiente, tanquam à principio, quod agit, provenit à forma, ut à principio, quo.
units.tr: 74. Action comes from the efficient as from the principle which acts; it comes from the form as from the principle by which it acts.

units.la: 75 Effecta virtutum & vitiorum sunt ab iis, tanquàm à principiis, quibus, non tanquam à principiis, quae.
units.tr: 75. The effects of virtues and vices come from those things as from the principles by which, not as from the principles which act.

units.la: 76 Omnis actio & passio proprie est totius compositi.
units.tr: 76. Every action and passion properly belongs to the whole compound.

units.la: 77 Idem motus est & actio & passio vario respectu.
units.tr: 77. The same motion is both action and passion, depending on the respect in which it is viewed.

units.la: 78 Subjectum naturâ sequitur effectum, ut subsistentia sequitur exsistentiam.
units.tr: 78. The subject naturally follows the effect, as subsistence follows existence.

units.la: 79 Non tantùm substantia sed etiam accidens potest esse subjectum.
units.tr: 79. Not only substance but also accident can be a subject.

units.la: 80 Non tantùm accidens, sed etiam substantia potest esse adjunctum.
units.tr: 80 Not only an accident but also a substance can be an adjunct.

units.la: 81 Locus est peculiaris modus subjecti.
units.tr: 81 A locus is a peculiar mode of a subject.

units.la: 82 Objectum est modus subjecti.
units.tr: 82 An object is a mode of a subject.

units.la: 83 Omnes facultates, habitus, & actiones habent sua objecta, circa quæ versantur vel occupantur.
units.tr: 83 All faculties, habits, and actions have their objects, with which they are concerned or occupied.

units.la: 84 Distinctio inter objectum materiale & formale non pertinet ad doctrinam objecti, sed fluit ex doctrina illa, quæ traditur de materia & forma, & applicanda est ad ens & non-ens.
units.tr: 84 The distinction between material and formal object does not belong to the doctrine of the object, but arises from that doctrine which is taught concerning matter and form, and is to be applied to being and non-being.

units.la: 85 Materia, quæ dicitur circa quam, non est materialis causa, sed objectum; materia in quâ est subjectum.
units.tr: 85 Matter, which is called that about which, is not a material cause but an object; matter in which is a subject.

units.la: 86 Plura sunt adjuncta quàm subjecta.
units.tr: 86 There are more adjuncts than subjects.

units.la: 87 Quidquid vel extrinsecùs vel intrinsecùs pertinet ad rem aliquam præter causas, & non est causa, est ejus adjunctum.
units.tr: 87 Whatever pertains to a thing, either extrinsically or intrinsically, apart from its causes, and is not a cause, is its adjunct.

units.la: 88 Quæ dici solent antecedentia, consequentia, & concomitantia, referri debent ad adjuncta.
units.tr: 88 What are usually called antecedents, consequents, and concomitants should be referred to adjuncts.

units.la: 89 Signum quamvis generali sensu æquè latè pateat atque argumentum, tamen maximè proprie pertinet ad adjunctum.
units.tr: 89 A sign, although in a general sense it extends as widely as an argument, nevertheless pertains most properly to the adjunct.

units.la: 90 Adjunctum non magis distribui potest in commune & proprium, quàm subjectum, effectum, & causa.
units.tr: 90 The adjunct can no more be divided into common and proper than can the subject, the effect, and the cause.

units.la: 91 Tempus est adjunctum.
units.tr: 91 Time is an adjunct.

units.la: 92 Omnis unitas & identitas rerum inter se fluit ex affectione consentanea, vel ejusdem causæ, vel ejusdem effecti, vel ejusdem subjecti, vel ejusdem adjuncti.
units.tr: 92 All unity and identity of things among themselves arises from a consistent affection: either of the same cause, or of the same effect, or of the same subject, or of the same adjunct.

units.la: 93 Nullæ duæ sunt res, quæ non inter se & consentiant & dissentiant.
units.tr: 93 There are no two things which do not both agree and disagree with each other.

units.la: 94 Consensio est prior dissensione.
units.tr: 94 Agreement is prior to disagreement.

units.la: 95 Dissentanea sunt in dissensione æqualia.
units.tr: 95 Things that disagree are equal in their disagreement.

units.la: 96 Diversa generatim dicuntur, quæ non sunt eadem.
units.tr: 96 Diverse things are generally said to be those which are not the same.

units.la: 97 Speciatim diversa appellantur, quæ ita non sunt eadem, ut possint tamen aliquo modo esse eadem, id est, eidem attribui.
units.tr: 97 Things are specifically called diverse which are not the same in such a way that they may nevertheless in some way be the same, that is, be attributed to the same thing.

units.la: 98 Diversa dissentiunt non tantùm ratione ratiocinante, vel conceptu nostro, sed etiam, ut loquuntur, ratione ratiocinatâ, vel ratione suâ.
units.tr: 98 Diverse things disagree not only in the reasoning reason, or our concept, but also, as they say, in the reasoned reason, or in their own reason.

units.la: 99 Dissensio hæc rationis, est quod duæ res non sint causæ ejusdem effecti, vel effecta ejusdem causæ, vel subjecta ejusdem adjuncti, vel adjuncta ejusdem subjecti.
units.tr: 99 This disagreement of reason is that two things are not causes of the same effect, or effects of the same cause, or subjects of the same adjunct, or adjuncts of the same subject.

units.la: 100 Omnia diversa si considerentur in natura sua abstracta sunt opposita, exempli gratiâ: hic formosus non est facundus, sunt diversa: forma non est facundia, sunt opposita.
units.tr: 100 All diverse things, if considered in their own nature abstractly, are opposites; for example, this handsome man is not eloquent are diverse; beauty is not eloquence are opposites.

units.la: 101 Opposita differunt non solâ ratione logicâ, sed etiam suâ naturâ vel essentiâ.
units.tr: 101 Opposites differ not only in logical reason but also in their own nature or essence.

units.la: 102 Opposita igitur non possunt convenire in uno objecto vel essentia.
units.tr: 102 Therefore opposites cannot agree in one object or essence.

units.la: 103 Opposita igitur non possunt convenire eidem, secundùm idem, ad idem, & eodem tempore.
units.tr: 103 Therefore opposites cannot belong to the same thing, in the same respect, in the same direction, and at the same time.

units.la: 104 Opposita non sunt opposita nisi ratione ejusdem.
units.tr: 104 Opposites are not opposed except by reason of the same thing.

units.la: 105 Disparata non semper eodem gradu inter se opponuntur, sed eodem genere oppositionis.
units.tr: 105 Disparates are not always opposed to each other in the same degree, but in the same kind of opposition.

units.la: 106 Omnia singularia seu individua sunt opposita disparata.
units.tr: 106 All singulars or individuals are disparate opposites.

units.la: 107 Individua igitur differunt essentialiter.
units.tr: 107 Individuals therefore differ essentially.

units.la: 108 Contraria sunt tantùm bina, non plura.
units.tr: 108 Contraries are only two, not more.

units.la: 109 Omnia igitur contraria, quæ contraria, sunt immediatè contraria, quia nullum tertium contrarium habent intercedens.
units.tr: 109 Therefore all contraries, as contraries, are immediately contrary, because they have no intervening third contrary.

units.la: 110 Illa quæ dici solent mediatè contraria sunt proprie disparata.
units.tr: 110 Those things that are commonly said to be mediately contrary are properly disparates.

units.la: 111 Illa etiam, quæ appellantur à quibufdam repugnantia, referri possunt ad disparata.
units.tr: 111 Those also which some call repugnants can be referred to disparates.

units.la: 112 Contraria proprie sunt generalia, non singularia, exempli gratia, hoc calidum, hoc frigidum, non sunt proprie contraria, sed disparata participantia contrariorum naturam: hic, hic pater, iste filius, non sunt proprie relata, sed disparata cum relatione adjuncta.
units.tr: 112 Contraries are properly general, not singular; for example, this is hot, this is cold are not properly contraries, but disparates sharing the nature of contraries; this man is a father, that man is a son are not properly relatives, but disparates with an added relation.

units.la: 113 Affirmatio vniuersalis non est axiomatis, sed est ratio alicujus rei positiva.
units.tr: 113 A universal affirmation is not an axiom, but is a positive account of some thing.

units.la: 114 Affirmatio prior est negatione.
units.tr: 114 Affirmation is prior to negation.

units.la: 115 Non tantum accidentia, sed etiam substantiæ sunt inter se contrariæ atque adversæ.
units.tr: 115 Not only accidents but also substances are mutually contrary and opposed.

units.la: 116 Relata sunt contraria, quia referuntur ad idem subjectum attributionis.
units.tr: 116 Relatives are contraries because they are referred to the same subject of attribution.

units.la: 117 Omnis relatio integra constat ex duabus quasi partibus: respectu unius, relatum est causa, correlatum est effectum: respectu alterius, relatum est effectum, correlatum est causa: respectu utriusque sive totius, sunt inter se mutuo & causæ & effecta.
units.tr: 117 Every complete relation consists of two parts, as it were: with respect to one, the relatum is the cause and the correlate the effect; with respect to the other, the relatum is the effect and the correlate the cause; with respect to both together, or as a whole, they are mutually both causes and effects of each other.

units.la: 118 Omnis relatio est mutua.
units.tr: 118 Every relation is mutual.

units.la: 119 In contrariis negantibus non sunt duæ res, ut in affirmantibus, sed una & eadem res affirmatur & negatur.
units.tr: 119 In negating contraries there are not two things, as in affirming ones, but one and the same thing is both affirmed and denied.

units.la: 120 Negatio hæc est ens rationis habens bens fundamentum in re.
units.tr: 120 This negation is a being of reason having a foundation in the thing.

units.la: 121 Prout est ens rationis, habet vim & rationem argumenti.
units.tr: 121 Insofar as it is a being of reason, it has the force and character of an argument.

units.la: 122 Negatio hæc topica alia est à negatione axiomatica.
units.tr: 122 This topical negation is different from the axiomatic negation.

units.la: 123 Simplex & mera negatio est negatio contradictionis.
units.tr: 123 The simple and bare negation is the negation of contradiction.

units.la: 124 Contradicentia sunt omnia; omnis contradictio complectitur sub se universa illa, quæ sunt, aut fingi possunt.
units.tr: 124 Contradictories are all things; every contradiction embraces under itself all those things which are, or can be imagined.

units.la: 125 Negatio contradicens est quasi genus eorum omnium quæ sub affirmatione non continentur.
units.tr: 125 A contradictory negation is as it were the genus of all those things which are not contained under the affirmation.

units.la: 126 Privatio est negatio cum aliquâ aptitudine ad affirmationem.
units.tr: 126 Privation is a negation together with some aptitude for affirmation.

units.la: 127 Habitus qui opponitur privationi est ens positivum, quod habetur vel haberi potest.
units.tr: 127 A habit which is opposed to privation is a positive being, which is or can be possessed.

units.la: 128 Habitus naturâ prior est privatione.
units.tr: 128 A habit is prior in nature to privation.

units.la: 129 Nulla privatio est de essentia alicujus rei positivæ.
units.tr: 129 No privation belongs to the essence of any positive thing.

units.la: 130 Privantia acerrimè omnium inter se contrariantur.
units.tr: 130 Privatives are of all things the most sharply opposed to one another.

units.la: 131 Comparata naturâ sunt posteriora simplicibus.
units.tr: 131 Comparatives are by nature posterior to simples.

units.la: 132 Omnis enim comparatio instituitur cum respectu ad aliquod simplex argumentum.
units.tr: 132 For every comparison is instituted with respect to some simple argument.

units.la: 133 Comparata semper distinguuntur ratione, sed non semper reipsâ.
units.tr: 133 Comparatives are always distinguished by reason, but not always in fact.

units.la: 134 Comparatio utrumque comparatum reddit æquè manifestum.
units.tr: 134 A comparison renders each of the things compared equally manifest.

units.la: 135 Omnis comparatio explicata redigi potest in contractam, & omnis contracta in explicatam.
units.tr: 135 Every explicit comparison can be reduced to a contracted one, and every contracted one to an explicit one.

units.la: 136 In explicata comparatione <bl>ἀντίθεσις</bl> continet argumentum, & <bl>ὑπόθεσις</bl> thema vel illud aliquid quod arguitur.
units.tr: 136 In an explicit comparison, <bl>ἀντίθεσις</bl> [antithesis] contains the argument, and <bl>ὑπόθεσις</bl> [hypothesis] the thesis, or that something which is argued.

units.la: 137 Omnis comparatio est vel in quantitate vel in qualitate.
units.tr: 137 Every comparison is either in quantity or in quality.

units.la: 138 Quantitas & qualitas Logica convenit omni enti & non enti.
units.tr: 138 Logical quantity and quality belong to every being and non-being.

units.la: 139 Paria sunt æqua, eandem habent mensuram quoad gradum, vel essentiæ, vel affectionis.
units.tr: 139 Equals are alike, having the same measure as to degree, whether of essence or of affection.

units.la: 140 Imparia sunt quæ diversam habent mensuram.
units.tr: 140 Unequals are those which have a different measure.

units.la: 141 Paritas vel imparitas rei vel rationis, vel probabilitatis non distinguuntur quoad rationem Logicæ comparationis.
units.tr: 141 Equality or inequality of a thing, of reason, or of probability are not distinguished with respect to the reason of logical comparison.

units.la: 142 A majore ad minus, si quantitas probabilitatis intelligatur, semper negativè concluditur.
units.tr: 142 From the greater to the less, if the quantity of probability is understood, the conclusion is always negative.

units.la: 143 A minore ad majus, si quantitas probabilitatis intelligatur, semper concluditur affirmatè.
units.tr: 143 From the less to the greater, if the quantity of probability is understood, the conclusion is always affirmative.

units.la: 144 Similia, & cætera etiam comparativa, ta, quamvis sunt fi&ta, possunt arguere res veras.
units.tr: 144 Similes, and other comparatives too, although they are fictions, can prove true things.

units.la: 145 Similitudo non tantum illustrat, sed etiam probat.
units.tr: 145 A similitude not only illustrates but also proves.

units.la: 146 Fabulæ, apologi, parabolæ, nihil aliud sunt, quam similitudinum propositiones.
units.tr: 146 Fables, apologues, parables are nothing other than propositions of similitudes.

units.la: 147 In similitudine disjunctâ sunt quatuor termini reipsa distincti, in similitudine continuâ sunt quatuor termini ratione tantum distincti.
units.tr: 147 In a disjunct similitude there are four terms really distinct; in a continuous similitude there are four terms distinct only in reason.

units.la: 148 Eadem arguendi affectio est in argumentis ortis, quæ fuit in primis, sed non eodem modo.
units.tr: 148 The same affection of arguing is found in derived arguments as in the first ones, but not in the same way.

units.la: 149 Orta argumenta perinde sunt ad id quod arguunt, sicut prima unde oriuntur, quoad essentiam, non quoad modum.
units.tr: 149 Derived arguments stand to that which they argue just as the first things from which they arise do, in essence, though not in manner.

units.la: 150 In conjugatis & in notatione tota ratio nominum continetur.
units.tr: 150 In conjugates and in notation the whole reason of names is contained.

units.la: 151 In conjugatis non est proprie conjugatio rerum sed nominum.
units.tr: 151 In conjugates there is properly no conjugation of things but of names.

units.la: 152 Conjugata oriuntur semper ex argumentis consentaneis.
units.tr: 152 Conjugates always arise from consistent arguments.

units.la: 153 Primum illud, vel jugum, quo inter se devincta sunt conjugata, est illud radicis, quod habent inter se commune.
units.tr: 153 The first thing, or the yoke, by which conjugates are bound together is that of the root which they have in common.

units.la: 154 Conjugata proprie sunt abstractum, concretum, & modus agendi.
units.tr: 154 Conjugates properly are the abstract, the concrete, and the mode of acting.

units.la: 155 Abstractum natura prius est concreto.
units.tr: 155 The abstract is prior in nature to the concrete.

units.la: 156 Abstractum est forma concreti.
units.tr: 156 The abstract is the form of the concrete.

units.la: 157 Concretum formam continet cum subjecto ipsius, quod ab ipsa denominatur.
units.tr: 157 The concrete contains the form together with its subject, which is denominated by it.

units.la: 158 Abstracta sunt genera vel species abstractorum, & concreta concretorum.
units.tr: 158 Abstracts are genera or species of abstracts, and concretes of concretes.

units.la: 159 Omnis abstractio est ultimata, id est, non potest resolvi in abstractius aliquid: idem est, ac si dicas, non datur abstractum abstracti.
units.tr: 159 Every abstraction is ultimate, that is, it cannot be resolved into something more abstract; this is the same as saying there is no abstract of an abstract.

units.la: 160 Posito abstracto ponitur concretum; posito concreto ponitur abstractum; posito modo ponitur & abstractum & concretum; sed posito abstracto & concreto non statim ponitur modus.
units.tr: 160 Given the abstract, the concrete is posited; given the concrete, the abstract is posited; given the mode, both the abstract and the concrete are posited; but given the abstract and the concrete, the mode is not posited at once.

units.la: 161 Omne nomen non admittit notationem, sed illa nomina, & sola, quæ certo consilio fuerunt imposita.
units.tr: Not every name admits of a notation, but only those names, and only those, that were imposed with deliberate purpose.

units.la: 162 Notatio arguit nomen, & nomen arguit notationem.
units.tr: A notation proves the name, and the name proves the notation.

units.la: 163 Omnis affectio orta, quæ est realis, pertinet vel ad distributionem vel ad definitionem.
units.tr: Every real affection that arises belongs either to distribution or to definition.

units.la: 164 Omnis distributio & omnis definitio debet esse reciproca.
units.tr: Every distribution and every definition must be reciprocal.

units.la: 165 Distributio oritur, partim ex consentaneis, partim ex differentiis.
units.tr: Distribution arises partly from things that agree and partly from differences.

units.la: 166 Accuratissima distributio est dichotomia, quia ibi est summa consensio & summa dissensio.
units.tr: The most exact distribution is dichotomy, because there is there the greatest agreement and the greatest disagreement.

units.la: 167 Doctrina de toto & partibus non est separanda à doctrina de distributione.
units.tr: The doctrine of whole and parts is not to be separated from the doctrine of distribution.

units.la: 168 Distributio passivè pertinet ad totum, activè ad partes.
units.tr: Distribution, taken passively, applies to the whole; taken actively, to the parts.

units.la: 169 Omne distributum est totum.
units.tr: Everything distributed is a whole.

units.la: 170 Omne totum est distributum vel actu vel potentiâ.
units.tr: Every whole is distributed either actually or potentially.

units.la: 171 Omne totum est majus qualibet suâ parte.
units.tr: Every whole is greater than any one of its parts.

units.la: 172 Totum & omnes partes simul sumptæ sunt reipsa idem, quamvis differant ratione.
units.tr: The whole and all its parts taken together are in reality the same, although they differ in concept.

units.la: 173 Nullum totum est, quod unicâ parte constat.
units.tr: There is no whole that consists of a single part.

units.la: 174 Totum continet partes singulas, ut majus quid; omnes, ut æquale & idem.
units.tr: The whole contains its individual parts as something greater; it contains all of them as equal to it and the same.

units.la: 175 Quicquid habet affectionem communem ad varia, prout ita consideratur, est totum.
units.tr: Whatever has a common affection extending to various things, as it is considered in this way, is a whole.

units.la: 176 Quæcunque inter se opponuntur sub affectione communi ad unam, prout ita considerantur, sunt partes.
units.tr: Whatever stands opposed to one another under a common affection tending to one thing, as they are considered in this way, are parts.

units.la: 177 Integrum accipit essentiam à membris.
units.tr: The integral thing receives its essence from its members.

units.la: 178 Omne membrum confert partem materiæ, partem formæ, integro.
units.tr: Each member contributes a part of the matter and a part of the form to the integral thing.

units.la: 179 Integrum non prædicatur de membro.
units.tr: The integral thing is not predicated of a member.

units.la: 180 Quicquid affirmatur de membro, affirmatur etiam de integro secundum partem.
units.tr: Whatever is affirmed of a member is also affirmed of the integral thing, in respect of a part.

units.la: 181 Posito integro perfecto ponuntur omnes ejus partes.
units.tr: Given the perfect integral thing, all its parts are given.

units.la: 182 Posito integro imperfecto ponuntur omnes partes principales.
units.tr: Given the imperfect integral thing, all its principal parts are given.

units.la: 183 Sublata parte principali, tollitur integrum.
units.tr: Remove a principal part, and the integral thing is removed.

units.la: 184 Sublata parte qualibet, tollitur perfectio integri.
units.tr: Remove any part, and the perfection of the integral thing is removed.

units.la: 185 Pars quæ dicitur singularis, qua talis, est potius species quam membrum.
units.tr: A part which is called singular, as such, is a species rather than a member.

units.la: 186 Genus est totum.
units.tr: The genus is a whole.

units.la: 187 Ipsa natura generis simpliciter consíderata, sine universalitate, est pars.
units.tr: The very nature of the genus, considered simply and without universality, is a part.

units.la: 188 Genus & universale idem sunt.
units.tr: Genus and universal are the same.

units.la: 189 Genus existit extra intellectum.
units.tr: The genus exists outside the intellect.

units.la: 190 Genus non existit extra suas species.
units.tr: The genus does not exist outside its species.

units.la: 191 Genus nihil aliud est quam communis illa natura, quæ variis rebus inest.
units.tr: The genus is nothing other than that common nature which inheres in various things.

units.la: 192 Quicquid essentiale affirmatur & negatur de genere, affirmatur etiam & negatur de specie.
units.tr: Whatever is essentially affirmed or denied of the genus is also affirmed or denied of the species.

units.la: 193 Sublato genere tollitur species.
units.tr: Remove the genus, and the species is removed.

units.la: 194 Posito genere ponitur aliqua species.
units.tr: Given the genus, some species is given.

units.la: 195 Posita specie necessariò ponitur genus.
units.tr: Given the species, the genus is necessarily given.

units.la: 196 Quicquid affirmatur & negatur de specie, etiam affirmatur & negatur de genere particulariter.
units.tr: Whatever is affirmed or denied of the species is also affirmed or denied of the genus, in a particular way.

units.la: 197 Individua sunt species specialifsimæ.
units.tr: Individuals are the most specific species.

units.la: 198 Quod proximè prædicatur de individuis est genus.
units.tr: That which is predicated most immediately of individuals is a genus.

units.la: 199 Nulla species, quâ species, est prædicabilis sed tantum subjicibilis.
units.tr: No species, as a species, is predicable, but only subjectable.

units.la: 200 Eadem res potest esse genus respectu inferiorum & species respectu superiorum.
units.tr: The same thing can be a genus with respect to lower things and a species with respect to higher things.

units.la: 201 Dantur legitimæ distributiones, quæ neque sunt integri in membra, neque generis in species.
units.tr: There are legitimate distributions which are neither of a whole into its members nor of a genus into its species.

units.la: 202 Omnis legitima distinctio est distributio.
units.tr: Every legitimate distinction is a distribution.

units.la: 203 Distinctionis partes referuntur ad argumenta dissentanea, sed tota distinctio ad distributionem.
units.tr: The parts of a distinction are referred to opposing arguments, but the whole distinction to distribution.

units.la: 204 Distributio subjecti in adjuncta, & aliæ distributiones ejusdem generis, non sunt imperfectæ distributiones, sed in suo genere perfectæ.
units.tr: The distribution of a subject into its adjuncts, and other distributions of the same kind, are not imperfect distributions but perfect in their own kind.

units.la: 205 Distinctio vocis ambiguæ pro varietate rerum quas significat, est distributio adjuncti in sua subjecta.
units.tr: The distinction of an ambiguous word according to the variety of things it signifies is the distribution of an adjunct into its subjects.

units.la: 206 Distinctio rei per varia nomina est distributio subjecti in sua adjuncta.
units.tr: The distinction of a thing by its various names is the distribution of a subject into its adjuncts.

units.la: 207 Idem argumentum primum potest esse & totum & pars respectu ejusdem, fi vario modo consideretur.
units.tr: The same first argument can be both a whole and a part with respect to the same thing, if it is considered in different ways.

units.la: 208 Quicquid perfecte definitur, est species.
units.tr: Whatever is perfectly defined is a species.

units.la: 209 Definitio ergo per distributionem investigatur, & ordine doctrinae sequitur distributionem.
units.tr: Definition, therefore, is investigated through distribution, and in the order of teaching it follows distribution.

units.la: 210 Per definitionem respondetur ad quaestionem, quid fit res.
units.tr: By definition we answer the question what a thing is.

units.la: 211 Per definitionem etiam explicatur qualis fit res, quoad qualitatem essentialem.
units.tr: By definition we also explain what kind of thing it is, with respect to its essential quality.

units.la: 212 quicquid essentiale reperitur in definito, debet etiam in definitione contineri.
units.tr: Whatever essential is found in the defined thing must also be contained in the definition.

units.la: 213 Materia & forma definiti explicantur in definitione per genus & differentiam.
units.tr: The matter and form of the defined thing are explained in the definition through genus and difference.

units.la: 214 Definitio & definitum sunt reipfa unum, ratione tantum differunt.
units.tr: The definition and the defined thing are in reality one, and differ only in concept.

units.la: 215 Omnis definitio debet esse perspicua & brevis.
units.tr: Every definition must be clear and brief.

units.la: 216 Genera generaliffima & species fpecialiffimae non possunt perfecte definiri
units.tr: The most general genera and the most specific species cannot be perfectly defined.

units.la: 217 Quod non est compositum, non potest perfecte definiri.
units.tr: What is not composite cannot be perfectly defined.

units.la: 218 Genus in definitione est membrum.
units.tr: The genus in a definition is a member.

units.la: 219 Accidentis definitio explicari solet let per genus, subjectum, & causam efficientem, quoniam effentia ejus pendet ab istis.
units.tr: The definition of an accident is usually explained through genus, subject and efficient cause, since its essence depends on these.

units.la: 220 Actio definitur per genus, objectum, causam & modum.
units.tr: An action is defined through genus, object, cause and manner.

units.la: 221 Relatum definitur per correlatum, addito genere, & fundamento, fi fit.
units.tr: A relative is defined through its correlative, with the genus added, and its foundation, if it has one.

units.la: 222 Quaecunque argumenta in defcriptione ponuntur, pertinere debent ad efsentiam rei aliquo modo explicandam.
units.tr: Whatever arguments are placed in a description ought to pertain to the essence of the thing, in some way to be explained.

units.la: 223 Omnis definitio & descriptio debet esse reciproca.
units.tr: Every definition and description must be reciprocal.

units.la: 224 Testimonium respectu testis est effectum, respectu rei testificatae simpliciter consideratum, est adjunctum; prout in fe solo consideratur, non est argumentum sed axioma; prout adhibetur ad fidem alicui rei faciendam, est argumentum inartificiale.
units.tr: Testimony, with respect to the witness, is an effect; considered simply with respect to the thing attested, it is an adjunct; considered in itself alone, it is not an argument but an axiom; applied to make someone believe a thing, it is an inartificial argument.

units.la: 225 Inartificialiter arguit quia vim arguendi neque habet a fe, ut argumenta prima: neque in fe, ut argumenta orta; sed per relationem quandam ad alia argumenta
units.tr: It proves inartificially, because it has its power of proving neither from itself, as the primary arguments do, nor in itself, as the arising arguments do, but through a certain relation to other arguments.

units.la: 226 Testimonium separatum ab omnibus aliis artificialibus argumentis nihil valet.
units.tr: Testimony separated from all other artificial arguments is worth nothing.

units.la: 227 Vis illa per quam testimonium valet, est authoritas testantis.
units.tr: That power by which testimony has weight is the authority of the one testifying.

units.la: 228 Authoritas testis pendet ex illa scientia scientiâ, quam habet de re testificanda, & veracitate in sententia ferenda.
units.tr: The authority of a witness depends on the knowledge he has of the thing to be attested, and on his truthfulness in giving his judgment.

units.la: 229 Divinum igitur testimonium est firmissimum.
units.tr: Divine testimony, therefore, is most firm.

units.la: 230 Humanum per se non multum valet, nisi in quaestionibus quibusdam de facto.
units.tr: Human testimony by itself counts for little, except in certain questions of fact.

units.la: 231 Testimonium potest esse falsum, ubi res testata est vera.
units.tr: Testimony can be false when the thing attested is true.

units.la: 232 Assensus, qui praebetur testimonio, proprie dicitur fides, prout distinguitur a scientia.
units.tr: The assent that is given to testimony is properly called faith, as distinguished from knowledge.

units.la: 233 Secunda pars Logicæ maximè proprie dicitur Dispositio.
units.tr: The second part of logic is most properly called Disposition.

units.la: 234 Argumenta inventionis non habent usum nisi in Dispositione.
units.tr: The arguments of invention have no use except in disposition.

units.la: 235 Omnis dispositionis fructus est vel judicium vel memoria.
units.tr: The fruit of every disposition is either judgment or memory.

units.la: 236 In axiomate judicium fertur sine discursu.
units.tr: In an axiom judgment is passed without discursive reasoning.

units.la: 237 Axioma igitur proprie declarat, non probat.
units.tr: An axiom, therefore, properly declares; it does not prove.

units.la: 238 Axioma non est primò in verbis neque proprie in mente, sed in rebus.
units.tr: The axiom is not primarily in words, nor properly in the mind, but in things.

units.la: 239 Non igitur tam recte dicitur propositio, enuntiatio, & similia, quam axioma.
units.tr: It is therefore not so correctly called a proposition, an enunciation, and the like, as an axiom.

units.la: 240 In omni axiomate duo saltem sunt argumenta, quæ sunt membra Axiomatis.
units.tr: In every axiom there are at least two arguments, which are the members of the axiom.

units.la: 241 Forma axiomatis est vinculum seu copula, vel ipsa dispositio horum argumentorum.
units.tr: The form of an axiom is the bond or copula, or the very disposition of these arguments.

units.la: 242 Illud in axionate dicitur thema, quod ex proposito disponentis arguitur, quæ maxima ex parte est pars antecedens vel subjectum; partis enim consequentis, sive prædicati, est lucem alteri parti inferre, & non recipere ab alia.
units.tr: In an axiom, that is called the theme which is argued for by the purpose of the one disposing; this is for the most part the antecedent part or subject, for it is the office of the consequent part, or predicate, to bring light to the other part and not to receive it from another.

units.la: 243 Vinculum non est distinctum membrum axiomatis, sed est formalis ratio ipsius dispositionis.
units.tr: The bond is not a distinct member of the axiom, but is the formal reason of the disposition itself.

units.la: 244 Affirmatio, negatio, veritas, falsitas, sunt affectiones vel adjuncta axiomatis.
units.tr: Affirmation, negation, truth and falsity are affections or adjuncts of the axiom.

units.la: 245 Affirmatio & negatio naturâ antecedit veritatem & falsitatem rei.
units.tr: Affirmation and negation precede, in nature, the truth and falsity of a thing.

units.la: 246 Affirmatio est prior negatione, ut habitus privatione.
units.tr: Affirmation is prior to negation, as a habit is prior to its privation.

units.la: 247 Affirmatio est conjunctio argumentorum: negatio est disjunctio argumentorum.
units.tr: Affirmation is the conjoining of arguments; negation is the disjoining of arguments.

units.la: 248 Argumenta affirmantia possunt in axiomate negari, & argumenta negantia possunt in axiomate affirmari.
units.tr: Arguments that affirm can be denied in an axiom, and arguments that deny can be affirmed in an axiom.

units.la: 249 Affirmatio & negatio non pendent ex argumentorum naturâ, sed ex eorum dispositione vel vinculo.
units.tr: Affirmation and negation depend not on the nature of the arguments but on their disposition or bond.

units.la: 250 Particulæ exclusivæ non efficiunt axioma negatum, sed negationem inferunt in aliquam partem axiomatis.
units.tr: Exclusive particles do not make an axiom negative, but they introduce negation into some part of the axiom.

units.la: 251 Interrogationes, quæstiones, & orationes omnes, vel imperantes vel optantes, sunt axiomata, & semper vel affirmantur vel negantur.
units.tr: All interrogations, questions and prayers, whether commanding or wishing, are axioms, and they are always either affirmed or denied.

units.la: 252 Argumentum potest affirmari & negari, ita ut maneat idem axioma.
units.tr: An argument can be affirmed and denied while the axiom remains the same.

units.la: 253 Cum idem axioma affirmatur & negatur, est contradictio axiomatica.
units.tr: When the same axiom is both affirmed and denied, there is an axiomatic contradiction.

units.la: 254 In contradictione idem debet esse antecedens, idem consequens, servatis legibus oppositionis, eidem, secundum idem, ad idem, & eodem tempore.
units.tr: In a contradiction the antecedent must be the same and the consequent the same, with the laws of opposition observed: the same thing, in the same respect, in the same relation, and at the same time.

units.la: 255 Veritas & falsitas proprie conveniunt axiomati, non argumentis.
units.tr: Truth and falsity properly belong to the axiom, not to the arguments.

units.la: 256 Veritas est congruentia axiomaticæ dispositionis cum affectione rerum dispositarum quam habent inter se.
units.tr: Truth is the agreement of the axiomatic arrangement with the actual relation that the things arranged have to one another.

units.la: 257 Axioma falsum est, cum in dispositione non servatur affectio, quam res habent inter se.
units.tr: An axiom is false when the arrangement does not preserve the relation that the things have to one another.

units.la: 258 Veritas illa, quæ dicitur moralis, est congruentia verborum cum mente, & consistere potest cum axiomate falso.
units.tr: The truth called moral is the agreement of words with the mind, and it can coexist with a false axiom.

units.la: 259 Contingentia & necessitas pendent ex natura argumentorum, quæ disponuntur; non ex certitudine quæ oritur ex circumstantia aliqua temporis.
units.tr: Contingency and necessity depend on the nature of the arguments that are arranged, not on the certainty that arises from some circumstance of time.

units.la: 260 Axioma igitur contingens potest esse certissimæ veritatis, sed non proprie necessariæ.
units.tr: 260 So a contingent axiom can have the most certain truth, but not properly necessary truth.

units.la: 261 Axiomatis contingentis nulla datur scientia proprie dicta, sed opinio.
units.tr: There is no science properly so called of a contingent axiom, but only opinion.

units.la: 262 Axioma necessarium est perpetuæ veritatis, cum impossibilitate falsitatis.
units.tr: A necessary axiom is of perpetual truth, with the impossibility of falsity.

units.la: 263 Quæ raro contingunt, & quæ maximâ ex parte contingunt, æquè constituunt axioma, atque illa quæ sunt mediæ contingentiæ.
units.tr: Things that happen rarely, and things that happen for the most part, make an axiom just as much as things of intermediate contingency do.

units.la: 264 Axioma potest esse <bl>κατὰ</bl> <bl>παντὸς</bl>, licet non sit universale.
units.tr: An axiom can be per omnis [κατὰ παντὸς] even if it is not universal.

units.la: 265 Nullum axioma est primæ veritatis, quod non est κατ' αὐτὸ καθ' αὑτό.
units.tr: No axiom is of first truth which is not per se [κατ' αὐτὸ καθ' αὑτό].

units.la: 266 Inanes repetitiones & confusio non potest vitari, nisi leges istæ ferventur in arte tradenda.
units.tr: Empty repetitions and confusion cannot be avoided unless these rules are observed in the art being taught.

units.la: 267 Omnis proprie dicta scientia fluit ab axiomate necessario.
units.tr: Every science properly so called flows from a necessary axiom.

units.la: 268 Unica distributio axiomatis in species qua est, vel est simplex vel composita.
units.tr: There is only one division of the axiom into kinds, namely that it is either simple or compound.

units.la: 269 In axiomate simplici unum disponitur cum uno.
units.tr: In a simple axiom one thing is arranged with one thing.

units.la: 270 Vinculum axiomatis simplicis est in verbo.
units.tr: The bond of a simple axiom lies in the verb.

units.la: 271 In verbo etiam continetur aliquando totum argumentum consequens.
units.tr: Sometimes the whole consequent argument is also contained in the verb.

units.la: 272 Simplici axiomate quodlibet argumentum potest disponi, exceptis plenis comparationibus & distributionibus.
units.tr: Any argument can be arranged in a simple axiom, except for full comparisons and distributions.

units.la: 273 Univerfalitas & specialitas pertinent tantum ad axioma simplex, non ad compositum.
units.tr: Universality and particularity pertain only to the simple axiom, not to the compound.

units.la: 274 Nullum datur axioma reipfa indefinitum, sed tantum verbis.
units.tr: No axiom is indefinite in fact, but only in words.

units.la: 275 In axiomate generali argumentum antecedens est genus.
units.tr: In a general axiom the antecedent argument is a genus.

units.la: 276 Axioma potest esse generale fine signo generali, quale est omne, nullum, &c.
units.tr: An axiom can be general without a general sign, such as all, none, etc.

units.la: 277 In axiomate particulari antecedens argumentum est species determinata.
units.tr: In a particular axiom the antecedent argument is a determinate species.

units.la: 278 In axiomate proprio antecedens argumentum est species fpecialiffima determinata.
units.tr: In a proper axiom the antecedent argument is a determinate most specific species.

units.la: 279 Axiomata collectiva (ut exempli causa, omnes Apostoli fuerunt duodecim) sunt propria.
units.tr: Collective axioms (for example, all the apostles were twelve) are proper.

units.la: 280 Antecedens commune praecise & rationaliter acceptum, fit singulare, ut animal est genus, Hoc axioma non est generale, sed proprium.
units.tr: A common antecedent, taken precisely and rationally, becomes singular, as in animal is a genus. This axiom is not general but proper.

units.la: 281 In composito axiomate sunt femper plura verba, vel expressa, vel intellecta.
units.tr: In a compound axiom there are always several words, either expressed or understood.

units.la: 282 Datur axioma compositum fine conjunctione grammatica.
units.tr: There is a compound axiom without a grammatical conjunction.

units.la: 283 Dantur axiomata composita, quae non possunt in duo vel plura simplicia resolvi.
units.tr: There are compound axioms which cannot be resolved into two or more simple ones.

units.la: 284 Sunt tres modi copulati axiomatis, 1. ubi conjunctio copulativa antecedit, 2. ubi sequitur, 3. ubi & antecedit & sequitur.
units.tr: 284 There are three modes of the copulative axiom: (1) where the copulative conjunction comes first; (2) where it follows; (3) where it both comes first and follows.

units.la: 285 Axioma copulatum verum non est, nisi omnes partes sint verae, sed falsum est, ex una parte falsa.
units.tr: A copulative axiom is true only if all its parts are true, but it is false if one part is false.

units.la: 286 Contradicitur axiomati copulato per negationem unius partis magis directè quam per negationem omnium.
units.tr: A copulative axiom is contradicted more directly by the denial of one part than by the denial of all.

units.la: 287 Contradictio in axiomate composito semper dividit verum à falso.
units.tr: In a compound axiom, contradiction always separates the true from the false.

units.la: 288 Affirmatio & negatio omnium partium axiomatis compositi non semper dividit verum à falso.
units.tr: The affirmation or denial of all the parts of a compound axiom does not always separate the true from the false.

units.la: 289 Cicero fuit neque rex, neque dictator, est axioma copulatum non proprie negatum, sed affirmatum.
units.tr: Cicero was neither king nor dictator is a copulative axiom that is not properly denied but affirmed.

units.la: 290 In omni axiomate connexo consequens in antecedentis virtute constituitur.
units.tr: In every connected axiom the consequent is set up in the force of the antecedent.

units.la: 291 Antecedens non semper est causa consequentis, sed consequentiae.
units.tr: The antecedent is not always the cause of the consequent, but sometimes of the consequence.

units.la: 292 Consequens antecedentis veritatem semper consequitur.
units.tr: The consequent always follows the truth of the antecedent.

units.la: 293 In axiomate connexo utraque pars potest esse vera, ita ut totum axioma sit falsum, ut si Socrates est Atheniensis, tunc est Philosophus.
units.tr: In a connected axiom both parts can be true while the whole axiom is false, as in if Socrates is an Athenian, then he is a philosopher.

units.la: 294 Utraque pars potest esse falsa, itaut axioaxioma sit verum: ut si Socrates est leo, est etiam quadrupes.
units.tr: Both parts can be false while the axiom is true, as in if Socrates is a lion, he is also a quadruped.

units.la: 295 Ex vero nil nisi verum sequitur.
units.tr: Nothing but what is true follows from what is true.

units.la: 296 Ex falso sequitur saepe verum, sed nunquam ex vero sequitur falsum.
units.tr: From what is false there often follows what is true, but from what is true there never follows what is false.

units.la: 297 Connexum axioma nihil absolutè ponit de antecedente vel consequente parte, sed infert consequentem partem ex antecedente suppositâ.
units.tr: A connected axiom asserts nothing absolutely about the antecedent or consequent part, but infers the consequent part from the antecedent supposed.

units.la: 298 Omne axioma connexum, quod est absolutè verum, est etiam necessarium: necessitas haec est necessitas consequentiae non consequentis.
units.tr: Every connected axiom that is absolutely true is also necessary; this necessity is the necessity of the consequence, not of the consequent.

units.la: 299 Necessitas haec consistere potest cum contingentia & antecedentis, & consequentis, imo cum falsitate & impossibilitate.
units.tr: This necessity can coexist with the contingency of both the antecedent and the consequent, indeed even with falsity and impossibility.

units.la: 300 Axiomata illa connexa quae non sunt necessaria sed tantum probabilia, vel sunt falsa, vel simplicia tantum continent veritatem.
units.tr: Those connected axioms that are not necessary but only probable are either false, or contain only the truth of simple statements.

units.la: 301 Relationes temporis & loci, si generaliter accipiantur, vim habent axiomatis connexi.
units.tr: Relations of time and place, if taken in general terms, have the force of a connected axiom.

units.la: 302 Propositiones exceptivae aliquando continent unum axioma connexum, aliquando duo.
units.tr: Exceptive propositions sometimes contain one connected axiom, and sometimes two.

units.la: 303 Contradicitur axiomati connexo proprie per negationem consequentiae.
units.tr: A connected axiom is properly contradicted by the denial of the consequence.

units.la: 304 In discreto axiomate non disponuntur argumenta consentanea.
units.tr: 304 In a discrete axiom, consistent arguments are not arranged.

units.la: 305 In discreto axiomate disponuntur opposita, sed non per conjunctionem, quæ proprie dicitur discretiva, sed per adversativam conjunctionem, ut Socrates non est lapis, sed homo.
units.tr: In a discrete axiom opposites are arranged, but not by the conjunction properly called discretive; rather by an adversative conjunction, as in Socrates is not a stone, but a man.

units.la: 306 In axiomate discreto maxime proprie disponuntur adversa.
units.tr: In a discrete axiom, adverse things are arranged most properly.

units.la: 307 In axiomate discreto una pars affirmatur, & altera pars vel expressè vel implicitè negatur.
units.tr: In a discrete axiom one part is affirmed and the other part is denied, either expressly or by implication.

units.la: 308 Ad veritatem discreti axiomatis requiritur, ut utraque pars sit vera.
units.tr: For the truth of a discrete axiom it is required that both parts be true.

units.la: 309 Per discretum axioma contradicitur & copulato axiomati, & connexo.
units.tr: A discrete axiom contradicts both a copulative axiom and a connected one.

units.la: 310 In disjuncto axiomate disponuntur proprie argumenta opposita.
units.tr: In a disjunctive axiom, opposed arguments are properly arranged.

units.la: 311 In disjuncto vero & proprio axiomate una pars debet esse vera, & unica.
units.tr: In a disjunctive and proper axiom, one part must be true, and only one.

units.la: 312 Itaque semper falsum est vel ineptum axioma disjunctum, cum omnes partes non solùm sunt falsæ, sed etiam veræ.
units.tr: Therefore a disjunctive axiom is always false or absurd when all its parts are not only false but also true.

units.la: 313 Disjunctum axioma potest esse necessarium, ubi nulla pars est necessaria.
units.tr: A disjunctive axiom can be necessary where no part is necessary.

units.la: 314 In eadem sententia commiscentur aliquando varia axiomata.
units.tr: Sometimes various axioms are mixed together in one sentence.

units.la: 315 Axioma distributum est p[?] tim copulatum, partim disjunctum.
units.tr: A distributed axiom is partly copulative and partly disjunctive.

units.la: 316 Syllogismus inservit axiomati.
units.tr: The syllogism serves the axiom.

units.la: 317 In Syllogismo judicium non fertur, sed per Syllogismum in axiomate.
units.tr: In a syllogism no judgment is passed; rather, judgment is passed through the syllogism in the axiom.

units.la: 318 Nullus est discursus aut consequentia determinata & necessaria, præterquam in Syllogismo.
units.tr: There is no determinate or necessary inference except in the syllogism.

units.la: 319 Omnis Syllogismus legitimus est necessarius quoad formam.
units.tr: Every legitimate syllogism is necessary as to form.

units.la: 320 Necessitas & contingentia non pertinent ad Syllogismi doctrinam, sed axiomata & argumenta.
units.tr: Necessity and contingency do not pertain to the doctrine of the syllogism, but to axioms and arguments.

units.la: 321 Enthymema est Syllogismus, cuius altera propositio deest.
units.tr: An enthymeme is a syllogism one of whose premises is missing.

units.la: 322 Inductio est enthymema partes numerans ad constituendum totum.
units.tr: Induction is an enthymeme that enumerates parts in order to constitute a whole.

units.la: 323 Dilemma est Syllogismus duplicatus.
units.tr: A dilemma is a doubled syllogism.

units.la: 324 Sorites est Syllogismus ex gradatione multiplicatus.
units.tr: A sorites is a syllogism multiplied by gradation.

units.la: 325 Syllogismus peccans in forma non est Syllogismus.
units.tr: A syllogism that errs in form is not a syllogism.

units.la: 326 Syllogismus non currit quatuor terminis.
units.tr: A syllogism does not run on four terms.

units.la: 327 Ex omnibus negatis & omnibus particularibus nihil concluditur.
units.tr: Nothing is concluded from all negative premises or from all particular premises.

units.la: 328 Nihil ponendum est in conclusione, quod non fuit in præmissis.
units.tr: Nothing should be put into the conclusion that was not in the premises.

units.la: 329 Non variæ tantum voces, sed & variæ varii sensus ejusdem vocis varia constituunt argumenta.
units.tr: Not only different words but also different meanings of the same word make different arguments.

units.la: 330 Tertium argumentum non ingreditur conclusionem.
units.tr: A third argument does not enter the conclusion.

units.la: 331 Syllogismus simplex confici potest ex axiomatis compositis.
units.tr: A simple syllogism can be made from compound axioms.

units.la: 332 In Syllogismo simplici tota pars consequens quæstionis disponitur in propositione, pars antecedens in assumptione.
